Computer Systems Fundamentals

From C down to the machine: MIPS assembly, data representation, and how programs really run. Weeks 1–9 are ready below; the rest of the term follows.

Arrays as address arithmetic, 1-D & 2-D layout, pointer arithmetic, and C structs with offsets and padding.

Calling with jal & jr, the $ra problem, arguments & return values, the calling convention, and saving registers on the stack with push/pop and begin/end.

Integers
Number bases (binary, hex, octal), two's complement for signed values, integer types and silent overflow, endian-ness, and signed vs unsigned byte/half-word loads.

Decoding a raw MIPS instruction by hand, then the six C bitwise operators — &, |, ^, ~, <<, >> — bit masks for checking, setting, clearing and toggling bits, shifts as multiply/divide, integers used as sets, and the MIPS bit-manipulation instructions.
byte decoder · instruction decoder · bitwise playground · mask workbench · shift explorer · bitset lab · live mipsy bits lab

Lecture 1 · Monday

The bitwise recap in one program, checking / setting / unsetting a bit at position n, the mask-building demos (set_low_bits, set_bit_range, extract_bit_range, pokemon.c, bitset.c) and the MIPS instruction tables — then fractions in binary, the radix point, why 0.1 never terminates, fixed point, and IEEE 754 in full: normalisation, the hidden leading 1, the biased exponent, zero / infinity / NaN, and where the rounding errors come from.

Lecture 2 · Wednesday
Floating point, operating systems & file systems
The IEEE 754 conversion procedure done by hand in both directions, the special patterns for zero / infinity / NaN, and the uneven number line that makes a + 1 == a above 253 — then the second half of the course begins: what an operating system is for, privileged vs non-privileged mode, system calls and their numbers, the three ways to make one (syscall, libc wrappers, stdio.h), Unix files and permissions, file descriptors, stderr and redirection, errno, and open / read / write / close.

No lectures, no tutorials, no labs, nothing due. Everything moved to Week 7.

Week 7
Lecture 1 · Monday
File systems: libc wrappers vs stdio.h
A recap of privileged mode, system calls and file descriptors, then the same job done at two levels: open with its flag mask and the octal mode you must not forget, read / write / close — then fopen, the opaque FILE *, fgetc / fputc, and the text-only family that destroys binary files. Plus the int-not-char bug, implementing cp, and the buffering that makes stdio 390× faster.
hello three ways · open() & mode · libc↔stdio rosetta · overflow lab · EOF type lab · cp bench + strace · buffering simulator
Lecture 2 · Wednesday
File systems: seeking, inodes, permissions & links
The rest of stdio.h — buffering, fflush and what a crash does to unflushed data — then writing your own FILE as an Assignment 2 warm-up. Then seeking: lseek, fseek, ftell, the gap of zeros past the end, and fuzz.c flipping one bit in place through r+. Then the file system underneath: what a file, a directory and an inode actually are, absolute and relative paths, the nine permission bits and chmod, hard versus symbolic links, the stat family and st_mode, mkdir / opendir / readdir, and why everything in Unix is a file.
fprintf vs fputc · the lost buffer · basic_stdio builder · seek playground · fuzz lab · chmod workbench · inode & links lab · stat explorer · directory walker
Week 8
Lecture 1 · Monday
Files, text encoding & Unicode
Four recap questions close out files — fwrite and the byte order it leaks, fseek/ftell to find a file's middle byte, chmod 755 read from C with S_IXOTH — then mkdir, opendir/readdir and the POSIX toolkit, ending on everything is a file. Then the question the course had been dodging: how do you represent an A? A lookup table, not a formula — from the five-needle telegraph and Morse code, through ASCII, the teletype, DEL and ^C, the bit tricks, the code-page chaos that produced mojibake, to Unicode's 1,114,112 code points, UTF-32's wasted bits and the variable-width encoding that fixed it: UTF-8.
fwrite byte order · the middle byte · the ASCII table · bit-trick workbench · mojibake machine · UTF-8 encoder · UTF-8 decoder · string inspector · bytes vs characters
Lecture 2 · Wednesday
Unicode in C, and processes
The encoding theory put into C: four ways to spell the same character in a source file, strlen returning 7 for a two-character string, a hand-written utf8_strlen, and three variables called total that look identical and are not — homographs, trojan source, and the editor setting that catches them. Then a new topic: what a process is, pid_t and the family tree rooted at init, the ps/top/kill toolkit, environment variables and getenv/setenv, multi-tasking, preemption and the context switch — and the two calls that make every program you have ever run: execve, which replaces you, and fork, which duplicates you and returns twice.
stream reader · the sloth encoder · byte classifier · four ways to write a sloth · strlen vs utf8_strlen · homograph trap · getpid chain · ps/top/kill · environ walker · getenv workbench · the scheduler · execve stepper · fork tree · fork bomb
Week 9
Lecture 1 · Monday
Processes & pipes
The rest of the process story: waitpid, the status word that is not the exit code and the macros that decode it, exit versus _exit and the stdio buffer fork duplicates, zombies and orphans. Then the three ways to start a program — fork+exec, system and its command-injection hole, and posix_spawn with its unusual error protocol and a child environment you choose. Then the machinery a shell is made of: dup2 and the three tables behind a file descriptor, file redirection in four lines, pipe, the closes that decide whether end-of-file ever arrives, popen, and posix_spawn file actions — ending with a working shell built from all five calls.
status word · the duplicated buffer · zombies & orphans · fork+exec stepper · injection lab · three ways · spawn workbench · child environment · the three tables · redirection · the pipe · closing the ends · popen · file actions · a shell
Lecture 2 · Wednesday
Concurrency & threads
Pipes finished — fdopen on a descriptor, which way popen's mode letter points, and which close actually delivers end-of-file — then the distinction the rest of the lecture rests on: concurrency is overlapping in time, parallelism is the same instant, and only one implies the other. Flynn's four boxes, MapReduce, and why processes are an expensive way to be concurrent. Then threads: one address space, so code, globals, heap and descriptors are shared while registers, stack and errno are not. pthread_create, pthread_join, and the three ways it goes wrong — data lifetime, race conditions on a global that ++ cannot protect, and deadlock from two locks in two orders. Fixed with mutexes, which are correct and slow, and atomics, which are neither — provided you never write x = x + 1. Every number measured by compiling and running the lecture's own demos.
pipe stepper · popen direction · which close matters · scheduler bench · Flynn · process or thread · shared/private prober · error protocol · join or not · ordering & streaks · one address two readers · scaling bench · the time trap · stack slot lifetime · MIPS race tracer · the sleep that hides it · the critical section · lock granularity · deadlock stepper · five ways to increment
Week 10
Lecture 1 · Monday
Concurrency finished & revision
The last content lecture, and it is two lectures in one. Concurrency is finished off: what threads share and the one thing they do not (errno), threads_return.c — where getting a value out of a thread hits the same lifetime wall, and GCC quietly rewrites return &local into return NULL — nested threads, a bank account raised from two threads to three, mutexes and what they cost, a deadlock that finally hangs on demand, the lock-ordering rule and why it is a theorem rather than a convention, and atomics: why x += 1 is one instruction and x = x + 1 is two. Then revision of Weeks 8–9: fork, exec, system, posix_spawn, environment variables, the status word, and posix_grep.c. Two demos that refused to misbehave in the lecture are broken here, with numbers.
shared or private · how main leaves · the changing argument · return-value storage · decoding the garbage · nested or siblings · the lost increment · duty-cycle model · critical section · lock granularity · deadlock stepper · three transfer schemes · four ways to add one · timeslices · who is my parent · environment workbench · which call · surviving exec · the fork tree · status word decoder · spawn workbench · posix_grep

No new content, and two lectures in one again. The first half is the exam: where every mark comes from, the two separate hurdles (50/100 overall and 18/45 on the paper — and the point above which the hurdle is the one that actually binds), the date and the corralling rule that stops you leaving early, the restricted environment to study against, the ten-question format, and how a partly-working answer is marked. From disk to execution

How a program actually runs (slides 48–52, 64–65, 70)

You can't just "run" hello.c. A program must become binary instructions + data, get loaded into memory, and then be executed one instruction at a time by the CPU.

Disk → RAM → CPU

The program file lives on non-volatile disk (survives power-off). To run it, the OS loads it into volatile RAM — faster, but lost on power-off. Picture RAM as a 1-D array: an address is just an index.

The fetch–decode–execute loop

The CPU loops forever: fetch memory[PC], advance the PC (program counter), then decode and execute. Most instructions just run the next one — but branches and jumps rewrite the PC themselves. That's how if and while exist at all.

fetch_execute — the CPU's core loop

Fetch · decode · execute

Step through a tiny loop that sums 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 into $t1. Watch the PC march down — and jump back when the branch is taken.

instruction memory · PC = 0
FETCH
DECODE
EXECUTE
Press Step to begin the cycle.
registers

Reading that program, line by line

The widget runs this exact program. It's a loop that adds 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 and leaves the total (15) in $t1:

0li $t0, 5$t0 = 5Load the constant 5 into $t0 — our counter.
1li $t1, 0$t1 = 0Start the running total in $t1 at zero.
2add $t1, $t1, $t0$t1 += $t0Add the counter into the total. (loop body)
3addi $t0, $t0, -1$t0 −= 1Count down by one. There's no subi, so we add −1.
4bgtz $t0, 2if $t0 > 0Branch: if the counter is still positive, jump back to line 2. This is the loop. When $t0 hits 0, we fall through.
5li $v0, 10$v0 = 10Pick syscall 10 (exit) — we'll meet syscalls properly in Lecture 2.
6syscall— done —Ask the OS to end the program.

Notice line 4 is where if/while actually come from: a branch rewrites the PC so execution loops instead of running straight down.

Where things live

The shape of memory (slides 53–55)

Once loaded, a process's memory is split into four regions — two come straight from the executable, two are built and reshaped at run time. They share one address space, with the heap growing up from the bottom and the stack growing down from the top, toward each other.

text / code
The machine instructions, loaded from the file. Typically read-only.
data
Global/static variables, also loaded from the file.
heap
Dynamic memory (malloc); grows upward at run time.
stack
Function locals & parameters; grows downward as calls happen.
Calls and returns

The call stack (slides 56–63)

Every function call pushes a stack frame — its locals and parameters. Returning pops it. The top frame is whatever is running right now. With no base case, recursion pushes frames forever: a stack overflow.

call_stack — frames push & pop

The call stack

Walk main → f → g → h and back, or trigger infinite recursion to watch the stack overflow.

void h(void) { /* deepest */ }
void g(void) { h(); }
void f(void) { g(); }
int  main(void) { f(); }

// infinite recursion:
void oops(void) { oops(); }
stack  (top = running)
Press Step to call main.
Ones and zeros to readable names

Machine code, assembly & ISAs (slides 66–69, 71–73)

The CPU only runs machine code — raw binary. Assembly is a human-readable name for each instruction; an assembler translates it to binary. The set of instructions a CPU understands is its ISA.

See the assembly yourself

gcc -S hello.c stops at the assembly step and writes hello.s instead of compiling all the way to a binary. Useful for seeing what your C becomes.

ISAs — a CPU's language

An Instruction Set Architecture is the finite set of instructions a CPU understands. Examples: x86, ARM, RISC-V, and MIPS. Code for one ISA won't run on another.

The emulator

Why MIPS, and how we run it (slides 74–77)

MIPS is simple, historic and foundational — easy to learn and read. Your laptop isn't a MIPS chip, so we use an emulator.

mipsy
A software emulator that recreates a MIPS CPU. Command-line based.
mipsy_web
A browser (WASM) version with a GUI — handy for stepping and inspecting.
VS Code
Recommended editor with CSE tooling for writing your .s files.
The docs are your friend
The MIPS instruction-set reference lists every instruction — and it's available in the exam. So is man (1 = commands, 2 = syscalls, 3 = library functions).
Computing in registers

Registers & your first computations (slides 80–88)

A register is a fast 32-bit slot inside the CPU; MIPS has 32 general-purpose ones. Almost everything happens in them.

The ones to use for now

$t0–$t9
Temporaries — scratch for calculations.
$zero ($0)
Always 0; writes are ignored.
$ra
Return address — jr $ra ends the program.

Compute with them

li loads a constant; add, sub, mul work between registers; addi adds an immediate. Try the worked chain in the MIPSY lab above — addi $t0,$zero,6 through to $t4 = 56 and $t6 = 42.

main:
        # YOUR CODE HERE
        li $v0, 0
        jr $ra
Active recall

Test yourself first

Try to answer before you flip. Each card is tagged to its slide.

Glossary

Keywords at a glance

Non-volatile vs volatile
Disk (HDD/SSD) keeps data without power; RAM loses it. Programs live on disk, run in RAM.
Program counter (PC)
Control register holding the address of the next instruction; edited by branch/jump.
Fetch–decode–execute
The CPU's core loop: read memory[PC], work out the op, do it, advance.
Stack frame
Per-call block of locals & parameters; pushed on call, popped on return.
Machine code vs assembly
Binary the CPU runs vs the human-readable names an assembler translates to it.
ISA
A CPU's finite instruction set / "language": e.g. x86, ARM, RISC-V, MIPS.
Register
A fast 32-bit slot inside the CPU. MIPS has 32 general-purpose registers.
li / add / sub / mul / addi
li loads a constant; the rest compute between registers. $zero is always 0.

One-screen summary

A program is binary instructions + data stored on non-volatile disk; to run it, the OS loads it into volatile RAM (a 1-D array of addresses) where memory is split into text · data · heap · stack. The CPU then loops fetch → decode → execute, advancing the program counter (branches just rewrite it). Function calls push and pop stack frames. CPUs run only machine code; assembly is its readable form, and the instruction set you get depends on the ISA. We learn MIPS — simple, historic, foundational — emulated by mipsy. Almost all work happens in registers: load constants with li, then compute with add / sub / mul / addi.

TL;DR · disk (binary) → load into RAM → CPU fetch·decode·execute (PC drives it) · stack frames push/pop on call/return · assembly = readable machine code · ISA = the CPU's language · we use MIPS via mipsy · compute in registers (li, add, sub, mul, addi; $zero = 0).

MIPS: Basics & Control

From single instructions to whole programs that decide and repeat. Today we add system calls (so a program can talk to the world), a disciplined way to translate C into MIPS, and the branch instructions that turn straight-line code into ifs and loops.

hex & binary syscalls simplified C + goto branches loops 3 interactive labs

Aside

Hexadecimal & binary (slides 5–6)

You'll see addresses and raw data written in hex all course. It isn't a new kind of number — it's just a compact way to write binary so you don't drown in ones and zeros.

The one rule that matters

A leading 0x — in C and in mipsy — means the number is hexadecimal. Hex uses sixteen digits: 0–9 then A–F for ten to fifteen.

The magic is that one hex digit = exactly four bits (a "nibble"). So two hex digits make a byte, and eight hex digits make a 32-bit word — the size of one MIPS register or instruction.

Why not just decimal?

Decimal doesn't line up with bit boundaries — you can't glance at 43981 and read off its bits. But 0xABCD maps cleanly: A=1010, B=1011, C=1100, D=1101.

Don't sweat it. This won't make or break the course. Play with the converter below and it'll click once you see it used for memory addresses.
base_converter — dec · hex · bin

Number base lab

Type in any box. The other two follow, and the nibble strip shows how each hex digit is four bits.

Recap from Lecture 1

What's in a MIPS CPU, and which registers we touch (slides 7–11)

A quick refresher before we build on it. A CPU is a small bundle of parts; for now we drive only a handful by hand.

Inside the CPU

Data registers, control registers (including the PC, program counter), a control unit, an arithmetic-logic unit, plus — ignored in this course — a floating-point unit and caches. It connects to memory (RAM), loading and storing values.

RAM is addressed in hex: 0x0000, 0x0004, … each word four bytes apart.

Registers to use for now

$t0–$t9
Temporaries — general-purpose scratch for calculations.
$v0, $a0
Needed for system calls (which syscall + its argument).
$zero ($0)
Always 0. Writes to it are silently ignored.
$ra
Return address — jr $ra ends every program.

Bare-bones program template

main:
        # YOUR CODE GOES IN HERE
        li   $v0, 0        # return 0
        jr   $ra
Recap exercise (slide 10). In mipsy Web: put 1 in $t0, 6 in $t1, sum them into $t2, then divide $t2 by 2. You can do this in the runner further down — try li / add / li / div.

The MIPS & mipsy documentation is, in the lecturer's words, "literally your best friend" — and it's available in the exam. It lists every register, the memory model, syntax, and all instructions.

More about MIPS instructions

Real instructions, pseudo-instructions, and naming (slides 12, 25–27)

There's almost a one-to-one mapping from an assembly line to a binary CPU instruction — but the assembler gives you a few conveniences on top.

Pseudo-instructions

Assemblers add pseudo-instructions for convenience. Each expands into 1–3 real CPU instructions. You'll meet many as you write more MIPS.

li $t0, 5      # pseudo-instruction…
addi $t0, $zero, 5  # …becomes this real one

Two names per register

Every register has a symbolic name and a numeric one. $t0 is also $8; $zero is $0. Prefer the symbolic names — they say what the register is for.

Many more registers exist ($s0–$s7, $sp, $fp…) — we meet those from Week 3.

Putting data in registers

li $t0, 7
Load immediate — a fixed value into a register.
la $t0, my_label
Load address — a label's address. (Labels are just addresses.)
move $t0, $t1
Copy a value from one register into another.
mipsy is flexible
li/la are interchangeable, but for readability use li for constants and la for labels.

Core integer arithmetic (from the MIPS Basics notes)

assemblymeaningnote
add $d,$s,$t$d = $s + $tsigned two's-complement
sub $d,$s,$t$d = $s − $t—
mul $d,$s,$t$d = $s * $t32-bit result
div $d,$s,$t$d = $s / $tpseudo-instruction
rem $d,$s,$t$d = $s % $tpseudo-instruction
addi $t,$s,I$t = $s + Ino subi — use a negative I

Naming convention: $d is the destination, $s and $t the sources. There's no subi; write addi $t7, $t4, -14 instead.

Assembly syntax, in one place (slide 26)

Labels — main:
End with : and stand for memory addresses.
Comments — # …
Everything after # to end of line.
Directives — .data .text .asciiz
Begin with a dot; instructions to the assembler, not the CPU.
Constants — MAX = 10
Like C's #define: QUIT = 'q'.
Talking to the world

System calls (slides 13–23)

A normal program's instructions can't touch hardware — they can't print or read input. Only the operating system can, because it holds the privileged instructions. So a program asks the OS: that request is a system call.

The syscall workflow

Three steps, every time:

1 · choose the service
Put its number in $v0. e.g. print_int is li $v0, 1.
2 · set the arguments
If any, e.g. li $a0, 42.
3 · hand over to the OS
syscall. Some services return a value — check the table.

Common mipsy syscalls (slide 15)

service$v0args / returns
printf("%d")1int in $a0
fputs (string)4string in $a0
scanf("%d")5→ int in $v0
fgets8$a0 line, $a1 len
exit(0)10—
printf("%c")11char in $a0
scanf("%c")12→ char in $v0

You'll use all of these — especially 1, 4, 5 and 11. (Float/double and file syscalls exist but aren't implemented in mipsy.)

Printing a string — the .data segment (slides 21–22)

An integer fits in a register, but a string lives in memory. You define it in the data segment, give it a label, and pass its address to the syscall:

        .text
main:
        li   $v0, 4              # syscall 4: print_string
        la   $a0, hello_msg      # address of the string
        syscall                  # printf("Hello COMP1521!!\n");
        li   $v0, 0
        jr   $ra                  # return 0;

        .data
hello_msg:
        .asciiz "Hello COMP1521!!\n"
.data
Switches to the data segment for global data.
.asciiz
Defines a nul-terminated string and labels it.
la
Loads the string's address into $a0.
mipsy_mini — assemble · step · run

mipsy mini

A small MIPS interpreter covering everything in this lecture: arithmetic, branches, labels, .data strings and syscalls 1/4/5/10/11/12. Pick a preset or edit the code, then Step through it or Run.

presets:

idle

registers
output
Exercise: integer average (slide 23). The integer average preset is the full translation of the C program that reads two numbers and prints their mean. Put two numbers in the stdin box (e.g. 10 20) and Run.
Style

Readable assembly (slides 4, 39)

Assembly is tedious and the tooling gives little help finding bugs, so layout matters more here than almost anywhere. Code written live in lectures won't always be tidy — but yours should be.

Do

Keep the C as inline comments
Each MIPS line shows the C it implements.
Indent instructions one step
Tabs, 8-wide is the recommendation.
Don't indent labels
They jump out, so you can find branch targets fast.
Vertically align comments
A clean right-hand column reads like a translation.

Don't

Don't indent to show structure — no extra indentation inside loops or ifs the way you would in C. The labels carry the structure instead.

For this course: optimise for readability, not for using the fewest registers or lines. There are full assembly and C style guides linked on the course site.
The translation method

Simplified C and goto (slides 24, 33–36)

Translating real C straight to MIPS is hard. The trick is a middle language — simplified C — where every line maps to roughly one MIPS instruction.

The recipe

1 · Write & test normal C
Get the logic correct first.
2 · Simplify it
No while, no compound conditions, no nested expressions — only simple if, goto, and one-operator steps. Compile it; check it still works.
3 · Translate line by line
Each simplified line → one MIPS instruction.

Wait — goto?

goto jumps to any label in a function. COMP1511/1911 hid it from you for good reason: Dijkstra's 1968 "Go To Statement Considered Harmful" still stands.

Don't use goto in real C. It hurts readability and stops the compiler optimising. We use it only as a stepping stone to MIPS, because a branch instruction is a goto.

Why a branch is a goto

A simplified-C line like if (tmp != 0) goto end; becomes one branch: bnez $t1, end. The label is the jump target; "fall through" to the next line is what happens when the branch isn't taken. Once you see this, the two languages line up.

transpiler — C › simplified C › MIPS

Three views of one program

Pick an example. Hover or tap any highlighted line to light up the matching lines in the other columns.

The orange links show how one idea — a condition, a body, a step — travels from C through simplified C into MIPS.

MIPS control

Branches, booleans, loops (slides 29–52)

So far programs run top to bottom. Branch instructions let us conditionally jump — and that's all we need for if, &&, || and every kind of loop.

Branch instructions (slide 31)

Each conditional branch reads "if <condition> is true, jump to this label". mipsy lets the second operand be a constant — handy in COMP1521.

instructionjumps to label if…
beq $s,$t,L / bne …$s == $t / $s != $t
blt / ble $s,$t,L$s < $t / $s <= $t
bgt / bge $s,$t,L$s > $t / $s >= $t
blez / bgtz $s,L$s <= 0 / $s > 0
bltz / bgez $s,L$s < 0 / $s >= 0
beqz / bnez $s,L$s == 0 / $s != 0
b Lalways (unconditional — same effect as j L)

Simple if — flip the condition

To enter an if-body only when a condition holds, branch away on the opposite condition — that skips the body.

// if (n % 2 == 0) { printf("even"); }
rem  $t1, $t0, 2     # tmp = n % 2
bnez $t1, end        # if (tmp != 0) goto end
# … print "even" …
end:

&& and ||: short-circuit

C stops evaluating once the answer is known. That maps directly to a sequence of branches.

&& — all must hold
Test each on its opposite; the first failure jumps to the else.
|| — any may hold
Test each as-is; the first success jumps into the then-body.

Boolean examples, side by side

in-bounds && (slide 42)

// if (x >= 0 && x <= 100)
blt $t0, 0,   else_oob
bgt $t0, 100, else_oob
# … in bounds …
b   bounds_end
else_oob:
# … out of bounds …
bounds_end:

milk || (slide 44)

// if (age >= 30 || level < 10)
bge $t0, 30, need_new
blt $t1, 10, need_new
# … drink milk …
b   milk_end
need_new:
# … get new milk …
milk_end:
Your turn, trickier (slide 47). if (y < 10 || (z > 50 && w < 5)). Test the lone || branch as-is; for the inner &&, branch out on the opposite of each part. See the worked answer in the transpiler's "trickier" example above.

Loops: peel them apart

A for loop becomes a while loop, and a while loop becomes if/goto. Name the pieces — init, cond, body, step, end — even if some labels go unused; the structure documents itself.

for vs while gotcha. In the for (int i = 0; …) version, i vanishes after the loop and never exceeds the bound. In the while version, i outlives the loop and ends up incremented one past the limit. Same output, different scope.

Capstone exercise — sum of 100 squares (slide 52)

Compute 1·1 + 2·2 + … + 100·100. As a loop in MIPS:

UPPER_BOUND = 100
        .text
main:
        li  $t0, 0                 # int sum = 0;
loop_init:
        li  $t1, 1                 # int i = 1;
loop_cond:
        bgt $t1, UPPER_BOUND, loop_end  # while (i <= 100) {
loop_body:
        mul $t2, $t1, $t1        #   tmp = i * i;
        add $t0, $t0, $t2        #   sum = sum + tmp;
loop_step:
        addi $t1, $t1, 1          #   i++;
        b   loop_cond             # }
loop_end:
        li  $v0, 1                 # printf("%d", sum);
        move $a0, $t0
        syscall
        li  $v0, 11                # putchar('\n');
        li  $a0, '\n'
        syscall
        li  $v0, 0
        jr  $ra
Load the sum 100 squares preset into mipsy mini above and run it — you should get 338350. Step through to watch $t1 climb and $t0 accumulate.

The through-line

Hex is just compact binary — one digit per nibble, eight digits per word. A program reaches the outside world only by asking the OS: load a service number into $v0, set $a0, then syscall. To get from C to MIPS, first rewrite in simplified C — simple ifs and gotos — because a branch instruction is a goto. From there: a simple if branches away on the opposite condition; && tests each part's opposite, || tests each part as-is; and loops peel into init · cond · body · step · end.

TL;DR · 0x = hex · 1 hex digit = 4 bits · syscall = ask the OS ($v0 = service, $a0 = arg, then `syscall`; 1 print_int, 4 print_string, 5 read_int, 11 print_char) · strings live in .data via .asciiz, load address with la · translate C → simplified C (if/goto) → MIPS · branch ≈ goto · if: branch on opposite cond · && opposite-each, || as-is · for → while → if/goto.

MIPS: control & first look at data

Loops become branches, and now data gets a home. This lecture finishes the control story (for, while, break, continue) and opens the data segment — global variables, load/store, alignment and your first pointer in MIPS.

Tooling

Debugging mipsy on the command line (slides 4–5)

MIPS is unforgiving and very literal: a value is either in the right register or it isn't. The fastest way to find a bug is to stop guessing and watch the machine one instruction at a time.

Three ways to step through code

All three let you pause execution and inspect registers and memory — the place most bugs hide.

Command line
1521 mipsy → an interactive prompt. Type h for the command list.
VS Code
The course extension gives a graphical debugger with a live memory pane.
mipsy web
The browser app shows registers and every memory cell as you step.

The commands you'll actually use

load fileassemble a .s file, ready to run
step [n]execute one (or n) instructions
runrun to completion
print $regshow a register's current value
hlist every command

Most MIPS bugs are small and mechanical — a swapped pair of registers, the wrong load width. Stepping makes them obvious.

mipsy — interactive debugger

Try the real workflow

A tiny program calc.s is already loaded: li $t0,2 · li $t1,3 · mul $t2,$t0,$t1. Type commands like step 6 then print $t2. Try h, run, reset.

[mipsy]
Recap

Where Lecture 2 left us (slides 6–9)

Two ideas carry into today: getting data into registers, and turning structured C into goto/branch.

Putting data in registers

li $t0, 7load immediate — a fixed value into a register
la $t0, labelload address — a label is an address; this loads that number
move $t0, $t1copy $t1 into $t0 (source on the right)
Key idea for today: la and li are cousins — both just plant a number in a register. Neither touches memory. The new instructions lw/sw are the ones that actually read and write memory.

A branch is a goto

The simplest loop in C, and its one-to-one MIPS shape:

int main(void) {
loop:
  printf("Forever!\n");
  goto loop;
}
main:
loop:
  la $a0, msg
  li $v0, 4
  syscall
  b loop      # goto loop

An unconditional b (or j) is a bare goto. A conditional branch is a goto guarded by a test — that's the whole trick behind if and loops.

Worked recap: range check (slide 9)

A two-part condition can't be one branch — MIPS branches test a single comparison. So we split n > MIN && n <= MAX by branching away on the opposite of each part.

C
scanf("%d", &n);
if (n > MIN && n <= MAX) {
  printf("In range\n");
} else {
  printf("Out of range\n");
}
simplified C
if (n <= MIN) goto out;
if (n > MAX)  goto out;
printf("In range\n");
goto end;
out:
printf("Out of range\n");
end:
MIPS
ble $t0, MIN, out
bgt $t0, MAX, out
la  $a0, in_msg
li  $v0, 4
syscall
b   end
out:
la  $a0, out_msg
li  $v0, 4
syscall
end:

For an && condition, branch out if either opposite holds. (For || you'd branch in if either part holds.) MIN and MAX here are assembler constants — MIN = 2 — which read better than bare numbers and are easy to change.

MIPS control

Loops, break and continue (slides 10–15)

Every loop becomes the same five labelled parts. Get this shape into your fingers — this week's lab leans on it.

C while
int i = 0;
while (i < 10) {
  printf("%d\n", i);
  i++;
}
→
simplified C — five parts
init:  i = 0;
cond:  if (i >= 10) goto end;
body:  printf("%d", i);
       putchar('\n');
step:  i++;
       goto cond;
end:

init runs once · cond tests the opposite and jumps to end · body does the work · step advances · then jump back to cond. A for loop simplifies to a while first, then to this. (The lecture's live "buggy MIPS" exercise is just this shape with one part out of place — fixing it means putting cond, step and the jump-back in the right order.)

break = jump to end

break leaves the loop immediately, so it's a goto straight to the loop's end label.

while (1) {
  int c = getchar();
  if (c == 'n')
    break;
}
loop:
  c = getchar();
  if (c == 'n')
    goto end;
  goto loop;
end:

continue = jump to step

continue skips the rest of the body but still advances the loop, so it jumps to the step label — not back to cond.

for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  if (i % 2 != 0)
    goto step;   // continue
  printf("%d\n", i);
step:
  i++;
}
The gotcha the lecturer demoed. Is a for with continue the same as the "obvious" while rewrite? No. In a for, continue still runs the i++ in the loop header. In the naïve while below, continue jumps over i++ entirely — so on the first odd i the counter freezes and the program hangs forever. 
for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  if (i % 2 != 0) continue;
  printf("%d\n", i);
}
// prints 0 2 4 6 8 ✓
i = 0;
while (i < 10) {
  if (i % 2 != 0) continue;
  printf("%d\n", i);
  i++;        // skipped on odd i
}
// prints 0, then hangs ✗

This is exactly why the five-part shape keeps step as its own label: continue has somewhere correct to land.

MIPS data

How memory is laid out (slides 16–21)

Registers are tiny and few. Anything bigger or longer-lived lives in memory — and on MIPS, memory is just one enormous array of bytes.

Memory is a 1-D array of bytes

Each byte (8 bits) has its own address, and the address is simply the index into that array. The byte at address 4 below holds the value 26 — exactly like memory[4] == 26.

Sizes you must know (slide 20)

C typebyteslives in
char1register or memory
int4register or memory
double8$f register or memory
pointer4register or memory

Same as your 64-bit laptop except pointers: mipsy is a 32-bit machine, so addresses — and therefore pointers — are 4 bytes, not 8. (sizeof would confirm this in C.)

Local vs global (slides 22–23)

Local variables (single values like int, char, pointers) live in registers for speed — unless their address is taken or registers run out, in which case they spill to the stack (next week).

Global variables live in the .data segment, reached by a label. That's what the rest of this lecture is about.

MIPS data

Defining and using global data (slides 24–37)

You reserve and initialise memory with directives in the .data segment, label it, then move bytes in and out with load/store instructions.

Directives reserve & initialise bytes

.word 42a 4-byte value = 42
.half 7a 2-byte value = 7
.byte 'a'a 1-byte value = 'a'
.asciiz "hi"a string, with a trailing '\0'
.space 88 uninitialised bytes

Shorthands exist too: .byte 0:4 = four zero bytes; .ascii is .asciiz without the '\0'.

The matching C, side by side

int  a = 42;       // .word 42
short b = 7;       // .half 7
char  c = 'a';     // .byte 'a'
char  d[6]="hello";// .asciiz "hello"
char  space[8];    // .space 8

Each global gets a label so you never hand-count addresses as the program grows.

Loading and storing — bytes, half-words, words

To compute on data you must first bring it into a register; to keep a change you must write it back. You move whole bytes, in groups of 1, 2 or 4:

Addressing modes — all of these are legal (slide 35)
sb $t0, 4($t1)store $t0 4 bytes past the address in $t1
sb $t0, 0($t1)store at exactly the address in $t1
sb $t0, ($t1)same as above — the 0 is optional
sb $t0, xstore at the byte labelled x (mipsy shortcut)
sb $t1, x+1515 bytes past label x
sb $t2, x($t3)$t3 bytes past label x — the array/struct pattern
Worked example: incrementing a global (slide 36)
C — global_increment.c
int global_counter = 0;

int main(void) {
  global_counter++;
  printf("%d", global_counter);
  putchar('\n');
}
MIPS — load, change, store back
main:
  lw   $t1, global_counter   # read the global into a register
  addi $t1, $t1, 1           # += 1   (registers can't add to memory)
  sw   $t1, global_counter   # write the new value back

  li   $v0, 1                # print_int
  la   $t0, global_counter
  lw   $a0, 0($t0)
  syscall                    # printf("%d", global_counter)
  li   $v0, 11
  li   $a0, '\n'
  syscall

.data
global_counter: .word 0     # int global_counter = 0;

The rhythm is always load → modify → store. Registers do the arithmetic; memory just holds the result between operations. sw $t1, global_counter is the mipsy shortcut for "compute the label's address, then store" — handy, though keeping the address in a register (the la+lw pair) is clearer when you'll reuse it. Exercise: change it to a char global_letter = 'A' — swap .word→.byte and lw/sw→lb/sb, and it prints B.

mipsy mini — run it, watch memory change

Step a program and watch the data segment

Pick a preset, then Step instruction-by-instruction (or Run). The registers and the memory panel update live — watch global_counter go 0→1, or a pointer rewrite answer from 42→27.

registers
data memory
console
MIPS data

Alignment — the rule that trips everyone (slides 38–41)

A value of size N bytes must sit at an address divisible by N. A 4-byte int needs an address divisible by 4; an 8-byte double, divisible by 8. MIPS enforces this — a misaligned lw/sw is a hard fault.

Debugging tip from the lecture: hex addresses ending in 0, 4, 8 or C are divisible by 4. If a lw/sw fails, glance at the last hex digit of the address first.

The classic trap: a 6-byte string leaves the next label at an odd spot. "hello" is 5 letters + a '\0' = 6 bytes, so g lands at 0x10000006 — not divisible by 4 — and sw $t0, g faults.

data-segment & alignment visualiser

See where each byte lands

Switch between the broken layout and each fix. The grid shows every byte's address; the ruler marks every multiple of 4. Watch where g sits and whether sw $t0, g would succeed.

Four ways to fix it

  1. Use .word — mipsy auto-aligns .word to 4. Simplest and recommended.
  2. .align 2 — force the next object onto a 2² = 4-byte boundary.
  3. Reorder — put the word-sized global first, where it's already aligned.
  4. Manual padding — .space 2 before g. Error-prone: it breaks if the string changes.

Why .word wins

Padding and reordering work but rely on you doing arithmetic in your head every time the data changes. .word (and .align) push that job onto the assembler, which never miscounts. Reach for manual padding only when you genuinely can't reorder.

Compound types (arrays, structs) must be aligned so every component is aligned — the same rule, applied to each field. More on that next lecture.
MIPS data

Pointers in MIPS (slide 42)

A pointer is just an address held in a register. In assembly that feels almost natural — you can see the box, its address, and what's inside it.

Worked example: pointer.c → MIPS
C — prints 42 then 27
int answer = 42;

int main(void) {
  int  i;
  int *p;
  p = &answer;   // p holds answer's address
  i = *p;        // i = 42
  printf("%d\n", i);
  *p = 27;       // overwrite answer
  printf("%d\n", answer);  // 27
}
MIPS
main:
  la $t0, answer   # p = &answer
  lw $t1, 0($t0)   # i = *p   (= 42)
  move $a0, $t1    # printf("%d", i)
  li $v0, 1
  syscall
  li $a0, '\n'
  li $v0, 11
  syscall
  li $t2, 27       # can't store a constant directly —
  sw $t2, 0($t0)   # *p = 27   (via a register)
  lw $a0, answer   # printf("%d", answer) → 27
  li $v0, 1
  syscall

.data
answer: .word 42

Note the one thing the lecturer flagged: you can't write a constant straight into memory. 27 goes into a register first (li $t2, 27), then sw stores it. Load the pointer example in the runner above to watch answer flip from 42 to 27 in the memory panel.

Closing exercise: sum of 100 squares (slide 43)

The Lecture-2 loose end, finished end-to-end. for → while → five-part shape → MIPS. It prints 338350.

C
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1;
     i <= 100; i++) {
  sum += i * i;
}
printf("%d\n", sum);
simplified C
sum = 0;
i = 1;
cond:
if (i > 100) goto end;
sum += i * i;
i++;
goto cond;
end:
printf("%d\n", sum);
MIPS
  li $t0, 0      # sum
  li $t1, 1      # i
cond:
  bgt $t1, 100, end
  mul $t2, $t1, $t1
  add $t0, $t0, $t2
  addi $t1, $t1, 1
  b cond
end:
  move $a0, $t0
  li $v0, 1
  syscall

Watch the loop counter: it's i that increments (addi $t1,$t1,1), and sum that accumulates — mixing those two up is the classic squares bug.

The through-line

When code misbehaves, step it and read the registers — most MIPS bugs are mechanical. Control flow is settled: loops are five labelled parts (init·cond·body·step·end), break jumps to end, continue to step. Data is the new frontier: memory is one big byte array, globals live in .data behind a label, and you compute by loading into a register, changing it, and storing it back. Mind alignment — size-N values need N-divisible addresses, and .word handles it for you. A pointer is just an address in a register: la to get it, lw/sw to follow it.

TL;DR · 1521 mipsy → load/step/run/print $reg · loop = init·cond·body·step·end · break→end, continue→step · memory = array of bytes, address = index · char 1 / int 4 / double 8 / pointer 4 · globals in .data via .word/.half/.byte/.asciiz/.space · load→modify→store with lb·lh·lw / sb·sh·sw · addr = reg + const · size-N needs N-aligned address; prefer .word · pointer = address in a register (la, then lw/sw).

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 2 — Lecture 2

MIPS: laying data structures out in memory

Memory is one long array of bytes. Once you accept that, every C data structure becomes address arithmetic: an array is base + i × size, a 2-D array is the same line folded into rows, and a struct is a set of fields at fixed offsets. This lecture turns each of them into MIPS you can step through.

Where Monday left off

Recap: memory is a byte array, and a pointer is an address (slides 4–6)

Lecture 1 opened the data segment. The whole model is small: memory is one giant array of bytes, each with a numeric address; the CPU can only compute on values held in registers; so the rhythm of every program is load → modify → store.

Only load/store touch memory

Everything else (add, mul, branches) works on registers. To change a value in memory you copy it into a register, change it there, and write it back.

lb / lh / lwload 1 / 2 / 4 bytes from memory into a register
sb / sh / swstore 1 / 2 / 4 bytes from a register into memory
laload the address of a label into a register

You load and store whole bytes, never individual bits. A word is 4 bytes; a half-word is 2.

Global variable warm-ups (slide 5)

Globals live in .data behind a label. Predicting the output of these two is a good test that the recap landed:

int max = 45;
int main(void) {
  max--;            // 44
  printf("%d", max);
}                   // prints 44
char x = 'Z';
int main(void) {
  x--;              // 'Z'(90) → 'Y'(89)
  printf("%c", x);
}                   // prints Y

A char is just a small integer. x-- on 'Z' walks one code-point back to 'Y'. In MIPS that's .byte + lb/sb instead of .word + lw/sw.

Worked recap: pointer.c → MIPS (slide 6)
C — prints 42 then 27
int answer = 42;
int main(void) {
  int  i;
  int *p;
  p = &answer;   // p holds answer's address
  i = *p;        // i = 42
  printf("%d\n", i);
  *p = 27;       // overwrite answer through p
  printf("%d\n", answer);  // 27
}
MIPS
main:
  la $t0, answer   # p = &answer
  lw $t1, 0($t0)   # i = *p   (= 42)
  move $a0, $t1
  li $v0, 1
  syscall             # printf("%d", i)
  li $a0, '\n'
  li $v0, 11
  syscall
  li $t2, 27        # constant into a register first…
  sw $t2, 0($t0)   # *p = 27 (store through the pointer)
  lw $a0, answer   # printf("%d", answer) → 27
  li $v0, 1
  syscall

.data
answer: .word 42

You can load this exact program (preset pointer) into the lab in §04 and watch answer flip 42 → 27 in the memory panel. Everything from here builds on this single move: an address in a register, followed with a load or store.

Reserving & initialising memory

Declaring data: directives and arrays (slides 7–8)

A directive (a line starting with a dot) is an instruction to the assembler, not the CPU. In the .data segment, directives reserve bytes and optionally fill them — that's how a C global declaration becomes laid-out memory.

The directive cheat-sheet

.space 18char a[18]; — 18 uninitialised bytes
.word 42int32_t i = 42; — one 4-byte value
.word 1,3,5int v[3] = {1,3,5};
.half 2,4,6int16_t h[3] = {2,4,6}; — 2-byte each
.byte 7:5int8_t b[5] = {7,7,7,7,7}; — repeat shorthand
.asciiz "abc"char s[4] = {'a','b','c','\0'};
.ascii "abc"char t[3] = {'a','b','c'}; — no terminator
.align 2push the next object onto a 2² = 4-byte boundary

.float exists but isn't used in this course.

Initialising a global array

The same value can be written several ways — pick the one that reads closest to the C you mean.

vec:   .space 40         # int vec[10] (or char vec[40])
nums:  .word 1,3,5,7,9   # int nums[] = {1,3,5,7,9}
nums2: .word 1:4         # int nums2[] = {1,1,1,1}
str:   .byte 'a','b','c','\0'
str2:  .asciiz "abc"     # same three chars + '\0'
chars: .ascii "abc"      # three chars, NO '\0'

Now the question the rest of the lecture answers: once it's laid out, how do you reach element i, and how do you loop over the whole thing?

Address arithmetic

1-D arrays: finding element i (slides 9–11)

An array is stored as one contiguous run of bytes. If you know the address of the start, every element's address is pure arithmetic — and the only thing that changes between a char array and an int array is how big each step is.

The one formula for every array.  &a[i] = &a + i × sizeof(element).  Bytes step by 1, halves by 2, ints by 4, doubles by 8. The C compiler does this multiply for you; in MIPS you do it — mul the index by the element size, then add it to the base.
element address — base + i × sizeof(element)

Element address calculator

Set the element size, the array's base address, and an index. The strip below highlights the element you've selected and shows the arithmetic the MIPS code has to do.

Worked example: read array elements by index (slide 12)
C
// my_char_array = {'k','f','c'}
// my_int_array  = {8, 99, 5}
printf("%c", my_char_array[0]);  // k
printf("%d", my_int_array[0]);   // 8
printf("%c", my_char_array[2]);  // c
printf("%d", my_int_array[2]);   // 5
MIPS — index × size, then load
la $t0, my_char_array
  lb $a0, 0($t0)    # [0]: offset 0×1
  li $v0, 11
  syscall
  la $t1, my_int_array
  lw $a0, 0($t1)    # [0]: offset 0×4
  li $v0, 1
  syscall
  lb $a0, 2($t0)    # char[2]: offset 2×1
  li $v0, 11
  syscall
  lw $a0, 8($t1)    # int[2]: offset 2×4 = 8
  li $v0, 1
  syscall

With a constant index the offset is known at assemble time, so it can ride in the offset(reg) part of the load — lw $a0, 8($t1). With a variable index you compute it at run time (next section). Note the .align 2 the assembler needs between the char array and the int array so the words land on a 4-byte boundary.

Putting it in motion

Looping over an array in MIPS (slides 12–13)

A variable index i means recomputing the address every iteration: load the base, multiply i by the element size, add. It's the same five-part loop from last lecture (init · cond · body · step · end) with an address calculation in the body.

Print an int array (print5.s)
Simplified C
int i = 0;
loop:
  if (i >= 5) goto end;
  int n = numbers[i];
  printf("%d", n);
  printf("%c", '\n');
  i++;
  goto loop;
end:
MIPS — recompute &numbers[i] each pass
li $t0, 0           # i = 0
loop:
  bge $t0, 5, end     # if (i >= 5) goto end
  la  $t5, numbers   # &numbers[i] =
  mul $t6, $t0, 4    #   base + i*4
  add $t7, $t5, $t6
  lw  $a0, 0($t7)   # n = numbers[i]
  li  $v0, 1
  syscall
  li  $a0, '\n'
  li  $v0, 11
  syscall
  addi $t0, $t0, 1   # i++
  b loop
end:

mul $t6, $t0, 4 then add is the address calculation made explicit. Changing the array instead of printing it (numbers[i] *= 42) is the same loop with an lw · mul · sw in the body — load it, scale it, store it back.

mipsy mini — arrays, pointers & structs, live

Step a real program and watch memory

Pick a preset, then Step instruction-by-instruction (or Run). Registers and the data memory panel update live — watch an index turn into an address, or a struct field get written at its offset. Edit the code freely; it re-assembles on the next Step.

registers
data memory

Walking through memory

Pointer arithmetic (slides 14–17)

In C, adding 1 to a pointer doesn't add 1 byte — it advances by sizeof the pointed-to type. The language hides the multiply so you can iterate without index arithmetic. In MIPS there's no such magic: you add the element size by hand.

C scales the step for you

char   *p = 0x6060; p++; // p == 0x6061  (+1)
int    *q = 0x6060; q++; // q == 0x6064  (+4)
double *r = 0x6060; r++; // r == 0x6068  (+8)

The pointer's type decides the stride. A char* steps a byte; an int* steps a word.

Style guide: prefer indices (slide 15)

Avoid pointer arithmetic; use array indices instead. Anything you can write with pointer arithmetic can be written with indices, and indices are easier to read and debug.

Experienced programmers reach for pointer arithmetic to write succinct idiomatic code — but it's a common way for novices to confuse themselves. Use it only when you're confident it genuinely reads better.

Worked example: print with two pointers (slide 17 · pointer5.s)
C — p ≤ q
int *p = &array[0];  // = array
int *q = &array[4];  // last element
while (p <= q) {
  printf("%d ", *p);
  p++;               // advance 4 bytes
}
MIPS — p in $t0, q in $t1
la   $t0, numbers      # p = &numbers[0]
  la   $t1, numbers      # q = &numbers[4]
  addi $t1, $t1, 16     #   = base + 4*4
loop:
  bgt  $t0, $t1, end    # if (p > q) goto end
  lw   $a0, 0($t0)     # *p
  li   $v0, 1
  syscall
  li   $a0, ' '
  li   $v0, 11
  syscall
  addi $t0, $t0, 4     # p++  → forward one int
  b    loop
end:

The pointer version drops the per-iteration mul + add: the address is the loop variable, nudged forward by 4 each pass. Faithful and fast — but compare it with the index version in §04 and decide which you'd rather debug at 2am. Load the pointer walk preset in the lab to step it.

Folding a line into rows

2-D arrays: one line, in row order (slides 18–21)

RAM is one-dimensional — just a long line of bytes. A 2-D array is that line folded into rows: every row laid down end-to-end, in order. So a pair of indices [row][col] has to be mapped to a single flat offset.

The 2-D offset formula.
Start of the row: (row × N_COLS) × sizeof(element)  ·  within the row: col × sizeof(element).
Together:  offset = (row × N_COLS + col) × sizeof(element)  — and &a[row][col] = &a + offset.
2-D → 1-D — (row × N_COLS + col) × sizeof(element)

2-D offset mapper

Set the shape and element size, then click any cell in the grid. The matching byte-range lights up in the flattened strip, and the arithmetic is spelled out below — the same computation the nested-loop MIPS does.

Worked example: sum a 2-D array (slide 20 · print2d.s)
C — nested loops
// int numbers[3][5], N_COLS = 5
int sum = 0;
for (row = 0; row < 3; row++) {
  for (col = 0; col < 5; col++) {
    sum += numbers[row][col];
  }
}
MIPS — offset = (row*5 + col)*4
li $t0, 0            # sum
  li $t1, 0            # row
loop1:
  bge $t1, 3, end1
  li  $t2, 0           # col
loop2:
  bge $t2, 5, end2
  la  $t3, numbers
  mul $t4, $t1, 20    # row * N_COLS * 4
  add $t6, $t3, $t4   # start of row
  mul $t5, $t2, 4     # col * 4
  add $t7, $t6, $t5   # &numbers[row][col]
  lw  $t8, 0($t7)
  add $t0, $t0, $t8   # sum += element
  addi $t2, $t2, 1
  b loop2
end2:
  addi $t1, $t1, 1
  b loop1
end1:

mul $t4, $t1, 20 is row × N_COLS × sizeof folded into one constant (5 cols × 4 bytes). The data is just numbers: .word 3,9,27,… — a flat list of 15 words; the loop's arithmetic is the only thing that makes it "2-D". Load the 2-D sum preset to watch the offset climb. The flag.c demo prints a 2-D char grid the same way, with sizeof = 1.

Fields at fixed offsets

Structs: variables at known offsets (slides 22–29)

A struct is just a set of variables packed together at fixed, known offsets from the start. Where an array element's offset is computed (i × size), a struct field's offset is a constant the assembler knows — so accessing a field is a single load or store at OFFSET($base).

Building up the offsets (slides 24–29)
struct student {
  int  zid;        // offset 0
  char first[20];  // offset 0 + 4  = 4
  char last[20];   // offset 4 + 20 = 24
  int  program;    // offset 24 + 20 = 44
  char alias[10];  // offset 44 + 4  = 48
};  // size: 48 + 10 + 2 padding = 60

Each field starts right after the previous one — unless alignment forces a gap. program is an int, so it must sit on a 4-byte boundary; here offset 44 already divides by 4, so no gap is needed. At the end, the struct is rounded up to a multiple of its largest field's size (4), turning 58 into 60 — those last 2 bytes are padding so the next struct in an array would still be aligned.

struct layout — offsets, padding & sizeof

Struct layout calculator

Add, remove, and reorder fields. The calculator applies C's alignment rules — each field's offset is rounded up to a multiple of its size, and the whole struct is rounded up to a multiple of its largest member — and shows where padding bytes appear.

Why padding? (slide 22)

MIPS can't load an int from an address that isn't divisible by 4. So the compiler inserts hidden bytes to keep every field aligned. Predict these, then check with the calculator:

{int x; int y;}= 8
{char c1; char c2;}= 2
{char c1; char c2; int x;}= 8 (2 pad before x)
{int x; char s[3];}= 8 (1 pad at end)

Access by offset, not name (slide 23)

In MIPS the field names are gone — you reach a field by its constant offset from the struct's base address.

.eqv can also be written with = :
OFF_ZID     = 0
OFF_PROGRAM = 44
  la $t1, stu1
  li $t0, 5012345
  sw $t0, OFF_ZID($t1)      # stu1.zid = …
  li $t0, 3778
  sw $t0, OFF_PROGRAM($t1)  # stu1.program = …

Load the struct preset in the lab to write zid and program into a .space 60 block and read them back.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slide 30)

Every C data structure is the same idea seen from a different angle: memory is a byte array, and access is address arithmetic. An array element is base + i × size. A 2-D array folds into one line, row by row, so [row][col] becomes (row × N_COLS + col) × size. A struct is fields at constant offsets, with padding inserted to keep each field aligned. Underneath all three, the moves never change: la to get an address, compute an offset, then lw/lb or sw/sb to follow it. Next lecture turns to functions in MIPS — and that's where the call stack arrives.

TL;DR · memory = array of bytes, address = index · only load/store touch memory; rhythm is load → modify → store · &a[i] = &a + i × sizeof (char 1 / half 2 / int 4 / double 8) · MIPS: la, mul index by size, add to base, then lw/lb · pointer arithmetic: p++ moves by sizeof the type (C scales it; in MIPS you add it) · prefer indices over pointer arithmetic · 2-D is row-major: offset = (row × N_COLS + col) × size · struct = fields at fixed offsets; align each field to its size, pad the whole struct up to its largest field · access fields by OFFSET($base).

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 3 — Lecture 1

MIPS: functions, the calling convention, and the stack

In C a function call is one line. Underneath, MIPS has to do it by hand: jump to the code with jal, come back with jr $ra, pass arguments in $a0–$a3, return in $v0 — and, because there is only one return-address register, save and restore it on a region of memory called the stack. The whole lecture is the story of how functions talk to each other without trampling each other's registers.

Where Monday left off

Recap: arrays and structs are address arithmetic (slides 5–10)

Last lecture's one idea: memory is a flat line of bytes, and reaching any element is arithmetic on a base address. Three shapes, three formulas — and the MIPS for each is just la, compute an offset, then lw/lb or sw/sb.

The three offset formulas

1-D array&a[i] = &a + i × sizeof(element)
2-D array&a[r][c] = &a + (r × N_COLS + c) × sizeof
struct field&s.field = &s + OFFSET (a constant)

For an array the offset is computed (mul the index by the size); for a struct it's a constant the assembler already knows, so a field access is one load/store at OFFSET($base).

Struct padding, again (slides 8–10)

A struct is a set of variables at fixed offsets, but MIPS can't load an int from an address that isn't divisible by 4 — so the assembler inserts padding to keep each field aligned.

# struct person { char fi; char li; int age; }
person:
  .space 1        # first_initial  @ 0
  .space 1        # last_initial   @ 1
  .align 2        # pad to a 4-byte boundary (skip 2,3)
  .space 4        # age (int)      @ 4

Two chars + one int wants 6 bytes but takes 8: the .align 2 pushes age onto offset 4 so the word lands on a multiple of 4.

Recap labs from Monday (slide 7 · read_array_words.c · modify_2d.c)

Two programs the lecturer re-derived live. They are the same five-part loop you already know, with an address calculation in the body — exactly the moves functions will soon wrap up and call.

read 5 ints into an array, then print them
li $t0, 0           # i = 0
read_loop:
  bge $t0, 5, print
  li $v0, 5          # read_int
  syscall
  mul $t2, $t0, 4    # offset = i*4
  sw  $v0, array($t2) # array[i] = input
  addi $t0, $t0, 1
  b read_loop
write into a 2-D array at [row][col]
# row in $t0, col in $t1, value in $t2
  mul $t3, $t0, 5    # row * N_COLS
  add $t3, $t3, $t1  # + col
  mul $t3, $t3, 4    # * sizeof(int)
  sw  $t2, numbers($t3) # numbers[row][col] = value

Note the label($reg) form: sw $v0, array($t2) stores at &array + $t2. That's the same la-plus-offset move written compactly — handy, but watch the element size. $t registers are fair game here because nothing is being called yet; once we add functions, that changes.

Named code you can call

What a function is, in C (slides 11–15)

You already write functions every day. The point of revisiting them is to name the four moving parts precisely, because in MIPS you'll implement each one by hand: the arguments going in, control transferring to the body, local work, and a value coming back.

Anatomy & signature (slides 12–13)

int times_two(int x) {  // takes an int
  int two_x = x * 2;     // does work
  return two_x;          // returns an int
}

A function's signature fixes the number and types of parameters and the type of the return value. A call must supply the right number of values, each of the right type.

In COMP1521 we only deal with a fixed number of arguments and a single return value. (Variadic functions like printf — "varargs" — are out of scope.)

What a call actually does (slide 14)

For result = func(expr1, expr2, …):

  1. each expression is evaluated and bound to a parameter,
  2. control transfers to the body of func,
  3. local variables are created for the call,
  4. a return value is computed,
  5. control returns to the caller, which uses the result.

Every one of those five steps becomes explicit MIPS. The next sections build them up one at a time.

A declaration comes first; the definition can come later.  C lets you declare a prototype (void f(void);) before main and define the body afterwards. In MIPS the equivalent is simply a label — f: — that you can jal to from anywhere, defined wherever you like in the file.
Jumping there — and back

Calling a function in MIPS: jal and jr $ra (slides 16–18)

A function is just a label, so your first instinct is to b or j to it. That gets you there — but how do you get back? The branch doesn't remember where it came from. MIPS solves this with one special instruction.

jal — jump and link

jal label is a special j that does two things at once:

1.sets $ra (return address) to the address of the next instruction,
2.then jumps to label.

It's jal, not jal1 — a common typo. The "link" is the saved return address; that's the mechanism that lets you come home.

jr $ra — return

jr $ra jumps to whatever address is in $ra. Put at the end of a function, it sends control back to the instruction right after the jal that called it.

So the round trip is: caller does jal f → $ra holds "the line after" → f runs → f does jr $ra → back to the line after. main itself returns the same way (the OS set $ra before calling it).

Worked example: a leaf function (slide 15 · call_return.c)
C
void f(void);
int main(void) {
  printf("calling f\n");
  f();
  printf("back from f\n");
  return 0;
}
void f(void) {
  printf("in f\n");
}
MIPS — f is a leaf, so it needs no setup
main:
  la $a0, msg0
  li $v0, 4
  syscall            # printf("calling f\n")
  jal f               # $ra = next line, jump to f
  la $a0, msg1
  li $v0, 4
  syscall            # printf("back from f\n")
  li $v0, 0
  jr $ra             # return from main
f:
  la $a0, msg2
  li $v0, 4
  syscall            # printf("in f\n")
  jr $ra             # return to caller

This works because f never calls anything itself, so it never disturbs $ra between the jal f and main's own jr $ra. A function that calls nothing is a leaf function — the simplest case. The moment main or f makes a second call, that lucky arrangement breaks…

Why one register isn't enough

The $ra problem: clobbering the return address (slides 17, 19–20)

There is only one $ra register. Every jal overwrites it. So as soon as a function that was called needs to call something else — or main calls the same function twice — the original return address is gone, and the program loops or crashes.

The tempting (wrong) fix (slide 19)

"Just stash $ra in a spare register like $t0 before the call, and move it back after." Two problems:

  • the function you call might itself clobber $t0 (you must treat callees as black boxes),
  • functions call functions call functions, and recursion has no fixed depth — you'd run out of the 32 registers fast.

The shape of the real fix (slide 26)

We need somewhere to keep a fresh copy of $ra for every active call — a place that grows and shrinks with call depth. Globals can't do it (recursion has unknown depth). The answer is a region of memory called the stack (§07).

Each call saves its own $ra on entry and restores it before returning.

$ra tracer — watch the link register get overwritten

Step the call sequence

Walk main → f → g one transfer at a time and watch $ra. In naive mode there's a single $ra and you'll see main's return address get clobbered. Switch to save on stack mode to see each call keep its own copy and everyone return correctly.

Talking to a function

Passing arguments and returning values (slides 21–24)

You've already been using this convention every time you call printf with a syscall. Arguments go in the $a registers; the result comes back in $v0. Same idea, now for your own functions.

Arguments → $a0–$a3 (slide 21)

The first four arguments are passed in $a0, $a1, $a2, $a3 (a for argument). A fifth argument, or one too big for a register (like a struct), would go on the stack — but you won't need that in COMP1521.

li $a0, 22       # first argument = 22
  jal f            # f(22)

Return value → $v0 (slide 23)

A function leaves its result in $v0 (the same register a syscall like read_int uses). In this course you only ever return a single value, so you only need $v0 — never $v1.

jal f            # call f
  move $a0, $v0  # use the result
The classic argument bug. The very first thing a function should do is move its arguments out of $a0–$a3 into safe registers. Why? The moment you call anything — even a printf syscall to debug — you clobber the $a registers and lose your argument. Grab $a0 into an $s (or, in a leaf, a $t) register at the top, before it can be overwritten.
Worked example: argument in, value out (slide 24)
C — int f(int x){ …; return x*2; }
int f(int x) {
  printf("in f\n");
  printf("%d", x);
  putchar('\n');
  x = x * 2;
  return x;
}
// main: int result = f(22);  // 44
MIPS — f is a leaf (no other calls)
f:
  move $t0, $a0   # save x before printing
  move $a0, $t0   # printf("%d", x)
  li $v0, 1
  syscall
  li $a0, '\n'
  li $v0, 11
  syscall
  mul $v0, $t0, 2   # return x * 2  → $v0
  jr $ra

In the lecture this was first written with $t registers to juggle $ra, $a0 and $v0 by hand — and it segfaulted, because a forgotten $ra save in main sent it off the rails. "It's so easy to make a mistake here… this is making you want the stack even more." That want is exactly what §06–§08 satisfy. Load the return value preset in the §08 lab to step the working version.

The rules everyone agrees on

The MIPS calling convention (slides 25, 32–36, 51)

Nothing in the hardware forces any register to mean anything — these are conventions, part of the MIPS ABI (application binary interface). Following them is what lets code from different sources work together, and what stops you making silly mistakes. The autotests for Assignment 1 deliberately trash registers to check you obeyed them.

$t registers — free real estate (slides 33–34)

A function may clobber any $t0–$t9 freely. The flip side: as a caller, you must assume any function you call destroyed every $t register. "Strict" autotesting will intentionally fill them with garbage — even if the callee never touched them. Treat callees as black boxes.

$s registers — saved across calls (slides 35–37)

A function must not permanently change any $s0–$s7 (or $sp, $fp) — that includes main. So a caller can rely on its $s values surviving a call. The catch: to use an $s register, a function must save the old value first and restore it before returning — and the place it saves it is the stack.

calling convention — who is responsible for each register?

The register contract

Pick a register group to see the deal from both sides: what a caller can assume after a jal, and what a callee is obliged to do. Green = you can trust it; coral = assume it's gone.

Caller's view — after jal callee

Callee's duty

The full contract (slide 51)

$a0–$a3arguments in; not preserved by callee (like $t)
$v0return value out
$rareturn address; preserve it if you overwrite it
$t0–$t9caller-saved — assume a call destroys them
$s0–$s7callee-saved — a call leaves them unchanged
$sp, $fpmust be restored to their original value

Why bother? (slide 32)

You could break the rules — the registers are just registers. But then your code can't interoperate with anyone else's, library updates would force you to rewrite your functions, and you'd lose the safety net that catches "I forgot to save that" bugs.

Conventions are about compatibility going forward — and about not shooting yourself in the foot.

Borrowing memory you give back

The stack: saving and restoring registers (slides 38–43)

The solution to both the $ra problem and the "how do I use an $s register" problem is the same: a region of memory that grows and shrinks with call depth. A function temporarily saves what it needs at the start and restores it at the end.

What the stack is (slide 38)

A region of memory you can grow and shrink. The $sp (stack pointer) register tracks the top of the stack. The stack grows downward — toward smaller addresses — and $sp is always 4-byte aligned.

Think of it like a pile of paper: each call drops a sheet on top; each return throws the top sheet away. Last in, first out.

The golden rule (slide 40)

A function may use the stack however it likes, as long as it restores $sp to its original value before returning. Whatever you pushed, you must pop.

Leave $sp wrong and you'll get spectacular, hard-to-find segmentation faults.

Two ways to save registers
The hard way — move $sp by hand (slide 41)
# prologue: allocate 8 bytes, save $ra and $s0
  addi $sp, $sp, -4
  sw   $ra, ($sp)
  addi $sp, $sp, -4
  sw   $s0, ($sp)
  # … body …
  # epilogue: reverse it exactly
  lw   $s0, ($sp)
  addi $sp, $sp, 4
  lw   $ra, ($sp)
  addi $sp, $sp, 4
The easy way — push / pop (slide 42)
# prologue
  push $ra      # $sp -= 4; sw $ra,($sp)
  push $s0
  # … body …
  # epilogue — REVERSE order
  pop  $s0      # lw $s0,($sp); $sp += 4
  pop  $ra

push Rt allocates 4 bytes ($sp = $sp − 4) and stores Rt there. pop Rt loads the top word into Rt and frees 4 bytes ($sp = $sp + 4). You must pop in the reverse order you pushed — last in, first out. Note: push/pop are mipsy pseudo-instructions; other MIPS assemblers may not have them, which is why it's worth understanding the $sp arithmetic underneath.

stack visualiser — push grows down, pop shrinks up

Push and pop the stack

Each push drops a word on top and moves $sp down 4 bytes; each pop lifts the top word off and moves $sp back up. Try to push in one order and pop in the same order — you'll see why it has to be reversed.

A function's story arc

Prologues, epilogues and the function skeleton (slides 44–51)

Put the convention and the stack together and every non-leaf function gets the same three-act shape: a prologue that saves what it must, a body that does the work, and an epilogue that restores everything in reverse and returns.

Prologue — the opening (slide 44)

  • begin — set up the frame pointer,
  • push $ra — so a nested call can't lose it,
  • push any $s registers you intend to use.

Epilogue — the close (slide 44)

  • pop those $s registers — reverse order,
  • pop $ra,
  • end — tear down the frame,
  • jr $ra — return to the caller.

What begin / end do (slides 47–49)

The frame pointer $fp marks the bottom of a function's frame — the value $sp had on entry. begin saves the old $fp and points it at the current $sp; end restores both. It's optional, but it makes debugging painless when you push and pop, so the course strongly advises always using it.

begin and end are mipsy pseudo-instructions, like push/pop.

Leaf functions skip all of it (slide 45)

A leaf function calls nothing else. It never executes jal, so it never disturbs $ra — no need to save it. It has no calls to preserve values across, so it can live entirely in $t registers — no $s registers, no prologue, no epilogue.

Just be sure it really is a leaf (a sneaky syscall doesn't count as a jal, but any jal does).

The function skeleton (slide 50)
func:
  # [header comment: what it does, args, return]
func__prologue:
  begin
  push $ra
  push $s0
  push $s1
func__body:
  # do stuff …
  li $a0, 42
  jal foo            # foo(42); result in $v0
func__epilogue:
  pop $s1            # reverse order of the pushes
  pop $s0
  pop $ra
  end
  jr $ra

Follow this formula and you avoid almost every function bug. The last thing pushed is the first thing popped, so the pop list is always the mirror image of the push list — with $ra popped last, right before end and jr $ra.

mipsy mini — functions, the stack & recursion, live

Step a real function call and watch the stack

Pick a preset and Step through it (or Run). Registers update live — watch $ra, $sp and $fp move — and the stack panel shows the words saved below $sp. The broken preset deliberately omits the $ra save, so Run hits a runaway loop; the others use the skeleton properly. Edit freely; it re-assembles on the next Step.

registers
stack  (top = $sp)
console
Out of scope for COMP1521, but good to know.  Floating-point registers pass and return float/double with similar conventions; the stack is also used to pass a 5th+ argument, to pass or return values too big for a register (like a whole struct), and to store local variables such as arrays. You'll only meet these in challenge questions.
What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 51–52)

A function in MIPS is a label you reach with jal (which records the return address in $ra) and leave with jr $ra. Arguments arrive in $a0–$a3; the result leaves in $v0. Because there is only one $ra, any function that calls another must save it — and the place to save it, along with any $s registers it borrows, is the stack: a downward-growing region tracked by $sp, used through push/pop and framed by begin/end. The calling convention ties it together: $t registers are fair game (assume a call destroys them), $s/$sp/$fp must come back unchanged, and the autotests will punish you for forgetting. Leaf functions, calling nobody, skip the prologue and epilogue entirely. Next lecture puts it all together in a full MIPS application.

TL;DR · a function = a label · jal f sets $ra = next instruction, then jumps · jr $ra returns · args in $a0–$a3, return in $v0 · only one $ra → a nested call clobbers it → save it · move your $a args to safe registers first thing · convention: $t caller-saved (assume destroyed), $s/$sp/$fp callee-saved (restored) · stack grows down, $sp = top, must end where it started · push Rt: $sp−=4; sw · pop Rt: lw; $sp+=4 · pop in reverse order · skeleton = begin · push $ra · push $s · body · pop $s · pop $ra · end · jr $ra · leaf = no calls → no prologue/epilogue.
