Where Monday left off

Functions in one breath (slides 5–10)

A function is a label you can call. The whole calling convention fits in five lines — say them out loud once and the rest of the lecture is just detail.

The five-line summary

Functions are named pieces of code (labels) which you can:

  1. call — with jal (jump-and-link),
  2. supply arguments — in $a0–$a3 (optional),
  3. compute using those arguments,
  4. return a value to the caller — in $v0,
  5. return from the function — with jr $ra.

We only deal with a single return value in this course. That's the entire contract.

C piece → MIPS piece

in Cin MIPS
the function's namea label, f:
calling f(...)jal f
arguments$a0 … $a3
the return value$v0
return;jr $ra

jal records the address of the next instruction in $ra, then jumps; jr $ra jumps back to it. The catch — there is only one $ra — is the whole reason the stack exists.

Why this lecture is a recap.  Monday introduced jal/jr, the $ra problem, arguments and return values, the calling convention and the stack. Today closes two gaps — the frame pointer and the complete register table — and then proves it all works by building a full application end to end.
A scratch region that grows and shrinks

The stack, revisited (slides 11–13)

The cliffhanger from Monday: where do we keep a fresh copy of $ra for every active call? The answer is the stack — a region of memory that grows as calls nest and shrinks as they return.

LIFO — like a stack of plates (slide 11)

A stack is last-in, first-out: you only ever add to the top and remove from the top. The last thing you pushed is the first thing you pop — exactly what nested function calls need, because the most recent call is always the first to return.

What the stack is, mechanically (slide 12)

The stack pointer $sp tracks the top. It's set up by the operating system before main runs, is always 4-byte aligned, and grows downward (towards smaller addresses). Move $sp down to allocate room; move it back up to free it.

Golden rule: a function must leave $sp exactly where it found it.

Two ways to write the same thing

Saving registers: the hard way and the easy way (slides 14–17)

To save $ra (and any $s registers you borrow), you write them to the stack on entry and read them back on exit. You can do that by hand with $sp arithmetic, or with two pseudo-instructions that do it for you.

Hard way vs easy way (slide 16)

Both snippets do the same thing: save $ra and $s0 at the start, restore them at the end. On the left, every save is two instructions on $sp; on the right, one word each.

the hard way — raw $sp
f:
  # prologue
  addi $sp, $sp, -4
  sw   $ra, ($sp)   # save $ra
  addi $sp, $sp, -4
  sw   $s0, ($sp)   # save $s0
  # ... body ...
  # epilogue (reverse order)
  lw   $s0, ($sp)   # restore $s0
  addi $sp, $sp, 4
  lw   $ra, ($sp)   # restore $ra
  addi $sp, $sp, 4
  jr   $ra
the easy way — push / pop
f:
  # prologue
  push $ra          # $sp-=4; sw $ra,($sp)
  push $s0


  # ... body ...

  # epilogue (reverse order)
  pop  $s0          # lw $s0,($sp); $sp+=4
  pop  $ra


  jr   $ra

push Rt allocates 4 bytes ($sp = $sp − 4) and stores Rt; pop Rt loads the top word into Rt and frees 4 bytes ($sp = $sp + 4). You must pop in the reverse order you pushed — last in, first out. That's the whole reason the saved $ra goes on the bottom and comes off last.

push/pop are mipsy pseudo-instructions (slide 17)

push and pop exist on mipsy, not on every MIPS emulator. The exam and the assignment use mipsy, so you can get through this course pushing and popping and never touch $sp directly.

You'd only reach for raw $sp arithmetic in challenge questions — storing local arrays, or passing a 5th+ argument.

The $t0 hack is finally retired (recap of Monday)

Monday's tempting-but-wrong fix was to stash $ra in a spare register like $t0 before a call. It fails because the callee may clobber $t0, and recursion has no fixed depth so you'd run out of registers.

The stack solves both: every active call gets its own saved copy, and it grows as deep as the recursion does.

A recipe to follow every time

Prologue, epilogue and the leaf-function shortcut (slides 18–19, 25)

Every non-leaf function gets the same three-act shape. Follow the skeleton and you sidestep almost every function bug — the lecturer's words: it's "a good recipe" worth following even when you think you don't need it.

Prologue — the opening (slide 18)

  • begin — set up the frame pointer (§05),
  • push $ra — so a nested call can't lose it,
  • push any $s registers you intend to use.

Epilogue — the close (slide 18)

  • pop those $s registers — reverse order,
  • pop $ra,
  • end — tear down the frame,
  • jr $ra — return to the caller.
The function skeleton (slide 25)
func:
  # [header comment: what it does, args, return]
func__prologue:
  begin
  push $ra
  push $s0
  push $s1
func__body:
  # do stuff …
  li $a0, 42
  jal foo            # foo(42); return value in $v0
func__epilogue:
  pop $s1            # mirror image of the pushes
  pop $s0
  pop $ra
  end
  jr $ra

The pop list is always the mirror image of the push list, with $ra popped last — right before end and jr $ra. Labelling the parts func__prologue / func__body / func__epilogue is optional but the lecturer recommends it: it keeps your labels unique and tells mipsy where errors live.

Leaf functions skip all of it (slide 19)

A leaf function calls nothing else. It never executes jal, so it never disturbs $ra — no need to save it. With no calls to preserve values across, it can live entirely in $t registers: no $s registers, no prologue, no epilogue.

A syscall doesn't count as a jal — but any real jal does. increase_price and print_pizza_t later are leaves; main is not.

Move your arguments out first (slide 27)

The very first thing a function should do is copy $a0–$a3 somewhere safe. The moment you call anything — even a debug printf syscall — the $a registers are overwritten and your argument is gone.

Same warning for $v0: move a return value out before you print, or the next syscall clobbers it.

A fixed landmark in a moving stack

The frame pointer: $fp, begin and end (slides 22–24)

The stack pointer keeps moving as a function pushes, pops and allocates. The frame pointer $fp is a second pointer that stays put — anchored to the bottom of the current frame — so there's always a fixed point to measure from.

What $fp points at (slide 22)

$fp marks the bottom of a function's stack frame — the value $sp had on entry, before any pushes or pops. While $sp chases the top of the stack, $fp stays anchored where this call began.

By saving the old $fp on the stack each time, the frame pointers form a linked list of frames — which is how a debugger prints a stack backtrace after a crash.

Optional, but strongly advised (slide 23)

Using a frame pointer is optional — compilers omit it when speed or code size matters. COMP1521 doesn't expect you to fully understand it. But it makes debugging far easier once you push and pop, so the course advises always using it.

You interact with it through two mipsy pseudo-instructions: begin and end.

What begin does (slide 24)

  • saves the old $fp onto the stack (linking to the previous frame),
  • sets $fp to the current $sp,
  • should be the first thing in the prologue.

What end does (slide 24)

  • restores $sp to the top of the previous frame,
  • restores $fp to its previous value,
  • should be right before jr $ra.
Why it matters: a growing stack can break the return.  Suppose a function reads a length at runtime and allocates a local array on the stack — so it subtracts an unknown amount from $sp mid-body. If the epilogue tries to read $ra back from a fixed offset of $sp, it reads the wrong word, because $sp has wandered. Measuring from the anchored $fp instead always lands on the saved $ra — that's the bug begin/end quietly prevent.
frame pointer — why $sp alone can't find $ra

Step a function that grows the stack

A function saves $ra, then allocates a local array (moving $sp down by a runtime amount). In $sp only mode the epilogue reads $ra from a fixed $sp offset and grabs garbage. Switch to frame pointer mode to measure from the anchored $fp and return correctly.

code
the stack  (top = $sp)
Conventions to prevent chaos

Register usage conventions (slides 26–27, 29)

MIPS has 32 registers. You can use 30 of them however you like — but everyone agrees on a convention so that functions don't trample each other. The single most important split: which registers survive a call, and which don't.

$t is free real estate — caller-saved (slide 27)

$t0–$t9 are temporaries. A called function may destroy them, so assume any jal wipes them. Use them for short-lived work — computing an offset, holding a value you're about to print — where you won't need them after a call.

In tests and assignments, the autotests deliberately scribble on $t registers. Don't trust them across a call.

$s is preserved — callee-saved (slide 27)

$s0–$s7 survive calls — but only because you save and restore them. If a value must outlive a jal (a loop counter you keep using, a pointer you need after the call), put it in an $s register and push it in your prologue.

The deal is symmetric: because you restore $s/$sp/$fp, callers can assume any function you call leaves them unchanged.

register file — the full convention (slide 26)

All 32 registers, by role

Tap a register to see its conventional use and — the question that matters most — whether its value survives a function call.

caller-saved (dies across a call) callee-saved (preserved) special / fixed role reserved
Select a register above.
The function rules, in one place (slide 27)
  • $a0–$a3 hold the first 4 arguments; $v0 holds the return value. Neither is preserved across a call (treat them like $t).
  • A function must restore $sp, $fp and $s0–$s7 to their original values — so callers may assume those are unchanged.
  • A function may destroy $t0–$t9 — so callers must assume those are changed.
  • A function must preserve $ra if it overwrites it (i.e. if it makes any call) — or it loses its way home.
Out of scope for COMP1521, but good to know.  Floating-point registers pass and return float/double with similar conventions; the stack is also used to pass a 5th+ argument, to pass or return values too big for a register (a whole struct can be any size), and to store local variables like arrays. You'll only meet these in challenge questions.
Choosing $t vs $s, live

Worked example: sum_to (slide 28)

A small program with one real decision in it: main keeps a value it needs after a call, so that value belongs in a saved register. The leaf it calls keeps nothing across a call, so it lives in temporaries.

C → MIPS
C
int sum_to(int n);
int main(void) {
  int max = 10;
  int result = sum_to(max);
  printf("sum 1..%d = %d\n",
         max, result);
  return 0;
}
int sum_to(int n) {
  int sum = 0;
  for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    sum += i;
  return sum;
}
MIPS — main saves max; sum_to is a leaf
main:
  begin
  push $ra
  push $s0          # max is needed AFTER the call
  li   $s0, 10       # -> use a saved register
  move $a0, $s0
  jal  sum_to        # result in $v0
  # ... print "sum 1..max = result" ...
  pop  $s0
  pop  $ra
  end
  li   $v0, 0
  jr   $ra
sum_to:                # leaf — only $t registers
  move $t0, $a0     # n  (move arg out first)
  li   $t1, 0        # sum
  li   $t2, 1        # i
sum_to__loop:
  bgt  $t2, $t0, sum_to__end
  add  $t1, $t1, $t2
  addi $t2, $t2, 1
  b    sum_to__loop
sum_to__end:
  move $v0, $t1     # return sum
  jr   $ra

The live lesson from lecture: putting max in a $t register looks fine until you call sum_to and then try to print max — the call has wiped it. The fix is one word: use $s0 (and push it). sum_to itself calls nothing, so it never needs an $s register or a prologue. Run it in the lab below — it prints sum 1..10 = 55.

Putting it all together

🍕 The MIPS Pizzeria (slides 30–35)

One program that uses everything: a global array of structs, a loop, a function that mutates a struct through a pointer, and a function that prints one. It's the full translation from C to MIPS — arrays as address arithmetic, structs as offsets, and the calling convention holding it together.

The C program (slides 31–33)
data & main
struct pizza_t {
  char size[10];
  int  price_cents;
};
struct pizza_t pizza_options[3] = {
  {"small",  300},
  {"medium", 550},
  {"large",  800}
};
int main(void) {
  printf("The available pizza options are:\n");
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    increase_price(&pizza_options[i], 100);
    print_pizza_t(&pizza_options[i]);
  }
  return 0;
}
the two functions
void increase_price(struct pizza_t *pizza,
                    int increase_cents) {
  pizza->price_cents += increase_cents;
}

void print_pizza_t(struct pizza_t *pizza) {
  printf("Size: %s, ", pizza->size);
  printf("price: %d cents\n",
         pizza->price_cents);
}

main walks the array, bumps each price by 100 cents, then prints it. Both helpers take a pointer to one element — so increase_price can change the array in place (there's no return value), and print_pizza_t can read its fields. Neither calls another function, so both are leaves.

The struct's shape decides the arithmetic

char size[10] takes bytes 0–9; the int price_cents must sit on a 4-aligned offset, so the assembler pads bytes 10–11 and places the price at offset 12. One element is 16 bytes.

PIZZA_STRUCT_SIZE  = 16
PIZZA_SIZE_OFFSET  = 0
PIZZA_PRICE_OFFSET = 12

Naming these constants (instead of sprinkling raw numbers) is exactly the style the lecturer pushes: it documents intent and makes the code easy to change and debug.

Reaching element i, field f

Same move as any array of structs:

la  $s1, pizza_options
mul $t0, $s0, 16     # i * STRUCT_SIZE
add $s1, $s1, $t0   # &pizza_options[i]
# then field at OFFSET($s1):
lw  $t2, 12($s1)    # ->price_cents

The base pointer goes in an $s register because it's needed after the increase_price call — to pass to print_pizza_t.

mipsy mini — the Pizzeria, sum_to & recursion, live

Run the whole application

Pick a preset and Run it, or Step instruction by instruction and watch the registers and the stack move. The Pizzeria mutates its struct array through a pointer and prints it; sum_to is §07; recursion grows the stack with begin/push on every call. Edit freely — it re-assembles on the next Step or Run.

registers
stack  (top = $sp)
console
Before you jump into MIPS (slides 34–35)
  • Simplify in C first. For each function, reduce it to simple statements, then recompile and rerun to check it still works — don't change everything at once without testing.
  • Plan your register usage. Decide up front what's temporary, what must survive a call, and what's a pointer you'll reuse. Most Pizzeria bugs are register-allocation slips.
  • Style counts. Consistent label names (function-name-prefixed), indentation, and a comment giving the equivalent line of C for each chunk of MIPS — and check the style marking rubric.
What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 36–39)

Today reinforced the function machinery and finished it. A function is a label reached with jal and left with jr $ra; arguments arrive in $a0–$a3 and the result leaves in $v0. Because there is one $ra, any function that calls another saves it on the stack — a downward-growing, LIFO region tracked by $sp, used through push/pop and framed by begin/end. The frame pointer $fp is a fixed anchor at the base of each frame: optional, but it keeps the return address findable even when $sp wanders, and it's how debuggers walk the stack. The register convention ties it together — $t caller-saved (assume a call destroys them), $s/$sp/$fp callee-saved (restored), arguments and $v0 volatile — and leaf functions skip the prologue entirely. The MIPS Pizzeria spent all of it at once: a struct array reached by i × 16, fields at fixed offsets, a pointer mutated in place, and the convention keeping main's state safe across two calls per loop. Next week leaves functions behind for integer representation and bitwise operations.

TL;DR · function = label · jal sets $ra, jr $ra returns · args $a0–$a3, return $v0 (both volatile) · stack = LIFO, grows down, $sp = top, must end where it started · push Rt: $sp−=4; sw · pop Rt: lw; $sp+=4 · pop in reverse · push/pop/begin/end are mipsy pseudo-instructions · skeleton = begin · push $ra · push $s · body · pop $s · pop $ra · end · jr $ra · leaf = no calls → no prologue · $fp = fixed anchor at frame base (begin saves old $fp & sets $fp=$sp; end reverses it) → return survives a growing stack · $t caller-saved, $s/$sp/$fp callee-saved · move args out of $a? first · Pizzeria: array of 16-byte structs, &options[i] = base + i*16, fields at 0 & 12, pointer mutated in place · next: integers & bitwise.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 4 — Lecture 1

Integers: bases, two's complement, types & endian-ness

Everything a computer does rests on integers — the bit patterns flowing through registers and memory are integers. Today decodes them end to end: how the same value wears binary, hex, octal and decimal costumes; how negatives are stored in two's complement so one adder does all the arithmetic; what each C type can hold and what happens when it overflows; and why the byte order — endian-ness — matters the moment you load a single byte.

A first taste of invalid C, then the foundation

Why learn about integers (slides 3–7)

The lecture opens with a couple of invalid C demos — a loop that writes past an array and silently clobbers its own counter, and a password check whose authenticated flag shares an address with an overflowed buffer. Both make far more sense now that you've seen how MIPS lays bytes out in memory. Then the main event: integers, the substrate everything else is built on.

Why it's worth your time (slide 6)

  • The disassembled MIPS you've been reading is just integers telling the processor what to do — understanding them is understanding the machine.
  • Knowing the limits of each type turns mystifying bugs (a big positive number printing as negative) into things you can predict and debug.
  • It sets up next lecture's bitwise operators, where you manipulate those bit patterns directly.

There are 10 types of people (slide 7)

Those who understand binary, and those who don't. The joke only lands once you read 10 in base 2 — it's two, not ten. That ambiguity is the whole problem this lecture solves: a string of digits means nothing until you know its base.

By the end you'll read 10 and instinctively ask "in which base?" — exactly the habit exams reward.

The same value, written in different alphabets

Bases & place value (slides 8–19)

A positional number system splits a number into place values, each a power of the base. Decimal is base 10 because we have ten fingers; computers use base 2 because a transistor is either on or off. The machinery is identical — only the base changes.

Decimal — base 10 (slides 8–11)

The digits 0–9, and place values that are powers of ten. 4705 is shorthand for a sum:

4705₁₀ = 4×10³ + 7×10² + 0×10¹ + 5×10⁰
       = 4000 + 700 + 0 + 5

Base 10 was an arbitrary choice — almost every ancient culture landed on it, fingers being the likely reason. To pull out one digit: n % 10 gives the ones, then divide by 10 and repeat.

Any base works — e.g. base 7 (slides 13–14)

Seven digits (0–6), place values that are powers of seven. The same expansion converts back to decimal:

1216₇ = 1×7³ + 2×7² + 1×7¹ + 6×7⁰
      = 343 + 98 + 7 + 6
      = 454₁₀

Without the subscript, 1216 could be base 7 (454) or base 10 (1216). Always know the base — especially in exams.

Binary — base 2, the language of hardware (slides 15–19)

Two digits (bits): 0 and 1, easy to realise as low/high voltage. Everything your computer does is pulses switching transistors on and off; high-level code is compiled all the way down to these. Place values are powers of two:

1011₂ = 1×2³ + 0×2² + 1×2¹ + 1×2⁰  = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11₁₀

Converting decimal → binary is repeated division by 2, reading remainders bottom-up (last remainder is the most significant bit):

25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1   ← least significant bit
12 ÷ 2 =  6 r 0
 6 ÷ 2 =  3 r 0
 3 ÷ 2 =  1 r 1
 1 ÷ 2 =  0 r 1   ← most significant bit
        → read up: 25₁₀ = 11001₂
Compacting long binary into readable chunks

Hexadecimal & octal (slides 20–35)

Binary gets unreadable fast — 12345678 is 10111100011000010100111 in bits. The fix is to group bits: every 4 bits become one hex digit (base 16), every 3 bits one octal digit (base 8). The bit pattern stays visible, but it's far shorter.

Hex — base 16, groups of 4 bits (slides 22–23, 27–30)

Sixteen digits: 0–9 then A B C D E F for 10–15. Since 16 = 2⁴, each hex digit maps cleanly to exactly four bits. To convert, slice the binary into nibbles from the right and translate each:

1011 1100 0110 0001 0100 1110₂
  B    C    6    1    4    E   = 0xBC614E

After a while, F just reads as four ones (15). In C, the 0x prefix marks hex.

Octal — base 8, groups of 3 bits (slide 34)

Eight digits (0–7). Since 8 = 2³, each octal digit is three bits. Less common than hex — the lecturer's verdict is it "exists" and is "just annoying" — but you'll meet it, so recognise it:

72₈ = 111 010₂ = 0x3A = 58₁₀

Humans recall things in groups of three (phone numbers), so octal isn't crazy — hex is just usually more convenient for byte-aligned data.

The one table worth memorising.  Hex digit ⇄ 4-bit nibble: 0=0000, 1=0001, … 9=1001, A=1010, B=1011, C=1100, D=1101, E=1110, F=1111. Once it's in your head, binary↔hex becomes a lookup, no maths. The converter below drills exactly this.
Type in any base, watch the rest update

Lab · live base converter (slides 8–35)

Edit any one field and the others convert instantly. The nibble strip underneath shows the 4-bit groups lining up with the hex digits — the grouping that makes binary↔hex a lookup rather than a calculation.

base converter — dec · hex · oct · bin

One value, four costumes

All four boxes hold the same number — the computer doesn't care which base you wrote it in. 32-bit unsigned range (0 to 4,294,967,295). Try 461, then 0xBC614E, then flip a bit in the binary box.

0x

0b
nibbles  (4 bits = 1 hex digit)
Addition works exactly as you'd hope

Doing maths in binary (slides 36–38)

Processors are built from arithmetic logic units that add bit patterns. The good news: binary addition follows the same carry rules as decimal — when a column overflows, carry one to the next.

Two worked additions (slides 36–38)

Add column by column from the right, carrying when a column reaches 2 (10₂). The result is just ordinary arithmetic on a different alphabet.

4 + 1 = 5
  00000100      (4)
+ 00000001      (1)
----------
  00000101      (5)
6 + 7 = 13 (watch the carries)
  00000110      (6)
+ 00000111      (7)
----------
  00001101      (13)

In the second sum, 1+1 in a column writes 0 and carries 1; 1+1+1 writes 1 and carries 1. The same hardware adder runs constantly inside your machine — even multiplication is built from repeated addition. (Subtraction reuses the same adder too, once we have two's complement.)

How C knows which base you mean

Integer constants in C & MIPS (slides 39–41)

You've already been writing these without noticing — disassembled MIPS shows memory in hex. A literal's prefix tells the compiler its base; the format specifier tells printf how to display it. They're independent.

Prefixes set the base of a literal (slide 40)

prefixbaseexample
0xhex (16)0x2A
0octal (8)052
0bbinary (2)0b101010
nonedecimal (10)42

All four examples above are the same value — 42. A lone leading 0 meaning octal trips people up: 052 is 42, not 52.

All four print 42 (slide 40)

printf("%d", 0x2A);      // prints 42
printf("%d", 052);       // prints 42
printf("%d", 0b101010);  // prints 42
printf("%d", 42);        // prints 42
Don't ship 0b. Binary literals were only recently added to C and some compilers (including dcc) reject them. Fine to experiment with, but use hex in submitted code — or the course's print_bits helper.

Format specifiers — choosing the display base

The prefix sets how a constant is read; the printf specifier sets how a value is shown. They're orthogonal — you can read in hex and print in decimal, or vice-versa.

specifiershows value as
%dsigned decimal
%uunsigned decimal
%xhexadecimal
%ooctal

There's a standard-library demo (integer_prefixes.c) that reads a number and prints its hex/octal equivalents — handy when you need a quick conversion without touching a calculator.

Negatives, stored so one adder does everything

Signed integers & two's complement (slides 42–52)

An unsigned 32-bit int holds 0 to 2³²−1 — all positive. To store negatives we must spend the patterns differently. The naive idea (a leading sign bit) gives two zeros and awkward arithmetic. The winning scheme is two's complement: it has one zero, and subtraction is just addition.

Unsigned — all the patterns are positive (slide 43)

A 32-bit unsigned int stores 0 … 2³²−1. Minimum is all zeros, maximum is all ones (4,294,967,295). No bits are spent on a sign, so every pattern is a positive value.

Why not just a sign bit? (slides 44–46)

Using the top bit as "negative" seems natural but creates +0 and −0, two patterns for the same value, and makes the adder hardware fiddly. Two's complement avoids both — there's exactly one zero, and the ordinary binary adder gets subtraction for free.

The two's complement rule (slides 50–53)

For an n-bit number, the representation of −b is 2ⁿ − b. Positive numbers and zero look normal; a negative number's top bit is 1. Counting down past zero wraps to all-ones:

 2 = 00000010      -1 = 11111111
 1 = 00000001      -2 = 11111110
 0 = 00000000      -3 = 11111101

So in 8 bits, −5 is 2⁸ − 5 = 251 = 11111011₂. And 11111011₂ reads back as −5 because 251 − 256 = −5. The signed int range becomes −2³¹ … 2³¹−1 — one bit goes to the sign, halving the positive range.

The flip-and-add-1 trick (slide 52)

The fast way to negate without subtracting from 2ⁿ: invert every bit, then add 1. To get −5 from +5:

+5:        00000101
invert:    11111010
add 1:     11111011   = -5

Run it again on 11111011 and you're back to 00000101 — the operation is its own inverse, a handy self-check.

Subtraction = negate, then add (slide 51)

Because negatives are stored to make this work, hardware almost never has a dedicated subtractor. To compute a − b it takes the two's complement of b and adds. One adder, used everywhere — that's the payoff that made two's complement universal.

It's done for the computer's convenience, not ours — but the explorer below makes the human side click.

Slide through −128…127, or toggle individual bits. Watch the sign bit (leftmost, red underline) decide positivity, and follow the flip-and-add-1 negation worked out live. The unsigned reading is shown alongside so you can see both interpretations of one byte.

How many bits, and what happens at the edge

Integer types, limits & overflow (slides 53–64)

A type is really just "how many bits, signed or unsigned". That fixes its range — and stepping outside the range doesn't error, it wraps. Knowing each type's limits is how you catch the bug before it ships.

Sizes on CSE machines (slides 60–61)

typebytesbits
char18
short216
int432
long864
double864

"Common, not universal" — an 8-bit microcontroller might make sizeof(int) 2. Use sizeof to ask the machine you're actually on.

Fixed-width types — stdint.h (slides 62–63)

When the exact width matters, #include <stdint.h> for guaranteed sizes. COMP1521 uses these heavily.

int8_t  / uint8_t    // ±128 / 0..255
int16_t / uint16_t   // ±32768 / 0..65535
int32_t / uint32_t   // ±2.1e9 / 0..4.3e9
int64_t / uint64_t   // ±9.2e18 / 0..1.8e19

<limits.h> gives the min/max of the built-in types (INT_MAX, INT_MIN, …).

Overflow & wraparound are silent.  INT_MAX + 1 wraps to INT_MIN — the biggest positive int becomes the most negative. For unsigned, 0 − 1 wraps to the largest value (4,294,967,295). dcc warns on signed overflow at runtime; production compilers usually say nothing, and that silence is precisely how a small slip becomes a security hole. In mipsy, signed add on overflow raises an exception and halts — useful for catching it.
integer types — ranges & wraparound

Pick a type, then push it past its edge

Tap a type to see its bit width and exact range. Then type a value and see how it's stored in that type — values outside the range wrap around, just like they do silently in C.

Select a type above.
store value:
Which byte goes at the lowest address?

Endian-ness (slides 65–66, 77)

A 32-bit value is four bytes. Endian-ness is the order they sit in memory. There's no winner — it's an architecture choice — but it bites the instant you read a single byte of a multi-byte value, or move data between machines.

Big-endian — big bits first (slide 65)

The most significant byte goes at the lowest address. For 0x12345678, address 0 holds 12, then 34, 56, 78. Reads left-to-right like we write numbers.

Little-endian — little bits first (slide 65)

The least significant byte goes at the lowest address. For 0x12345678, address 0 holds 78, then 56, 34, 12. mipsy and most modern machines are little-endian.

How to test it in C (slide 77).  Store 0x03040506 in a uint32_t, then read its first byte through a uint8_t *. You get 6 on a little-endian machine (LSB first) and 3 on a big-endian one. On CSE — and in the visualiser below — the answer is 6: little-endian.
endian-ness — byte order in memory

Watch a word land in memory

Enter a 32-bit hex value, toggle the byte order, and see which byte sits at the lowest address. The highlighted cell is what a single-byte load from the base address would read.

value:
Filling a 32-bit register from a smaller piece

Loading bytes & half-words in MIPS (slides 67–76)

A register is 32 bits, but lb loads 8 and lh loads 16. So what fills the rest? It depends on signedness: signed loads sign-extend (copy the top bit up), unsigned loads zero-extend. That's why bytes and halves come in two flavours — and why words don't.

Sign-extend vs zero-extend (slides 68–70)

Load 0x80 into a 32-bit register. As unsigned (lbu) the upper bytes are zeros → 0x00000080. As signed (lb) the top bit is 1, so the sign extends with ones → 0xFFFFFF80, a negative value.

// lbu 0x80: 00 00 00 80
// lb  0x80: FF FF FF 80

Why no lwu? (slide 67)

A word already fills all 32 bits — there's nothing to extend. Its own top bit is the sign bit, so lw needs no signed/unsigned variants. Only the partial loads (lb/lh) must decide how to fill the gap.

Endian-ness decides which byte/half you grab; signedness decides how it's extended into the register.

The four partial loads on 0x1234ABCD (slides 71–76)

Memory is little-endian, so byte 0 = CD, byte 1 = AB. Loading from the base address picks the low byte(s); the result depends on signed vs unsigned. CD and ABCD both have their top bit set, so the signed loads go negative.

instructionreadsextendsresult in $t0
lbbyte CDsign (1s)0xFFFFFFCD
lbubyte CDzero0x000000CD
lhhalf ABCDsign (1s)0xFFFFABCD
lhuhalf ABCDzero0x0000ABCD

Run all four in the lab below — they're verified against these exact values. The "signed" load makes sense only if the byte genuinely represents a small negative number; reach for the unsigned variant whenever you just want the raw bits.

mipsy mini — endianness, signed loads, overflow, live

Run the integer demos

Pick a preset and Run, or Step through it watching the registers and memory. endianness stores a word and reads back its lowest byte; signed loads contrasts lb/lbu/lh/lhu on the same word; overflow and wraparound push values past their limits. Edit freely — it re-assembles on the next Step or Run.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 78–80)

Integers are the substrate of computing, and a bit pattern means nothing until you fix its base: decimal for humans, binary for hardware, and hex/octal as compact stand-ins where each digit is a fixed group of bits (4 for hex, 3 for octal). Binary arithmetic follows the same carry rules as decimal, which is why one hardware adder suffices. Negatives use two's complement — −b is 2ⁿ−b, or equivalently "flip the bits and add 1" — giving a single zero and turning subtraction into addition. A type is just a bit-width and a signedness, which fixes its range; stepping outside that range wraps silently (INT_MAX+1 = INT_MIN), and knowing the limits is how you catch the bug. Finally, endian-ness sets the byte order in memory (mipsy is little-endian), and signedness decides how a partial load fills a register — lb/lh sign-extend, lbu/lhu zero-extend, and lw needs no variant because a word is already full. Next lecture: bitwise operators — the shifts and masks that read and rewrite these patterns directly.

TL;DR · a digit string means nothing without its base · decimal (humans), binary (hardware), hex = 4 bits/digit, octal = 3 bits/digit · C prefixes: 0x hex, 0 octal, 0b binary (don't ship it), none = decimal · printf %d/%u/%x/%o · binary addition carries like decimal → one adder does subtraction too · two's complement: −b = 2ⁿ−b = flip bits + 1 · one zero, subtraction = add the negation · signed int range −2³¹…2³¹−1, unsigned 0…2³²−1 · type = width + signedness → fixed range · overflow wraps silently (INT_MAX+1 = INT_MIN, 0−1 unsigned = UINT_MAX) · stdint.h for guaranteed widths, limits.h for ranges · endian-ness = byte order; mipsy little-endian (LSB at low address) · lb/lh sign-extend, lbu/lhu zero-extend, lw needs no variant · next: bitwise operators.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 4 — Lecture 2

Bitwise operators: masks, shifts & bit manipulation

Last lecture said a bit pattern means nothing until you know its type. Today we stop interpreting bits and start manipulating them. First we finish the loading story and decode a raw MIPS instruction by hand — proof that even code is just an integer. Then the six C bitwise operators (& | ^ ~ << >>), the masks built from them to check, set, clear and toggle individual bits, shifts as multiplication and division by powers of two, integers used as sets, and the MIPS instructions that do all of it in one cheap gate.

You cannot read bits without a type

Recap: bits, bytes & what a pattern represents (slides 5–14)

The lecture opens by putting 32 bits on the screen and asking what they represent. Your brain immediately says "a binary number" — but that's a guess, not an answer. The same 32 bits are a different value in every type, and the machine only knows which one because you told it.

What does this represent in C? (slides 5–6)

10110110111110001110110101110110

We can't know without knowing its type. Is it an int? An unsigned int? A float? A Unicode character? A MIPS instruction? Every one of those readings is legal, and they all disagree.

The course notes make the same point with one byte: 0b10100011 is −93 as a signed byte, 163 as an unsigned byte, and something else again as part of a character or an instruction.

The two readings you must have cold (slides 7–9)

Unsigned — a 4-byte unsigned int holds 0 … 2³²−1. All zeros is the minimum, all ones is the maximum. No bit is spent on a sign.

Signed — a 4-byte int holds −2³¹ … 2³¹−1 in two's complement: positives and zero look normal, and for an n-bit number −b is stored as 2ⁿ − b.

8-bit "-5"  =  2⁸ − 5 = 251 = 1111 1011₂
1111 1011₂  =  251 − 2⁸ = −5
Worked exercise — the same two bytes, two types (slides 10–14)

What do 01000011 and 11000011 mean in decimal, first as uint8_t and then as int8_t? Only the second pattern changes — because only it has the top bit set.

as uint8_t (unsigned)
01000011 = 2⁶ + 2¹ + 2⁰
         = 64 + 2 + 1        =  67

11000011 = 2⁷ + 2⁶ + 2¹ + 2⁰
         = 128 + 64 + 2 + 1  = 195
as int8_t (signed)
01000011 = 64 + 2 + 1       =  67
           (top bit 0 → positive, unchanged)

11000011 = 195 − 2⁸
         = 195 − 256         = −61
           (top bit 1 → negative)

The rule in one line: if the top bit is 0, signed and unsigned agree. If the top bit is 1, subtract 2ⁿ to get the signed reading. Everything else in this lecture — masks, shifts, sign extension — is downstream of that one bit.

Closing out the end of Monday's lecture

Endian-ness & partial loads, finished (slides 15–26)

A quick finish to Lecture 1's last topic before the new material. Two independent questions decide what a partial load puts in a register: endian-ness picks which bytes you grab, and signedness decides how the rest of the register is filled.

Endian-ness — which byte is "first"? (slides 15–16)

"What order to put things in" has no right answer, so there are two schools:

  • Big-endian — most significant byte at the low address. Big bits first.
  • Little-endian — least significant byte at the low address. Little bits first.
li  $t0, 0x12345678
sw  $t0, my_word    # mipsy-web is little-endian:
                        # memory reads  78 56 34 12

What fills the other 24 bits? (slides 17–20)

Store 0x80 into a 32-bit register and three bytes are left over. Fill them with zeros and 0x80 is 128. But 0x80 as a signed byte is −128 — so a signed load must extend the sign bit instead:

// lbu (unsigned) → zero-extend
00000000 00000000 00000000 10000000
// lb  (signed)   → sign-extend
11111111 11111111 11111111 10000000

There is no lwu: a word already fills the register, so there is nothing left to extend.

The load examples, side by side (slides 21–26)

Both words are stored little-endian, so a byte load takes 78 / CD and a half-word load takes 5678 / ABCD. Notice that 78 and 5678 have their top bit clear, so signed and unsigned agree — while CD and ABCD have it set, and the signed loads go negative.

stored wordinstructionreadsextends withresult in $t0
0x12345678lbbyte 78zeros (top bit is 0)0x00000078 = 120
0x12345678lhhalf 5678zeros (top bit is 0)0x00005678
0x1234ABCDlbbyte CDones — sign extend0xFFFFFFCD
0x1234ABCDlhhalf ABCDones — sign extend0xFFFFABCD
0x1234ABCDlbubyte CDzeros0x000000CD
0x1234ABCDlhuhalf ABCDzeros0x0000ABCD

Short version: lb/lh hand you a signed number, and adding a u hands you an unsigned one. Which you want depends entirely on what that byte is supposed to mean — and the Lecture 1 load lab runs all four if you want to watch it happen.

Your code is an integer too

Decoding a MIPS instruction by hand (slides 27–35)

The decompiled view in mipsy shows numbers like 0x01288820. That number is the instruction — a 32-bit pattern that switches control logic on and off inside the CPU. With the instruction format in hand you can read it the way the processor does.

What a MIPS instruction looks like (slide 29)

Every MIPS instruction is exactly 32 bits and specifies an operation (the thing to do) plus zero or more operands (the things to do it to). Fields sit at fixed positions, so decoding is pure slicing:

00100001000010010000000000001100
              ↓
     addi $t1, $t0, 12

Everything you write in MIPS becomes one of these words. Assembly is the readable skin; this is the machine's actual language.

Working through 0x01288820 (slides 27–35)

0x01288820
= 0000 0001 0010 1000 1000 1000 0010 0000
= 000000 01001 01000 10001 00000 100000
    ↓      ↓     ↓     ↓      ↓     ↓
   op     rs    rt    rd   shamt funct

op = 000000 and funct = 100000 together mean add. Then rd = 10001₂ = 17, rs = 01001₂ = 9, rt = 01000₂ = 8:

add $17, $9, $8
add $s1, $t1, $t0     # same thing, friendly names
Registers really are numbers.  $t0, $s1 and friends are just aliases the assembler understands — the hardware only knows $8, $17, $9. Open the register pane in mipsy and you can see both names for every slot. Paste add $s1, $t1, $t0 into mipsy web and the disassembly comes back as 0x01288820, closing the loop.
instruction decoder — hex → fields → assembly

Type a hex word and watch it split into fields. R-format instructions (op = 000000) are named by their funct; everything else is named by its op. Try the two from the slides, then invent your own.

Six operators, one idea

Why bitwise, and what C gives you (slides 36–39)

Integers are everywhere — and where accuracy and speed matter, integers are what you reach for rather than floating point. Bitwise operators are how you get underneath an integer and work on the individual bits.

Where this actually gets used (slide 37)

  • Optimisation — a shift or an AND is a single gate; a division or a remainder is not.
  • Embedded systems — hardware registers pack a dozen flags into one word.
  • Data compression — packing values into fewer bits than a byte.
  • Security & cryptography — XOR is the workhorse of both.
  • Graphics and computer networks — pixel channels, headers, flags, checksums.

And in this course: heavily, for the rest of the term.

The six C operators (slide 38)

CPUs provide instructions to manipulate individual bits — MIPS has 13 bit-manipulation instructions. C exposes six operators:

x & ybitwise AND
x | ybitwise OR
x ^ ybitwise XOR (exclusive OR)
~xbitwise NOT (negation / inversion)
x << nleft shift
x >> nright shift

All of them take 1, 2, 4 or 8-byte values and return a result with the same number of bits as the input.

Logical && is not bitwise & (slide 39).  && works on whole values and answers true/false — it's what belongs in if (x > 10 && x < 20), and it only ever gives you 1 or 0. & works on every individual bit of both values at once. So 5 && 6 is 1 ("both are non-zero, so true"), while 5 & 6 is 4 (101 & 110 = 100). Mixing them up is a classic silent bug.
Beware: other subjects use other symbols.  Discrete maths, electrical engineering and other languages all write AND, OR and NOT differently — you'll meet overbars, wedges, ! and more. For this course and C, the symbols are the six above. Learn them here; translate elsewhere.
Four operations, four truth tables

AND, OR, NOT & XOR (slides 40–62)

Each operator lines the two values up bit by bit and applies one tiny rule per column. Learn the four truth tables and the two identities that go with each, and everything after this is bookkeeping.

AND & (slides 40–42)

  00100111        AND | 0  1
& 11100011        ----+------
  --------          0 | 0  0
  00100011          1 | 0  1

Identities: x & 0 = 0 (a zero destroys), x & 1 = x (a one preserves).

Use it to: check whether a particular bit is set, and clear particular bits to 0.

OR | (slides 51–54)

  00100111         OR | 0  1
| 11100011        ----+------
  --------          0 | 0  1
  11100111          1 | 1  1

Identities: x | 0 = x (a zero preserves), x | 1 = 1 (a one forces).

Use it to: set particular bits to 1.

NOT ~ (slides 55–57)

~ 00100111        NOT | 0  1
  --------        -----+------
  11011000            | 1  0

Use it to: build one mask from another — ~0x7 turns a "these three bits" mask into an "everything but these three bits" mask.

~ does not make a number negative. It flips every bit, nothing more. Whether the result reads as negative depends on the type you stored it in. (Two's complement negation is ~x + 1 — flip, then add one — which is a different operation.)

XOR ^ (slides 58–62)

  00100111        XOR | 0  1
^ 11100011        ----+------
  --------          0 | 0  1
  11000100          1 | 1  0

Identities: x ^ 0 = x (pass through), x ^ 1 = ~x (flip).

Use it to: toggle bits, compare two values (result bits are 1 exactly where they differ), hash, and encrypt — because XOR is its own inverse.

XOR is its own inverse — the toy cipher (slides 62–63, xor.c)

Apply the same mask twice and you're back where you started. That's the whole idea behind xor.c: XOR every byte of the input with a key to "encrypt", XOR again with the same key to get it back.

uint8_t x      = 0x13;   // 0001 0011
uint8_t mask   = 0x07;   // 0000 0111
uint8_t once   = x ^ mask;      // 0001 0100  = 0x14
uint8_t twice  = once ^ mask;   // 0001 0011  = 0x13  — back to x

Run at the shell: echo Hello | xor 42 produces gibberish, and echo Hello | xor 42 | xor 42 produces Hello. Real cryptography is a great deal more than this — but this is the shape of it.

The four things you ever want to do to a bit

Bit masks: check, set, clear, toggle (slides 43–50, 56–57)

A mask is just a bit pattern you build so that the operators hit the bits you care about and leave the rest alone. Pair the right operator with the right mask and you get exactly four moves — and every piece of bit manipulation you'll write is some combination of them.

The four moves, as C (slides 43–45, 54, 57, 61)
goalcodewhy it worksx = 0x13, mask = 0x07
test / extractx & mask&1 keeps, &0 zeroes0x03
set to 1x | mask|1 forces 1, |0 keeps0x17
clear to 0x & ~mask~mask is 0 where you want to clear0x10
togglex ^ mask^1 flips, ^0 keeps0x14

The clear case is the one worth staring at: you write the mask for the bits you want to affect, then ~ it so those positions become zeros and everything else becomes ones. ~0x07 is 1111 1000 — zeros exactly where the original had ones.

Building the mask you need

One bit, and the low n bits

// bit n only
mask = 1 << n;              // n=2 → 00000100

// the low n bits (set_low_bits.c)
mask = (1 << n) - 1;        // n=3 → 00000111

The −1 trick is worth memorising: one bit set at position n, minus one, borrows all the way down and leaves n ones.

A range of bits, and pulling it out

// bits low..high (set_bit_range.c)
int size = high - low + 1;
mask = ((1 << size) - 1) << low;

// extract them (extract_bit_range.c)
uint32_t bits = (value & mask) >> low;

Mask off everything outside the range, then shift the range down so its lowest bit becomes bit 0 — which is precisely how the instruction decoder above pulls out op, rs, rt and the rest.

Reading one bit — get_nth_bit (print_bits.c, slide 75)

Rather than build a fresh mask for every position, shift the bit you want down to position 0 and use the same mask every time. This is the helper the whole print_bits family is built on.

// extract the nth bit from a value
int get_nth_bit(uint64_t value, int n) {
    uint64_t shifted_value = value >> n;   // n-th bit is now the LSB
    int bit = shifted_value & 1;           // zero everything else
    return bit;
}

// print the bottom how_many_bits bits, most significant first
void print_bits(uint64_t value, int how_many_bits) {
    for (int i = how_many_bits - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        printf("%d", get_nth_bit(value, i));
    }
}

Same idea, one level up: to print a value in hex, shift by 4 * digit and mask with 0xF to get one hex digit at a time — that's all of print_int_in_hex.c. And going the other way, hex_string_to_int.c builds a value with value = (value << 4) | digit, one digit at a time.

Case study: is this number odd? (slides 46–50)

The pattern in binary

0  000     4  100
1  001     5  101
2  010     6  110
3  011     7  111

Every odd number has a 1 in the least significant bit — necessarily, since that's the only place a 1 contributes an odd amount. So testing oddness is testing one bit:

int is_odd(int n) {
    return n & 1;
}

…but should you write it that way?

Two defensible answers, and it's worth holding both:

  • The hardware argument (lecture). An AND gate is one gate drawing a minuscule amount of power; a division-with-remainder is orders of magnitude more work. On embedded or power-constrained systems that difference is real.
  • The readability argument (course notes). Write the obvious code — n % 2 != 0 — and let the compiler emit andi for you. It will. Clever code that saves nothing costs you a reader.

The skill being taught is recognising that the two are the same operation. Which one you type is a judgement call about your compiler and your audience.

Sliding the bits sideways

Left shift, right shift & the bugs they bring (slides 64–73)

A shift moves every bit a fixed number of positions. Bits that fall off the end vanish; the vacated positions are filled with zeros. The result has the same width as the input — so shifting is lossy, and that loss is where both the maths and the bugs come from.

Left shift << multiplies by 2ⁿ (slides 64–67)

expressionresultdecimal
00000001 << 1000000102
00000001 << 2000001004
00000001 << 3000010008
00000001 << 40001000016

Each position is worth twice the one to its right, so sliding left one place doubles the value. shift_as_multiply.c uses exactly this to compute 2ⁿ without a multiply.

Right shift >> divides by 2ⁿ (slides 68–72)

expressionresultdecimal
00010000 >> 1000010008
00010000 >> 2000001004
00010000 >> 3000000102
00010000 >> 4000000011

When a 1 falls off the right it's simply lost: 0111 >> 1 = 0011, i.e. 7 / 2 = 3. That's not a bug — it's integer division, exactly what C does anyway.

Shifting signed values is a trap (slide 73, shift_bug.c).  Shifts involving negative values are implementation-defined or undefined — the standard doesn't promise you an answer, and different compilers give different ones. It is a common source of bugs in COMP1521 and everywhere else. Always use unsigned values and variables when shifting.
Four ways to get this wrong (shift_bug.c)
int16_t i;
i = -1;      i = i >> 1;   // undefined — right shift of a negative value
i = -1;      i = i << 1;   // undefined — left shift of a negative value
i = 32767;   i = i << 1;   // undefined — result doesn't fit, goes negative

uint64_t j;
j = 1 << 33;                // undefined — the constant 1 is an int (32 bits)
j = ((uint64_t)1) << 33;    // ok — shift a 64-bit value

The last pair is the sneakiest: the variable you assign into is 64 bits, but the expression 1 << 33 is evaluated as a 32-bit int before it ever gets there. Cast the operand, not the result.

Logical vs arithmetic right shift

C hides this behind the type; MIPS makes you choose the instruction. Shifting 0xFFFFFFF0 (which is −16 as a signed word) right by 2:

srl — logical:    1111...11110000 >> 2 → 0011 1111 ... 1100  = 1073741820
sra — arithmetic: 1111...11110000 >> 2 → 1111 1111 ... 1100  = −4

Logical shifts zeros into the top — which is what C's >> does for an unsigned value. Arithmetic copies the sign bit down, which keeps a negative number negative and makes the shift a genuine divide by 2ⁿ. Pick the wrong one and −16 becomes a billion.

One integer, sixty-four yes/no answers

Using an integer as a set (course notes, pokemon.c & bitset.c)

Give every possible member its own bit and a single integer becomes a set. A uint16_t holds any subset of 16 things; a uint64_t any subset of 64. Union, intersection and membership then cost one instruction each — which is why this pattern is everywhere in systems code and in every hardware driver you'll ever read.

One bit per member (pokemon.c)

#define FIRE_TYPE      0x0001   // bit 0
#define FIGHTING_TYPE  0x0002   // bit 1
#define WATER_TYPE     0x0004   // bit 2
#define FLYING_TYPE    0x0008   // bit 3
#define POISON_TYPE    0x0010   // bit 4
// … up to
#define FAIRY_TYPE     0x8000   // bit 15

Each constant is a single set bit — i.e. 1 << n written out in hex.

The three moves, in the operators you just learned

uint16_t p = BUG_TYPE | POISON_TYPE | FAIRY_TYPE;

if (p & POISON_TYPE)  { … }  // test  → &
p |= GHOST_TYPE;              // add   → |
p &= ~POISON_TYPE;            // remove→ & ~

Test with &, add with |, remove with & ~ — the same check / set / clear trio from the mask section, just with a friendlier name on each mask.

The general version (bitset.c)

With typedef uint64_t set; the classic set operations are one line each — and they are all operators from this lecture.

set set_add(int x, set a)          { return a | ((set)1 << x); }
set set_union(set a, set b)        { return a | b; }
set set_intersection(set a, set b) { return a & b; }
int set_member(int x, set a)       { return (a >> x) & 1; }

int set_cardinality(set a) {
    int n_members = 0;
    while (a != 0) {
        n_members += a & 1;   // count the low bit
        a >>= 1;              // then look at the next one
    }
    return n_members;
}

Note the cast in set_add: (set)1 << x, not 1 << x. Without it the constant is a 32-bit int and any member above 31 is undefined behaviour — the same shift_bug.c trap, in real code.

The same six ideas, in assembly

MIPS bit-manipulation & shift instructions (slides 76–78)

Everything above has a direct MIPS instruction. Register–register forms are R-format; the i variants take a 16-bit immediate instead of a second register — exactly the two layouts the decoder in §03 pulls apart.

Bit manipulation

assemblymeaning
and rd, rs, rtrd = rs & rt
or  rd, rs, rtrd = rs | rt
xor rd, rs, rtrd = rs ^ rt
nor rd, rs, rtrd = ~(rs | rt)
andi rt, rs, Irt = rs & I
ori  rt, rs, Irt = rs | I
xori rt, rs, Irt = rs ^ I
not rd, rsrd = ~rs

There's no real not instruction — mipsy translates not rd, rs into nor rd, rs, $0. Since x | 0 = x, "NOR with zero" is just "NOT".

Shifts

assemblymeaning
sll  rd, rt, Ird = rt << I
srl  rd, rt, Ird = rt >> I  (zeros in)
sra  rd, rt, Ird = rt >> I  (sign in)
sllv rd, rt, rsrd = rt << rs
srlv rd, rt, rsrd = rt >> rs  (zeros in)
srav rd, rt, rsrd = rt >> rs  (sign in)
  • srl / srlv shift zeros into the most significant bit — this matches C's >> on an unsigned value.
  • sra / srav propagate the most significant bit, so the sign is maintained and a negative number really is divided by two.
  • The v suffix means the shift amount comes from a register rather than being fixed at assembly time.

mipsy also provides rol and ror pseudo-instructions, which rotate bits around instead of dropping them — real instructions on some MIPS versions, with no simple C equivalent.

Exercises (slides 41–42, 52–53, 59–63, 74)

Every one of these is a two-line calculation once you have the truth tables. Work them on paper first, then check with the playground above.

Exercise 1 — logical vs bitwise, and the beer joke (slide 63)

A software developer walks into a bar and orders 5 ^ 6 beers. Evaluate:

5 && 6      5 & 6      5 ^ 6
Show the answers 
5 = 101₂     6 = 110₂

5 && 6  →  both operands are non-zero, so the whole
           condition is TRUE  →  1

5 & 6   →  101
           110  &
           ---
           100  →  4

5 ^ 6   →  101
           110  ^
           ---
           011  →  3   (three beers — he survives)

A mathematician would read 5^6 as exponentiation — 15,625 beers — which is a rather different evening. Different notation, different subject; see the warning in §04.

Exercise 2 — the seven expressions (slide 74)

Given these declarations, what is the value of each expression?

uint8_t x = 0x55;   // 0101 0101
uint8_t y = 0xAA;   // 1010 1010

uint8_t a = x & y;      uint8_t e = x >> 1;
uint8_t b = x ^ y;      uint8_t f = y >> 2;
uint8_t c = x << 1;     uint8_t g = x | y;
uint8_t d = y << 2;
Show the answers

The two values were chosen to be perfect opposites: every position where x has a 1, y has a 0. So AND is empty and OR and XOR are full.

expressionbinaryhexdecimal
a = x & y0000 00000x000
b = x ^ y1111 11110xFF255
c = x << 11010 10100xAA170  (= y)
d = y << 21010 10000xA8168
e = x >> 10010 10100x2A42
f = y >> 20010 10100x2A42
g = x | y1111 11110xFF255

Watch d: 1010 1010 << 2 would be 10 1010 1000, but the two bits that slid past the top of an 8-bit type are gone, leaving 1010 1000. And c is a small joke of its own — shifting x left by one turns it into y.

Exercise 3 — bit manipulation, 8-bit (course notes)

Assuming 8-bit quantities and writing your answers as 8-bit bit-strings:

  • What are 25, 65, ~0, ~~1, 0xFF, ~0xFF?
  • What are (01010101 & 10101010) and (01010101 | 10101010)?
  • For any x: what are (x & ~x) and (x | ~x)?
  • How do you ensure the 3rd bit from the right is set to 1? To 0?
Show the answers 
25    = 0001 1001        ~0    = 1111 1111
65    = 0100 0001        ~~1   = 0000 0001   // ~ twice = unchanged
0xFF  = 1111 1111        ~0xFF = 0000 0000

01010101 & 10101010 = 0000 0000   // no column has two 1s
01010101 | 10101010 = 1111 1111   // every column has one

x & ~x = 0000 0000   // a bit and its opposite are never both 1
x | ~x = 1111 1111   // one of them always is

// "3rd bit from the right" is bit index 2 → mask 0000 0100 = 0x04
x |= 0x04;    // set   it to 1
x &= ~0x04;   // clear it to 0

x & ~x = 0 and x | ~x = all ones hold for every x — they're the bitwise versions of "P and not-P is false, P or not-P is true".

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slide 79)

A bit pattern still means nothing without a type — the same byte is 195 unsigned and −61 signed, and the same 32 bits can be an integer, a float, a character or an instruction. Decoding 0x01288820 into add $s1, $t1, $t0 by slicing out op, rs, rt, rd and funct makes that concrete: your code is an integer, and reading it is just masking and shifting. C gives you six operators to do that work — & tests and clears, | sets, ^ toggles and compares, ~ builds the complement of a mask, and << / >> slide bits sideways, multiplying and dividing by powers of two while quietly discarding whatever falls off the end. Combine an operator with a mask and you get the only four moves that exist: x & mask, x | mask, x & ~mask, x ^ mask. Build masks with 1 << n, (1 << n) - 1 and ((1 << size) - 1) << low, and one integer becomes a set where union, intersection and membership each cost a single instruction. Shift only unsigned values — signed shifts are undefined and will bite you. In MIPS it's and/or/xor/nor plus the i immediate forms, with srl zero-filling and sra sign-propagating. Next lecture: a few more bitwise examples, then floating point.

TL;DR · bits need a type: 11000011 is 195 unsigned, −61 signed · an instruction is an integer — 0x01288820 = op·rs·rt·rd·shamt·funct = add $s1, $t1, $t0 · six C operators: & | ^ ~ << >> · && (whole values, gives 1/0) ≠ & (per bit) · x&0=0, x&1=x, x|0=x, x|1=1, x^0=x, x^1=~x · masks: test x&m, set x|m, clear x&~m, toggle x^m · build them with 1<<n, (1<<n)-1, ((1<<size)-1)<<low · get_nth_bit = (v>>n)&1 · odd = n&1 (but n%2 reads better and compiles the same) · << ×2ⁿ, >> ÷2ⁿ with integer truncation · never shift signed values — undefined · XOR is its own inverse · an int is a set: add |, remove &~, test & · MIPS: and/or/xor/nor + andi/ori/xori, not = nor rd,rs,$0, srl/srlv zero-fill vs sra/srav sign-propagate · next: floating point.

masks, shifts & bit manipulation — reaching underneath the integer.
COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 5 — Lecture 1

Bitwise examples & the arrival of floating point

Two halves. First we finish bitwise: the six operations recapped in one program, the three questions you will always be asked about a bit (check it, set it, unset it) answered for position 3 and for position n, five C demos that build masks for you, and the MIPS instructions that do all of it. Then the pivot the whole course has been building to — how do you store 0.75? We put a radix point in a binary number, convert fractions by repeated multiplication, watch 0.1 refuse to terminate, and then take the IEEE 754 standard apart: sign, biased exponent, the leading 1 that is never stored, and the special patterns for zero, infinity and NaN. It ends where floating point always ends — with the errors.

Six operations, one program

Bitwise operators, recapped (slides 4–5)

Everything from last lecture in one paragraph, then in one program. A bitwise operator looks at each bit position independently and produces a bit there — unlike && and ||, which look at whole values and answer true or false.

The six, in the lecturer's words (slide 4)

  • ~ NOT — "take a number and flip all the bits. A zero becomes a one and a one becomes a zero."
  • & AND — "anything ANDed with a zero is zero. The only time we get a one is when a one is ANDed with a one."
  • | OR — "if either of them is one, we get a one. It's only when they're both zero that we get a zero."
  • ^ XOR — "both bits have to be different. Same → zero, different → one."
  • >> right shift — "like a division by two."
  • << left shift — "like a multiplication by two."

Bitwise vs logical — the trap worth repeating (slide 4)

Take x = 0x55 and y = 0xAA. Neither is zero, so:

x && y   // both non-zero  → 1  (one bit of truth)
x &  y   // 0101 0101
         //  & 1010 1010
         //  = 0000 0000  → 0

Same symbol doubled, completely different question. && asks "are both of these true?"; & asks that question once per bit position and hands back a whole new number.

Demo: bitwise.c — the whole recap in one run (slide 5)

The demo program reads three numbers — a, b and a shift distance c — then prints every operation in binary, hex and decimal. This is the exact run from the lecture, at 16 bits wide:

$ dcc bitwise.c print_bits.c -o bitwise
$ ./bitwise
Enter a: 23032
Enter b: 12345
Enter c: 3
     a = 0101100111111000 = 0x59f8 = 23032
     b = 0011000000111001 = 0x3039 = 12345
    ~a = 1010011000000111 = 0xa607 = 42503
 a & b = 0001000000111000 = 0x1038 = 4152
 a | b = 0111100111111001 = 0x79f9 = 31225
 a ^ b = 0110100111000001 = 0x69c1 = 27073
a >> c = 0000101100111111 = 0x0b3f = 2879
a << c = 1100111111000000 = 0xcfc0 = 53184

Three things to read off that output. ~a is not -a — it's 42503, the complement inside 16 bits. a >> 3 = 2879 is 23032 / 8 with the remainder thrown away. And a << 3 should be 23032 × 8 = 184256, but the answer is 53184 — the top three bits fell off the end of the 16-bit type and are simply gone.

bitwise.c — live

Run the recap demo on your own numbers

Type a, b and a shift distance c, or click a bit to flip it. Every row is recomputed at 16 bits, exactly like print_bits.c does it — so you can watch bits fall off the end of a << c just like they do in the C program. Note the width: this runs at 16 bits like the lecture demo, so ~a here is a 16-bit complement — the 8-bit uint8_t answers in the §11 exercise will differ in the top byte.

The three questions you will always be asked

Check it, set it, unset it (slides 6–7)

"Especially at the low level where we're dealing closely with hardware, we might want to see if a particular bit is set, or what value it has — that might tell us something about whether the file is readable, or writable, or what kind of function we're doing." Three operations cover it, and each one is a mask plus one operator.

Bit numbering.  Positions run 0 to 7 in a uint8_t, with 0 being the least significant bit — the rightmost one, the 1s place. So "bit 3" is the fourth bit from the right, worth 8. Getting this backwards is the single most common way to lose marks on a bit question.
Worked at the whiteboard — bit 3 of an unknown byte (slide 7)

Start with eight bits you know nothing about. The lecturer wrote them as xs, because the whole point is that the answer must work whatever they are:

      x x x x x x x x        // bit:  7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0
                ↑
              bit 3
1 · check it  →  & with a single 1
  x x x x x x x x
& 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0     // 0x08
  ---------------
  0 0 0 0 x 0 0 0

// everything else is forced to 0;
// what's left tells you what x was
value & 0x08
2 · set it  →  | with a single 1
  x x x x x x x x
| 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0     // 0x08
  ---------------
  x x x x 1 x x x

// OR with 0 leaves a bit alone,
// OR with 1 forces it to 1
value | 0x08
3 · unset it  →  & with a single 0
  x x x x x x x x
& 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 1     // ~0x08
  ---------------
  x x x x 0 x x x

// AND with 1 leaves a bit alone,
// AND with 0 forces it to 0
value & ~0x08

Notice the symmetry that makes this memorable: OR can only turn bits on, AND can only turn bits off, and in both cases the other mask value (0 for OR, 1 for AND) is the "do nothing" value. Pick the operator by what you want to happen, then build the mask so every bit you care about gets the active value and every bit you don't gets the identity.

Now for an arbitrary position n (slide 7, questions 4–6)

"Whatever the position is, that's where we create the mask — and the masks all look the same." The only change is that the single 1 is no longer written by hand, it's shifted into place:

// the one mask that generates all three
uint8_t mask = 1 << n;        // n = 3  →  0000 1000

// 4) check  — non-zero means the bit was set
if (value & (1 << n)) { ... }
//    want a clean 0 or 1 instead?
int bit = (value >> n) & 1;

// 5) set
value |= (1 << n);

// 6) unset
value &= ~(1 << n);

// bonus: toggle — XOR flips exactly the masked bits
value ^= (1 << n);

Three lines, and they are the same three lines forever — in file permission flags, in graphics, in device drivers, in the assignment. & asks, | turns on, &~ turns off, ^ flips.

Drag n to move the target bit. The mask row rebuilds itself as 1 << n (or ~(1 << n) for unset), the result row shows what comes back, and the C echo underneath is the line you would actually write. Click any bit of value to change it.

Five programs that build masks for you

The code demos (slides 8–15)

"It's sort of just all these little building blocks that you can use." Each demo is a handful of lines, and between them they cover every mask you will need: a set of flags, a run of low bits, a run anywhere, and pulling a field back out.

pokemon.c — one integer, sixteen flags (slides 9–11)

Sixteen types, each given a distinct single-bit value, so a Pokémon's whole type is a combination built with | and queried with &:

#define FIRE_TYPE     0x0001
#define FIGHTING_TYPE 0x0002
#define WATER_TYPE    0x0004
#define FLYING_TYPE   0x0008
#define POISON_TYPE   0x0010
#define ELECTRIC_TYPE 0x0020
// ... 10 more, doubling each time ...
#define BUG_TYPE      0x0400
#define STEEL_TYPE    0x4000
#define FAIRY_TYPE    0x8000
0000010000000000 BUG_TYPE
0000000000010000 POISON_TYPE
1000000000000000 FAIRY_TYPE
1000010000010000 our_pokemon type (1)

Poisonous
1001010000000000 our_pokemon type (2)

Scary

Building the type is BUG_TYPE | POISON_TYPE | FAIRY_TYPE — the OR just lights up each bit. Asking a question is if (our_pokemon & POISON_TYPE), which is non-zero exactly when that one bit survives.

"While you probably don't want to use this for Pokémon, you can see it can be useful when you're using codes to describe things, combining codes and working out what your code comprises of."

bitset.c — the same trick as mathematics (slide 15)

Give bit i the meaning "i is in the set" and a 64-bit integer becomes a set of 0–63, where the discrete-maths operations are single instructions:

Enter set a: 1 2 4 8 16 32 -1
Enter set b: 5 4 3 33 -1

a = 0x100010116 = 4295033110
b = 0x200000038 = 8589934648

a = {1,2,4,8,16,32}
b = {3,4,5,33}
a union b        = {1,2,3,4,5,8,16,32,33}
a intersection b = {4}
cardinality(a)   = 6
is_member(42, a) = 0
set operationbitwise
union  a ∪ ba | b
intersection  a ∩ ba & b
difference  a − ba & ~b
add ia |= 1UL << i
remove ia &= ~(1UL << i)
is_member(i)(a >> i) & 1
cardinalitycount the 1 bits

This one is "left for you to look at" on the slide — worth doing, because a bitset is how you get set operations at the speed of a single AND.

The three mask-building programs (slides 12–14)

These three are the ones worth memorising, because they compose. Each builds on the one before it, and the last one is how you would pull the op or rs field out of the MIPS instruction you decoded last lecture.

programthe ideathe line that matters
set_low_bitsbottom n bits all ones(1 << n) - 1
set_bit_rangebits low…high all ones((1 << size) - 1) << low
extract_bit_rangeread the value of that field(v >> low) & ((1 << size) - 1)
set_low_bits.c  (slide 12)
mask = 1;
mask = mask << n;   // 1 000...0
mask = mask - 1;    // 0 111...1

$ ./set_low_bits 3
The bottom 3 bits of 7 are ones:
00000000000000000000000000000111

$ ./set_low_bits 19
The bottom 19 bits of 524287 are ones:
00000000000001111111111111111111

$ ./set_low_bits 29
The bottom 29 bits of 536870911 are ones:
00011111111111111111111111111111
set_bit_range.c  (slide 13)
size = high - low + 1;
mask = (1 << size) - 1;  // n ones, at the bottom
mask = mask << low;      // slide into position

$ ./set_bit_range 0 7
Bits 0 to 7 of 255 are ones:
00000000000000000000000011111111

$ ./set_bit_range 8 15
Bits 8 to 15 of 65280 are ones:
00000000000000001111111100000000

$ ./set_bit_range 8 23
Bits 8 to 23 of 16776960 are ones:
00000000111111111111111100000000

$ ./set_bit_range 1 30
Bits 1 to 30 of 2147483646 are ones:
01111111111111111111111111111110
extract_bit_range.c  (slide 14)
size = high - low + 1;
mask = (1 << size) - 1;
bits = (value >> low) & mask;
     // shift down FIRST, then mask

$ ./extract_bit_range 4 7 42
Value 42 in binary is:
00000000000000000000000000101010
Bits 4 to 7 of 42 are:
0010

$ ./extract_bit_range 10 20 123456789
Value 123456789 in binary is:
00000111010110111100110100010101
Bits 10 to 20 of 123456789 are:
11011110011

Why (1 << n) - 1 works: 1 << n is a single 1 sitting above the n bits you want, and subtracting one from any power of two borrows all the way down, turning every bit below it into a 1. It is the cheapest way to say "n ones" that exists. And in extract, the order matters — shift down first so the field lands at position 0, then mask; masking first would leave the value multiplied by 2low.

mask builder — set_low_bits · set_bit_range · extract_bit_range

Build the mask, then use it

Move low and high and watch the three-step construction: 1 << size, minus one, shifted into place. Switch to extract and the widget also shows the value being shifted down and masked, the way extract_bit_range.c does. All 32 bits, exactly like the demos.

The same ideas, in assembly

MIPS bit manipulation & shift instructions (slides 16–17)

"Just like we did it on a piece of paper" — creating masks in MIPS is the same as in C, only you write the shift yourself. Register–register forms are R-format (named by funct); the i forms are I-format with a 16-bit immediate. Lecture 4.2's decoder pulls both apart if you want to see the fields.

Bit manipulation (slide 16)

assemblymeaningbit pattern
and  rd, rs, rtrd = rs & rt000000ssssstttttddddd00000100100
or   rd, rs, rtrd = rs | rt000000ssssstttttddddd00000100101
xor  rd, rs, rtrd = rs ^ rt000000ssssstttttddddd00000100110
nor  rd, rs, rtrd = ~(rs | rt)000000ssssstttttddddd00000100111
andi rt, rs, Irt = rs & I001100sssssttttt IIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
ori  rt, rs, Irt = rs | I001101sssssttttt IIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
xori rt, rs, Irt = rs ^ I001110sssssttttt IIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
not  rd, rsrd = ~rspseudo-instruction

There is no real not — the assembler turns it into nor rd, rs, $0. Because x | 0 = x, "NOR with zero" is "NOT".

Shifts (slide 17)

assemblymeaningbit pattern
sllv rd, rt, rsrd = rt << rs000000ssssstttttddddd00000000100
srlv rd, rt, rsrd = rt >> rs000000ssssstttttddddd00000000110
srav rd, rt, rsrd = rt >> rs000000ssssstttttddddd00000000111
sll  rd, rt, Ird = rt << I00000000000tttttdddddIIIII000000
srl  rd, rt, Ird = rt >> I00000000000tttttdddddIIIII000010
sra  rd, rt, Ird = rt >> I00000000000tttttdddddIIIII000011
  • srl and srlv shift zeroes into the most-significant bit. This matches shift in C of unsigned values.
  • sra and srav propagate the most-significant bit. This ensures the sign is maintained — so a negative number really is divided by two.
  • The v suffix means the shift amount comes from a register, so it can be decided at run time; without it the amount is fixed in the instruction's shamt field.

"If you had a negative number and you shift to the right, sra would fill it up with ones to maintain the negative — or the logical type, which just shifts the bits like we do in C."

The pattern just keeps going to the right

Fractions in different bases (slides 19–24)

"We've got integers down — hex, octal, we're all good. But what about 0.75?" Half the difficulty of floating point evaporates once you accept that the place-value pattern you already know does not stop at the point. It just keeps halving.

0.75 in three bases (slide 19)

The decimal fraction 0.75 means:

7×10⁻¹ + 5×10⁻² = 0.7 + 0.05 = 0.75
or equivalently  75/10² = 75/100 = 0.75

Similarly 0.11₂ means:

1×2⁻¹ + 1×2⁻² = 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75
or equivalently  3/2² = 3/4 = 0.75

And 0.C₁₆ means:

12×16⁻¹ = 0.75
or equivalently  12/16¹ = 3/4 = 0.75

"This is a monstrous way to write anything — the only time anyone would ever do this is to trip you up in an exam."

It's called a radix point (slide 19)

"We want to call it a decimal point, but because this is a binary number it's actually called the radix point." Decimal point only makes sense in base 10; radix point is the name that works in any base.

Everything to the left of it is the powers of two you already use. Everything to the right continues the same sequence downwards — each step halves:

2³  2²  2¹  2⁰  .  2⁻¹   2⁻²    2⁻³
 8   4   2   1  .  0.5   0.25   0.125

So 1010.1011₂ is 8 + 2 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0625 = 10.6875. No new rule — the same rule, extended.

The conversion algorithm — multiply by the base, harvest the whole part (slide 22)

To convert a decimal fraction into another base:

  • Take the fractional part of the number and multiply it by the base you are converting to.
  • The whole number part of the result becomes the next digit after the radix point.
  • Repeat with the remaining fractional part.
  • Continue until the fractional part becomes zero, or you have enough digits for the accuracy you need.
This process does not always terminate.  Some fractions have repeating representations in some bases. That single sentence on slide 22 is the seed of every floating-point bug in the rest of the lecture.
0.3125 → base 2  (slide 23)
0.3125 × 2 = 0.625
0.625  × 2 = 1.25
0.25   × 2 = 0.5
0.5    × 2 = 1.0   ← fraction is 0, stop

0.3125₁₀ = 0.0101₂

check: 0.25 + 0.0625 = 0.3125 ✓
12.625 → base 2  (slide 24)
whole part:  12 = 1100₂

0.625 × 2 = 1.25
0.25  × 2 = 0.5
0.5   × 2 = 1.0   ← stop

12.625₁₀ = 1100.101₂

check: 8 + 4 + 0.5 + 0.125 = 12.625 ✓
0.1 → base 2  (slide 24)
0.1 × 2 = 0.2
0.2 × 2 = 0.4
0.4 × 2 = 0.8
0.8 × 2 = 1.6
0.6 × 2 = 1.2
0.2 × 2 = 0.4   ← 0.2 again. Loop.

0.1₁₀ = 0.00011 0011 0011…₂

"Will I ever stop?"  No.

The 0.1 case is the one to remember. There is no finite string of halves that adds to one tenth, so no binary computer can store 0.1 exactly — not with 32 bits, not with 64, not with a million. Everything strange that happens later in this lecture traces back to that.

radix point explorer & fraction converter

Convert a decimal fraction, step by step

Type a value and watch the multiply-by-two algorithm run exactly as it was done on the whiteboard, one row per digit. If a fractional part repeats, the row is flagged in red and the repeating block is bracketed — that's a number your computer can never hold exactly. Click bits on the strip to build a value the other way round.
