The simple answer, and what it costs

Fixed point representation (slide 25)

Before the clever solution, the obvious one: multiply everything by a constant and store an integer. It is genuinely used — and understanding why it survives tells you exactly what floating point is buying you.

The trick (slide 25)

Every value is multiplied by a particular constant and stored as an integer:

scale = 1000

56125  represents  56.125
  3141 represents   3.141

// but 3.141592 cannot be represented at all —
// the scale decides your smallest step, forever

Splitting a 32-bit word as 16 bits of integer and 16 bits of fraction (a scale factor of 216) gives:

  • minimum step 2⁻¹⁶ ≈ 0.000015
  • maximum value 2¹⁵ ≈ 32768

Every bit you spend on the fraction is a bit you no longer have for whole numbers. The range and the precision are in direct competition — that is the "major limitation".

Why anyone still uses it

Used on small embedded processors with no floating point hardware — but that is not the only reason, and a student in the lecture supplied the better one:

Determinism. "Fixed point will give you the same number regardless of how floating point is represented on different types of hardware. That's really important, because every Tuesday someone's upgrading their hardware and changing how they're implementing something, and then you can't be sure the mathematical operations you did today give the same answers tomorrow."

So fixed point is chosen when anything that needs operations to be deterministic is on the line — and when losing range and precision is an acceptable price for that certainty.

The design question this forces on you.  "You kind of have to decide what is the smallest delta I can tolerate." Porting a TensorFlow model onto an Arduino and finding you have four bits per weight is exactly this decision. "For some things, certainty is absolutely imperative — if you're doing medical devices, you don't want to be off by some random decimal value and that means somebody has a heart attack and doesn't get the help they need."
Uh oh

IEEE 754, and why you must understand its limits (slides 26–30)

"The industry standard, used by almost all computers." Slide 26 puts a picture of a plane crash next to it, which sets the tone. The standard is excellent; the trouble is entirely in what people assume it does.

Three things it is crucial to understand (slide 26)

  • Why using floating point for finance is unwise. Money is exact; binary fractions of a dollar are not. "Anyone that does the tax, you never put the decimals — it's always done in whole numbers, otherwise things can go kooky."
  • Why sometimes a + 1 == a. Once the gap between representable values exceeds 1, adding 1 lands you back on the number you started from.
  • Why if (x == y) is not a good idea. Two calculations that should agree can each be rounded a different way, so the equality test fails on values that are mathematically identical. Compare with a tolerance instead.

C's three floating point types (slide 27)

typetypicallynotes
float32-bitlower precision, narrower range
double64-bithigher precision, wider range
long double128-bitoften only 80 bits actually used

Literal floating point values are double by default: 3.14159, 1.0/3, 1.0e-9.

Reminder: dividing two ints gives an int. 1 / 2 == 0, not 0.5. "This is a really easy mistake to make — you might be looking to get 0.5 and what you'll get is 0." Fix it by making one operand a double: 1 / 2.0.

Code demo: double_output.c — the same value printed with %lf, %e, %g and explicit precisions like %.9lf, to see what you are actually being shown.

This course does not use the MIPS floating point unit. MIPS has one; we look at floating point purely from C.

The unavoidable consequence (slide 28)

A fixed number of bits means:

  • a finite number of bit patterns,
  • so only a finite subset of the reals can be represented,
  • so almost every real value has no exact representation — and neither does the result of most arithmetic,
  • so every result must be rounded to the closest value that is representable,
  • and that rounding introduces an error into your calculation.

"Often it does not matter. Sometimes it can be disastrous — pacemakers, finance." Approximation is usually fine: "we build bridges basically using Newtonian physics and don't care about relativity most of the time." It is knowing when you are in the other case that matters.

Code demo: double_imprecision.c.

What you get for those 4 and 8 bytes (slide 29)

typebytesminmax
float41.17549e−383.40282e+38
double82.22507e−3081.79769e+308
unsigned int404294967295
unsigned long801.84467e+19

Same number of bytes, and the range explodes from 109 to 1038. That is not magic and it is not free — it is bought by not storing every value in between.

Code demo: floating_types.c, which prints these out of <float.h>.

The idea that buys the range: scientific notation (slide 30)

In decimal you already write huge numbers as a small mantissa times a power of ten — Avogadro's number is 6.0221515 × 10²³. Do the same in binary:

10.6875  =  1010.1011₂            // the plain binary form
         =  1.0101011 × 2³        // radix point moved 3 places left

Store the digits and the exponent separately and the point can sit anywhere: 8 bits of exponent reaches from about 10−38 to 1038, and 11 bits reaches 10−308 to 10308. "This allows a much bigger range of values than fixed point" — the radix point floats, which is where the name comes from.

Sign, exponent, fraction

Taking IEEE 754 apart (slides 31–34)

Three fields, and one hack. float in C is the single precision format; double is the double precision format. The fraction part is also called the significand or the mantissa — three names for the same field.

Sign and fraction (slide 32)

Sign bit — 0 for positive, 1 for negative. That's the whole rule; this is not two's complement.

Fraction — first we normalise, so that there is exactly one digit in front of the radix point:

1.1001 × 2³      // ✓ normalised
1100.1 × 2⁰      // ✗ same value, different pattern
11.001 × 2²      // ✗ same value again

Why bother? "Better to have only one representation representing a value — multiple representations would make arithmetic slower on the CPU."

The weird hack.  In binary, a normalised number's leading digit is always 1 — there is nothing else it could be. So we don't store it. To represent 1.1001 × 2³ the fraction field holds 1001000000…, and the hardware puts the 1 back when it reads it. You get 24 bits of precision from 23 bits of storage, for free. The price: zero has no leading 1, so it needs a special pattern — see §09.

The exponent, and its bias (slide 33)

The exponent must be able to go negative, but the field is a plain unsigned number. The fix is a bias: to represent an exponent of x, store x + B.

// for float, B = 127
1.1001 × 2³   →   store 3 + 127 = 130
                =   10000010₂

Where 127 comes from — with an 8-bit exponent:

B = 2⁸⁻¹ − 1 = 127     // the middle of 0…255

valid patterns   00000001 … 11111110   (1…254)
exponents        −126 … +127

All-zeros and all-ones are reserved for the special values, which is why the usable range stops one short at each end. Putting the bias in the middle means "we have as many fractional numbers as we do numbers above zero" — roughly as much reach below 1 as above it.

For double, the exponent is 11 bits, so B = 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023 and exponents run −1022 … +1023.

Worked example — 150.75 as a float (slide 34)

The full procedure, in the order you should always do it:

150.75    = 10010110.11₂          // 1. plain binary, both sides of the point

          = 1.001011011 × 2⁷      // 2. normalise: one digit before the point.
                                  //    the point moved 7 places, so e = 7

sign      = 0                     // 3. positive
exponent  = 7 + 127 = 134         // 4. add the bias
          = 10000110₂
fraction  = 001011011            // 5. drop the leading 1, pad right to 23 bits
          = 00101101100000000000000

result    = 0 10000110 00101101100000000000000
          = 01000011000101101100000000000000

Read the three colours back off: sign 1 bit, exponent 8 bits, fraction 23 bits. Check yourself with explain_float_representation.c or an online floating point calculator — the widget below is the same idea and does both directions.

IEEE 754 explorer — both directions

Decimal → bits, and bits → decimal

Type a decimal number to encode it, or click any bit to decode. The three fields are colour-coded like the slide: sign, exponent, fraction. The readout shows the raw exponent field, the bias subtracted, the reconstructed 1.fraction, and — when the value can't be stored exactly — the actual number your computer holds.

Three patterns the standard reserves

Zero, infinity and NaN (slides 36–38)

The hidden leading 1 means the format cannot represent zero by normal means, so the standard carves out the two exponent patterns it deliberately left unused — all zeros and all ones — and gives them jobs.

valueexponentfractionproduced by
0 (+ve or −ve)all 0'sall 0's0.0
inf (∞ and −∞)all 1'sall 0's1.0/0
nan (not a number)all 1'snot all 0's0.0/0

Because the sign bit is separate, there is a +0 and a −0, and a +inf and a −inf. They compare equal where you'd want them to and behave sensibly everywhere else.

infinity.c — it propagates sensibly (slide 37)

double x = 1.0/0.0;

printf("%lf\n", x);           // prints inf
printf("%lf\n", -x);          // prints -inf
printf("%lf\n", x - 1);       // prints inf
printf("%lf\n", 2 * atan(x)); // prints 3.141593
printf("%d\n",  42 < x);      // prints 1 (true)
printf("%d\n",  x == INFINITY);// prints 1 (true)

Every one of those is the mathematically right answer. Infinity minus one is still infinity; 2 × arctan(∞) really is π; every finite number really is less than infinity. "You can handle infinity properly using floating point numbers — there's no special thing you need to do, you can just treat it in your equations as required."

nan.c — errors that don't hide (slide 38)

double x = 0.0/0.0;

printf("%lf\n", x);        // prints nan
printf("%lf\n", x - 1);    // prints nan
printf("%d\n",  x == x);   // prints 0 (FALSE)
printf("%d\n",  isnan(x)); // prints 1 (true)

NaN is the representation for an invalid result, and its defining property is that it infects everything it touches — any arithmetic involving a NaN produces a NaN, so a bad value cannot quietly turn back into a plausible-looking number halfway through your computation.

x == x is false.  This is the one that catches people. NaN is not equal to anything, including itself — "it's a very philosophical thing." Never test for NaN with ==; use isnan(x) from <math.h>. It is also, incidentally, a one-line NaN detector: if (x != x).
Try them in the explorer above.  The 0, inf, −inf and nan presets in §08 show these patterns directly — zero is genuinely just 32 zero bits, and infinity is an exponent of all ones with an empty fraction. Toggle one fraction bit of infinity and watch it become a NaN.
Where the bugs actually come from

Distribution of floating point numbers (slides 39–43)

Integers are boring in the best way: each one is exactly 1 from its neighbours, and every integer in range is exact. Floating point is not like that at all, and almost every surprising bug is a consequence of the difference.

Integers (slide 39)

A subset (a range) of the mathematical integers:

  • can represent all integer values in that subset,
  • each integer is 1 away from the next one and the previous one,
  • all integers are represented accurately.

"Each step is the same. It's happy days."

Floating point (slide 40)

A subset of the mathematical reals, and not evenly distributed:

  • numbers closer to 0 have higher precision, which is good,
  • representations get further apart as values get bigger,
  • this works well for most calculations but can cause weird bugs.

The cause is structural: the exponent picks an interval, and the fraction divides that interval into equal steps. Bigger interval, bigger steps.

The counting argument (slide 41)

A 64-bit double uses 52 bits for the fraction. Fix the exponent and the fraction can take 252 values — so between 2n and 2n+1 there are 252 doubles, evenly spaced. That is true for every n:

between 2⁻⁴³ and 2⁻⁴²   →  2⁵² doubles
between 0.5  and 1      →  2⁵² doubles
between 1    and 2      →  2⁵² doubles
between 2    and 4      →  2⁵² doubles
between 4    and 8      →  2⁵² doubles
between 2⁴²  and 2⁴³    →  2⁵² doubles

The interval [2⁴², 2⁴³) is about 4.4 trillion units wide and the interval [1, 2) is one unit wide — and they get the same number of representable values. That single fact is the whole story of floating-point precision loss.

What that means in practice (slide 42)
doubles near…are about this far apartso…
0.0010.0000000000000000002absurd precision
10000.0000000000002still excellent
1000000000000000≈ 0.25you have lost the cents
above 2⁵³more than 1a + 1 == a

The slide rounds these; the spacing explorer above computes them exactly — near 10¹⁵ the true gap is 0.125, and near 1000 it is 1.14×10⁻¹³. Same story either way: by 10¹⁵ a double can no longer tell you the cents. That last row is where double_disaster.c lives: the smallest integer that cannot be represented exactly as a double is 2⁵³ + 1 = 9007199254740993. Ask for it and you get 9007199254740992 back. A loop that keeps adding 1 climbs happily up to 2⁵³ and then stops moving — "it just keeps on printing out the same number, because this is the biggest one that it can do."

spacing explorer — how far is the next double?

The gap between neighbouring values, at any magnitude

Pick a magnitude and the widget reports the exponent interval it falls in, the gap to the next representable value (the ULP — unit in the last place), and whether x + 1 == x at that scale. The ladder underneath is the same calculation across the whole range, so you can see precision draining away as the numbers grow.

value:
The demo everybody remembers — ten tenths is not one (slide 28 demo)

Remember from §05 that 0.1 is a repeating binary fraction, so it cannot be stored exactly. Now subtract it from 1 ten times and ask whether you get zero:

double a = 0.1;
double b = 1 - a - a - a - a - a - a - a - a - a - a;

if (b == 0) printf("b is zero\n");
else        printf("b is NOT zero: %.20lf\n", b);
b is NOT zero
a = 0.10000000000000000555111512312578
b = 0.00000000000000013877787807814457

"Those bits at the end come directly from this situation — we can't represent 0.1 with a fixed number of bits, it's recursive. So depending on how we represent it we're going to have these little garbage bits at the end, and those garbage bits become real as we add them all together." The stored value of 0.1 is very slightly too big; ten of those errors accumulate into a residue of about 1.4×10−16 — small, but emphatically not zero. This is precisely why if (x == y) is a bad idea.

imprecision lab — run the disasters

Four experiments, real IEEE 754 doubles

These run on your machine's actual 64-bit doubles — the same hardware arithmetic C uses, so the output is what dcc would print. Each one demonstrates a different failure mode: accumulated representation error, the equality trap, the spacing wall, and catastrophic cancellation.

double_catastrophe.c — when a tiny error becomes the whole answer (slide 43)

This one is the advanced example, and it is the one worth being frightened by. Compute (1 − cos x) / x² for a small x. Mathematically the answer tends to 0.5. In doubles:

x = 1.1e-08
(1 - cos(x)) / (x*x)          = 0.917  ← should be 0.5
2 * pow(sin(x/2)/x, 2)        = 0.500  ← the same maths, rearranged

For tiny x, cos x is so close to 1 that 1 − cos x throws away almost every significant digit — what's left is pure rounding noise, and dividing that noise by an equally tiny x² amplifies it back up to full size. The error is almost double the size of the real answer. Rewriting the same expression with sin avoids the subtraction entirely and gives 0.5 to fifteen digits, which is what the lecturer meant by "using the sin might actually be better". Nothing about the hardware changed — only the order of operations.

Why this matters beyond the exam.  "If this is some calculation you're doing to determine your entry angle into the atmosphere, any small change and you kind of burn up. Approximations are happening here, and errors in every single bit — especially as we get to smaller and smaller fractions — and those can accumulate and give you the wrong results." Pacemakers, brain implants, rockets, finance. The rounding is not a bug in the standard; failing to account for it is a bug in your program.
Do these before you look

Exercises (slides 6, 7, 24, 35)

Four sets, straight off the slides. The bitwise ones are two-line calculations; the floating point ones are the five-step procedure from §08, run forwards and then backwards.

Recap Exercise 1 — seven expressions (slide 6)

Given these declarations, what is the value of each expression?

// an unsigned 8-bit value
uint8_t x = 0x55;
uint8_t y = 0xAA;

uint8_t a = x & y;        uint8_t e = x >> 1;
uint8_t b = x ^ y;        uint8_t f = y >> 2;
uint8_t c = x | y;        uint8_t g = y << 2;
uint8_t d = ~x;
Show the answers

The two values are perfect opposites — 0x55 is 0101 0101 and 0xAA is 1010 1010. Every position where one has a 1, the other has a 0. So AND is empty, OR and XOR are full, and ~x is literally y.

expressionbinaryhexdecimal
a = x & y0000 00000x000
b = x ^ y1111 11110xFF255
c = x | y1111 11110xFF255
d = ~x1010 10100xAA170  (= y)
e = x >> 10010 10100x2A42
f = y >> 20010 10100x2A42
g = y << 21010 10000xA8168

Watch g: 1010 1010 << 2 would be 10 1010 1000, but the type is only 8 bits wide, so the two bits that slid off the top are gone — leaving 1010 1000 = 168, not 680. And e and f landing on the same answer is not a coincidence: shifting 0101 0101 right once and 1010 1010 right twice produce the same surviving pattern.

Recap Exercise 2 — the six bit operations (slide 7)

If bit positions are 0 to 7, with 0 being the least significant bit, how can we:

  1. Check the bit at position 3 of a uint8_t?
  2. Set the bit at position 3?
  3. Unset the bit at position 3?
  4. Check the bit at position n?
  5. Set the bit at position n?
  6. Unset the bit at position n?
Show the answers 
// position 3 — the mask is 0000 1000 = 0x08
1)  value &  0x08          // non-zero ⇔ the bit was set
2)  value |= 0x08;
3)  value &= ~0x08;        // ~0x08 = 1111 0111

// position n — build the same mask with a shift
4)  value &  (1 << n)      // or, for a clean 0/1:  (value >> n) & 1
5)  value |= (1 << n);
6)  value &= ~(1 << n);

Two habits worth forming. First, value & (1<<n) returns 8, not 1, when bit 3 is set — fine for an if, wrong if you want to store the bit, so use (value >> n) & 1 there. Second, in a wider type write 1U << n (or 1UL): shifting a signed 1 into the top bit is undefined behaviour.

Exercise 3 — binary fractional conversion (slide 24)

Convert the following decimal values into binary: 12.625 and 0.1.

Show the answers 
12.625
whole:  12 = 1100₂
frac:   0.625 × 2 = 1.25
        0.25  × 2 = 0.5
        0.5   × 2 = 1.0    ← fractional part is 0, done

12.625₁₀ = 1100.101₂        // 8+4 + 0.5+0.125 ✓

0.1
0.1 × 2 = 0.2
0.2 × 2 = 0.4
0.4 × 2 = 0.8
0.8 × 2 = 1.6
0.6 × 2 = 1.2
0.2 × 2 = 0.4     ← 0.2 has come back; the cycle repeats

0.1₁₀ = 0.0 0011 0011 0011 …₂   // never terminates

The test for "will this terminate?" is simple: a decimal fraction has a finite binary expansion only when, in lowest terms, its denominator is a power of two. 0.625 = 5/8 ✓. 0.1 = 1/10 ✗ — the factor of 5 can never be built from halves.

Exercise 4 — floating point conversions (slide 35)

Question 1. Convert the decimal number 1 to IEEE 754 single precision.
Question 2. Convert these single-precision patterns to decimal:

1 10000000 11000000000000000000000

0 01111110 10000000000000000000000
Show the answers 
Q1 — encode 1
1 = 1.0₂ = 1.0 × 2⁰           // already normalised, e = 0
sign     = 0                  // positive
exponent = 0 + 127 = 127 = 01111111₂
fraction = 000…0              // nothing after the hidden 1

1.0f = 0 01111111 00000000000000000000000
     = 0x3F800000
Q2a — decode 1 10000000 11000000000000000000000
sign     = 1        → negative
exponent = 10000000₂ = 128,  128 − 127 = 1
fraction = 11000…   → put the hidden 1 back: 1.11₂

1.11₂ = 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 1.75
1.75 × 2¹ = 3.5
answer = −3.5
Q2b — decode 0 01111110 10000000000000000000000
sign     = 0        → positive
exponent = 01111110₂ = 126,  126 − 127 = −1
fraction = 1000…    → put the hidden 1 back: 1.1₂

1.1₂ = 1.5
1.5 × 2⁻¹ = 0.75
answer = 0.75

// or, straight from the powers:
//   2⁻¹ + 2⁻² = 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75

"The key thing is always to remember that one out the front of the radix point — that's a really common thing to forget to do." Also useful for spot-checking: 01111111 is exactly 127, so an exponent field of 01111111 means ×1, anything larger means ×2 or more, anything smaller means a fraction. Check all three against the explorer in §08.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slide 44)

The bitwise half closes with three moves you now own outright: value & (1<<n) asks about a bit, value |= (1<<n) turns it on, value &= ~(1<<n) turns it off — and every mask you will ever need is built from (1 << n) - 1, optionally slid into place with another shift. pokemon.c and bitset.c show what that buys: an integer used as a set, with union, intersection and membership costing one instruction each. In MIPS it's and/or/xor/nor and their i forms, with srl zero-filling and sra sign-propagating. Then the pivot. Put a radix point in a binary number and the place values keep halving to the right, so 0.11₂ is 0.75; convert a decimal fraction by repeatedly multiplying by two and harvesting the whole part — a process that does not always terminate, which is why 0.1 is stored as a very slightly wrong number forever. Fixed point dodges that by fixing the scale, buying determinism at the cost of range. IEEE 754 instead stores sign, a biased exponent (add 127 for a float, 1023 for a double) and a normalised fraction whose leading 1. is never written down — giving 10±38 from four bytes, with all-zeros and all-ones exponents reserved for zero, ±infinity and NaN. The price is spacing: 252 doubles fit between any 2n and 2n+1, so precision drains away as values grow until, past 253, a + 1 == a. Rounding error is not a defect to be avoided; it is a property to be budgeted for. Next lecture: an introduction to operating systems and file systems.

TL;DR · bit n: check v & (1<<n), set v |= (1<<n), unset v &= ~(1<<n), toggle v ^= (1<<n) · | only turns bits on, & only turns them off · n low ones = (1<<n)-1 · a range = ((1<<size)-1)<<low · extract = (v>>low) & ((1<<size)-1) · an int is a set: | add, &~ remove, & test · MIPS srl zero-fills, sra sign-propagates, v suffix = amount from a register · right of the radix point the places are 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 … · convert a fraction by ×2 and harvesting the whole part · 0.1₂ repeats forever — no computer stores 0.1 exactly · fixed point = one scale, deterministic, tiny range · IEEE 754 float = 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 fraction; double = 1 + 11 + 52 · exponent is biased: store e + 127 (float) or e + 1023 (double) · the leading 1. is implied and never stored · 150.75 = 0 10000110 00101101100000000000000 · zero = all zeros; inf = exp all 1s + frac 0; NaN = exp all 1s + frac ≠ 0 · NaN != NaN, so use isnan() · 2⁵² doubles between every 2ⁿ and 2ⁿ⁺¹ · above 2⁵³, a+1 == a · never write if (x == y) on floats · next: operating systems & file systems.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 5 — Lecture 2

Floating point revisited, then the machine you have been standing on: operating systems & files

The last twenty minutes of floating point, done the slow way — the lecturer at the whiteboard converting 150.75 and −42.5 by hand, dividing and multiplying by two, counting the shift, adding the bias — plus the special patterns, the uneven number line, and the two demos where the arithmetic quietly lies to you. Then the course turns a corner. What is an operating system actually for? The answer is a stack of abstractions: your printf calls write, write traps into the kernel through a numbered system call, and the kernel — the only code allowed to touch the hardware — does the work and hands control back. We take that ladder apart rung by rung, then meet the objects it moves: Unix files (just bytes), file descriptors (just small integers), stdout and stderr, errno, and the four calls you will use for the rest of the course — open, read, write, close.

The whiteboard, not the calculator

IEEE 754, converted by hand (slides 5–7)

Nothing new in the standard itself — last lecture introduced it. What this lecture added was the procedure, run slowly on the whiteboard, twice, including the part where the lecturer converted a binary answer and forgot to turn it back into decimal. That mistake is the useful bit: the algorithm is mechanical, so the errors are always bookkeeping errors.

IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. "They have these big groups of people, they get together and work out what a standard should be" — and you will meet their standards constantly through a computing degree. The point of 754 is that it is the same on every platform: the same bit pattern means the same number on your laptop, on a Mac, on the CSE servers.
150.75, the long way (slide 6)

Five steps, and the first two are just base conversion — the integer part by repeated division, the fraction part by repeated multiplication.

Step 1 — 150 by repeated ÷2, read remainders upwards
150 / 2 = 75  r 0   ← least significant
 75 / 2 = 37  r 1
 37 / 2 = 18  r 1
 18 / 2 =  9  r 0
  9 / 2 =  4  r 1
  4 / 2 =  2  r 0
  2 / 2 =  1  r 0
  1 / 2 =  0  r 1   ← most significant

150 = 10010110
Step 2 — 0.75 by repeated ×2, read whole parts downwards
0.75 × 2 = 1.5    keep 1, carry 0.5
0.5  × 2 = 1.0    keep 1, carry 0.0
                    ← nothing left, stop

0.75 = 0.11

150.75 = 10010110.11
3. NormaliseSlide the radix point left until exactly one 1 sits in front of it. 10010110.11 → 1.001011011, and the point moved 7 places, so the value is 1.001011011 × 27. "The power of seven tells you how many bits you have to jump that radix point."
4. Sign150.75 is positive, so the sign bit is 0.
5. Bias the exponentStore e + 127, not e. Here 7 + 127 = 134 = 10000110. Keep in mind 10000000 = 27 = 128, so 134 is just "128 + 6".
6. FractionEverything after the leading 1. — that 1 is assumed and never stored. So 001011011, then zero-padded out to 23 bits.
150.75 = 0 10000110 00101101100000000000000
       = 01000011000101101100000000000000

       // red = sign, green = exponent, blue = fraction

The lecturer's summary of the whole thing: "it's very kind of laborious — but just to kind of reinforce it for you. Obviously your calculator can do a great job at it as well." That is exactly the right attitude: know the procedure, then check it with explain_float_representation.c or the online Floating Point Calculator.

ieee754_by_hand — step-by-step encoder & decoder

Type a decimal and watch every step the lecturer wrote on the board: the division ladder, the multiplication ladder, the normalisation shift, the bias sum and the assembled bits. Or flip to decode and paste 32 bits back the other way. Repeating fractions are flagged in red, and the panel always reports the exact value actually stored — which is often not the number you typed.

value:

Recap exercise — the two the lecturer did live (slide 7)

Keep in mind 10000000 = 27 = 128. Try both before opening the answers; they are also loaded as presets in Lab 1 above.

  1. Convert −42.5 to an IEEE 754 float.
  2. Convert 00111110100000000000000000000000 back to decimal.
Show the working

1. −42.5 → bits. Divide 42 down — 42, 21, 10, 5, 2, 1 giving remainders 0,1,0,1,0,1 read upwards, so 42 = 101010. The fraction is easier by inspection: 0.5 is exactly 2−1, so 0.1. Together 101010.1.

42.5   = 101010.1
       = 1.010101 × 25       // radix point moved 5 places

sign     = 1                 // negative
exponent = 5 + 127 = 132 = 10000100
fraction = 01010100000000000000000

-42.5  = 11000010001010100000000000000000  // = 0xC22A0000

2. Bits → decimal. Split the pattern into 0 | 01111101 | 000…0.

sign     = 0                → positive
exponent = 01111101 = 125   → 125 - 127 = -2
fraction = all zeros        → significand = 1.0

value = 1.0 × 2-2 = 0.012 = 0.25
The rookie mistake, live on stream. The lecturer got to 0.01, typed it into the calculator, and got a wrong-looking answer — because 0.01 was still binary. "Oh right — that's still a binary number. So then we've got to change it into a decimal number. Rookie mistake." 0.012 = 2−2 = 0.25. Finish the conversion.
Patterns the standard reserves

Zero, infinity and NaN (slides 8–10)

Three exponent patterns are not ordinary numbers. They exist so that a calculation which goes wrong keeps going and tells you about it at the end, instead of crashing in the middle.

valueexponentfractionexample that produces it
0  (+ve or −ve)all 0'sall 0's—
inf  (∞ and −∞)all 1'sall 0's1.0 / 0
nanall 1'snot all 0's0.0 / 0

Because the sign bit is separate from everything else, −0 exists and is a distinct bit pattern from +0. Flip the leading bit of all-zeros in Lab 1 and you will see it. "There might be mathematical cases where that's a thing" — and there are: it records which side a value underflowed from.

infinity.c — infinity propagates sensibly (slide 9)

double x = 1.0/0.0;
printf("%lf\n", x);          // inf
printf("%lf\n", -x);         // -inf
printf("%lf\n", x - 1);      // inf
printf("%lf\n", 2*atan(x)); // 3.141593
printf("%d\n", 42 < x);      // 1 (true)
printf("%d\n", x == INFINITY); // 1 (true)

Every one of those behaves the way the mathematics says it should. atan(∞) is π/2, so doubling it prints π correctly. 42 really is less than infinity. "Infinity in your code will work properly."

nan.c — and so does not a number (slide 10)

double x = 0.0/0.0;
printf("%lf\n", x);        // nan
printf("%lf\n", x - 1);    // nan
printf("%d\n", x == x);    // 0 (FALSE)
printf("%d\n", isnan(x)); // 1 (true)

Once a NaN enters a calculation it contaminates everything downstream, which is the point — the error survives to where you can see it. "Quite often with calculations you want to at least indicate that the operation failed somehow."

The one that catches everyone. x == x is false when x is NaN — it is the only value in C for which that happens. So you cannot test for NaN with ==. Use isnan(x) from <math.h>. (Some people exploit the quirk deliberately: x != x is a NaN test.)
Where the bugs actually live

The uneven number line (slides 11–15)

Integers march. Floats cluster. That one difference explains almost every floating point surprise you will ever hit, and the lecturer framed it as an engineering question rather than a curiosity: "working out whether this is acceptable for your task is really important."

Integers (slide 11)

  • A subset (a range) of the mathematical integers.
  • Every integer inside that subset can be represented.
  • Each one is exactly 1 away from the next and the previous.
  • All of them are exact. a + 1 != a, always.

Floating point (slide 12)

  • A subset of the mathematical reals — but a strange one.
  • Numbers close to 0 have higher precision. "Really tiny steps around zero" — which is good.
  • Representations get further apart as values get bigger.
  • Works well for most calculations, but can cause weird bugs.
The counting argument (slide 13)

A 64-bit double spends 52 bits on the fraction. Fix the exponent and those 52 bits enumerate 252 evenly spaced values. Bump the exponent by one and you get another 252 values — spread over an interval twice as wide.

between 2-43 and 2-42 … 252 doubles
between 0.5   and 1     … 252 doubles
between 1     and 2     … 252 doubles
between 2     and 4     … 252 doubles
between 4     and 8     … 252 doubles
between 242  and 243  … 252 doubles

Same count, ever-wider interval — so the step size doubles every time the exponent does. "Lots of tiny tiny little steps, but as we move up... the step size is changing exponentially." That is why precision is measured relatively (significant figures), never absolutely.

doubles near…slide 14 saysexact gap
0.001≈ 0.00000000000000000022.168×10−19
1000≈ 0.00000000000021.137×10−13
1015≈ 0.250.125
above 253more than 12, then 4, then 8…

Slide 14 rounds; Lab 2 below computes the gap exactly. The 1015 row is the one to remember — a double counting cents can no longer tell 0.125 apart at a quadrillion, which is why money is not stored in floating point. That last row is where double_disaster.c lives.

double_disaster & double_catastrophe — precision lab

Lab 2 · How wrong is it, exactly?

Pick a value and see the true gap to its neighbour, whether it survives a round trip, and what x + 1 > x actually does there. The two code demos from slide 15 run underneath — both with real IEEE 754 arithmetic, not a description of it.

value:
Why the lecturer keeps hammering this. "That is an issue if you're doing biomedical sciences, or your rocket sciences — being aware that your numbers are going to be biased in a particular way using floating point, and working out whether this is acceptable for your task, is really important." The rounding is not a defect in the standard. Failing to budget for it is a defect in your program.
Switching brain into a different gear

What an operating system is actually for (slides 16–21)

This is the hinge of the course. Everything so far has been downwards — C to assembly to bits. From here we go sideways: what surrounds your program while it runs. The lecture opened the topic with two questions to the room, and got the silence every 9am lecture gets.

Question 1: what is your favourite operating system? "It's really just three to choose from… nobody's talking this morning. Fair enough." The lecturer's own answer, as a practising engineer who has had to use all of them: least favourite is Windows ("it takes forever to boot up and randomly shuts things down to update things"), daily driver is macOS ("they always work, and they work for a long time"), but "for engineering stuff you can't really go past Linux." The real point is the one underneath: be flexible. "As a computer scientist or engineer you really have to be a bit flexible. It's good to understand all of them." Also worth noting how much has changed — portability across operating systems used to be nearly impossible, and "operating systems are not something people go to war for like they did back in the day."
Question 2: a world without operating systems (slides 18–19)

The fastest way to see what an OS does is to delete it and list what breaks.

  • Boot your computer manually. No OS means no automatic boot into a familiar environment. You start from nothing, every time.
  • Write your own file system. No file names, no directories — your hard drive is raw data and you must remember where you put things.
  • Run programs… if you can. Multi-tasking? "Good luck."
  • Security? Your dodgy game can read the password you typed into online banking — if you could connect to the internet at all, because…
  • …no OS means no drivers. Mouse, printer, USB port, network: every program must talk to each device directly.
  • And you would do all of it again for every machine. Different hardware configuration, different code. "You would not be too keen to use a different device. Or to get an upgrade."

This is not hypothetical for everyone — it is still daily life in deep embedded work. "As an embedded engineer I've had to write a lot of dodgy code to get things working because I haven't had an operating system, and it takes a long time… and sometimes it's for nothing, because then a new version of something comes out and you've spent a lot of time and it's not portable."

What you get (slide 21)

  • Abstraction — use the machine without knowing voltages or device specifics. "I couldn't tell you what the voltages are on the CPU. I don't know any device specifics in this computer."
  • Portability — write here, push to GitHub, run there. "It seems like that's just how it should be, but it's not magic."
  • Resource management — files, memory, devices and many processes at once, coordinated safely.
  • Reliability — the complex, error-prone low-level work happens once, in the OS, instead of in every program.

The result, made concrete

Apple shipped Intel processors, then ARM, then their own silicon — and to the user the machine barely changed. "The Mac experience for me has remained pretty much the same, and that's because of all the cool stuff they do at the operating system layer… it makes all of that architectural stuff in the hardware invisible to me."

That is the deliverable: users and programs see the same interface even when the underlying hardware is different. You get to concentrate on writing good programs instead of on the nitty-gritty of the hardware.

Two modes, one doorway

Privileged mode and the system call (slides 22–25)

An operating system cannot enforce anything unless the hardware helps it. What the hardware provides is two modes of execution — and one controlled doorway between them.

Privileged mode (slide 22)

  • Code can access all hardware, all memory, and every CPU instruction.
  • The OS kernel runs here — and only the kernel.
  • The kernel is the core of the operating system: it manages the hardware and the system resources. "This is the bit where hardware meets software."

Non-privileged mode (slide 22)

  • Code cannot touch hardware directly.
  • Code can only access the memory it was allocated — which is what stops your dodgy game reading the banking tab.
  • All user code runs here, including everything you have written this term.
You have done this already. Every syscall instruction you wrote in MIPS was exactly this pattern — a number in $v0 saying what, arguments in $a0 saying with what, and a trap into the tiny operating system mipsy provides. "We had to do the raw syscall in order to send data to standard output or read data in from standard input… the OS will check, are these proper codes? I'm sure you've written the wrong arguments in some of those system calls — you'll get an error thrown back to you, because the operating system has checked and said no, this isn't right."
mipsy's tiny operating system (slide 25)

mipsy gives you two things: a virtual machine that executes MIPS instructions, and a miniature OS behind the syscall instruction.

  • A small number of very specific system calls — print an integer, read an integer, print a string, exit.
  • Designed for students writing small programs with no library functions, so the calls are high-level and convenient rather than general.
  • Real hardware works the same way at the instruction level: MIPS programs on real hardware and a real OS also use syscall. On Linux, syscall passes execution to operating system code, which carries out the request specified in the registers.

The difference is generality. mipsy call 1 is "print an integer". Linux call 1 is "write n bytes from this address to this file descriptor" — and printing an integer is something you build on top of it. "It's sort of, you know, kind of turtles all the way down."

400+ of them, and how to look them up

System call numbers, and the Linux manual (slides 24, 26–27, 32)

Different operating systems have completely different system calls — Linux system calls are very different from Windows system calls — and even different Linux kernel versions differ. Linux provides over 400. Each one has a number, and the numbers live in a header file you can read.

$ cat /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/asm/unistd_64.h
...
#define __NR_read  0
#define __NR_write 1
#define __NR_open  2
#define __NR_close 3
...
#define __NR_set_mempolicy_home_node 450

The lecturer scrolled this list live and stopped at the end: "and it goes to… yeah, 462 and counting." Which kernel version you are on genuinely matters — "when you do things like embedded systems development, sometimes you have to change the whole operating system in order to add features or to get things working."

The six that matter for this course (slide 32)
idnamewhat it does
0readread some bytes from a file descriptor
1writewrite some bytes to a file descriptor
2openopen a file system object, returning a file descriptor
3closeclose a file descriptor
4statget file system metadata for a pathname
8lseekmove a file descriptor to a specified offset within a file

Other examples of things a system call might provide: create a process (run a program) or terminate one, request more memory, send information over the network. "Nobody knows what all of those are — but for this course at least a bit of vague awareness around it would be pretty useful." Memorising 0, 1, 2, 3 is genuinely worth it.

The manual is available in the exam. "Get used to using it — now." man is split into numbered sections, and the section number disambiguates names that appear in more than one: man 2 write is the system call, man 1 write is the shell command that messages another user. The sections that matter here:
1Executable programs and shell commands — ls, cp
2System calls — the whole of the rest of this lecture
3Library functions, types and constants — strcpy, scanf, ssize_t
7Miscellaneous and headers — limits.h
And man man describes the rest. "Sometimes a little bit cryptic, I have to say — it takes you a while to go 'what? what?'. But we're not supposed to remember everything, so it's a really useful library of information."
man — the pages you will need this term

Type a real man command. The pages here are trimmed to the parts that matter for COMP1521, laid out the way the real ones are — SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, RETURN VALUE, ERRORS — so that the layout stops being unfamiliar before you meet it under exam conditions. Try man 2 write, then man 2 open, then man errno.

Libraries on libraries on libraries

Three ways to make a system call (slides 29–31, 33–36)

The same job — put twelve bytes on standard output — written at three different heights. Each layer calls the one below it. "It's really important that you understand that there's libraries on libraries on libraries on libraries, and that all helps make your hardware… you don't need to know what's going on in that hardware."

1 · syscall() — the raw floor (slide 29)

  • Makes a system call without writing assembler.
  • Not usually used by programmers. Use it to experiment and learn.
  • Syscall numbers vary between operating systems, so the code is not portable.
  • Cryptic to use and to read — the first argument is a bare number.
  • Genuinely handy in one case: a brand-new syscall that has no wrapper yet.

2 · libc wrappers — write(), read() (slide 30)

  • Meaningful names instead of numbers. "That makes more sense."
  • Helps with type checking — the compiler can tell you the arguments are wrong.
  • More portable than syscall, but still not portable: works across POSIX systems like Linux and macOS, not on Windows.
  • Still low level — you are still counting bytes yourself.

3 · stdio.h — where you already live (slide 31)

  • Useful most of the time — and it calls the syscall wrapper for you.
  • Portable, because it is part of the standard C library and exists on every platform that can do I/O.
  • Does other cool stuff to make things easier: formatting, and buffering for efficiency.
  • You have been using these to indirectly do your system calls the whole time. Every #include <stdio.h> you have ever typed was an opt-in to this layer.
The same twelve bytes, three ways (slides 33–35)
hello_syscalls.c
char bytes[13] = "Hello, Zac!\n";

// arg 1 = syscall number
//   (1 is write)
// arg 2 = fd, 1 == stdout
// arg 3 = address of bytes
// arg 4 = how many bytes
syscall(1, 1, bytes, 12);
hello_libc.c
#include <unistd.h>

char bytes[13] = "Hello, Zac!\n";

// same 3 arguments,
// but the name says
// what it does
write(1, bytes, 12);
hello_stdio.c
#include <stdio.h>

char bytes[] = "Hello, Zac!\n";

// no fd, no byte count,
// no numbers at all
printf("%s", bytes);

Watch the byte count disappear as you move right. In the first two you must know that "Hello, Zac!\n" is 12 bytes — and the array is declared as 13 because of the terminating '\0', which you deliberately do not write out. "It's a real pain in the neck to count how many bytes there are in whatever you're wanting to print out." Miscount by one and you lose the newline; the lecturer demonstrated exactly that, live. printf counts for you.

strace ./hello — the abstraction ladder

Lab 4 · Follow one call all the way down

Pick an entry point and step it. Each rung is a real layer of software on your machine; the ones above your entry point grey out, because you skipped them. The right-hand panel is the strace view — what the kernel sees, which is identical for all three.

idle

what happens at this rung
$ strace ./hello
What strace really showed. The lecturer ran it on a program whose entire body was one printf, and scrolled. Dozens of calls: mapping libraries into memory, opening and closing files, reading configuration — all before the single write that produces the output. "Just running that really simple printf statement, a lot of stuff is going on underneath. You can see how crazy it would be if you had to know what all this is." The reason to know about it anyway: writing good code, especially around security, and portability — "the code bit is sometimes the easiest part."
Reading a byte, the same three ways (slide 36 — read_char.c)

Reading inverts everything: file descriptor 0 instead of 1, syscall number 0 instead of 1, and you supply a buffer for the byte to land in rather than a buffer to send.

syscall
char c;
// 0 = read
// 0 = stdin
syscall(0, 0, &c, 1);
libc wrapper
char c;

read(0, &c, 1);
stdio.h
int c;

c = getchar();

"We're going to store what's written in standard input in this little block of memory — we're going to point to this little block of memory — and we're only going to take in one byte." That &c is the whole reason read needs a pointer: the kernel writes into your memory, so it must be told where.

A file is less than you think

Unix files (slides 37–39)

On a Unix-like system a file is a sequence of zero or more bytes. That is the entire definition. There is no structure, no type and no meaning attached to those bytes by the file system.

What the metadata does not say (slide 37)

The file's metadata does not record that it is ASCII, or MP4, or JPG. File extensions are just hints — a convention for humans and for the programs that open them, not a fact the kernel enforces. Rename photo.jpg to photo.txt and nothing about the file changes; only your expectations do.

"It's just zeros and ones. File extensions are really just a nice thing that have been added to help you determine what the file is."

Files live somewhere else (slide 39)

Files typically live on a mechanical or solid-state drive. To interact with their data they must be read into RAM — you cannot operate on them where they are stored. Getting them across that boundary is precisely what system calls are for: one to open, some to read or write bytes, one to close when you finish.

And the file system is the mapping from the name you typed to where the bytes actually sit on the drive.

Seven file types, one character (slide 38)

Run ls -l and the very first character of each line tells you what kind of thing it is.

symbolfile typewhere you meet it
-Regular fileeverything in your home directory
dDirectory/boot, /home, …
lLink/bin → usr/bin on most modern distributions
cDevice file (character)/dev/tty, /dev/null — a device you read a byte at a time
sSocketnetwork and inter-process endpoints
pFIFO / named pipeone program's output plumbed into another's input
bBlock device/dev/sda — a disk you read a block at a time

The lecturer went looking for live examples and reported honestly: "I tried to find some of these other things, but it was actually pretty hard." Directories and links are everywhere near the top of the hierarchy; sockets, pipes and device files are specific to peripherals and networking. All of them are opened, read and written with the same four system calls — that uniformity is the famous "everything is a file" design.

ls -l / chmod — permission bit explorer

Lab 5 · Those little rwx codes are a bit mask

Click any permission bit, or type an octal mode. This is Week 4's bitwise material wearing a different hat: each octal digit is three bits, one group of three per audience. "Six is 1 1 0 — that means we can read and write this file but we can't execute it."

octal mode:
Where you have already seen this. When you chmod 755 a script, you are writing three octal digits — user, group, other. "Seven is everything, 111. And then five is: I'll give you read permission and I'll give you execution permission, but I won't give you write permission." The permissions on your COMP1521 files are why the tutors can read your work: "you can all read and execute all the files in this — and so you have access to it, you can pull it out."
Small integers doing a lot of work

File descriptors (slides 40–41)

A file descriptor is a small integer. That is all it is on your side of the boundary. On the kernel's side it is an index into a per-process table, and that table points at everything the kernel actually knows about the open file.

What the number is (slide 40)

  • Uniquely identifies a stream or file that is open within a process.
  • It is an index into a per-process, kernel-maintained file descriptor table.
  • Two processes can both have fd 3 open, pointing at completely different files. The number is only meaningful inside one process.

What the kernel stores for it (slide 40)

  • File offset — the current position in the file. Every read and write moves it.
  • File status — read-only, write-only, append, and so on.
  • Information to locate the actual bytes — where on the drive the data lives.
The four rules (slide 41)
  • Every process starts with the three standard streams: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr.
  • When a file is opened, the next available free descriptor is used. "If we've got nothing else open then we open something, we'll just take the next one, which is three."
  • When a file is closed, the descriptor is released — some other file can take that number later.
  • When a file is read from or written to, the file offset is updated.

There is a hard cap. "There's only a finite number — depending on your operating system, maybe 1024. There might be situations where for whatever reason you've opened more than there are file descriptors, and there will be an error associated with that. It's just good practice, once you've opened a file and done something with it, that you close it, just to free up that file descriptor."

fd_table — allocation, reuse and offsets

Lab 6 · Watch descriptors get handed out and given back

Open and close files and watch the table. The rule to internalise: always the lowest free number. Close fd 3 while 4 and 5 are open, open something new, and it comes back as 3 — not 6. Reading also moves the offset, which is why the second read gives you different bytes than the first.

per-process file descriptor table

3 descriptors in use · next free: 3

actions
close fd:
program output
"What on earth is stderr?"

Standard error, and redirection (slides 42–43)

There are three standard streams in Linux, and Linux treats them like files — because they are a sequence of bytes, which is exactly what a file is. That is why they get file descriptors at all.

fdstreamconnected by default towhat belongs in it
0stdinthe keyboardinput your program consumes
1stdoutthe terminalthe program's actual results
2stderrthe terminal — alsoerrors, warnings, progress, debug chatter

Because both 1 and 2 land on the terminal by default, they look identical when you run the program normally. The distinction only becomes visible when you redirect — which is exactly the point of having two.

stderr_example.c — the demo, in full (slide 43)
#include <stdio.h>

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    printf("hello\n");                                  // goes to stdout (fd 1)

    if (argc < 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "error: no argument given\n");   // goes to stderr (fd 2)
    }

    printf("goodbye\n");                                // stdout again
    return 0;
}

printf always writes to stdout — there is no version of it that does anything else. To choose a stream you need fprintf, whose first argument is the destination. "printf will default itself to printing to standard output; here we use this type of printf statement so that we can specify which file descriptor we need." Note the type difference: stderr here is a FILE * from stdio.h, which wraps file descriptor 2 — the shell's 2> talks about the descriptor directly.

./stderr_example — redirection playground

Lab 7 · Where does each line end up?

Choose whether to pass an argument, then choose a redirection. Watch the three output lines split between the terminal and the files. Run it with no redirection first and notice you cannot tell the two streams apart — that is the problem redirection solves.

terminal
file: temp
file: errs
Use this while you debug. "This is actually a really good way of debugging — you can collect all your errors and filter out all the output to standard output. If you use printing to standard errors for some of your debug statements, it can help you work out which is which." Two practical habits: send progress and diagnostics to stderr so they never pollute a pipeline, and keep stdout clean enough that ./prog > out produces exactly the result and nothing else.
Why did that fail?

errno (slides 44–45)

Unix-like systems have a C library wrapper for most system calls — open, read, write, close. They share one convention, and it is an old one: return −1 on error, and put the reason somewhere else.

The convention (slide 45)

  • The function returns −1 to indicate an error.
  • It sets errno to an integer value indicating why.
  • You can think of errno as a global integer variable.
  • The values are #define-d in <errno.h>; man errno has more.

"You can see that there's uh, you know, probably you get this one quite a bit… permission denied. Not a directory — definitely got that one before. All these are what the integer will return. It has meaning behind it; it's not just some random number."

Turning the number into English

fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);
if (fd < 0) {
    printf("errno = %d\n", errno);
    perror("could not open file");
    // or:
    // puts(strerror(errno));
    return 1;
}

perror() looks at errno and prints your message followed by the reason. strerror() just converts the number to a string. To list every code on the command line: errno -l.

The ones you will actually hit

Not portable. This whole mechanism is libc — the layer closest to the hardware. "You're better off always using your higher level functions from stdio, but this is a good way to see the mechanics that go underneath." One piece of history worth knowing: errno looks like a global variable but cannot be one on a multi-threaded system, since two threads would overwrite each other's error. The workaround is that errno is #define-d to a function call returning the address of a per-thread variable.

The API for the rest of the term

open, close, read, write (slides 46–52)

Four functions, one shared shape. Every one of them takes or returns a file descriptor, and every one of them returns −1 with errno set when something goes wrong.

open — two forms (slide 46)
int open(char *pathname, int flags);
    - open the file at pathname, according to flags
    - flags is a bit-mask defined in <fcntl.h>

int open(char *pathname, int flags, mode_t mode);
    - use this version when potentially CREATING a new file
    - mode is an octal number giving sensible access permissions

if successful  → returns a file descriptor (small non-negative int)
if unsuccessful → returns -1 and sets errno to the reason

Use the three-argument form whenever O_CREAT is in the flags — otherwise the new file gets whatever permission bits happen to be on the stack. The mode is exactly the octal number from Lab 5: 0644 is readable by everyone and writable by the owner.

open() — flag mask builder & error probe

Lab 8 · Build the flags, then watch open() succeed or fail

The flags argument is a bit mask — the same | from Week 4. Click flags to OR them together and see the number the kernel receives. Then run open() against a tiny pretend file system and read the return value: a descriptor, or −1 with an errno you can look up in §11.

access mode — pick exactly one
extra flags — OR in as many as you like
pathname: mode:
The flags (slide 47)
flagoctaluse
O_RDONLY0open for reading
O_WRONLY01open for writing
O_RDWR02open the object for reading and writing
O_APPEND02000append on each write — every write goes to the end
O_CREAT0100create the file if it doesn't exist
O_TRUNC01000truncate to size 0 — throw away what was there

Flags combine with |, and the classic combination is (O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC) — "open for writing, make it if it isn't there, and empty it if it is". That is 1 + 64 + 512 = 577 = 0x241. Note that O_RDONLY is zero, so it contributes nothing to the mask; "read only" is the absence of the write bit rather than a bit of its own.

read (slide 49)

ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);
  • Read up to count bytes from fd into buf.
  • buf must point to an array of at least count bytes — read cannot check this. Getting it wrong is a buffer overflow.
  • Success → the number of bytes actually read, which may be fewer than you asked for.
  • 0 → no more bytes to read (end of file).
  • Error → −1, and errno is set.
  • The descriptor's current position advances by the number of bytes read.

write (slide 50)

ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count);
  • Attempt to write count bytes from buf into the stream identified by fd.
  • Success → the number of bytes actually written.
  • Error → −1, and errno is set.
  • The descriptor's current position advances too.

Note const on the buffer: write promises not to modify what you hand it, while read exists precisely to modify what you hand it. The type signature tells you the direction of travel.

close — and why you bother (slide 48)
int close(int fd);
    - release open file descriptor fd
    - if successful, return 0
    - if unsuccessful, return -1 and set errno
        - e.g. if fd is not an open file descriptor
        - e.g. if fd has already been closed

Note the asymmetry that trips people up: open returns a non-negative descriptor on success, but close returns 0. Both return −1 on failure, so if (result < 0) is the check that works for all four calls.

The three types you keep seeing (slide 51)
typesigned?used for
ssize_tsigneda count of bytes or an error indication — it must be signed so it can hold −1. Range [−1, SSIZE_MAX].
size_tunsigneda count of bytes you are supplying. Range [0, SIZE_MAX] — unsigned, because an object cannot have negative size.
off_tsignedfile sizes and offsets. Signed so you can seek backwards from the current position or from the end.

This is a direct callback to Week 4's integers lecture: signedness is not decoration, it is what makes −1 expressible. If read returned size_t, an error would come back as a colossal positive number — and if (n < 0) would silently never fire.

open_read.c — the full pattern (slide 52)
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <errno.h>

int main(void) {
    int fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);       // 2 args: not creating
    if (fd < 0) {                              // ALWAYS check
        printf("errno = %d\n", errno);
        perror("could not open file");
        return 1;
    }
    printf("file descriptor = %d\n", fd);      // prints 3

    char byte;
    while (read(fd, &byte, 1) == 1) {          // one byte at a time
        putchar(byte);
    }

    close(fd);                                 // give the fd back
    return 0;
}

Run against a missing file it reports errno = 2 and "No such file or directory". Run against a file that exists, the descriptor is 3 — 0, 1 and 2 are taken. Run it twice and it is 3 again, because close gave it back. That is the whole of §09 demonstrated in one program.

open_write.c — creating a file (slide 52)
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc < 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s <filename>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }
    int fd = open(argv[1], O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0666);
    if (fd < 0) { perror("open"); return 1; }

    char *msg = "potato\n";
    write(fd, msg, 7);                       // 7 bytes, counted by hand
    close(fd);
    return 0;
}

Three flags, three arguments, and a mode. Afterwards ls -l shows the new file with rw-rw-rw- — because 0666 granted read and write to everyone and execute to nobody. "It's got read and write permissions because we set it to 666." The byte count 7 is the same manual counting from §07: p-o-t-a-t-o-\n.

Do these before you look

Exercises

Six sets. The first is straight off slide 7; the rest are built from the material the lecture demonstrated live — the layers, the descriptor numbers, the permission bits, the flag mask and the return-value convention. Every answer can be checked in one of the labs above.

Exercise 1 — floating point, both directions (slide 7)

Keep in mind 10000000 = 27 = 128, and that the bias for a 32-bit float is 127.

  1. Convert −42.5 to IEEE 754 single precision.
  2. Convert 00111110100000000000000000000000 to decimal.
  3. Harder: convert 0.15625 to IEEE 754 single precision.
  4. Harder: convert 11000000101000000000000000000000 to decimal.
Show the answers

1. 42.5 = 101010.1 = 1.010101 × 25. Sign 1, exponent 5 + 127 = 132 = 10000100, fraction 0101010…:

11000010001010100000000000000000   // 0xC22A0000

2. Sign 0; exponent 01111101 = 125, so e = 125 − 127 = −2; fraction all zeros, so the significand is 1.0. Value = 1.0 × 2−2 = 0.012 = 0.25. Remember to finish converting out of binary.

3. 0.15625 has no integer part at all. By repeated ×2: 0.3125 → 0, 0.625 → 0, 1.25 → 1, 0.5 → 0, 1.0 → 1, stop. So 0.001012, which normalises to 1.01 × 2−3. Exponent = −3 + 127 = 124 = 01111100:

00111110001000000000000000000000   // 0x3E200000

4. Sign 1 → negative. Exponent 10000001 = 129, so e = 2. Fraction 01000… → significand 1.012 = 1.25. Value = −1.25 × 22 = −5.0.

Exercise 2 — name the layer

For each line, say which of the three levels it belongs to, and what it turns into on the level below.

a)  fputc('x', stdout);
b)  syscall(1, 2, msg, 6);
c)  write(1, buf, n);
d)  fprintf(stderr, "oops\n");
e)  read(0, &c, 1);
Show the answers
linelayerbecomes
astdio.h (highest)a buffered write(1, …), then syscall 1. Note it may not write immediately — stdio buffers.
braw syscall (lowest)nothing — it is already the bottom. This one writes 6 bytes to fd 2, i.e. stderr.
clibc wrappersyscall(1, 1, buf, n)
dstdio.hwrite(2, "oops\n", 5), then syscall 1 with fd 2
elibc wrappersyscall(0, 0, &c, 1) — syscall number 0 is read, and fd 0 is stdin

The trap in (b): the first argument is the syscall number and the second is the file descriptor. It is easy to read syscall(1, 2, …) as "write to fd 1" when it actually means "call write, on fd 2".

Exercise 3 — predict the descriptors

A freshly started process runs this. What does each printf print? Assume every open succeeds.

int a = open("one.txt",   O_RDONLY);   printf("%d\n", a);
int b = open("two.txt",   O_RDONLY);   printf("%d\n", b);
int c = open("three.txt", O_RDONLY);   printf("%d\n", c);
close(b);
int d = open("four.txt",  O_RDONLY);   printf("%d\n", d);
close(a); close(c);
int e = open("five.txt",  O_RDONLY);   printf("%d\n", e);
Show the answers 
3
4
5
4   // b was closed, so 4 is the lowest free number — not 6
3   // a and c were closed; 3 is lower than 5, so 3 wins

The rule is lowest free descriptor, not "next number I have not used yet". 0, 1 and 2 are never free, because stdin, stdout and stderr are open for the life of the process. Step this exact sequence in Lab 6 if the last two surprise you.

Exercise 4 — permission bits
  1. Write 754 as nine rwx characters.
  2. Write -rw-r----- as an octal mode.
  3. A file shows drwxr-xr-x. What kind of object is it, and what is the octal mode?
  4. Why does a directory need the execute bit set to be useful?
Show the answers 
1)  7 = 111 = rwx    5 = 101 = r-x    4 = 100 = r--
    754 → rwxr-xr--

2)  rw- = 110 = 6    r-- = 100 = 4    --- = 000 = 0
    -rw-r----- → 640

3)  leading 'd' → a directory;  rwx r-x r-x = 755

4. On a directory the bits mean something slightly different: r is "list the names inside", w is "create or delete entries", and x is "traverse it" — permission to name anything through this directory. Without x you cannot cd into it or open a file inside it even if you know the exact path, which is why directories are almost always 755 and not 644.

Exercise 5 — build the mask

Given O_RDONLY=0, O_WRONLY=1, O_RDWR=2, O_CREAT=64, O_TRUNC=512, O_APPEND=1024:

  1. What integer is O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC?
  2. What flags would you pass to append to a log file, creating it if it does not exist?
  3. Why is passing O_RDONLY | O_CREAT a suspicious thing to write?
Show the answers 
1)  1 | 64 | 512 = 577 = 0x241 = 01101 octal

2)  O_WRONLY | O_APPEND | O_CREAT
    = 1 | 1024 | 64 = 1089 = 0x441
    // and use the 3-argument open(), because O_CREAT is present

3. Because O_RDONLY is 0. It contributes no bits at all, so O_RDONLY | O_CREAT is indistinguishable from plain O_CREAT — you have asked to create a file you are then only allowed to read. It compiles, it may even succeed, and it is almost never what you meant. This is the practical consequence of an access mode that is encoded as the absence of bits rather than the presence of one.

Exercise 6 — what came back, and why

Each of these runs and returns. State the return value and, where relevant, the errno.

a)  open("file_that_does_not_exist", O_RDONLY)
b)  close(7)                // fd 7 was never opened
c)  read(fd, buf, 4096)     // fd is at end of file
d)  read(fd, buf, 4096)     // 12 bytes remain in the file
e)  close(fd)               // fd is a valid open descriptor
Show the answers
returnserrnonote
a-12 — ENOENT"No such file or directory". This is the one the lecturer hit live.
b-19 — EBADF"Bad file descriptor" — also what you get closing something twice.
c0unchanged0 is not an error. It means end of file. This is why read loops test > 0, not != -1.
d12unchangedA short read. You asked for 4096 and got what was there — that is normal, not a failure.
e0unchangedclose returns 0 on success, unlike open which returns a descriptor.

(c) and (d) together are the whole reason read returns a count rather than a success flag. A program that assumes it always gets exactly count bytes is broken the first time it reads from a pipe, a socket or a slow disk.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slide 53)

The floating point half closed the loop by hand: convert the integer part by repeated division and the fraction by repeated multiplication, normalise until one 1 sits before the radix point, count the shift, add the bias of 127, and drop the leading 1 because it is always there. Reserved patterns catch what arithmetic cannot: all-zero exponent for zero, all-ones with an empty fraction for ±infinity, all-ones with anything else for NaN — the value that is not equal to itself. And the number line is uneven: 252 doubles fit between every 2n and 2n+1, so the gap doubles as the exponent does, until above 253 adding 1 changes nothing at all. Then the pivot. An operating system exists because the alternative is writing device-specific code for every machine you ever touch; it presents a consistent virtual machine over wildly different hardware, and it enforces that with two hardware modes. Only the kernel runs privileged. Your code asks, through a numbered system call, and gets control back afterwards. Above that sits a ladder you have been standing on since your first C program: printf calls write, write traps to syscall 1, and only the bottom rung is non-portable. The things being moved are deliberately simple — a Unix file is just bytes, a file descriptor is just a small integer indexing a kernel table, and the lowest free one is always the one you get. Everything else is convention: 0, 1, 2 for the standard streams, > and 2> to re-plumb them, −1 plus errno to report failure, and open / read / write / close to do the work. Next: flex week — nothing due. Then in Week 7, working with the stdio.h library and files, and much more about file systems and other system calls.

The sign-off. "Make sure that you catch up on all the stuff that you have to do — life, also, you know, self-care. Give yourself a bit of a break. I know it's the nitty-gritty, but this is how everything works… None of us are going on holidays, so reach out. We will answer you. We're not going missing. And of course, if you need any help in any way, please ask for it." Content questions go to the forum; admin questions to cs1521@cse.unsw.edu.au.

inf = exp all 1s + frac 0; NaN = exp all 1s + frac ≠ 0 · x == x is false for NaN → use isnan() · 252 doubles between every 2n and 2n+1 → gaps double as values do · above 253, a+1 == a · an OS = abstraction + portability + resource management + reliability, over a consistent virtual machine interface · hardware supplies privileged mode (kernel only) and non-privileged mode (all your code) · a system call is the doorway: args in, OS checks & performs, control returns · Linux has 400+ syscalls, numbered in unistd_64.h · 0 read, 1 write, 2 open, 3 close, 4 stat, 8 lseek · three ways to call: raw syscall() (cryptic, unportable), libc wrappers read/write (named, typed, POSIX-only), stdio.h (portable, buffered — what you already use) · man section 1 = commands, 2 = syscalls, 3 = library functions, 7 = headers; COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 7 — Lecture 1

Files, two layers deep: the libc wrappers, the stdio.h library, and the buffer sitting quietly between you and the disk

Back from flex week, and the course picks up exactly where it left off. First a recap of the machinery — privileged and non-privileged mode, the numbered system call, the file descriptor table — then the same job done twice. Once the hard way, with the libc wrappers: open with a bitmask of flags and an octal mode you must not forget, read and write that count bytes for you and nothing else, close that hands the descriptor back. Then the way you already write C: fopen, a FILE * you are not allowed to look inside, fgetc and fputc, and the text-only family that quietly destroys binary files. The lecture ends on the question that makes the whole distinction worth caring about: copying a 10 MB file one byte at a time takes 63 seconds through libc and 0.16 seconds through stdio — identical-looking code, 390× apart. The answer is buffering.
