Two questions from the board

Recap: privileged and non-privileged mode (slides 5–7)

The lecture opened with the two questions from Week 5 Lecture 2 put straight back up on the screen: what is the difference between privileged and non-privileged mode, and how can user code access hardware? Everything in this lecture is an answer to the second one, at increasing distance from the metal.

Privileged mode (slide 6)

Everything is allowed

Code running here can touch all hardware, all memory, and every CPU instruction. Only the OS kernel runs in this mode — the part of the operating system that manages hardware and system resources, and that knows the intricacies of whichever platform you happen to be standing on. The lecturer's description: "this is like, you know, the core operating system — like the reptilian brain of a CPU. It's the bit that does all the basic kind of stuff, accesses the hardware, and knows the intricacies of the different hardware platform that you might be running on."

Non-privileged mode (slide 6)

Where you actually live

Code here cannot touch hardware directly and can only access the memory it was allocated. All user code runs in this mode — including every program you have written in this degree. "This is basically where we usually are playing. This doesn't give us any actual hardware access unless we use specific system calls… we can get some memory allocated to us, but other than that we don't have really deep access into the hardware guts."

The MIPS exception — and why it felt so unrestricted. "When we do our MIPS stuff, we're essentially, you know, kind of being god of the CPU, and we're allowed to do things at that level. Most of the time that's not something that can happen." That is worth pausing on: for six weeks you wrote code with unrestricted access to registers and memory, because mipsy is a simulator that hands you the whole machine. Real hardware does not. The privilege boundary is the single biggest difference between the machine you have been imagining and the one you are actually running on.
The round trip (slide 7)

A system call is not a function call into a library. It is a controlled transfer of execution out of your program and into the kernel, and back again. Four things happen, in order:

1You ask. Execution transfers to OS kernel code, now running in privileged mode. The request includes arguments specifying the details — which operation, on which object, with what data.
2The OS checks. Is this operation valid? Are you permitted to do it? This is the step that makes privilege separation mean anything — it is where "permission denied" comes from.
3The OS carries it out. The kernel — and only the kernel — touches the device.
4You get control back. Execution returns to your code in non-privileged mode. "And then instantly you're transported back to your non-privileged mode."

Note what is not in that list: your program never runs privileged, not even for an instant. It stops, the kernel runs, your program resumes. The privilege never travels — only the request does.

Same operation, three altitudes

Three ways to make a system call (slide 8)

This slide is a repeat, and the repetition is deliberate: the rest of the lecture is a tour of levels two and three. What changes as you climb is not what happens — the same bytes reach the same device — but how much of the machine you have to know about, and how much the library is allowed to do behind your back.

Level 1 · the syscall function

Not portable, and no type checking at compile time

"This is not at all portable. This is very hardware specific, and you need to have at least some information about the hardware that you're using." You pass the syscall number, not a name, and the compiler cannot check any of the arguments because they are all variadic. Get the number wrong and you have silently asked for a different operation entirely.

syscall(1, 1, bytes, 6);   // write, to fd 1, 6 bytes — and nothing checks any of it
Level 2 · libc named wrappers — man section 2

More portable, type-checked, less cryptic

"It's a lot more portable. It's likely to work if you've got a Mac and on other Linux systems." You get a real function with a real prototype, so the compiler checks your arguments, and a name instead of a number. What you do not get is much abstraction: "it's not that much less complex than syscall, except that there's a few things that have increased the abstraction a little bit."

write(1, bytes, 6);        // same operation, named, and the types are checked
Level 3 · stdio.h — man section 3

Portable, and it does other helpful stuff behind the scenes

"You need to know a lot less about what's under the hood. All that kind of gets done for you. It's very portable — you can compile C code with this library on a Windows computer, a Mac, a Sun systems computer, an embedded computer, and usually things will work out okay for you." It calls the named wrapper for you. And — the part that matters most in this lecture — it does other helpful stuff behind the scenes, which slide 8 states without explaining. The explanation is buffering, and it arrives in §13.

printf("hello\n");        // no fd, no byte count, and possibly no write() — yet
Why Windows is the odd one out. "The Windows operating system is quite a lot different to Macs and Linux, and that adds some complications with things." That is the whole portability story in one line: macOS, Linux and the BSDs are all POSIX-like, so they share the section-2 names — open, read, write, close. Windows does not; it has its own API entirely. stdio.h survives the jump because it is part of the C standard rather than the operating system, so every C implementation that can do I/O at all must provide it.
An aside that is really about your career. The lecturer stepped sideways here, and it is the most quotable thing in the recap: "this is where kind of abstraction starts to happen in terms of hardware and software. Hardware engineers need to know how much memory and what bytes you're using and so forth. As software engineers, you need to more think about security and speed of running and portability across different platforms. And this is where the multiple different priorities can affect how you write a piece of code." The three levels on this slide are not a difficulty ladder — they are three different sets of things somebody decided to care about.
Six numbers and two tables

The file system calls, and the descriptors they hand out (slides 9–10)

Every system call has an ID number. "So a zero means you're going to do a read, a one means you're going to do a write, and so forth — this is basically just saying what you're going to do within that syscall function." Six of the 400-odd matter for files, and four of them are this lecture.

IdNameFunction
0readread some bytes from a file descriptor
1writewrite some bytes to a file descriptor
2openopen a file system object, returning a file descriptor
3closeclose a file descriptor
4statget file system metadata for a pathname — next lecture
8lseekmove file descriptor to a specified offset within a file — next lecture
Read the numbers as an archaeology. read is 0 and write is 1 because they were the first two things anybody needed. open is 2 and close is 3 because you need those to have anything to read and write. The gap between 4 and 8 is filled by fstat, lstat, poll — and the numbers keep climbing to 400-plus as the operating system grew. They are an ABI, so they can never be reordered.
The four rules, restated (slide 10)
1Every process starts with the three standard streams already open: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. You did not open them and you generally should not close them.
2When a file is opened, the next available free descriptor is used — always the lowest one. "You'll open a file, if there's nothing else open it'll just take file descriptor three. If you open another file before closing that, it'll take descriptor four, and so on."
3When a file is closed the descriptor is released, and goes straight back into the pool. "Say you open something, it took number three; you open something else, it took number four. Then you close number three, and then you open another file — and that file could take number three instead of number five."
4When a file is read from or written to, the file offset is updated. The descriptor remembers where you are. Nothing you write ever needs to say "and put it here".

And a warning attached to rule 2. "It does mean that there's a natural maximum number of files that you can have open in your system, and so that's something to keep mind of. You can definitely crash things by opening too many files. There are ways that systems have to deal with that, but it's a good idea not to go crazy with it." The usual ceiling is 1024 per process — a number that comes back in §07 as the reason to call close.

Counting bytes on your fingers

hello.c, written three times (slide 11 · live demo)

Slide 11 says only "hello.c" — the rest happened live, and it is the clearest thing in the lecture. The same six bytes go to the same terminal three times, and each version deletes one thing you had to know.

Version 1 — the raw system call

Built up on screen, argument by argument. "If we want to write to the output, we can go back and look up here — a write has an ID of one. So we have one. Now, where we want to write this: if we want to write it to the standard output, then that's got a file descriptor of one."

// hello, the hard way
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/syscall.h>

int main(void) {
    syscall(1, 1, "hello\n", 6);
    //      ^  ^     ^        ^
    //      |  |     |        `-- how many bytes. Count them yourself.
    //      |  |     `----------- the bytes
    //      |  `----------------- fd 1 = stdout
    //      `-------------------- syscall 1 = write
    return 0;
}

The counting, out loud. "Then we need to specify how many bytes is in the string that we're writing. So go through and count. There's 1, 2, 3, 4, five — and then the carriage return is six. We don't include the null here." That last clause is the trap. The string literal "hello\n" occupies seven bytes in memory, because C appends a terminating '\0'. You want to write six. Write seven and a stray NUL byte lands in your output.

Why this gets old fast. "You can see how annoying that is. Imagine if every time you wanted to print something out to standard output you had to count how many bytes were in everything. It gets rather tedious after a while." Every level above this exists to stop you counting.
Version 2 — the libc wrapper

One improvement, and the lecturer was precise about how small it is.

#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
    write(1, "hello\n", 6);   // returns ssize_t: 6, or -1 on failure
    return 0;
}

"So the only improvement in abstraction here is that the function is called write and we don't have to remember what the ID for writing is. Otherwise it's pretty much the same sort of information that we need." You still name the descriptor. You still count the bytes. What you gain is a prototype — the compiler now knows the second argument should be a pointer and the third a size_t.

Version 3 — stdio.h
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("hello\n");
    return 0;
}

"The nice thing about this is it is a function that's built for printing to the standard output, so we don't need to specify the file descriptor here. And we also don't need to specify the number of bytes that we're writing out. All that kind of happens under the hood." Two facts deleted: which descriptor, and how many bytes. The program printed hello three times, once per version. "There's obvious advantages to working really close to the hardware and knowing how many bytes you're moving around… but in general terms, this is obviously a lot easier."

hello.c — the same six bytes, three ways

Type any message. The panel shows it as bytes — including the ones you cannot see — and writes the three versions of the program for you, with the count filled in. The NUL terminator is drawn in red so you can watch it sit there being excluded. Try the "off-by-one" button to write it anyway and see what lands in the output.

How C says "no"

errno, and the three types you will keep seeing (slides 13–14)

Both of these were covered in Week 5; both were repeated here because every single function in the rest of the lecture uses them. "The C library has an interesting way of returning error information."

The convention (slide 13)
  • Functions typically return −1 to indicate an error — "not always," the lecturer added, which is why the next bullet matters.
  • And set errno to an integer value indicating the reason.
  • "You can think of errno as a global integer variable." (It is not quite one — on a threaded system each thread gets its own — but that is exactly the right mental model here.)
  • The values are #defined in <errno.h>; man errno for more.

The homework attached to it: "whatever functions you're using, make sure that you read the man page — see what it might return with an error, and also what it returns with a success, so that you understand what that should look like and you can write good loops."

Turning a number into a sentence
perror(char *s)
Looks at errno and prints s, a colon, and the reason. The one you actually want. "It's very useful when you're doing debugging and checking what happened."
strerror(int e)
Converts errno to a string describing the reason, for when you want to format the message yourself.
errno -l
On the command line, lists every code. "There's 133 of them. Some of them super interesting."
The ones you will actually meet

"Generally, those ones at the top are going to be the ones that you'll see the most of." Three of them account for nearly every failure in this course:

2 ENOENTNo such file or directory. You misspelled the pathname, or you are not in the directory you think you are in. By far the most common.
13 EACCESPermission denied. The file exists; the mode bits say no. This is the one the lecturer produced live in §06 by forgetting an argument.
3 ESRCHNo such process. Turns up when you are closing or signalling something that has already gone.
$ ./open_read hi.txt
hi.txt: No such file or directory        // ← that whole line came from one perror() call

The pattern in code is always the same three lines: call it, compare against the documented failure value, perror with something identifying, then bail out.

Three types, and what each one is for (slide 14)
ssize_tA count of bytes, or an error indication. Signed, storing [-1, SSIZE_MAX]. This is what read and write return, and the sign is doing real work: "generally that's either a negative one that it's going to give you when there's a return with an error, or the size in terms of number of bytes of the operation that you've just done. So if you've just written hello, the return would be six."
size_tA count of bytes. Unsigned, [0, SIZE_MAX]. This is what you pass in. "This type is used in write functions where you're saying how many bytes you want to write — you can't specify that as a negative number."
off_tFile sizes and offsets. Signed — deliberately, so that lseek can move backwards. "We look at this a little bit, I think, in the next lecture."

The asymmetry is the whole design: unsigned going in (a request for a negative number of bytes is meaningless), signed coming out (so one value can be stolen to mean "it didn't work").

Filling in a gap from the room. A student asked how to printf a size_t, and the lecturer — live, under time pressure — couldn't get it to print and cast to int instead: "there's probably a way to print size_t's, I would say… for this platform, where you're just using a very standard kind of system, ints will be more than sufficient." There is a way, and it is one letter: %zu for size_t, %zd for ssize_t. The z is a length modifier meaning "this argument is size_t-sized", and it has been standard since C99. 
ssize_t n = write(1, buf, 6);
printf("wrote %zd bytes\n", n);   // %zd, not %d — no cast needed
The undefined-behaviour digression. The casting question turned into the liveliest exchange of the lecture, when a student made the case for Rust: "one of the main advantages is that it does not have weird undefined behaviours… if you have a single undefined behaviour in C then the compiler can do any optimization that's as weird as whatever the compiler writer wants it to be — you might just trigger a bomb or something." The lecturer's reply: "That's terrifying." The serious version: undefined behaviour does not mean "unpredictable result", it means the compiler is entitled to assume it never happens and optimise on that assumption. That is why the safe move is to use the type the man page names, rather than one that happens to work on your machine today.
Two prototypes and one forgotten argument

open(), its flags, and the mode you must not forget (slides 15–16)

Writing to a file starts by opening it, and open is the only call in this lecture with two different prototypes. Choosing the wrong one produced the lecture's most instructive failure.

The two forms (slide 15)
int open(char *pathname, int flags);
//   open the file at pathname, according to flags
//   flags is a bit-mask defined in <fcntl.h>

int open(char *pathname, int flags, mode_t mode);
//   use THIS version when you might be creating a new file
//   mode is an octal number giving the new file sensible permissions
Successreturns a file descriptor — a small non-negative int. "That integer number that comes after two — 0, 1, 2 are reserved for standard input, output and error, and then after that all the numbers get used up."
Failurereturns −1 and sets errno.

Note the check: open returns −1 on failure, so if (fd < 0) is the guard. Compare this with fopen in §09, which returns NULL instead — the same idea wearing different clothes, and a genuine source of bugs when you switch layers mid-program.

The flags (slide 16)

"Sounds like a dog has made these ones up." They are defined in <fcntl.h>, and they are bits — which is why the next line of the slide says they can be combined.

FlagUse
O_RDONLYopen for reading
O_WRONLYopen for writing
O_RDWRopen the object for reading and writing
O_APPENDappend on each write — "that means that you would continue on from the end of file"
O_CREATcreate the file if it doesn't exist
O_TRUNCtruncate to size 0 — "if the file exists it's just going to start at the front of the file and then write over everything"
open("out.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
//    "open for writing; make it if it isn't there; and if it is there, empty it first"

"This is where some of your bitwise logic comes in. You can combine them — you can say I'm opening this file for write only, if it doesn't exist create it, and if it does I'm going to start it from the top of the file." Straight out of Week 4 Lecture 2: each flag owns a bit, | turns bits on, and the kernel tests them with &. The choice between truncate and append is the one you must make consciously: "whether you want to just rewrite the whole file even if it exists, or if you want to continue the file from where the end of file is."

The failure, live. The lecturer opened a file with O_CREAT, using the two-argument form, and the program ran. The file appeared. And then nothing worked, because the file had been created with whatever garbage happened to be on the stack as its permission bits. "I did do something wrong, didn't I? And this is going to cause me pain later on… The thing that I forgot was — my errors are very instructive in this course — when we open for writing, we need to write the mode."
The rule: if O_CREAT is in your flags, you must pass a third argument. C will not stop you — open is variadic — so the compiler is silent and the bug shows up as a permission error later.
The mode argument — three octal digits

"So mode is the sort of bunch of octal numbers that we use to say: can you read to the file, can you write to the file, can you execute the file? And they kind of work as a bit mask." Three bits per digit, three digits:

4r — read
2w — write
1x — execute

"So if you've got a mode of seven, that means that you can read, write and execute it. You kind of do bitwise OR with this. If you've got an octal of six, it means that you can read it and write it but you can't execute it. If you've got an octal of four, it means you can read it, but you can't write to it and you can't execute it."

rwx  r-x  r--
111  101  100
 7    5    4      →  chmod 754 f.txt   →  open(..., O_CREAT, 0754)

Leading zero, always. 0644 is octal; 644 is decimal 644, which in octal is 1204 — a completely different set of bits. In C a leading 0 means "read this as base 8", and file modes are the main place you will ever use that notation.

The question the lecture left open — and its answer. The ordering of the three digits was genuinely uncertain in the room: "if I put a six here and then 0 0, it means that I can read and write but no one else can see it or do anything with it… I can't remember which way around all these are. We'll need to look this up later. I think that's me, that's my group, and that's… I don't know who that is. Yeah, I will work this out and tell you." Then it was settled empirically, with ls -l: "so it's read, write, executable for me and for my group, whomever that is — but you guys, who are down here, you don't have any access to it."
The order is user, then group, then other, left to right — the same order ls -l prints them, which is exactly how the lecturer confirmed it. 0640 is "I can read and write it, my group can read it, everyone else gets nothing."
Read implies copy — a security point worth keeping. A student asked why read permission alone is useful if someone can just copy the file. The answer turned into the best security observation of the lecture: "that's actually a really good point. Letting somebody read it always lets them see what's inside it, and that means that they can make copies of it and do things with it as well — which is an important security thing to remember. Letting someone read a file is giving them access to that information, whatever it may be." Write permission controls the file; read permission controls the information, and once information has left, no mode bit can call it back.
The fourth digit — contributed from the floor. A student pointed out that the mode is really four octal digits, not three: "usually it's like three digits octal, right? It's actually four digits — the first one is the set-user-ID and set-group-ID and sticky attributes. When something is set-user-ID, whenever someone runs it, it runs as that user. One of the most famous set-UID binaries is sudo… sudo always runs as root." That is exactly right, and it is how an ordinary user is able to do a privileged thing at all: sudo is owned by root with the set-UID bit on, so running it hands you root's identity for the duration. chmod 4755 sets it. The lecturer's response: "So we do this in a couple of times — I won't go into too much now, but I'll probably call on you." Permissions and stat are the next lecture.
Where users and groups come from. "There's you as the creator, and then it's your group — which in different instances you're going to be part of different groups. You're part of the group COMP1521 semester 2, that's one of your groups, but you're also probably part of different class groups and year groups, and depending on how the Linux system is set up, you may or may not be allowed to access files because of your group." And on how blunt the mechanism is: "this is like super kind of dumb low-level stuff. It's not that intelligent." Nine bits. That is the entire model, and everything richer — ACLs, roles, capabilities — is built on top of it.
open() — flags, mode, and the missing third argument

Pick your flags on the left and your permission bits on the right, then run it. The panel ORs the flags into a real mask, works out whether you have supplied the arguments open actually needs, and prints the ls -l line the file would end up with. Three functions, one moving position

read, write and close (slides 17–19)

Once the file is open, everything else is these three. Notice what they have in common: none of them takes a position, because the descriptor is already holding one, and every operation moves it.

read (slide 17)
ssize_t read(int fd, void *buf, size_t count);
DoesReads up to count bytes from fd into buf. "Up to" is not a formality — a short read is normal and correct.
SuccessReturns the number of bytes actually read.
End of fileReturns 0. This is not an error: "remember, zero will give us back when there's no more bytes to read. So it's not an error, it just means there's nothing left."
ErrorReturns −1 and sets errno.
Side effectThe descriptor's current position in the file is updated. "That will become important later on."

The warning on the slide, in bold on purpose: buf should point to an array of at least count bytes, and read cannot check that it does. "So if you've only sort of allocated a character — say you've only got one byte allocated to it — and then you read a buffer that's five bytes, then that will throw an error at you… that's kind of up to you." There is no bounds check anywhere in this function. You pass a pointer and a count, and the kernel believes both.

write (slide 18)
ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count);

The mirror image. "Same sort of game — you put in the file descriptor, where you're writing to, which file; you put in the buffer of what you're writing and how big it is." Returns the number of bytes actually written, or −1 with errno set; the position moves by however much went out.

The const on buf is the only asymmetry, and it is a promise: write reads your memory but never modifies it.

close (slide 19)
int close(int fd);
DoesReleases the open file descriptor fd, returning the number to the pool.
SuccessReturns 0 — note, not the descriptor, and not a byte count.
FailureReturns −1 and sets errno — most often because fd was not an open descriptor in the first place, "e.g. if fd has already been closed."

Always close your files. "It's a common mistake when you're writing your code — you forget. It's one little tiny little line." The reason is the ceiling from §03: the number of descriptors is limited, "somewhere like 1,024, so always making sure you close is just best practice." A program that opens files in a loop and never closes them will run perfectly on your three test files and fail on the marker's thousand.

Three different success values, three different checks. This is the single easiest thing to get wrong when you are moving between these calls, so it is worth memorising as a block:
opensuccess = a small non-negative int  →  check if (fd < 0)
readsuccess = bytes read, 0 = EOF  →  loop while ((n = read(...)) > 0)
writesuccess = bytes written  →  check if (n < 0), and compare n to what you asked for
closesuccess = 0  →  check if (close(fd) != 0)
A habit that saves you: close returning 0 for success is the opposite polarity to the other three, and it is the same convention main uses. Zero means "nothing went wrong", not "nothing happened".
On error checking, and the assignment. "So here I'm not really doing any of the error checking — for your assignment two, error checking please do it. There will be definitely weird things that will be thrown at your code, and so make sure that you're fully equipped for weird things." Every code sample in this lecture has its error handling stripped for legibility. Yours should not.
Written on screen, mistakes included

open_read.c and open_write.c (slide 20 · live demo)

Slide 20 is a list of two filenames and three flags. Everything below happened live — including the part where it didn't work.

The headers, and why each one is there

"Here we have just put all the headers and everything in beforehand, otherwise that'll take forever." Four includes, and the lecturer named the job of each:

#include <fcntl.h>    // the O_ flags — "this one has all of our flags in there"
#include <unistd.h>   // read, write, close
#include <errno.h>    // "so that we get error codes, so we can decode our errors"
#include <stdio.h>    // "this one is only in here so I can print to the standard output"

That last comment is worth noticing: even a program written to demonstrate the low-level API pulls in stdio.h, because nobody wants to write printf by hand. "The actual reading of the file and everything will be done with our low-level library." Mixing layers is normal — just be deliberate about which one is doing what.

open_read.c — one byte at a time
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc != 2) {                          // "if there's no file name, this will throw an error"
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <file>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    int fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);       // name from the command line, read only
    if (fd < 0) {
        perror(argv[1]);                        // "we're going to use this to tell us what that error was"
        return 1;
    }

    int c;                                    // int, not char — see §11
    while (read(fd, &c, 1) > 0) {           // one byte at a time; 0 means EOF
        printf("%c", c);
    }

    close(fd);                                // "at the end I remembered to put close"
    return 0;
}

The loop condition is the whole design. read returns a count, so > 0 means "we got something", == 0 means end of file, < 0 means error. "So as long as what we're reading is greater than zero, we're going to keep on reading it." Hold onto this: in §11 the same loop written with fgetc tests a completely different thing, and that is where the bug lives.

It ran, and then it failed on purpose
$ ./open_read data.txt
… the entire file, byte for byte …

$ ./open_read hi.txt
hi.txt: No such file or directory        // ← perror(), doing its job

The test file had something planted in it for later: "I've got some weird characters in here for something later on, but it's essentially the standard Latin. There's nothing to see here." The character is ÿ — byte 0xFF — and it is the reason §11 exists.

open_write.c — and the potato

The write side, built the same way, and this is where the missing mode from §06 bit. Once the third argument was added, it worked:

int fd = open(argv[1], O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0770);
if (fd < 0) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; }

int o = write(fd, "potato", 6);   // p-o-t-a-t-o — counted on screen, again
printf("%d\n", o);                    // prints 6

close(fd);

"So six bytes were written out… the number of bytes I wrote is the number of bytes that was output by the write." And then a useful aside about return values in general: "you could get rid of this — you wouldn't have to do this, you could just say write potato and it just writes potato. Sometimes the return values are not useful to you. If this was part of a loop and you were looping through and writing something, then this would obviously be important to you."

Two potatoes — O_TRUNC vs O_APPEND

The most memorable thirty seconds of the lecture. The file already contained potato. The program was run again, unchanged:

$ cat class.txt
potato
$ ./open_write class.txt      // flags: O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC
6
$ cat class.txt
potato                         // still ONE potato — truncate wiped it, then rewrote it

// change O_TRUNC to O_APPEND, recompile:
$ ./open_write class.txt
6
$ cat class.txt
potatopotato                   // "okay, now we got two potatoes"

"So that's the difference with those flags. Truncate will, if the file exists, just go to the beginning of it, write over it — all is lost. And append goes to the end of file and then carries on from that point in time." One had to be recompiled to see the difference, which is the other lesson: the flags are baked in at compile time, so the behaviour of your program on an existing file is a decision you made in the source, not at runtime.

Why the byte counting still happens here. Look at that write(fd, "potato", 6) and notice we are still counting on our fingers, three sections after §04 complained about it. That is the honest state of the libc layer: it renames things, it type-checks things, and it does absolutely nothing about the tedium. The next section is where that changes.
Same job, one floor up

fopen, the FILE *, and fclose (slides 21–24)

"If we want to do the same things with our standard IO library, we have a different set of functions to use." Everything from here on does the same work as §06–§08 — but the flag mask becomes a short string, and the small integer becomes a pointer to something you are not allowed to look inside.

fopen (slide 22)
FILE *fopen(const char *pathname, const char *mode);

Returns NULL if the open failed — not −1. Different sentinel, same idea, and the reason is obvious once you see the return type: there is no "negative pointer" to hand back.

ModeMeaningThe libc flags it stands for
"r"open for readingO_RDONLY
"w"open for writing — truncated to 0 length if it exists, created if it does notO_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC
"a"open for writing — writes append if it exists, created if it does notO_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPEND
"r+"reading and writing; the file must already existO_RDWR
"w+"reading and writing; truncated or createdO_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC
"a+"reading and appending; created if neededO_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_APPEND

This is the compression that makes stdio worth using. "So the w by itself — it's those two flags that we had. It's the writing flag and the truncate flag." (And O_CREAT, which the slide states and the lecture assumed.) Three flags and a mode argument become one character. "You can see the abstraction has gone up a little bit more here: where we had to specify these flags, now we're using kind of more logical symbols to represent what we're doing… it's kind of all compressed down into this idea of r, which is read, which I think is a lot more intuitive."

Notice what disappeared. There is no mode argument. fopen asks the OS for 0666 and lets your umask knock bits off — typically producing 0644. That is a real trade: the failure from §06 is now structurally impossible, and in exchange you have lost the ability to say "create this one private". If you need 0600, you need open.
What a FILE * actually is (slide 23)

"It's a special kind of structure… and we can't access the fields of this structure." Four facts, and the fourth is punctuated aggressively on the slide:

1FILE is an opaque struct — we cannot access its fields. Not "should not". The header genuinely does not promise you any member names.
2FILE stores a file descriptor. Underneath everything, there is still one of the small integers from §03. "You can imagine that under the hood here somewhere, FILE has the file descriptor and has used the really low-level functions."
3FILE may also, for efficiency, store buffered data. This is the sentence the entire second half of the lecture turns on.
4FILE may store other things too!!!!! — five exclamation marks, on the actual slide. Position, error and EOF flags, the buffer size, whether the buffer is yours or the library's, a lock on threaded systems.

Why opaque is the point, not an inconvenience. Because you cannot reach into it, the library is free to implement it differently on every platform — and that is what makes the same source compile on Linux, macOS and Windows. The abstraction only holds because the door is locked.

fclose (slide 24)
int fclose(FILE *stream);
  • Calls close. The descriptor inside goes back to the pool.
  • The number of streams open at any time is limited (to maybe 1024) — the same ceiling as before, because it is the same ceiling.
  • Writes unwritten buffered data to the stream. This is the one that will bite you: data you "wrote" may not have left the process yet.

The third bullet means fclose is not merely tidying up — it is part of writing the file. Skip it, and the last few thousand bytes exist only in your process's memory. They do get flushed when the program exits normally, which is exactly why the bug hides: it only appears when the program doesn't exit normally.

The same reader, rewritten

Side by side with §08. "There's kind of analogies here."

libc — §08
int fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
if (fd < 0) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; }

int c;
while (read(fd, &c, 1) > 0)
    printf("%c", c);

close(fd);
stdio — the same program
FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "r");
if (f == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; }

int c;
while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF)
    putchar(c);

fclose(f);

Three differences, and every one of them is a trap. The failure test changed from < 0 to == NULL. The loop condition changed from "did the call return bytes?" to "is the byte itself EOF?" — a completely different question, and the subject of §11. And the error-handling shape stayed identical: "instead of less than zero for the file descriptor it's just: is f equal to NULL? And then you can do your file checking… the same procedure works here with the perror, because we included — well, it's sort of wrapped in with stdio — and we then will be given a description of what the reason was for this NULL return."

One family for bytes, one for text

Reading and writing with stdio.h (slides 25–28)

Four slides of function signatures, and the organising idea is a split that the slides state flatly and the lecture demonstrated by breaking it: some of these functions work on any bytes, and some of them only work on text. Using the second group on a binary file destroys the file.

Group 1 — safe for any bytes (slide 25)
int fgetc(FILE *stream);                // read a byte
int fputc(int c, FILE *stream);          // write a byte

size_t fread (void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);
size_t fwrite(const void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);

"So we can use the fgetc — get a character from a file. Here the only argument is the file that you've just opened. The opposite of that for write is fputc: you say what it is that you're putting and what file it's going to. So these are your sort of low-level, just like our read and write in libc — these are our stdio reading and writing functions."

On fread/fwrite, with feeling. "These funky ones here are related to particularly things like binary files… We won't look into it too much here, but it's worth perusing the man pages if you are in need of sleeping material — because I don't think you're going to use it in your life. I can honestly say I've never used these things in my life. That's not really saying a lot, but it's good to know they exist. See what they are, see how you can use them. You'll all come to me later and say 'I used them extensively in my assignment', and I'll be like: there you go, don't listen to me." The course notes agree, gently: "fgetc/fputc + loop often better."

Group 2 — text only (slide 26)
char *fgets(char *s, int size, FILE *stream);   // read a line
char *fputs(char *s, FILE *stream);            // write a string

int fscanf (FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);  // formatted input
int fprintf(FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);  // formatted output
The restriction, in the slide's own words: these functions cannot be used for binary data as they may contain zero bytes. You can use them to read text (ASCII / Unicode); you cannot use them to read a .jpg. "There's a lot of weird stuff in binary files, so only use them to read text… and don't use them to read a JPEG."

The mechanism is the one you have known since your first C string: these functions delimit with '\0'. A binary file is full of 0x00 bytes that mean nothing in particular, and every one of them looks like the end of the string. §12 shows the damage.

"Although I strongly recommend you try this at home, because it's fun. And that's with all these things — the best way to understand how these things work is to just try them and see what happens, and cast things to the wrong types and see what happens. That's my suggestion for the best way to do things."

Group 3 — the convenience wrappers (slide 27)

Every function you have used since your first week of C is one of these with stdin or stdout already filled in. "You can see they're kind of defined very much the same, except with the f in front you need to specify what file you're writing to. That's the only difference in the syntax."

ConvenienceIs exactly
getchar()fgetc(stdin)
putchar(c)fputc(c, stdout)
puts(s)fputs(s, stdout) — plus a newline
scanf(fmt, ...)fscanf(stdin, fmt, ...)
printf(fmt, ...)fprintf(stdout, fmt, ...)

Which closes a loop opened in §04: the printf("hello\n") that looked like magic is fprintf(stdout, "hello\n"), which is a buffered write(1, "hello\n", 6), which is syscall(1, 1, "hello\n", 6). Four names, one operation.

The never-use list (slide 27)
These should never be used: security vulnerability, buffer overflow. 
char *gets(char *s);        // NEVER USE
scanf("%s", array);        // don't use with %s
sprintf(str, fmt, ...);      // use snprintf instead

"These guys here have fun security vulnerabilities that have been discovered, and so don't use these — ever — because bad things could happen. And I suggest that, just because they're very tricky, in this course I wouldn't use them for your assignments either. So just use the fun guys, the ones that we know don't cause problems."

The single flaw they share: none of them takes the size of the destination. You hand over a pointer and a promise. If the input is longer than the array, the extra bytes are written past the end — over whatever happened to be next in memory. gets is so unfixable it was removed from the C standard entirely in C11; there is no correct way to call it.

I/O to strings — the aside (slide 28)

"There's a lot in stdio.h — open it up, have a look, see all the things that are defined in there." Two that are worth knowing now:

// like scanf, but the input comes from the char array str
int sscanf(const char *str, const char *format, ...);

// like printf, but the output goes to the char array str
// handy for creating strings to pass to other functions
// size is the size of str — which is the whole point
int snprintf(char *str, size_t size, const char *format, ...);

snprintf is sprintf with the missing argument restored. That one extra parameter is the entire difference between a standard tool and a documented security vulnerability — "do not use the similar function sprintf as it is a security vulnerability." A closing caution from the room, worth keeping: "some of these more obscure ones, I don't know how strongly they've been tested, so just be aware of that."

rosetta — libc ↔ stdio, both directions

int, not char — the fgetc return-type bug (slide 29)

This is the one slide in the deck written as a deliberate sabotage exercise: "to make a buggy version, use char instead of int for fgetc". It is also the one demo that fought back, and the fight is the most useful thing in the lecture.

The counting argument

"Reminder: getchar and fgetc return int." Here is why they must:

0…255Every possible byte value. A file can contain any of them, and fgetc must be able to report each one distinctly.
−1EOF. A value that is not a byte, meaning "there are no more bytes."
= 257Possible return values. This cannot fit in signed char or unsigned char — both hold exactly 256 distinct values.

The pigeonhole is exact and unarguable: 257 things, 256 boxes. Whatever type you choose that is one byte wide, two of those values must collide. The only question is which two, and that depends on the signedness.

signed char — the silent truncation

Range −128…127. It can store −1, so it can detect EOF — but the byte 0xFF, a perfectly legal byte, also becomes −1 when narrowed. Result: the loop stops early, in the middle of the file, the first time a 0xFF shows up. "Valid byte value 0xFF gets mistaken for EOF."

unsigned char — the infinite loop

Range 0…255. It cannot store −1 at all — assigning EOF to it produces 255. The test c != EOF is therefore never true. Result: the loop never ends, spinning on whatever the last state was. "Unsigned char can't store −1 and can't detect EOF."

The demo that refused to break — and why

The lecturer tried to break the libc reader from §08 with a char, and it kept working. Repeatedly. On stage.

"You might be tempted to sort of use a character… and generally it will [work]. I actually tried really hard to break it with char and it worked… Even though my data.txt has these funny characters, it still prints them out, for reasons that we will get into in a few lectures time… I used unsigned char because I wanted it to die, but it did not die. And it should die, but it does not… It's me, it's not you. It just constantly works for me. I wanted to see crazy, but crazy did not happen."

Here is the reason, and it is not mysterious. Look at the two loops side by side. They test different things:
libc — survives a bad type
char c;
while (read(fd, &c, 1) > 0)
    putchar(c);

End-of-file is detected from read's return value — a separate ssize_t that is 0 at EOF. The type of c never participates in the decision. c is only ever a one-byte mailbox, so char, unsigned char and int all behave identically. There is no bug to find.

stdio — breaks immediately
unsigned char c;
while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF)
    putchar(c);

End-of-file is detected from the value itself. fgetc has only one channel to say both "here is a byte" and "there are no bytes", so the width of c is load-bearing. Narrow it and the two meanings collide. This is where the bug lives.

Which is exactly what happened next in the room. The moment the same experiment was repeated on the stdio reader, it failed instantly — and loudly.

And then it did die
$ dcc open_read_stdio.c -o open_read_stdio
warning: comparison is always true due to limited range of data type
       // ← "see, it's warning me that it won't work"

$ ./open_read_stdio data.txt
…ÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿÿ
       // forever, until you press ^C

"So why this didn't work was because we created an unsigned char, which then doesn't know how to handle end of file. So end of file comes and it's like: what is this character? And then it's just kind of freaking out, and it keeps seeing end of file. So it's like — I still don't know, tell me again. So it just endlessly loops with garbage." The moral, delivered with feeling: "the man page told us to, so it's a very brave person to go against the man page. Cast it to an int and everything will work."

The compiler told you first. warning: comparison is always true due to limited range of data type is not noise — it is the compiler having done the pigeonhole argument for you and noticing that c != EOF can never be false. In this course dcc will shout about it. Read the warnings.

The exercise, and where it breaks

Implementing cp (slides 30–31)

The set exercise: implement the Linux cp command, twice — (1) a byte at a time with stdio.h, and (2) using fgets and fprintf/fputs. Slide 30 attaches a question to the second one: "what is the problem with this approach?" The answer is on slide 31, and it was demonstrated live.

What cp has to do

"You've got a file… and I want to copy it into something else. And you can do a diff between these two after you've done a copy, and they come up with nothing because they're identical. So it's just copying the contents of one file into another file."

$ ./cp data.txt data2.txt
$ diff data.txt data2.txt        // silence = success
$

Two files open at once — one for reading, one for writing — which makes it the first program in the course that needs two descriptors live simultaneously. Descriptors 3 and 4, by rule 2 of §03.

Version 1 — byte at a time, fgetc/fputc

Built live. Note "r" for the source and "w" for the destination — and the reasoning for "w": "right now, the way copy works is that if the file already existed, it just writes over it. So that means we're doing the truncate thing."

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc != 3) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s <src> <dest>\n", argv[0]);
        return 1;
    }

    FILE *f1 = fopen(argv[1], "r");      // the file we read
    if (f1 == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; }

    FILE *f2 = fopen(argv[2], "w");      // "w" = O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC
    if (f2 == NULL) { perror(argv[2]); return 1; }

    int byte;                             // int. See §11.
    while ((byte = fgetc(f1)) != EOF) {
        fputc(byte, f2);
    }

    fclose(f1);
    fclose(f2);                           // "make sure that you close both of the files"
    return 0;
}

Ten lines of substance, and it copies anything — text, JPEGs, executables, whatever. It also looks appallingly slow, one byte per call, and §13 is about why it is not. "I mean, it's a bit laborious. We're doing one character at a time."

Version 2 — fgets in chunks, and the trap (slide 31)

"Here's one I prepared earlier, with a stream… With the stream, you need to define what's your chunk size, how you're chunking this up."

char buf[4096];                       // how big? "it's kind of a design choice"
while (fgets(buf, sizeof buf, f1) != NULL) {
    fputs(buf, f2);
}

On text files it works and it is faster. "That works fine as well… fgets is if you know it's just, say, you're copying Moby Dick for unknown reasons — this would be the right thing to do because it's quicker, it's getting big chunks of data at a time, so it's just more efficient."

Then it was pointed at a binary file. The lecturer picked the nearest one to hand — the compiler's own output. "This is completely unplanned, but your output a.out is a binary file, so we could see if we can copy it to a different file." 
$ ./cp_fgets a.out b.out
$ diff a.out b.out
Binary files a.out and b.out differ      // ← the copy is wrong

$ ./cp_fgetc a.out b.out
$ diff a.out b.out
$                                        // ← silence. fgetc copied it perfectly.
"It just says the binary files a.out and b.out differ — it doesn't tell you more than that, because otherwise it just looks like a bunch of rubbish. So that's just to illustrate: fgets is really bad at binary files."

Slide 31 states the mechanism: it seems to work fine when copying text files, but breaks for binary files with 0x00 bytes — they are interpreted as the end-of-string '\0' character. fgets hands you a NUL-terminated string; fputs writes bytes until it hits a NUL. Every 0x00 in the source silently truncates that chunk, and everything after it in the chunk is dropped. "Reminder: only use fgets, fprintf, fscanf, or fputs for text."

Choosing between them. "fgetc would be a safer option if you didn't really know what kind of characters were inside the file, if there was some weird stuff. fgets is faster, more efficient for text. fgetc — use it when you've got weird files, binary files, and also text files, but it's not as efficient. It's really about file size and sort of how long you have for computing." And on the buffer size: "one of the things to think about is how big to make this buffer size. It might come with what you know about what you're actually reading — it's kind of a design choice that is somewhat linked to the file and somewhat linked to performance. And it might be that you need to experiment a little bit with your system to see what's the optimum buffering size."
Worth being precise about the "efficiency" claim, though, because §13 complicates it: fgets is faster than fgetc only by a small margin, and both are hundreds of times faster than the same loop written with read. The big win is not the chunk size in your source code. It is the buffer stdio is keeping either way.

Buffering, and why stdio is 390× faster (slides 33–35)

Slide 33 sets up a race and slide 34 explains the result. In the room, time ran out: "I'm mindful of time here, so I might just do it at the beginning of next lecture. This will tell you how long it takes to do the operation — and, spoiler, it's quicker when you use something like fgets because it takes bigger chunks of file." The numbers below are the course's own measured results, from the files notes.

The experiment (slide 33)
$ clang -O3 cp_x.c -o cp_x
$ dd bs=1M count=10 </dev/urandom >random_file
10485760 bytes (10 MB, 10 MiB) copied, 0.183075 s, 57.3 MB/s

$ time ./cp_x random_file random_file_copy

Ten megabytes of random bytes — deliberately, because random data is incompressible, contains every byte value including 0x00, and cannot be cheated by any clever special case. -O3 so nobody can blame the optimiser. Then the same 10 MB copied by four programs that all look about equally reasonable in source form.

The numbers
cp_libc_one_byteread/write, one byte per call — real 1m2.878s · user 0m2.248s · sys 1m0.555s
cp_fgetcfgetc/fputc, one byte per call — real 0m0.160s · user 0m0.063s · sys 0m0.027s
cp_libcread/write, 4096 bytes per call — real 0m0.105s · user 0m0.000s · sys 0m0.037s

Read the sys column. That is time spent inside the kernel, and for the first program it is 60.5 of the 62.9 seconds. The program is not computing anything; it is paying the toll to cross the privilege boundary, nearly 21 million times. At the user level cp_fgetc copies one byte at a time too — "much faster than copying 1 byte at a time using read/write" — and cp_libc is faster still "because we copy 4096 bytes at a time while avoiding the buffering of fputc."

How stdio does it (slide 34)

Goal: reduce the number of system calls, because system calls are expensive. Assume BUFSIZ is 4096, which is typical.

Reading
  • Uses one read system call to fill the whole buffer.
  • Subsequent reads get bytes from the buffer.
  • Does not do another read until it runs out of data.

Concretely: the first fgetc requests 4096 bytes via read, returns 1 byte, and stores the other 4095. The next 4095 fgetc calls touch no kernel at all. The 4097th triggers the next read.

Writing

Delays calling write by storing data in a buffer instead. It calls write only when:

  • the buffer is full;
  • a newline is encountered, for line-buffered output (e.g. a terminal);
  • fflush is called;
  • the file is fclosed;
  • and note: files are closed and buffers flushed on exit.

4096 calls, 1 crossing. That single ratio is the entire 390×. Nothing clever is happening — stdio is not compressing, not threading, not predicting. It is just refusing to knock on the kernel's door for one byte at a time.

Why the boundary is expensive. A system call is not a jump. The CPU switches privilege level, saves your register state, enters kernel code, validates the arguments, does the work, restores everything and switches back. That is on the order of a microsecond — nothing, unless you do it twenty million times, at which point it is a minute. §01's tidy four-step round trip has a price tag, and this is it.
Seeing it — strace (slide 33)
$ strace ./cp_fgetc random_file random_file_copy

"strace just traces through how many calls are happening at the lower level. So if you run some of these compiled programs and do strace, it'll show you all the system-level calls that it's doing underneath — and you can see how these stdio functions are really being optimised, how often it's calling down to the low level. And that's where you get your speed advantage, because it's not doing every single call one at a time; it's kind of chunking them up."

"These efficiencies are not written into the lower-level libraries. This is why the higher-level libraries run so much faster." Which is worth stating precisely, because it sounds backwards: the higher-level library is faster because it is higher level. The abstraction is not a tax you pay for convenience — it is where the optimisation had room to live.

fflush — forcing the issue (slide 35)
int fflush(FILE *stream);

fflush(stdout);   // forces a write() to stdout and empties the output buffer
DoUse it on stdout when you need output to appear now — a progress indicator, a prompt without a newline, a debug print just before something crashes.
DoUse it on files opened for writing, when something else needs to see the data before you close.
Don'tUse it on stdin, or on files opened read-only. Slide 35 says so flatly; the behaviour is not defined by the C standard.

The debugging bug this explains. If your program prints something and then segfaults, and the print never appears — it did run. The bytes were sitting in the output buffer, and the crash meant nothing ever flushed them. The demos fflush_line.c and fflush_full.c are on the course site; the lecture ran out of clock before reaching them.

bufsim — BUFSIZ 4096, one call at a time

Exercises

Six sets. The first two are the translation drill this lecture is really about; the rest are the traps, in the order they will catch you. Every answer can be checked in one of the seven labs above.

Exercise 1 — translate the layer

Rewrite each line at the other level. Assume the pathname is in argv[1] and that you want sensible permissions on anything you create.

a)  int fd = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);          // → stdio?
b)  FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "a");              // → libc?
c)  write(1, "hi\n", 3);                       // → stdio?
d)  while (read(fd, &c, 1) > 0) putchar(c);   // → stdio?
e)  What replaces the check if (fd < 0) when you move to stdio?
Show the answers
aFILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "r");
bint fd = open(argv[1], O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPEND, 0644); — "a" is three flags, and because O_CREAT is one of them the third argument is mandatory.
cfputs("hi\n", stdout); or printf("hi\n"). Note what vanished: the descriptor and the count.
dint c; while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(c); — and c must be int here, where in the libc version it did not matter. See Exercise 4.
eif (f == NULL). open returns −1 on failure because it returns an int; fopen returns NULL because it returns a pointer. perror() works identically for both.

The trap in (b): it is tempting to write O_APPEND alone. Without O_WRONLY you have asked for read-only access with an append flag attached, and every write will fail.

Exercise 2 — build the mask

For each description give (i) the open flags, (ii) whether a third argument is required, and (iii) the fopen mode string that does the same job.

  1. Read an existing configuration file. Fail if it isn't there.
  2. Write a fresh output file, wiping any previous contents.
  3. Add a line to a log file, keeping everything already in it.
  4. Open an existing database file to read and modify in place, without wiping it.
Show the answers
#flags3rd arg?fopen
1O_RDONLYno"r"
2O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNCyes"w"
3O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPENDyes"a"
4O_RDWRno"r+"

The rule for column three: the third argument is required exactly when O_CREAT is present, because that is the only case in which a new file might need permission bits. Nothing in the language enforces this — open is variadic, so the compiler will happily accept the two-argument call and the file will be created with whatever garbage was on the stack.

Why (4) is "r+" and not "w+": "w+" also reads and writes, but it truncates first — which for a database is the difference between an update and a catastrophe.

Exercise 3 — permissions, both directions
  1. Write 0644 as nine rwx characters.
  2. Write rwxr-x--- as an octal mode.
  3. The lecturer's file came back from ls -l as read/write/execute for the owner and the group, and nothing for anyone else. What mode created it?
  4. Why is open(p, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT) a bug, and what will you see when you run the program?
  5. A file you own has mode 0444. Can you delete it?
Show the answers

1. 6 = 4+2 = rw-, 4 = r--, 4 = r--, so rw-r--r-- — the owner reads and writes, everyone else reads.

2. rwx = 4+2+1 = 7, r-x = 4+1 = 5, --- = 0 → 0750.

3. rwxrwx--- = 7, 7, 0 → 0770. The order is user, group, other — which is exactly the question that was left open in the room and settled by reading the ls -l output.

4. O_CREAT is present with no third argument, so the new file's permission bits come from whatever happened to be in that stack slot. The compiler says nothing, because open is variadic. What you see is the file appearing and then being unusable — typically Permission denied (EACCES) the next time anything touches it. This is the failure the lecturer produced live.

5. Yes — and this surprises almost everyone. Deleting a file means removing its name from a directory, so what you need is write permission on the directory, not on the file. The mode bits on the file itself govern reading, writing and executing its contents. (Next lecture takes this apart properly: directories, hard links, and what a name actually is.)

Exercise 4 — predict the failure (slide 29)

A file t.dat contains exactly three bytes: 'A' (0x41), 0xFF, 'B' (0x42). For each loop, say exactly what is printed and whether the program terminates.

a)  int c;            while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(c);
b)  char c;           while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(c);
c)  unsigned char c;  while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(c);
d)  char c;           while (read(fd, &c, 1) > 0)  putchar(c);
Show the answers
aPrints A, ÿ, B and terminates. int holds all 257 possible returns, so 0xFF (255) and EOF (−1) stay distinct.
bPrints A and stops early. 0xFF narrowed into a signed char is −1, which compares equal to EOF, so the loop exits in the middle of the file. Terminates — with silently truncated output, which is the worst kind of bug.
cPrints A, ÿ, B and then never stops. unsigned char cannot hold −1, so c != EOF is always true. This is the garbage loop from the live demo.
dPrints A, ÿ, B and terminates — even though c is a char. End-of-file comes from read's return value, not from the byte, so the width of c is irrelevant. This is why the lecturer could not break the libc version.

The general principle: a function that reports data and end-of-data through the same value needs a type wider than the data. One that reports them through separate values does not.

Exercise 5 — count the crossings (slides 33–34)

Copy a 10,000-byte file with BUFSIZ = 4096. Count the system calls each program makes — count open, read, write and close, and remember that a read returning 0 is still a call.

  1. cp_fgetc — fgetc/fputc, one byte at a time through stdio.
  2. cp_libc_one_byte — read/write, one byte at a time.
  3. What is the ratio, and which column of time does it show up in?
Show the answers

1. cp_fgetc — 11 system calls.

2open — one per file
4read — 4096, 4096, 1808, then one more returning 0 to signal EOF
3write — the buffer fills at 4096 and at 8192, and fclose flushes the last 1808
2close

2. cp_libc_one_byte — 20,005 system calls. 10,000 reads returning 1, plus one returning 0, plus 10,000 writes, plus 2 open and 2 close.

3. Roughly 1,800× — and it appears in the sys column, the time spent inside the kernel. On the real 10 MB test that is sys 1m0.555s against sys 0m0.027s. The user column barely moves, because neither program is computing anything.

Check yourself in Lab 6: switch implementations and watch the syscall counter. Then in Lab 7, drag BUFSIZ down to 16 and see the ratio collapse — the buffer is the optimisation.

Exercise 6 — will it survive a JPEG? (slides 26, 31)

For each function, say whether it can be used to copy a binary file, and if not, what exactly goes wrong.

a) fgetc / fputc      b) fread / fwrite     c) fgets / fputs
d) fprintf(f, "%s", b)  e) read / write
Show the answers
aSafe. Moves one byte at a time as an int in 0…255, with no interpretation. Slower to write, impossible to get wrong.
bSafe. These take an explicit length, so no byte value is special. This is what they are for — even if "I can honestly say I've never used these things in my life."
cNot safe. fgets NUL-terminates what it read, and fputs writes until it hits a NUL. Every 0x00 in the source silently ends the chunk, so everything after it in that chunk is dropped. fgets also stops at newlines, which are just ordinary bytes in binary data.
dNot safe — same reason. %s means "print bytes until you reach a NUL".
eSafe. Byte counts in, byte counts out; no byte value means anything to these two.

How you find out you got it wrong: diff prints Binary files a.out and b.out differ and nothing else — "it doesn't tell you more than that, because otherwise it just looks like a bunch of rubbish." Reproduce it in Lab 6 by copying a.out with cp_fgets.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 36–37)

Two APIs for one job, and by the end the choice is not close. The libc wrappers from man section 2 — open, close, read, write — hand you exactly what the kernel offers and nothing more: a bitmask of flags you assemble with |, an octal mode you must remember whenever O_CREAT appears, byte counts you compute yourself, and −1 plus errno when it fails. The stdio.h functions from section 3 — fopen, fclose, fgetc, fputc, fgets, fputs, fread, fwrite — compress the flag mask into "r", "w" or "a", hide the descriptor inside an opaque FILE *, return NULL instead of −1, and split into two families you must not confuse: anything goes for fgetc/fputc/fread/fwrite, text only for fgets/fputs/fscanf/fprintf, because a 0x00 byte ends a C string and binary files are full of them. Two traps carry real consequences. fgetc returns an int because it must express 257 different things, so a char loop variable truncates the file at the first 0xFF and an unsigned char one never terminates at all — while the same mistake in a read loop is harmless, because there the end of file arrives through the return value rather than the byte. And stdio's "other helpful stuff behind the scenes" turns out to be a buffer: one read fills 4096 bytes, the next 4095 calls never leave your process, and writes accumulate until the buffer fills, a newline arrives on a line-buffered stream, you call fflush, or you fclose. That single ratio is why copying 10 MB one byte at a time takes 62.9 seconds through libc and 0.16 through stdio. The higher-level library is faster because it is higher level — the abstraction is where the optimisation had room to live. Next lecture: file metadata — permissions and the stat system call — hard links and symbolic links, and working with directories.

The sign-off. "We learned stuff today — hopefully. Well, we didn't, but we had a good sit down for two hours. Hope you all get your assignment — hope you all enjoy the assignment. Sorry, you've already got yours in. It'll be out in like seven minutes. It'll be up there glowing. Extreme excitement. I will see you on Wednesday morning. Thank you for your attention." Content questions go to the forum; admin questions to cs1521@cse.unsw.edu.au.
The advice that actually generalises. Said twice in this lecture, about two different things: "the best way to understand how these things work is to just try them and see what happens — and cast things to the wrong types and see what happens." And, on reading a JPEG with fgets: "I strongly recommend you try this at home, because it's fun." Every trap in §11 and §12 takes about ninety seconds to reproduce, and you will never forget one you have watched fail.
TL;DR · only the kernel runs privileged; your code asks via a numbered system call and gets control back · 0 read, 1 write, 2 open, 3 close, 4 stat, 8 lseek · fd 0/1/2 are stdin/stdout/stderr, new files get the lowest free number, close returns it to the pool, limit ~1024 · write(1,"hello\n",6) — six, not seven: the NUL is not written · open returns fd or −1; fopen returns FILE * or NULL; both use perror() · flags are bits: O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC · O_CREAT ⇒ you must pass a third argument, an octal mode · mode digits are user, group, other; r=4 w=2 x=1; 0644 = rw-r--r-- · the 4th (leading) digit is setuid/setgid/sticky — sudo is setuid root · read returns bytes read, 0 at EOF, −1 on error; close returns 0 on success · ssize_t out (signed, so −1 fits), size_t in (unsigned), off_t for offsets · print them with %zd / %zu · "r"=O_RDONLY, "w"=O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, "a"=O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPEND · FILE is opaque: holds an fd, a buffer, and other things · fclose flushes — it is part of writing the file · fgetc/fputc/fread/fwrite = any bytes; fgets/fputs/fscanf/fprintf = text only · never gets, never scanf("%s"), never sprintf — use fgets and snprintf · fgetc returns int: 256 bytes + EOF = 257 values · char → stops at 0xFF; unsigned char → never stops; the same bug in a read loop is harmless · fgets+fputs destroys binary files at every 0x00 · stdio buffers: 1 read per 4096 fgetcs; writes flush on full buffer, newline (line-buffered), fflush, fclose or exit · 10 MB byte-at-a-time: libc 1m2.9s vs stdio 0m0.16s, almost all of it sys time · strace shows you the crossings · next: stat, permissions, hard & symbolic links, directories.

One deviation worth flagging. The lecture explains stdio's speed advantage as "it's quicker when you use something like fgets because it takes bigger chunks of file" — true, but it is not where the 390× comes from. The course's own measurements show cp_fgetc, which reads one byte per call at the user level, already running 390× faster than the identical byte-at-a-time loop written with read. The win is the buffer, not the chunk size in your source. §12 and §13 keep the lecture's phrasing and put the measured figures beside it.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 7 — Lecture 2

File systems: seeking to a position, and everything the file system knows about your file apart from its bytes

Last lecture a file was a stream you read from the front and wrote to the end. Today it gets an address space and a dossier. First the rest of stdio.h: why buffering makes stdio fast, why fflush exists, and what a crash does to data still sitting in a buffer. Then seeking — lseek, fseek, ftell — which let you jump to byte 41, read it, back up one, and write over it. Then the file system itself: inodes, the metadata table that holds the size, the owner, the permissions and the timestamps; paths, absolute and relative; permissions as nine bits in three octal digits; hard and symbolic links, two very different ways to give a file a second name; the stat system call that hands you the whole dossier; and finally mkdir, opendir and readdir, because a directory is just a file with a strange shape. It ends on the sentence the whole of Unix is built on: everything is a file.

Three questions from the board

Recap: which function, which mode, how many bytes (slide 5)

The lecture opened the way the last one did — questions on screen, answered out loud before any new material. All three are the kind of thing that costs marks in a test and hours in an assignment.

Question 1 — fgetc, fgets or fscanf?

The honest answer is "it depends what is in the file", and the lecture gave the rule in one line: "Fgetc and fgets, they're fine for text. Fgetc you can use for binary files as well, but don't use fgets, because it skips over a bunch of stuff and doesn't work properly."

FunctionTextBinaryWhy
fgetc✓✓One byte at a time, and it returns an int so all 256 byte values plus EOF fit. Nothing is special-cased.
fgets✓✗Stops at '\n' and terminates the buffer with '\0'. A binary file full of 0x00 and no newlines defeats both assumptions — see last lecture's a.out demo.
fscanf✓✗Parses formatted text. Useful when the file really is columns of numbers; wrong for anything else.

And a warning about testing. "Sometimes the things that aren't supposed to work will work. It really depends on your file." A text file with no 0x00 bytes will copy perfectly with fgets — and then fall over on the first JPEG. Choose by what the file could contain, not by what your test file happens to contain.

Question 2 — fopen("data", "w") when data already exists

Two halves, and both matter for Assignment 2.

ModeFile existsFile does not existStarting position
"r"opened read-onlyNULL, errno = ENOENTstart
"w"truncated to length 0createdstart
"a"keptcreatedend — every write appends
"r+"opened read and write, not truncatedNULLstart
"w+"truncated, read and writecreatedstart
"a+"kept, read and writecreatedreads at start, writes at end

"If it already exists then we'll just move to the start of the file and we'll write over the file — so it'll go into truncation mode. If it doesn't exist, then it'll create the file. It's not going to append to the output; you need the a mode for append, and that will start writing to the file from the bottom of the file. Otherwise w writes from the top." The lecturer demonstrated this live with a program that writes hello — run twice with "w", the file still says hello; change to "a", run again, and now it says hellohello. §07 comes back to r+, which is the one you will actually need.

Question 3 — how many bytes does each of these write?
fprintf(f, "%d", 255);

Three bytes. '2', '5', '5' — the characters that spell the number, one byte each. 0x32 0x35 0x35.

fputc(255, f);

One byte. The single byte whose value is 255 — 0xFF. cat shows it as a replacement glyph because 0xFF is not valid UTF-8 on its own.

"Test one is three bytes, and it's three bytes because it's printing the characters 255 — there's three characters, three bytes. Whereas test two is just printing a byte… it prints one byte at a time, one character at a time. Even though this is an integer, when we're actually printing it out we're printing it out as characters." This is the same distinction as printf("%d", 65) versus putchar(65): one gives you 65, the other gives you A. Lab 1 lets you check it against a hex dump.

The demo that would not run

Comparing libc wrappers with stdio.h (slides 6–7 · live demo)

This was meant to be the headline demo, and the machine fought back for most of the hour — "it really is a cursed morning, I think", after the terminal died for the third time. The numbers below are the course's own measurements, which is what the slide points you at. The lecturer rebuilt all four programs live first.

cp_libc_one_byte.c
int fd1 = open(argv[1], O_RDONLY);
int fd2 = open(argv[2],
        O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0644);

int c;
while (read(fd1, &c, 1) > 0) {
    write(fd2, &c, 1);
}
close(fd1);
close(fd2);

Two system calls per byte. Built up on screen argument by argument, including a nice aside on the type of buf: "its type is void in the man pages, so it can be whatever you want… I'm using an int here in case we get characters that are bigger than a byte, but either would work." And on the loop condition: "zero means we've reached the end of the file, and negative one means that there's an error — so we're going to keep doing this as long as we don't have an end of file or an error."

cp_libc.c — a buffer, by hand
char buf[4096];
while (1) {
    ssize_t bytes = read(fd1, buf, 4096);
    if (bytes <= 0) break;
    write(fd2, buf, bytes);   // not 4096!
}

The detail worth stealing. You write bytes, not the buffer size. "Instead of the number of bytes that the buffer has, we just put bytes, because this is the return value that tells you how many bytes were read. That way we're not kind of falling over the edge creating some big errors." The last read of a file almost never fills the buffer; writing 4096 every time would append garbage.

The stdio versions
cp_fgetc.c — one byte at a time
FILE *f1 = fopen(argv[1], "r");
FILE *f2 = fopen(argv[2], "w");

int c;
while ((c = fgetc(f1)) != EOF) {
    fputc(c, f2);
}
fclose(f1);
fclose(f2);
cp_fgets.c — a line at a time
char line[1000];
while (fgets(line, 1000, f1) != NULL) {
    fputs(line, f2);
}

"We know from before that fgets is not great with binary files — in fact you shouldn't use it with that. But for big text files this goes through things a lot quicker. Well, at least it should."

Note the shape. The stdio versions have no descriptors, no flags, no octal mode, no bytes_read bookkeeping — and the byte-at-a-time one is still faster than the byte-at-a-time libc one. That is the whole point of §03.

Measuring it: time and strace (slide 7)
$ clang -O3 cp_x.c -o cp_x
$ dd bs=1M count=10 </dev/urandom >random_file
10485760 bytes (10 MB, 10 MiB) copied, 0.183075 s, 57.3 MB/s
$ time ./cp_x random_file random_file_copy
$ strace ./cp_x random_file random_file_copy

time prints three numbers. "System, how long it took; user, how long it took; real, how long it took. I don't know what this means actually — user and system make sense to me. Real, I guess that's really how long it took." The honest version: real is wall-clock time from start to finish; user is CPU time spent running your code; sys is CPU time spent inside the kernel on your behalf. For these programs almost all the time is sys, and that is the tell — the cost is in the crossings, not in your loop. strace prints every system call the program makes, which is how you see the crossings directly.

measured — 10 MB, clang -O3
