cp_fgetc is 393× faster than cp_libc_one_byte — and both copy one byte per call at the source level.
the difference is sys time: 60.5s of kernel crossings versus 0.027s.
The caveat the lecturer put on it, out loud. "Sometimes the answers it gives is kind of not making sense to me — it's worth doing this more times than one, because it's odd… I feel like to properly demonstrate this we'd need to run it many, many times and look at averages." That is correct and worth internalising: a single time run on a shared machine measures the machine's mood as much as your program. The 390× gap is far too large to be noise; a 10% gap on one run is not a result.
The exercise attached to it. "It's worthwhile having a look at running this on the cp_fgets version and comparing it to the cp_fgetc one, and just seeing how many more system calls you run. You could write all this data to two different files and then you could see the increase in calls." Concretely: strace -o a.txt ./cp_fgetc f g and strace -o b.txt ./cp_fgets f g, then wc -l a.txt b.txt. Or count just the reads with grep -c '^read' a.txt.
One array, between you and the kernel

stdio.h buffering, and why it is worth 390× (slide 8)

The explanation is short and it is the whole answer to §02. "When we need to make a system call we need to go out of our unprivileged mode into privileged mode, do the thing, come back out. This is time consuming… so for reading, the ideal is to use a system call and fill a whole buffer rather than constantly system call, system call, system call."

Reading
  • The first fgetc() issues a read() for a whole buffer — typically BUFSIZ = 4096 bytes.
  • It returns you one byte and keeps the other 4095 in an array.
  • The next 4095 fgetc() calls are served from that array. No system call at all.
  • The 4097th call runs the buffer dry and issues the next read().
Writing
  • Calls to write() are delayed; your bytes go into an array instead.
  • write() is only called when one of five things happens:
  • 1. the buffer is full   2. a newline is written to a line-buffered stream (a terminal)   3. fflush is called   4. the stream is fclosed   5. the program exits normally
Play with the numbers. The buffering simulator in Week 7 Lecture 1 §13 (Lab 7 there) lets you set BUFSIZ, switch between full, line and no buffering, and watch library calls turn into system calls at whatever ratio you dial up. This lecture builds on it rather than repeating it — what is new here is the failure mode, in §04.
A phrasing to be careful with. The lecture describes stdio's advantage as "it helps with improving how many lower-level commands that you give — it kind of buffers things so that you can do things a lot more efficiently", which is right. But it is easy to hear that as "because fgets reads bigger chunks". The measurements in §02 rule that out: cp_fgetc reads one byte per call in your source and is still 390× faster than the identical read loop. The chunking that matters happens inside stdio, not in your code.
When the buffer is the problem

fflush — and the crash that eats your output (slide 9 · demos fflush_line.c, fflush_full.c)

Buffering is invisible right up until the program dies with data still in the buffer. Then it is very visible, because that data is simply gone.

int fflush(FILE *stream);
fflush(stdout)Forces a write() system call for whatever is in the standard-output buffer, and empties it.
fflush(fp)Same, for any stream opened for writing.
fflush(stdin)Do not. Undefined behaviour in standard C. "You shouldn't use it for standard input or files open for read only, for obvious reasons." There is nothing buffered from you to push out.
fflush(NULL)Flushes every output stream at once. Occasionally handy; not in the slides.
The demo, twice — fflush_full.c

The lecturer's own summary of the setup: "I print to standard output hello, and then I assign a pointer to null and then I add one to that — and that's going to throw me an error." The same shape is then run against a file, which is where it gets expensive.

without fflush — the file ends up empty
FILE *fp = fopen("my_file", "w");
fprintf(fp, "important information\n");

// deliberately crash
int *p = NULL;
*p = *p + 1;          // SIGSEGV

fclose(fp);              // never reached

"So now if we interrogate our file — it's got nothing in it, right? So that important information wasn't printed." 21 bytes went into a 4096-byte buffer, the process died, and the kernel never heard about them.

with fflush — the data survives
FILE *fp = fopen("my_file", "w");
fprintf(fp, "important information\n");
fflush(fp);              // force the write() now

int *p = NULL;
*p = *p + 1;          // still crashes

fclose(fp);

"So we still — the file still crashes as expected. But now when we go more, the important information has been printed to that file." The crash is unchanged. What changed is that the bytes were already on the other side of the boundary when it happened.

Why hello survived but goodbye never appeared. In the stdout version, printf("hello\n") ends in a newline and stdout attached to a terminal is line-buffered — so the newline itself flushed it. goodbye is after the crash in the source, so it never runs at all. Redirect that same program to a file and stdout becomes fully buffered, the newline no longer flushes, and hello disappears too. Same program, same code, different buffering discipline, different output. "Doing things using the lower-level system calls, you're not guaranteed to have those buffers flushed."

The debugging trap this creates. A program that segfaults halfway through often prints less than it actually executed, because the tail of its output died in a buffer. If you are hunting a crash with printf, either end every message with \n on a terminal, or call fflush(stdout), or print to stderr — which is unbuffered by default, precisely so that error messages survive the thing that caused them.
And the disclaimer. "Although it is not normal to purposely do something that would destroy your program." Quite. The realistic versions are: the machine loses power, someone sends SIGKILL, the program calls _exit() or abort() (neither of which flushes), or a long-running program writes a log you want to be able to tail in real time.

Assignment 2 warm-up

Writing your own FILE (slide 10 · basic_stdio.c · live demo)

The best way to stop finding FILE * mysterious is to write one. The task on the slide is deliberately tiny: a struct with a single field, and two functions that wrap open and read.

The brief, as written
basic_FILEA type containing an int file descriptor.
basic_fopenA minimal fopen: read only, no buffering, no error checking.
basic_fgetcA minimal fgetc: no error checking, does not consider EOF, no buffering.

The three "does not"s are the point. Everything real stdio does beyond this — the 4096-byte array, the EOF and error flags, the mode handling, the ungetc pushback slot — is what makes the real FILE struct big enough that you are not allowed to look inside it. Strip them and what is left is one integer.

Building it, in the order it was built on screen
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

// 1. the type — one field, because that is all we were asked for
typedef struct {
    int fd;
} basic_FILE;

// 2. open: get a descriptor, wrap it, hand back a pointer
basic_FILE *basic_fopen(char *pathname) {
    int fd = open(pathname, O_RDONLY);
    basic_FILE *f = malloc(sizeof (basic_FILE));
    f->fd = fd;
    return f;
}

// 3. getc: read exactly one byte into an int, return it
int basic_fgetc(basic_FILE *f) {
    int c = 0;
    read(f->fd, &c, 1);
    return c;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    basic_FILE *f = basic_fopen(argv[1]);
    printf("%c", basic_fgetc(f));
    printf("%c", basic_fgetc(f));
    close(f->fd);
    return 0;
}

The malloc is not optional. "In order to do this we're going to have to allocate some space, which is equal to the size of the structure." If you declare the struct as a local and return its address, that address points at a stack frame which no longer exists the moment basic_fopen returns. This is exactly why the real fopen returns a pointer rather than a FILE by value — the object has to outlive the call.

What it proves. "The reason to do this is just to sort of understand how the standard library creates these kind of wrapping functions around the libc library functions, and allows you to perhaps do multiple reads or make some efficiencies in there. Under the hood of fgets or fgetc is a read operation." Run it on a text file and it prints the first two characters — the lecturer's ran on data.txt and printed ll, "the first two letters are L and the first two letters it prints out there is L". Two basic_fgetc calls, two read() system calls. Real stdio would have made one.
Two things to put back for the assignment. "For your assignment make sure that you put some error checking in — unless otherwise stated not to — because obviously you won't know where you went wrong if you don't have it." Concretely: if (fd == -1) { free(f); return NULL; } after the open, and a real EOF signal from basic_fgetc, since as written a read of 0 bytes leaves c untouched and returns whatever was there. That is the bug Lab 3 lets you trigger.
basic_stdio.c — build a FILE from one integer

A file is not a queue

Seeking — lseek (slides 11–13)

Everything so far has been sequential: open at one end, walk to the other. Slide 12 asks the three questions that break that model — where am I?, how do I skip to the end?, how do I go back and read earlier data again? — and the answer to all three is that the descriptor's current position is a number you are allowed to set.

The mental model. A file descriptor is not just "which file". It is which file, and where in it. Every read and every write moves that position forward by the number of bytes transferred — that is why repeated reads walk through the file without you tracking anything. lseek is the one call that moves it without transferring bytes. "Firstly you need to know where you are in the file, and then you need to be able to write to that particular place — not just the beginning or the end, as we do when we open things." 
off_t lseek(int fd, off_t offset, int whence);
fdWhich open file. The position belongs to the descriptor, not to the file.
offsetIn bytes, and it can be negative. off_t is a signed 64-bit integer for exactly this reason — see W7L1 §05 on the POSIX types.
whenceWhat the offset is measured from. Three constants, below. "Whence, which is extraordinarily Shakespearean of whoever wrote this."
whenceNew positionTypical use
SEEK_SEToffsetAbsolute. lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET) rewinds to the start.
SEEK_CURcurrent + offsetRelative. Negative offsets step backwards. lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR) asks "where am I?" without moving.
SEEK_ENDsize + offsetFrom the end. lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) gives you the file's size; -1 puts you on the last byte.
lseek(fd, 42, SEEK_SET);   // move to after the 42nd byte
lseek(fd, 58, SEEK_CUR);   // 58 bytes forward from here
lseek(fd, -7, SEEK_CUR);   // 7 bytes backward from here
lseek(fd, -1, SEEK_END);   // move to before the last byte
Return value

The new position as an off_t, or −1 with errno set. Note the shape: this is a call whose success value is a number you actually want, not just a "yes". lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) is the standard idiom for "how big is this file" when you cannot be bothered with stat.

Two edges, and they behave differently
  • Past the end: allowed. It leaves a gap which reads as zeros. Nothing is written until you write.
  • Back before the start: an error. Returns −1, sets errno to EINVAL, and the position does not move.
Do not let these two blur together. "It's important to remember this bit about seeking beyond the end of the file, because that's important to know that it's not going to throw you a negative one error." Seeking forward into nothing is a legitimate, useful operation — it is how sparse files are made. Seeking to a negative absolute position is meaningless, so it fails. A loop that walks backwards through a file with SEEK_CUR, -1 and never checks the return value will spin at position 0 forever.
The gap that costs nothing — create_gigantic_file.c (slide 14, advanced)
FILE *f = fopen("sparse_file.txt", "w");
fprintf(f, "Hello, Andrew!\n");
fseek(f, 16L * 1000 * 1000 * 1000 * 1000, SEEK_CUR);
fprintf(f, "Goodbye, Andrew!\n");
fclose(f);

A 16-terabyte file on a laptop. ls -l reports 16 TB; du reports about 8 KB. Almost all of it is zeros the file system never bothered to store — it records "there is a hole here" in the inode's block pointers instead. Read the hole and you get zeros, exactly as promised. This is a sparse file, and it is why the "gap of zeros" rule is a feature rather than a curiosity.

The same idea, one level up

fseek and ftell (slide 14 · demo fseek.c)

The stdio equivalent, with three differences and one addition.

int  fseek(FILE *stream, long offset, int whence);
long ftell(FILE *stream);
lseekfseek
First argumentint fdFILE *stream
Offset typeoff_t (64-bit)long
Returnsthe new position, or −10, or −1
Buffersnone to worry aboutinfluences the stdio buffers — a pending read buffer is discarded, a pending write buffer is flushed
"Where am I?"lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_CUR)ftell(stream)
whence survived the promotion. "They couldn't get rid of whence, because that's like the coolest thing ever — that remains as it was in the libc version." SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR and SEEK_END mean exactly the same thing in both APIs, which makes translating between them mechanical.
Is fseek faster than lseek? No — and that is fine. A student asked, and the answer is worth keeping: "When you look at fseek versus lseek, you're not getting too much efficiency gain from this. For something like fread, where it's holding lots of things in a buffer instead of writing lots of system calls — that's where you're getting the gains. But this kind of function, it's not going to be massively…" Buffering pays off when it lets you avoid system calls. A seek is one call either way; you use fseek because you are already holding a FILE *, not because it is quicker. 
fseek(stream, 4, SEEK_SET);   // move to after the 4th byte
fseek(stream, 2, SEEK_CUR);   // 2 bytes forward from current position
fseek(stream, -3, SEEK_CUR);  // 3 bytes backward from current position
fseek(stream, -1, SEEK_END);  // move to before the last byte in the file
The demo — fseek.c, five moves and a deliberate failure
FILE *in = fopen(argv[1], "rb");   // b for binary

fseek(in, -1, SEEK_END);
printf("last byte of the file is 0x%02x\n", fgetc(in));

fseek(in, 0, SEEK_SET);
printf("first byte of the file is 0x%02x\n", fgetc(in));

fseek(in, 41, SEEK_SET);
printf("42nd byte of the file is 0x%02x\n", fgetc(in));

fseek(in, 58, SEEK_CUR);
printf("100th byte of the file is 0x%02x\n", fgetc(in));

fseek(in, -1, SEEK_SET);              // deliberately invalid

Read it as a tour of the three whence values. -1 from the end lands on the last byte. 0 from the start rewinds. 41 from the start jumps into the middle — "we've moved to the 41 bytes from the start… the next byte we read is the 42nd." Then 58 from the current position walks forward without needing to know where "here" is. And the last line is there to fail: "this will throw an error — you can't seek back from the start. Remember, we can seek forward from the end and it'll give us a bunch of zeros, but we can't seek back from the start."

An off-by-one in that demo, worth catching yourself. The fourth message is labelled "100th byte". Count it through: fseek(in, 41, SEEK_SET) puts the position at 41, then fgetc reads the byte at index 41 — the 42nd byte, correctly labelled — and advances the position to 42. fseek(in, 58, SEEK_CUR) therefore lands at 100, and the fgetc that follows reads index 100, which is the 101st byte. The lecture's arithmetic ("41 and then 58, so that's 99… the next byte we read is the 100th") forgets that the intervening fgetc moved the position. To genuinely land on the 100th byte you want fseek(in, 57, SEEK_CUR). Step it in Lab 4 and watch the caret.
seek — a file is an address space

Reading and writing the same file

fuzz.c — go in, change one bit, come out (slide 14 · live demo)

The program that puts every piece together: r+, fseek, ftell, a pseudo-random number generator, an XOR from Week 4, and a write that lands exactly on top of the byte it just read. "This is a very odd thing to want to do, but it just shows you what you can do."

First, the mode — r+ versus w+
"r+"Read and write. The file must already exist. It is not truncated, and the stream starts at the beginning.
"w+"Read and write. The file is created if it does not exist and truncated if it does. Also starts at the beginning — of a now-empty file.

"r+ means read and write, and this is how you're going to want to open a file if you want to make changes to that file. Really useful to know for your assignment… w+ will create the file if it doesn't exist, and r+ is going to just open the file and position itself at the beginning. It doesn't truncate. It just means that when you start writing into it, it'll start from the beginning, not from the end — but you can use seek in order to move around the file to different places." If you want to edit a file, r+ is the only mode that does not destroy it first.

The program
FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "r+");  // read AND write, no truncate

fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END);              // jump to the end …
long n_bytes = ftell(f);            // … and ask where that is = the size

srandom(time(NULL));                // seed the PRNG with the clock
long target_byte = random() % n_bytes;

fseek(f, target_byte, SEEK_SET);    // go to that byte
int byte = fgetc(f);                // read it — position moves +1

int bit      = random() % 8;        // pick a bit, 0–7
int new_byte = byte ^ (1 << bit);   // XOR flips exactly that bit

fseek(f, -1, SEEK_CUR);             // back one — undo the fgetc
fputc(new_byte, f);                 // overwrite in place
fclose(f);

The two lines that make it work are the seeks around the fgetc. Reading the byte moves the position past it, so writing immediately would hit the next byte. fseek(f, -1, SEEK_CUR) puts it back. "We're going to go back one byte from our current location, then we're going to put our new byte that has been created with the bit flip into the file." The file's length never changes — this is an overwrite, not an insert. There is no such thing as inserting a byte into the middle of a file; you rewrite the tail.

Why ^ (1 << bit)?

1 << bit is a mask with a single 1 in position bit. XOR with 1 flips; XOR with 0 leaves alone. "So if the bit is a one then it'll flip to a zero, and if the bit is a zero then it'll flip to a one. That's why we're doing an XOR." Straight out of Week 4 Lecture 2: & to test, | to set, & ~ to clear, ^ to toggle.

Why srandom(time(NULL))?

A pseudo-random generator is a deterministic sequence chosen by its seed. "If you ran the same pseudo-random number with the same seed it would give you the same sequence of pseudo-random numbers. That's why it's pseudo." Seeding from the clock gives a different sequence per run. Seeding from a constant is what you want while debugging — the same "random" fuzz every time, so a crash is reproducible.

This has a name, and a job. Random changes made to a file in order to search for errors or vulnerabilities are called fuzzing. Point a fuzzer at a parser — a JPEG decoder, a font renderer, a PDF reader — and let it flip bits until something crashes; each crash is a candidate bug. The lecturer's run reported "the file contains 242 bytes… we changed byte 73 of that file from 75 to 55", and the text file still opened and still read fine, one letter different. Point the same program at an executable and it usually will not.
fuzz.c — one byte, one bit

Second half of the lecture

What a file system actually is (slides 15–17)

Three definitions, and they are worth taking literally because every complication later follows from how thin they are.

File

A named sequence of bytes, stored on a device. That is the entire definition. There is no type. The metadata does not record that it is ASCII or MP4 or JPG. "Files will take up a certain number of bytes and you can point to the beginning and end of that." A .jpg extension is a hint to humans and to xdg-open; the file system has never heard of it.

Directory

A set of files or directories. Not a container that the files live inside — a list of names and what each name points at. This distinction is invisible until §13, where one file turns out to have two names in two directories and no way to say which is "the real one".

File system

The thing that maps names to locations on a device and maintains metadata. "Right down at the hardware level the file exists as ones and zeros somewhere, and so the file system helps us organise it, find it, open it, close it, change it. So the file system creates some kind of metadata: what permissions does this file have, when was it created, how big is it, who can access it." Two jobs: find the bytes, and remember everything about them that is not the bytes.

Tree, with an asterisk. "Some of these files are linked to other places, and so you can kind of be climbing around the tree forever." A directory tree is acyclic by construction — you cannot hard-link a directory, which is exactly why that restriction exists (§13). Symbolic links can point anywhere, including at an ancestor, so anything that walks a file system recursively must either not follow symlinks (lstat, §14) or keep a set of visited inodes.
Two forbidden bytes

File names, path names, and the working directory (slides 18–20)

A file name is a sequence of one or more bytes. Almost any bytes — the restrictions are shorter than you would guess, and they are both structural.

ByteWhy it is banned
0x00 — ASCII '\0'It terminates the name. The kernel receives file names as C strings, so a name containing a NUL would simply end early.
0x2F — ASCII '/'It separates path components. A name containing a slash would be read as two names.

Everything else is legal, including spaces, newlines, control characters and emoji. Maximum length depends on the file system, typically 255 bytes. "There are definitely file systems that allow you to do bigger file names, but at some point it just becomes ridiculous."

The practical consequence. Because a name may contain a newline or a space, shell one-liners of the form for f in $(ls) are broken by construction — they split on whitespace. This is why find -print0 and xargs -0 exist: they separate names with the one byte that cannot appear in a name.
Two names you cannot use, because they already mean something
.The current directory. Present in every directory, pointing at itself.
..The parent directory. Present in every directory, pointing one level up. In / it points at /.

And a convention that is not a rule. Names starting with a dot are hidden — but only by convention: ls and the shell choose not to show them. "If you do ls it's not going to give you any files that start with a dot." ls -a shows them. The behaviour is a famous accident: an early ls filtered out . and .. with a test on the first character, and every dotfile since has been living in that bug.

Absolute and relative (slides 19–20)
absolute — starts with /
/usr/include/stdio.h
/cs1521/public_html/
/home/z5555555/lab07/main.c

The full path from the root. Means the same thing from anywhere, for anyone. Read /usr/include/stdio.h as: start at the root, enter usr, enter include, take stdio.h.

relative — does not
main.c
./a.out
../../another/path/prog.c

Resolved against the process's current working directory. "It only works from whatever directory you did the ../.. from — it wouldn't work from somewhere else."

Every process has a CWD, and it is an absolute path. The shell command pwd prints it; getcwd() is the C function (§15). Resolution is pure string work: if the CWD is /home/z5555555/lab07/ then main.c means /home/z5555555/lab07/main.c, and ../a.out means /home/z5555555/lab07/../a.out, which is /home/z5555555/a.out. "If I wanted to know its absolute path I'd go pwd, it gives me the full absolute path, and I append /fuzz.c to it."

Everything except the bytes

Inodes — the metadata table (slides 21–24)

The name is not part of the file. The size, owner, permissions and timestamps are not stored with the bytes either. They live in a separate record called an inode, and understanding that one fact makes hard links, symbolic links and stat all obvious at once.

What an inode holds (slide 21)
locationWhere the file's contents actually are on the device — the data block pointers.
typeRegular file, directory, symbolic link, device, … This is the character at the front of ls -l. "This guy has just regular files — there's nothing other than that. If I go up then I do the same thing, I see that it starts with a d: that means they're directory types. If it starts with an l, it's a link type."
sizeIn bytes.
ownershipThe owning user and the owning group, as numeric IDs.
permissionsWho may read, write and execute — nine bits, §12.
timestampsLast access, last modification, last status change.

Notice what is not in the list: the name. The name lives in the directory, as one half of a (name, inode-number) pair. That asymmetry is the whole of §13.

The inode number (slide 22)

A file system holds a large array of inodes. An inode's index in that array is its inode number (or i-number), and it identifies the file uniquely within that file system. The analogy from the room: "it's very similar to a zID. Here at UNSW we all have a number, and that number is unique — nobody else can use it. Same for the inodes."

$ ls -i file.c
109988273 file.c

One caveat on "unique". Uniqueness is per file system, and a running machine usually has several mounted. Two files on different file systems can share an inode number without being related at all — which is also why a hard link cannot cross a file-system boundary (§13). A truly unique identity is the pair (st_dev, st_ino), both of which stat gives you (§14).

Opening a file, step by step (slide 24)
1Open the directory and scan for the name. Not found → ENOENT, "No such file or directory".
2Found as (name, i-number) → look up inodes[i-number] in the inode table.
3Check the permissions against the current user and group. Not permitted → EACCES, "Permission denied".
4Update the access timestamp. "Even if you didn't actually get access to it, it'll be updated."
5Use the size and location in the inode to reach the contents.

Read that list for an absolute path and it repeats. /usr/include/stdio.h is four lookups, not one: scan / for usr, scan usr for include, scan include for stdio.h. Each step needs execute permission on the directory, which is why §12's "execute on a directory means you can enter it" matters more than it sounds — a directory you cannot execute blocks everything beneath it, no matter how open those files are.

Nine bits, three digits

Permissions and chmod (slides 25–27)

Every file and directory carries read, write and execute rights for three classes of user. Ten characters of ls -l say all of it, and the lecturer was candid about the ordering: "I never remember this, so this is quite instructive for me."

The type character
-Normal file
dDirectory
lSymbolic link
r, w and x mean different things for files and directories (slide 26)
On a fileOn a directory
rView the contents of the file.View the names of the items in it — i.e. run ls.
wModify the file.Create, delete and rename entries in it.
xRun it as an executable.cd into it — and it is also required to reach anything inside, whatever that thing's own permissions say.

The three that surprise people. (1) Deleting a file needs write on the directory, not on the file — the name lives in the directory, and that is what you are removing. (2) r without x on a directory lets you list the names but not stat or open any of them. (3) x without r lets you open a file whose name you already know, but not discover it by listing — the classic way to publish a download directory without publishing its index. "There will be directories where you cannot ls into them because you don't have access to those."

Bits to octal (slide 27)
rwx  r-x  r-x
111  101  101
 7    5    5

Three bits fit exactly into one octal digit, which is the entire reason permissions are conventionally written in octal rather than decimal or hex. r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, and you add them: rw- is 6, r-x is 5, rwx is 7. "That's why we can use interchangeably the letters and numbers." Change them with chmod and a three-digit octal code:

$ chmod 700 f.txt      # rwx------  only you
$ chmod 644 notes.txt  # rw-r--r--  the default for a data file
$ chmod 755 script.sh  # rwxr-xr-x  the default for a program
Why the lecturer's course files are 775. "Seven is read, write, execute; seven read, write, execute; and then five is read and execute… I have read write execute access to them, people in my group do, and you guys have read and execute access. So you can't come in and change them — you can't write to them, but you do have permission to read them and execute them." The group here is the course's administrators, who need to be able to update the material; students are other. And a fair observation from the room: "it's kind of silly that these files are executable, because they're not executable files." True — 775 on a .c file is harmless but meaningless. 664 would be the tidy choice.
Every open you have ever done ran this check. §11's step 3 is these nine bits being compared against your user and group IDs. When fopen hands you back NULL and perror says Permission denied, this is the table that said no. And once a file is open, the check is not repeated — permissions are tested at open time, so a descriptor opened before a chmod keeps working.
chmod — nine bits, three ways of writing them

One file, two names

Hard links and symbolic links (slides 28–29 · live demo)

Because the name lives in the directory and everything else lives in the inode, a file can have more than one name — and there are two quite different ways to arrange that. "It's really useful, especially for a lot of the library files: rather than giving people full access to the tree, you can link to it and then just allow them access into the part of the tree that you want them to have."

Hard links — ln fileA fileB
  • Multiple names referencing the same inode.
  • Both entries must be on the same file system — inode numbers are only unique within one.
  • You cannot create an extra hard link to a directory.
  • All hard links have equal status. There is no original.
  • The file is destroyed when the last hard link is removed.
Symbolic links — ln -s fileA fileB
  • Points at another path name, stored as text.
  • Accessing it accesses the file being pointed to (by default).
  • Can point at a directory.
  • Can point across file systems.
  • Has no permissions of its own — it is only a pointer, so ls -l always shows lrwxrwxrwx.
The demo, as it ran
$ ln copy copyB              # hard link
$ ls -i copy copyB
109988273 copy    109988273 copyB   # same inode number

$ echo potato >> copyB
$ cat copy
…potato                          # it is the same file

"You can see here that copy and copyB have the same inode number. So when you're doing that hard link, you're basically saying: same file, just different name… copy has potato in it now too, because they're essentially the same files. And vice versa, if I took the potato out — yeah, potato is gone from both of them. When you make a change to one, the change happens to the other."

$ ln -s test1 ltest          # symbolic link
$ ls -li test1 ltest
109988301 -rw-r--r-- 2 … test1
109988344 lrwxrwxrwx 1 …  ltest -> test1   # different inode

"You can see they've got different inode numbers, so they're still existing as separate files… but they're going to mirror each other." Worth being precise about the mechanism, because it explains everything else in this section: they are not two copies kept in sync. The symlink's own inode holds nothing but the six characters test1. When you open ltest, the kernel reads that string and restarts the lookup. There is exactly one copy of the data, which is why an edit through either name is visible through both.

Which one to use — the difference that actually decides it

The lecturer got as far as "the reason to do one over the other… the symbolic link, you can crack that link, or you could remove ltest and it's not going to remove test1, because it's a separate file" — and then, fairly: "I can't think of any use cases here, but I'm sure you'll come across some." Here are the ones you will.

Hard linkSymbolic link
Delete the linkFile survives while any other name remains.Target untouched.
Delete the targetMeaningless — there is no target, only names of equal status. The data survives until the last one goes.The link dangles. It still exists and still points at a name that resolves to nothing; opening it gives ENOENT.
Rename the targetIrrelevant — links point at the inode, not the name.Breaks. The stored string no longer resolves.
Across file systemsImpossible.Fine.
To a directoryNot permitted — it would let you build a cycle and destroy the tree.Fine, and common.
Where you meet them/bin/gzip, /bin/gunzip, /bin/zcat — one program, three names, behaviour chosen from argv[0]. Also how every incremental backup tool avoids storing unchanged files twice./usr/lib/libfoo.so → libfoo.so.1.2.3 — a stable name in front of a versioned one, so an upgrade is a one-line repoint. Also /bin → /usr/bin on modern Linux.

And the reason directories are excluded. Hard-linking a directory into one of its own descendants would create a cycle with no way to detect it — rm -r would never terminate, and the "tree" from §09 would stop being a tree with no marker to say where the loop is. A symlink can create the same loop, but it is labelled: the type character is l, and any traversal that uses lstat can decline to follow it.

a directory, an inode table, and some data blocks

The left panel is a directory: a list of names and inode numbers. The right panel is the inode table. Select an entry, then link it, unlink it or write to it, and watch which numbers move. The thing to look for: ln adds a row on the left and changes one number on the right; ln -s adds a whole new inode.

selected:hello new name:
directory — (name, i-number) pairs
inode table + data blocks
Show me the code

stat, lstat and fstat (slides 30–35 · demo stat.c)

Everything in §11 to §13 is readable from a program with one call. "All of these functions and everything, they all exist as code."

#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

int stat (const char *pathname, struct stat *statbuf);
int lstat(const char *pathname, struct stat *statbuf);
int fstat(int fd,               struct stat *statbuf);
statMetadata for a path name. Follows symbolic links — ask about ltest and you get facts about test1.
lstatSame, but does not follow symbolic links. "It'll just give you the file that's in the path name that you're looking at, not go through symbolic links." This is the one a directory walker must use — "important not to get stuck in infinite loops."
fstatSame, but via an already open file descriptor. No second lookup, and no window in which the file could be renamed underneath you.
returns0 on success. −1 and sets errno if the metadata is not accessible — the file does not exist, or you lack execute permission on a directory along the path.
Three man pages, three different sections. man 2 stat for the system call (and a good sample program at the bottom of it — the slide points this out explicitly). man 3 stat for struct stat. man 7 inode for the masks and macros. "So all of these different types, you can use the man page to have a look at what they do." The section numbers matter: type man stat on its own and you get section 1, the shell command.
struct stat (slide 33)
struct stat {
    dev_t     st_dev;      /* ID of device containing file */
    ino_t     st_ino;      /* Inode number                 */
    mode_t    st_mode;     /* File type and mode           */
    nlink_t   st_nlink;    /* Number of hard links         */
    uid_t     st_uid;      /* User ID of owner             */
    gid_t     st_gid;      /* Group ID of owner            */
    dev_t     st_rdev;     /* Device ID (if special file)  */
    off_t     st_size;     /* Total size, in bytes         */
    blksize_t st_blksize;  /* Block size for file I/O      */
    blkcnt_t  st_blocks;   /* Number of 512B blocks        */
    struct timespec st_atim;  /* last access       */
    struct timespec st_mtim;  /* last modification */
    struct timespec st_ctim;  /* last status change */
};

Read it against §11 and it is the same list. st_ino is the inode number from ls -i. st_nlink is the hard-link count from §13 — the number that goes to 2 when you run ln, and the number that has to reach 0 before the data is freed. st_dev plus st_ino is the genuinely unique identity. And the three timestamps are distinct: atime when the contents were read, mtime when the contents changed, ctime when the inode changed — a chmod moves ctime and nothing else.

st_mode is a bitwise-or of type and permissions (slide 34 · man 7 inode)
/* type — the high bits */
S_IFLNK  0120000  symbolic link
S_IFREG  0100000  regular file
S_IFDIR  0040000  directory
/* permissions — the low nine */
S_IRUSR  0000400   S_IRGRP  0000040
S_IWUSR  0000200   S_IWGRP  0000020
S_IXUSR  0000100   S_IXGRP  0000010
S_IROTH  0000004   S_IWOTH  0000002
S_IXOTH  0000001

One integer, two fields. A regular file with rw-r--r-- has st_mode == 0100644: the 0100000 says "regular file", the 644 says the permissions. Test a bit the way you tested bits in Week 4 Lecture 2 — if (s.st_mode & S_IRUSR) — and test the type with the macros rather than by hand, because the type field is not a single bit: S_ISREG(s.st_mode), S_ISDIR(s.st_mode), S_ISLNK(s.st_mode). "If you man inode it'll give you the bit values, and you can or these to have multiple things."

Using it — stat.c
struct stat s;
if (stat(pathname, &s) != 0) {
    perror(pathname);
    exit(1);
}
printf("ino   = %10ld # Inode number\n", s.st_ino);
printf("mode  = %10o # File mode\n",    s.st_mode);   // %o — octal!
printf("nlink = %10ld # Link count\n",   (long)s.st_nlink);
printf("uid   = %10u # Owner uid\n",     s.st_uid);
printf("gid   = %10u # Group gid\n",     s.st_gid);
printf("size  = %10ld # File size (bytes)\n", (long)s.st_size);
printf("mtime = %10ld # seconds since 1/1/70\n", (long)s.st_mtime);

Two details in the format strings. %o prints st_mode in octal, which is the only base in which it is readable. And the casts to long are there because the exact widths of nlink_t, off_t and time_t vary between systems — casting to a known type is the portable way to pick a conversion specifier. "It's worthwhile playing around with this, seeing what other information you can pry out of it. Look at the man pages — we've added them in there so that you know what to look at."

stat.c — the whole dossier

A directory is a file with a strange shape

Making and reading directories (slides 36–38)

A directory stream works almost exactly like a file stream, which is the point. "That structure, similar to the file structure, is: you use an opendir and then the name that you want. There's a structure related to it that points to the next directory entry, and then you can closedir in the same sort of way. It mirrors what you can do with files, but with directories."

mkdir (slide 36)
int mkdir(const char *pathname, mode_t mode);

mkdir("newDir", 0755);   // note the leading 0 — octal
returns0 if successful, −1 and sets errno otherwise.
for a/b/c/da, b and c must all already exist — mkdir creates one level, not a chain. That is what mkdir -p does for you at the shell.
c must be writable to the caller — you are adding an entry to c's list (§12).
d must not already exist — otherwise EEXIST.
contentsThe new directory already has two entries: . pointing at itself, and .. pointing at its parent.

Which is why a brand-new empty directory has a link count of 2, not 1 — its own name in the parent, plus its own .. Every subdirectory you add to it makes 3, 4, 5… because each child's .. is another hard link back. This is the one place the kernel creates directory hard links, and it is exactly why you are not allowed to.

opendir / readdir / closedir (slide 37, man 3)
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <dirent.h>

DIR *opendir(const char *name);        // open a directory stream
struct dirent *readdir(DIR *dirp);     // next entry, or NULL at the end
int closedir(DIR *dirp);               // close it
for (int arg = 1; arg < argc; arg++) {
    DIR *dirp = opendir(argv[arg]);
    if (dirp == NULL) {
        perror(argv[arg]);      // prints why the open failed
        return 1;
    }
    struct dirent *de;
    while ((de = readdir(dirp)) != NULL) {
        printf("%ld %s\n", de->d_ino, de->d_name);
    }
    closedir(dirp);
}

Line up the three APIs and the pattern is identical. open → read → close on an int; fopen → fgetc → fclose on a FILE *; opendir → readdir → closedir on a DIR *. Each returns a pointer or NULL, each has an end-of-stream sentinel, each must be closed. And note what struct dirent gives you: d_ino and d_name — exactly the (name, i-number) pair from §11, because that is genuinely all a directory contains. Everything else needs a stat. readdir also returns . and .., so a recursive walk that does not skip them will not terminate.

The rest of the POSIX toolkit (slide 38)
chmod  (char *pathname, mode_t mode)   // change permissions
unlink (char *pathname)                 // remove a name — this is rm
rename (char *oldpath, char *newpath)  // rename a file/directory
chdir  (char *path)                     // change working directory
getcwd (char *buf, size_t size)         // get working directory
link   (char *oldpath, char *newpath)  // hard link — this is ln
symlink(char *target, char *linkpath) // symbolic link — this is ln -s

unlink is the honest name for rm. It removes a name, not a file — it decrements st_nlink, and the data is only reclaimed once the count hits zero and no process still holds an open descriptor. That last clause is why you can rm a log file that a running program is writing to and free no disk space at all until the program exits: the directory entry is gone, the inode is not. "The file (inode and data) persists until all references from directories are removed and all processes accessing it close their file descriptor."

Not covered in the room, but on the slide and in the code directory: getcwd.c climbs to the root with repeated chdir(".."); nest_directories.c builds a 1000-deep tree; many_links.c and chain_links.c push the link machinery until it breaks. "On the website you can always go to files and look at codes — any code that's mentioned that we didn't get time to look at is usually going to be in here, and way better commented as well."

list_directory.c — a directory stream, one entry at a time

The sentence the rest of Unix hangs off

Everything is a file (slide 39)

"Originally files only managed data stored on a magnetic disk. The Unix philosophy is: everything is a file." Which sounds like a slogan until you notice that it is a design decision with consequences you have already used.

What it isWhere it appears as a file
Ordinary files and directoriesEverything above.
Storage devices/dev/sda — the raw disk. dd bs=1M count=10 </dev/urandom from §02 read a random-number generator with read().
Peripherals/dev/input/mouse0, /dev/ttyUSB0. Move the mouse and bytes become readable.
System information/proc/cpuinfo, /proc/self/status. Not on any disk — the kernel manufactures the bytes when you read them.
Inter-process communicationPipes and Unix sockets. A shell pipeline is one process's fd 1 wired to another's fd 0.
NetworkSockets are descriptors. read and write work on them.
Why it is worth the trouble. One interface — open, read, write, close, lseek, plus permissions on a path — covers all of it. A program that copies bytes works on disks, terminals, pipes and network sockets without being told which it has. Redirection and pipes in the shell exist because fd 1 can be pointed at anything. And the permission bits from §12 turn out to be a general access-control system for hardware, not just for documents. "Essentially everything is a file in Unix, so we can do very similar things to them."
Where the abstraction shows its seams. lseek is the honest test. It works on a regular file, which has an address space; it fails with ESPIPE on a pipe, a socket or a terminal, which do not. Some things really are streams and nothing else — which is also why fseek(stdin) does not do what you might hope.
Do these before you look

Exercises

Six sets. The first two are the recap questions done properly; the middle two are the arithmetic that seeking and permissions actually require; the last two are the file-system model. Every answer can be checked in one of the nine labs above.

Set 1 — bytes, modes and what lands on disk
  1. How many bytes does fprintf(f, "%d", 1521) write? And fprintf(f, "%c", 65)? And fputc(1521, f)?
  2. A file data contains 100 bytes. You run FILE *f = fopen("data", "w"); fclose(f); and nothing else. What does ls -l data report now?
  3. You want to add a line to the end of a log file without destroying it, then read the whole thing back. Which fopen mode? Name two that would be wrong and say what each would do.
  4. Why is fgets unsafe for a binary file but fgetc fine? Give both reasons.
Show the answers

1. fprintf(f,"%d",1521) writes 4 bytes — the characters '1' '5' '2' '1'. fprintf(f,"%c",65) writes 1 byte, 0x41, the letter A — %c converts the int to a single character, unlike %d. fputc(1521, f) also writes 1 byte: fputc converts its argument to an unsigned char, so 1521 becomes 1521 mod 256 = 241 = 0xF1. The top bits are silently discarded.

2. 0 bytes. Mode "w" truncates on open, and it does so immediately — you do not have to write anything for the damage to be done. This is the single most common way to lose a file by accident.

3. "a+" — append, plus read. "w" or "w+" would truncate the log to nothing. "r+" opens for read and write without truncating, but positions you at the start, so your first write would overwrite the beginning of the log rather than extend it.

4. Two independent reasons. (i) fgets stops at '\n', so a binary file with no newlines is read in one enormous chunk or not at all; (ii) it terminates its buffer with '\0' and the matching fputs stops at the first '\0', so every zero byte in the data truncates the write. fgetc returns one byte as an int, treats all 256 values alike, and signals end-of-file with a value (EOF, −1) that no byte can produce.

Set 2 — buffering and fflush
  1. A program does 10,000 fgetc calls on a file. Assuming BUFSIZ is 4096, how many read() system calls does that cause? Now the same program written with read(fd, &c, 1): how many?
  2. This program prints nothing when run, but prints working… when you press Ctrl-C. Why? 
    printf("working");
while (1) { }
  3. You add fprintf(stderr, "checkpoint %d\n", i) to a loop and the messages appear immediately even redirected to a file, while your printf messages do not. Why?
  4. Name the five events that cause stdio to actually call write(). Which two of them does a segfault prevent?
Show the answers

1. Three for stdio — ceil(10000/4096) = 3 — and a fourth returning 0 if the loop runs to EOF. 10,000 for the libc version, plus one returning 0. That ratio, roughly 2500:1, is the 390× from §02 in one line.

2. Trick premise — it actually prints nothing either way, but the shape is the point: "working" has no newline, so on a line-buffered terminal nothing flushes it, and the infinite loop means the program never exits or closes the stream. (Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, whose default action terminates without flushing, so the output is lost.) Add \n, or fflush(stdout), and it appears.

3. stderr is unbuffered by default, precisely so diagnostics survive whatever they are diagnosing. stdout is line-buffered on a terminal and fully buffered when redirected — which is why redirecting a program to a file can change the apparent order of its stdout and stderr output.

4. Buffer full · newline on a line-buffered stream · fflush · fclose · normal program exit. A segfault prevents the last two — the process dies without running exit()'s cleanup, so anything still buffered is lost.

Set 3 — seek arithmetic
  1. A file is 24 bytes. Give the position after each, starting from 0 each time: lseek(fd,0,SEEK_END); lseek(fd,-1,SEEK_END); lseek(fd,30,SEEK_SET); lseek(fd,-1,SEEK_SET).
  2. Write the one-line idiom for "how many bytes is this file?" using lseek, and the stdio version using fseek and ftell.
  3. You want to read the byte at index 41 and then the byte at index 99. You have already done fseek(f, 41, SEEK_SET); fgetc(f);. What is the correct second fseek? Give it both as SEEK_CUR and as SEEK_SET.
  4. Explain the difference in outcome between lseek(fd, 1000000, SEEK_END) followed by write(fd,"x",1), and simply writing a million bytes of zeros.
Show the answers

1. 24 (which is why this is the size idiom) · 23, sitting on the last byte · 30 — legal, six bytes past the end, and reads there return 0 until something is written · −1, position unchanged at 0, errno = EINVAL. Forward past the end is fine; backward past the start is an error.

2. off_t size = lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END); and fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(f); — exactly the first two lines of fuzz.c. (For a path you have not opened, stat and s.st_size is better: no descriptor, no position to restore.)

3. After the fgetc the position is 42, not 41. To read index 99 you need fseek(f, 57, SEEK_CUR) or, unambiguously, fseek(f, 99, SEEK_SET). This is the off-by-one in the fseek.c demo: 58 from SEEK_CUR lands on index 100, the 101st byte, not the 100th.

4. Both produce a file that reads identically — a million zeros then an x. The seek version creates a sparse file: the file system records a hole in the inode and allocates almost no blocks, so ls -l says ~1 MB and du says ~8 KB. Writing the zeros explicitly allocates a real megabyte. Same contents, hugely different storage — this is create_gigantic_file.c at small scale.

Set 4 — permissions
  1. Translate both ways: rwxr-x--- to octal, and 640 to the ls -l string.
  2. A directory is drwx--x--x. As "other", can you ls it? Can you cat a file inside it whose name you already know and which is rw-r--r--? Explain both.
  3. A file you do not own is rw-rw-rw-, and the directory it sits in is rwxr-xr-x owned by someone else. Can you edit the file? Can you delete it?
  4. Why are permissions written in octal rather than hexadecimal?
Show the answers

1. rwx r-x --- = 111 101 000 = 750. 640 = 110 100 000 = rw-r-----.

2. No to ls — listing names needs r on the directory, and other has only x. Yes to cat — x is what permits traversing into the directory to reach an entry, and the file itself grants you read. This is the 711 pattern: a directory you can fetch from but not browse.

3. Yes, you can edit it — w for other is set on the file. No, you cannot delete it — deleting removes a name from the directory, which needs w on the directory, and other has only r-x there. Permissions on the file and on its directory answer different questions.

4. Because the bits come in groups of three, and one octal digit is exactly three bits. A hex digit is four, so it would straddle the user/group/other boundaries and no digit would line up with anything meaningful.

Set 5 — inodes and links
  1. ln a b, then rm a. Is the data still reachable? Now instead ln -s a b, then rm a. Same question, and what does cat b print?
  2. You have two path names. Write the test that decides whether they are the same file. Why is comparing st_ino alone not enough?
  3. Why can a hard link not cross a file system, and why can a symbolic link?
  4. A program is writing to big.log. You rm big.log and df shows no space freed. Explain, using st_nlink.
  5. A brand-new empty directory has st_nlink == 2. Where are the two links? What happens to the number when you mkdir a subdirectory inside it?
Show the answers

1. Hard link: yes — st_nlink drops from 2 to 1, b still names the same inode, the data is untouched. There was never an "original" to lose. Symbolic link: no — b still exists but now dangles; cat b prints No such file or directory, because the kernel resolves the stored string a and finds nothing. ls -l still shows the arrow; ls in some shells colours it red.

2. stat both and compare st_dev and st_ino together. Inode numbers are only unique within one file system, and a running machine has several mounted, so two unrelated files on different file systems can share an i-number.

3. A hard link is a directory entry pointing at an inode number, and inode numbers are meaningful only within the file system that owns the table — the number would be ambiguous elsewhere. A symbolic link stores a path string, which is resolved from the root and therefore means the same thing everywhere.

4. rm is unlink: it removed the name and took st_nlink to 0, but the inode and its data blocks are only reclaimed when the link count is zero and no process holds an open descriptor. The writer still has one, so the file lives on with no name. Space returns when the program exits. (This is also a tidy trick: a program can create a file, unlink it immediately, and keep a private scratch file no other process can open.)

5. Its name in the parent directory, and its own . entry. Each subdirectory adds one more, because the child's .. is a third hard link back — so st_nlink on a directory is 2 + (number of subdirectories). These are the only directory hard links that exist, and the kernel makes them itself.

Set 6 — stat and directories
  1. latest.txt is a symbolic link to a 4096-byte file report.txt. What does stat("latest.txt", &s) report for s.st_size, and what does lstat report? Why those numbers?
  2. A regular file is rw-r--r--. Write st_mode in octal. Write the test for "the owner may execute this".
  3. Why must a recursive directory walker use lstat rather than stat?
  4. mkdir("a/b/c/d", 0755) fails. List all four things that could be wrong.
  5. What does readdir give you about each entry, and what does it not? What must you call to get the rest, and what do you have to build first?
Show the answers

1. stat follows the link and reports 4096 — the size of report.txt. lstat reports the size of the link itself, which is the length of the stored path string: "report.txt" is 10 characters, so 10. A symlink's contents are its target's name.

2. S_IFREG | 0644 = 0100000 | 0644 = 0100644. The test is if (s.st_mode & S_IXUSR). Use the macro S_ISREG(s.st_mode) for the type rather than masking by hand — the type is a multi-bit field, not a flag.

3. Because stat follows symbolic links, so a symlink pointing at an ancestor directory would send the walk round the same subtree forever. lstat reports on the link itself, letting you see S_ISLNK and decline to descend. "Important not to get stuck in infinite loops."

4. (i) one of a, b, c does not exist — mkdir creates one level only; (ii) c is not writable by you, so you cannot add an entry to it; (iii) d already exists → EEXIST; (iv) you lack execute permission on one of the directories along the path, so the lookup cannot even reach c.

5. readdir gives you d_ino and d_name — the (name, i-number) pair, which is genuinely all a directory stores. It does not give you size, permissions, owner, timestamps or reliably the type. For those, call stat (or lstat) — and you must first build the path by joining the directory you passed to opendir with d_name, because d_name is a bare component, not a path.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slide 40)

Two halves that turn out to be one idea. The first half finished stdio.h by showing what the buffer costs you as well as what it buys: 390× fewer boundary crossings, and a program that can die with your last 4095 bytes still in an array. fflush is the escape hatch. Then seeking gave the descriptor's position a name and made it settable, which is the difference between a file you can append to and a file you can edit — r+, fseek, ftell, and the trick of stepping back one byte to overwrite the one you just read.

The second half went underneath all of it. A file is bytes; a directory is a list of (name, i-number) pairs; an inode holds everything else — type, size, owner, the nine permission bits, three timestamps, and where the data actually sits. Once the name is separated from the file, hard links and symbolic links stop being two flavours of the same thing and become two genuinely different mechanisms: a second entry pointing at the same inode, versus a small file containing a path. stat hands you the entire inode as a struct; opendir and readdir hand you the directory as a stream, in exactly the shape fopen and fgetc taught you.

The through-line, if you want one sentence. A file descriptor answers which bytes and where in them; an inode answers everything about those bytes except the bytes; a directory answers what we call them. Every function in this lecture belongs to exactly one of those three, and knowing which one tells you what it can and cannot do.
Coming up next (slide 40). "Next week we're going to look at Unicode, processes. Fun times." Unicode picks up the thread from §01 — what a byte with value 255 means when it is meant to be text — which the lecturer flagged during the fputc(255, f) demo: "we'll talk about what this means in, I think, next lecture." Processes pick up the other thread: the file descriptor table is per-process, and it is about to matter that a process can make another one. → Week 8 Lecture 1: text encoding & Unicode.
TL;DR · stdio buffers so it can make one system call per 4096, not one per byte — 10 MB byte-at-a-time: libc 1m2.9s vs stdio 0m0.16s, nearly all of it sys · write() happens on: buffer full, newline if line-buffered, fflush, fclose, normal exit — a crash prevents the last two and the data is gone · stderr is unbuffered on purpose · fprintf(f,"%d",255) = 3 bytes, fputc(255,f) = 1 · "w" truncates, "a" appends, r+ reads and writes without truncating · lseek(fd,off,whence) returns the new position or −1; fseek(f,off,whence) returns 0 or −1; ftell is "where am I" · SEEK_SET / SEEK_CUR / SEEK_END · lseek(fd,0,SEEK_END) = the size · past the end is legal and reads as zeros (sparse files); before the start is an error · reading a byte moves the position, so fseek(f,-1,SEEK_CUR) before you overwrite it — that is fuzz.c, plus byte ^ (1 << bit) · file = named sequence of bytes, no type; directory = set of (name, i-number) pairs; file system = names → locations, plus metadata · names may contain any byte except 0x00 and 0x2F /; max usually 255; . and .. are taken · absolute paths start with /, relative ones resolve against the process's CWD · inodes hold location, type, size, ownership, permissions, timestamps — not the name; ls -i prints the i-number; unique per file system, so identity is (st_dev, st_ino) · open = scan directory → inode table → permission check → touch atime → read contents · permissions are 9 bits, 3 octal digits, user/group/other, r=4 w=2 x=1; 755 = rwxr-xr-x; on a directory r = list, w = create/delete/rename, x = enter — so deleting needs write on the directory · chmod 700 f.txt · hard link = same inode, same file system, not for directories, equal status, data dies with the last one; symlink = a file containing a path, crosses file systems, works on directories, lrwxrwxrwx, dangles if the target goes · stat follows symlinks, lstat does not, fstat takes an fd — all return 0 or −1 · st_mode = type | permissions, e.g. 0100644; use S_ISREG/S_ISDIR/S_ISLNK, print with %o · st_nlink is the hard-link count; a new directory starts at 2 · mkdir(path, 0755) makes one level, parent must be writable, target must not exist · opendir/readdir/closedir mirror fopen/fgetc/fclose; struct dirent gives you only d_ino and d_name · unlink removes a name, not a file · everything is a file: disks, devices, /proc, pipes, sockets — but lseek fails on the ones that are only streams · next: Unicode, then processes.

Two places these notes correct the source, both flagged in place. (1) Seeking before the start of a file. Slide 13 and the lecture both say it is an error, which matches POSIX — lseek returns −1 with EINVAL. The course's own files notes say instead that it "sets position to start of file", which is wrong; §06 follows the slide. (2) The "100th byte" in fseek.c. The fgetc after fseek(in, 41, SEEK_SET) advances the position to 42, so fseek(in, 58, SEEK_CUR) lands at 100 and the next fgetc reads the 101st byte, not the 100th. §07 keeps the demo as written and puts the arithmetic beside it; Lab 4 lets you step it.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 8 — Lecture 1

Text encoding: how a number becomes a letter, and why that took two hundred years to get right

The first half closes out files — the four recap questions from the board, then mkdir, opendir/readdir and the rest of the POSIX toolkit, ending on everything is a file. The second half asks a question the course has been quietly dodging since Week 1: you know how to represent an unsigned integer, a signed integer and a float — so how do you represent an A? The answer is a lookup table, not a formula, and the story runs from a telegraph with five needles and no letter Q, through Morse code, through ASCII and the teletype it was designed to drive, through the code-page chaos that gave us mojibake, to Unicode — 1,114,112 code points — and the encoding that made it practical: UTF-8, variable width, 1 to 4 bytes, ASCII-compatible for free. You will encode € and 字 and 😀 by hand, and then decode a byte string back.

Sections §01–§04 here finish that thread — four recap questions and the last few POSIX calls. From §05 the lecture changes subject completely and starts a new one: how text is represented. It is the last piece of the "how is data stored" arc that began with integers and continued through floating point. Next lecture: processes.
Four questions from the board

Recap: what exactly lands in the file? (slides 3–4)

Two files open for writing, FILE *f1 and FILE *f2. The question is deliberately narrow: which bytes end up on disk, in what order, and what does the call return? It introduces one function the course had not used yet.

The new function — fwrite

"We're using this command fwrite, which I don't think we looked at… so let's look at the man pages, see what they say." Which is the actual lesson of the segment: you will have man pages in the exam, so practise reading them now.

size_t fwrite(const void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);
size_t fread (void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, FILE *stream);
ParameterMeaning
ptrAddress of the bytes to write. Not a string — a raw void *, so anything at all can go through it.
sizeSize of one item, in bytes.
nmembHow many such items.
streamThe open FILE *.
returnsThe number of items written — not bytes. Fewer than nmemb means an error.

"It's kind of similar to fputc, except we can say how many bytes we're putting in — so rather than one byte at a time, we can say put in two bytes or three bytes." The total number of bytes moved is always size × nmemb; the split between the two is your choice, and it only changes the return value.

Question 1 — two ways to write the same two bytes
uint8_t data[] = {0xAB, 0xCD};
size_t n = fwrite(&data, 1, 2, f1);

Two items of one byte each. The file gets AB CD, in that order, because that is the order they sit in the array. n == 2 — two items written.

uint16_t x = 0xABCD;
size_t n = fwrite(&x, 2, 1, f2);

One item of two bytes. On CSE's x86 machines the file gets CD AB — backwards. n == 1 — one item written. Same two bytes of data, different order, different return value.

Why the second one flips. fwrite copies the object's bytes out of memory exactly as they lie there, and on a little-endian machine a uint16_t lies least-significant-byte first. This is Week 2's endianness, showing up somewhere you did not ask it to. "If the file isn't big-endian or little-endian in this case, then it's going to flip the bytes and we're going to get the wrong thing written down."

Question 2 — is this portable? (slide 4)
uint16_t x = 0xABCD;

uint8_t low_byte  = x & 0xFF;   // 0xCD
uint8_t high_byte = (x >> 8);    // 0xAB
fputc(low_byte,  f3);
fputc(high_byte, f3);

It writes CD AB, and yes — it is portable. That is the whole point of the question, and it is the opposite of the intuition most people have. The bytes come out in that order on every machine, because you never asked the machine where its bytes live: & 0xFF means "the low eight bits of the value" and >> 8 means "the next eight bits of the value", and shifting and masking are defined on values, not on memory layout. You chose little-endian on purpose, by hand.

"This is a way to make your code portable, putting one byte in at a time… writing bytes at a time means that you're not going to get into trouble with endians. It means you're not going to get into trouble with different types of encodings, which we're going to look at later today." That last clause is the hinge of the whole lecture: a file format is a byte-order agreement plus a character-encoding agreement, and both of them have to be written down.

The class of bug this is. "These sorts of things, if you don't pick up on them, can really lead to errors that you don't notice later on." Nothing crashes. The file is written, the program exits 0, and the corruption only shows up when someone reads it on a different machine — or, worse, when your own reader makes the same mistake in reverse and the round trip appears to work.
A slide typo worth knowing about. Slide 3 writes uint8_t data = {0xAB, 0xCD}; — a scalar with a two-element initialiser, which is not valid C (clang will warn about excess elements and leave data == 0xAB). It should be uint8_t data[] = {0xAB, 0xCD};, which is what the demo actually ran and what is written above. The question the slide is asking is unaffected.
fwrite — what actually lands on disk

Written live, from the man page up

Recap: print the middle byte of a file (slide 5 · live demo)

One sentence on the slide, and a whole program built from nothing in front of the room. It is a good exercise precisely because the file's length is not known in advance — you have to ask the file how long it is, and the only way to do that is to seek to the end and look at where you landed.

The two functions, from the man page
int  fseek(FILE *stream, long offset, int whence);
long ftell(FILE *stream);
whencePosition becomesThe lecture's reading
SEEK_SEToffset"You're going from the start. fseek(f, 0, SEEK_SET) would be zero bytes from the start of the file."
SEEK_CURcurrent + offset"Where you currently are in the file… you might go a certain number of bytes and then do a SEEK_CUR, and then you can maybe change the byte there."
SEEK_ENDsize + offset"You go back to the end of the file — and this offset could be negative, so you go to the end and then back five or six bytes."

fseek returns 0 on success and −1 on failure; ftell returns the current offset, which is the only reason the size trick works. Full treatment, including lseek and what happens past the end of the file, is in Week 7 Lecture 2 §06–§07.

The program, in the order it was typed
FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "r");        // read only — we're not changing anything

fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END);                  // 1. jump to the end
long bytes = ftell(f);                  // 2. where am I? → that's the size
printf("the file has %ld bytes\n", bytes);

long middle = bytes / 2;                 // 3. integer division — it just rounds

fseek(f, middle, SEEK_SET);             // 4. back to the start, then forward
int c = fgetc(f);                       // 5. read that one byte
printf("byte %ld is 0x%x\n", middle, c);

fclose(f);                              // 6. don't forget

Step 2 is the idea. There is no filesize() in stdio. ftell after SEEK_END is the file size, because the position at the end of a file is exactly the number of bytes in it. On the run in the lecture the middle came out at offset 277 holding 0x64 — "which I think is 100 integer", and it is: 0x64 = 100 = the character 'd'.

And the closing note, which is not really about this program. "Don't forget to close the file once you've opened it… you might want to access the file from somewhere else and then it's locked, and — worst case — you've opened so many files that you've run out of file descriptors and really bad things have [happened]." A process has a finite descriptor table. Leaking one per iteration of a loop is a real and common way to kill a long-running program.
Two rounding details the demo glosses over. For a file of even length there is no single middle byte — bytes / 2 picks the first of the two middle bytes (0-indexed, so for 10 bytes it reads index 5, the sixth byte). And for an empty file, bytes == 0, middle == 0, and fgetc returns EOF — which prints as 0xffffffff with %x, because EOF is -1. Check for it.
