Two questions, one on the shell and one in C

Recap: chmod 755 f — and checking it from code (slide 6 · live demo)

Part A is a reading exercise; part B is the reason stat exists. Both were answered by a student from the floor before the slide had finished.

A — does "others" get execute?

Yes. Nine bits, three groups of three, rwx each, most significant first:

chmod 755 f

  7        5        5
 111      101      101
 rwx      r-x      r-x
owner    group    others
                   ^^^
        others: read = yes, write = no, execute = yes

"Seven octal is going to give us three bits — so that means we can read, we can write, we can execute. Now five is 101, so that means we can read and we can execute." Note the ordering is fixed and worth memorising: r is 4, w is 2, x is 1, and the columns run owner → group → others left to right. Full treatment in Week 7 Lecture 2 §12.

The live ls -l, which makes it concrete

The lecturer listed the course directory and read the permissions off it. Two different pictures in the same listing:

What you sawModeWhat it means for you, as "other"
the ordinary course files775"I can read, write, execute and my group can read, write, execute… so that would be a 775." You get r-x: you can read them and list into them.
test1, test2, test3700-ish"You guys are others — you can't read or execute these files." Which is the point of the demo later in §04, where chmod from C makes them readable in front of you.
data764Read for you. stat data reported size 455, 8 blocks, regular file, one inode number, and the access rights as rw-rw-r--.
B — how do I check that from C?

Two layers, and the lecture showed both. First the shell command — stat data — then the same information through the system call of the same name.

#include <sys/stat.h>

struct stat s;
if (stat(pathname, &s) != 0) { perror(pathname); return 1; }

printf("size  %ld\n", (long)s.st_size);
printf("mode  %o\n",  s.st_mode);          // octal!

if (S_ISREG(s.st_mode)) printf("regular file\n");
if (s.st_mode & S_IRUSR) printf("owner can read\n");
if (s.st_mode & S_IXOTH) printf("others can execute\n");   // ← the answer to A

S_IXOTH is the answer. It is the single bit that chmod 755's last digit turned on. "You can use these as defined terms to then ask questions about the file… it's kind of like a mini stat. stat gave us a lot of information; this just pulls out some stuff that we asked." The header is <sys/stat.h>, and reading it is genuinely useful — "this header will give us the definition of the stat structure."

The word that went missing, live. Working through struct stat, the lecturer described hard links ("you share the inode number, and if it deletes somewhere then it deletes everywhere"), then reached for the other kind and came up short: "the other types of links which I've forgotten what it's called — virtual — anyway, the other type has its own inode number… The word I was looking for was symbolic." Both are in W7L2 §13, and the distinction is exactly as described: a hard link shares the inode, a symbolic link has one of its own.
The last of the file system, at speed

Directories, the POSIX toolkit, and "everything is a file" (slides 7–10 · live demos)

Four slides that mostly re-run last lecture's material with the demos actually working this time. What is new is the framing: every one of these exists twice — once as a shell command you already use, and once as a C function with almost the same name.

mkdir — and the demo that failed usefully (slide 7 · mkdir.c)
int mkdir(const char *pathname, mode_t mode);   // 0 on success, -1 and errno otherwise

mkdir("newDir", 0755);
RuleDetail
one level onlyFor a/b/c/d, the directories a, b and c must already exist. mkdir is not mkdir -p.
parent writablec must be writable by you — creating d means adding an entry to c.
target must not existd must not already exist, or you get EEXIST.
two free entriesThe new directory already contains . (itself) and .. (its parent). You get them whether you want them or not.

The demo. "So I tried to make a directory called Bob, but Bob exists" — the error path firing correctly on the first run, which is a better demonstration than success. Retried as hob, it worked. Then the aside that is worth chasing: the new directory showed up as 770, not the 0755 passed in. That is umask: the process's file-creation mask clears bits from the mode you request, so the mode argument is a maximum, not a guarantee. "This is just making sure that I have access to be able to do this, not that it's going to give those permissions."

Reading a directory — the third stream type (slide 8 · list_directory.c)
#include <dirent.h>

DIR           *opendir(const char *name);   // open a directory stream
struct dirent *readdir(DIR *dirp);         // next entry, or NULL at the end
int            closedir(DIR *dirp);        // close it

DIR *d = opendir(argv[1]);
if (d == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; }

struct dirent *e;
while ((e = readdir(d)) != NULL)
    printf("%8lu  %s\n", (unsigned long)e->d_ino, e->d_name);

closedir(d);

"Even though everything is a file, directories have kind of different information stored about them… it's a struct that is kind of specific for a directory." Run on . it printed the inode number and the name of every entry — which is all a directory stores. Everything else (size, permissions, timestamps) requires a separate stat call on the joined path. Note the shape: opendir / readdir / closedir is deliberately fopen / fgetc / fclose with the nouns changed. Found in man 3.

The rest of the toolkit (slide 9)
C functionDoes whatShell equivalent
chmod(path, mode)change permissionschmod
unlink(path)remove a name — the file goes when the last name and the last open descriptor dorm
rename(old, new)rename or movemv
chdir(path)change the process's working directorycd
getcwd(buf, size)ask where you arepwd
link(old, new)hard link — a second name for the same inodeln
symlink(target, path)symbolic link — a small file containing a pathln -s

Demos on the slide, most deferred to the course website for time: chmod.c, rm.c, rename.c, my_cd.c, getcwd.c, nest_directories.c, many_links.c, chain_links.c. "We try to keep a library of everything… this is where you'll find some model code that you can use. Sometimes I fall over with which header files I need to include — so this is a good place to come check what you need for that."

The chmod demo, run on the room

The best moment of the first half, because the audience could verify it themselves. test1 and test2 were unreadable to the class; the program made them readable while everyone watched.

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    char *end;
    long mode = strtol(argv[1], &end, 8);   // base 8 — it's an octal mode
    if (*end != '\0') { fprintf(stderr, "bad mode\n"); return 1; }

    if (chmod(argv[2], (mode_t)mode) != 0) { perror(argv[2]); return 1; }
    return 0;
}

Base 8 is the detail that bites. strtol(argv[1], &end, 8) — if you pass 10 there, chmod 755 sets mode 0o1363 and you will spend a while wondering why. "So before I did it, test1 — you couldn't even see it was there. Now you should be able to read it."

Man page sections — the numbering, explained properly. This came up because chmod exists in two of them, and it is worth writing down. "Level one is sort of at that Unix/Linux level. Level two is our standard C library and level three is our standard I/O C library functions that have a lot more portability and sort of optimization built into them so that they don't make so many system calls."
SectionWhat lives thereExample
man 1Shell commands you typeman 1 chmod
man 2System calls — thin wrappers that cross into the kernelman 2 chmod, man 2 stat
man 3Library functions — stdio and friends, buffered, portableman 3 fseek, man 3 opendir

Strictly, man 3 is the whole C library rather than stdio specifically, and man 2 entries are themselves thin libc wrappers around the real syscall — but the working distinction the lecture draws is the right one: section 2 crosses the boundary, section 3 mostly avoids it. That is why fgetc is 390× faster than a read loop (W7L2 §02).

Everything is a file (slide 10)

"Originally the file system only managed data stored on a magnetic disk." It grew. The Unix philosophy is that if you can name it, you can open it, and then read and write already work on it.

CategoryWhere you meet it
filesThe obvious case.
directories§04 above — a file whose contents are (name, inode) pairs.
storage devices/dev/sda. dd reads a raw disk with the same calls that read a text file.
peripherals"If you plug something in to a POSIX-type system, a Linux-type system, you'll see that a new directory is created for that device… it will then have an inode associated with it."
system information/proc — cat /proc/cpuinfo reads a file that does not exist on any disk.
inter-process communicationPipes and FIFOs. Next lecture's territory.
networkSockets — a descriptor you read and write, though lseek on one fails.

"If you go on further in your degree and do driver writing, compiler writing, operating systems — all these really detailed things — you'll start to look at [this] in a lot more depth." The payoff of the abstraction is that a program which copies a file also copies a keyboard to a network socket, without being recompiled.

From the break — the fourth octal digit. A student asked what the setuid bit does on a file that is not executable. The answer, correctly given from the floor: a Unix mode is really four octal digits, and the leading one carries setuid (4), setgid (2) and the sticky bit (1). "If the first digit is four, that's a setuid bit, which means that — at least for executables — you always run with the effective user ID of the user that owns it." On a non-executable file it does essentially nothing; on a directory, setgid still matters (new entries inherit the directory's group), and the sticky bit is what makes /tmp safe — mode 1777, so anyone can create a file there but only the owner can delete their own. The honest summary from the room: "generally it's not going to make much difference — it's a bit of a throwback."
Second half — a new subject entirely

How should we represent text? (slides 11–13)

Every representation this course has taught you so far is a formula. Text is the one that isn't, and that turns out to change everything about it.

WHAT YOU ALREADY HAVE

Three representations, all arithmetic

unsignedRaw binary. 100 = 11001002. W4L1
signedTwo's complement. −745 = 111…101000101112. W4L1
realIEEE 754. 3.14159 = sign, exponent, mantissa. W5L1

All three are computable. Give me the number and I can derive the bits with a pen. Nothing needs to be looked up, and nothing needs to be agreed.

WHAT IS MISSING

Text

"Text is arguably the most important data type… and it's just important because at the end of the day, someone reads the output of what your file is doing."

And it subsumes the rest. Turning objects into text is called serialization — JSON, XML, YAML — and it is how most systems talk to each other. The slide names the reason it wins: no endianness issues like binary formats. A JSON number is the characters 255, and those characters mean the same thing on every machine, which is exactly the guarantee §01 had to be built by hand.

The chain the lecture builds. Text is a sequence of characters → so we need a way to encode one character → once we can do that, an array of them is a string. "This is how we represent text in C. Other languages use more complex structures than arrays, but the basics are the same." Everything from here is about the middle step, and it is the only step where the answer is a table rather than a formula.

So: how? "By default in C and MIPS we have used ASCII… modern computers use something called Unicode to represent the individual characters. But other things came before." And a disclaimer that the notes repeat more strongly than the slides: this timeline is very Western-centric. "There are many other encoding schemes from around the world" — and specifically, the course notes add, East Asian languages have very interesting encoding schemes of their own, because a writing system with tens of thousands of characters poses a completely different problem from one with twenty-six.

Two encodings from before the computer

The telegraph, Morse code, and the two lessons they teach (slide 14 · course notes 7–15)

These are not history for its own sake. Each one demonstrates exactly one property that ASCII and UTF-8 later inherit — and the lecture is explicit that people have been doing this "from very early on in caves."

Cooke and Wheatstone, 1837 — five needles, twenty letters

The five-needle telegraph put five magnetic needles on a board. One needle deflected left, another right, and the letter was where the two pointed — you read it off a diamond grid painted behind them.

ConstraintConsequence
only 20 charactersC, J, Q, U, X and Z were simply omitted. Operators spelled around them. The alphabet was negotiable; the wire was not.
one wire per needleConnecting two telegraphs 1 km apart needed 5 km of wire. Wire was the entire cost of the system.
a shared circuitThe whole thing was one circuit — one needle carried the positive voltage, one the negative — which is why exactly two deflect at a time.
wires brokeAnd when one did, they did not replace it — they switched to a new encoding that needed fewer wires. The code was cheaper to change than the infrastructure.

Formally it is a 5-trit ternary encoding (a trit being base 3 what a bit is to base 2): each needle is left, right, or still. "Hello" comes out as 120003, 102003, 000123, 000123, 002103 — 135, 99, 5, 5, 21 in decimal. Five trits gives 35 = 243 possible values of which 20 were used: an 8.23% efficiency. Hold on to that number; the argument in §13 for abandoning UTF-32 is the same argument.

The lesson, and it is the most important sentence in the section. Character encoding is done by a lookup table — not a mathematical expression like two's complement or IEEE 754. There is no derivation for why A is 65. Someone decided, wrote it down, and everyone else agreed. Every argument in the rest of this lecture is therefore an argument about which table, and every bug is two programs using different tables.
Morse code, 1844 — and a problem it creates

Dots and dashes. "Dots are short taps and dashes are elongated taps." Write dot as 0 and dash as 1 and encode "Hello":

LetterMorseBinaryDecimal
H····00000
E·00
L·—··01004
L·—··01004
O———1117

H and E are both 0. That is not a mistake in the table — it is the defining property of a variable length encoding: one zero and four zeros are different values, and the number alone cannot tell you which you have. You also need the length. This is precisely the problem UTF-8 has to solve in §14, and it solves it by putting the length inside the first byte.

Why Morse is not really binary at all
time is part of itA dot is one unit, a dash is three. Both are "on", so both are 1 in any naive binary reading — they differ only in duration. Unlike the five-needle telegraph, where all five trits went at once, Morse sends sequentially.
the gaps carry meaning1 unit between parts of a letter, 3 between letters, 7 between words. "One of the biggest problems is where you put the spaces between each character that you want to send." Silence is data.
it is frequency-optimisedLetter lengths are inversely proportional to how common the letter is. E is one dot; Q is four symbols. This is Huffman coding, a century early.
standardised in 1848International Morse has not changed since — which makes it memorisable, and memorisable makes it fast for a trained operator. It also makes it impossible to improve. There are still several variants: American (Morse), Continental (Gerke), International (ITU).

Two lessons, and UTF-8 takes both. (1) Standardisation is good — it lets different people in different places communicate at all. (2) Variable length encodings are efficient, in bits and in time, because common things get short codes — but they are more complex. That trade is the entire content of §14.

The context the lecture puts around it. "Nowadays we kind of don't realise how mind-blowing that must have been back in the day. You could send a message that might have taken days by horse — you could do it within seconds. So even though we think our times are changing very quickly, that would have been an absolutely massive thing for most humans." And on the gap between 1897 and 1943: "certainly a couple of world wars were actually quite useful in terms of improving how quickly we send information."
Seven bits, 128 values, all of them used

ASCII: 1963 (slides 15, 18–19)

American Standard Code for Information Interchange. Created by the American Standards Association, which became ANSI — "the first organization to standardize the C programming language", which is why you still see the phrase "ANSI C".

THE SHAPE OF IT
7 bitsFixed size. Not 8 — the eighth bit was free, and §10 is the story of what people did with it.
128 values0x00 to 0x7F.
all usedThere is no spare room. "It's completely full." Nothing can be added to ASCII, ever.
WHY 128 IS NOT ENOUGH

"If you think about today, probably all of you have sent an emoji to someone today. I've probably done like 300 already — and it's not even three [pm]." Uppercase, lowercase, digits, punctuation, then every other writing system on Earth, then emoji. "We've got a lot of characters that we want to send."

The layout — "sticks" (slides 18–19)

ASCII is split into eight sticks of sixteen characters. The word is a hangover from the physical hardware; what matters is that the sticks are not arbitrary.

SticksCodesContents
0–10x00–0x1FControl characters — '\0', '\n', '\t', BEL. Not printable, and §08 is why they exist.
20x20–0x2FSpace first, then punctuation. Space leads the stick deliberately — it is both a control character and a printable one, and putting it lowest makes sorting strings by ASCII value behave the way people expect.
30x30–0x39The digits '0'–'9', then a few more punctuation marks.
4–50x41–0x5AUppercase 'A'–'Z' (65–90), plus brackets and friends.
6–70x61–0x7ALowercase 'a'–'z' (97–122), plus the rest, ending at DEL.

The course notes add a nice observation: sticks 2–5 are a usable alphabet by themselves — space, punctuation, digits and uppercase letters, in 64 codes, which is what a 6-bit machine could manage. And "the next several characters [after space] are commonly used as word separators", again by placement rather than by accident.

Reading the 1963 table. The original printed chart is transposed from how you would draw it now — columns are the high bits, rows the low. And, as the lecture noticed: "back in the 60s when this came about, they hadn't embraced starting with a zero", so the bits are numbered from 1. Two other things visible on it: NUL is all zeros, and BEL is 0000111 — "which is still here. I don't know what anyone uses this for. It's probably used by someone, because it's there." (It still rings: printf("\a").) And the gap that mattered: there is no £, "so even the UK couldn't really use ASCII."
the ASCII table — all 128 of it

Lab 3 · The table, and the patterns hiding in it

Eight sticks across, sixteen rows down — the layout the standard actually specifies. Click any cell for its full details. The highlight buttons colour a group; case pairs draws the link between each letter and its opposite case, which is the pattern §09 exploits.

control punctuation digits uppercase lowercase
Thirty-three codes that are not characters

Control characters, the teletype, DEL and ^C (slides 16–17 · course notes 21–25)

The single most useful fact about ASCII's design: when it was created, computers did not have monitors. Every oddity in the first two sticks follows from that.

What a computer's output device was in 1963

A teletype — an electromechanical typewriter with a keyboard for input and a printer for output, drivable either by a human typing or by a computer sending codes. "These could be controlled by a human (typing) or by a computer (printing)."

Because it was a physical device, it had to be physically controlled. So the encoding needed codes that were not letters at all but instructions to the machinery:

CodeNameWhat it physically did
0x0DCRCarriage return — slam the print head back to the left margin.
0x0ALFLine feed — roll the paper up one line.
0x07BELRing the bell. An actual bell.
0x08BSBackspace — move left one, without erasing anything.
0x09HTHorizontal tab — advance to the next mechanical tab stop.

And this is why Windows line endings are \r\n. On a teletype you genuinely needed both instructions, in that order: return the carriage and feed the line. Unix decided one code could imply both and kept only \n; DOS kept the pair. Half a century of text-file incompatibility descends from a decision about a printer.

The lecturer's own footnote on the bell. "Has anyone ever played with a mechanical typewriter? When you go back to the new line, it goes bing and then you start typing again. Bing, start typing again. I used a mechanical typewriter when I did my primary school assignments, so I've had the joy of the ding. But even though there's no dinging any more — which is, you know, sad for humankind — these actual functionalities have been encoded." Also offered, on printers that would not die: "my father-in-law is an accountant and he still insists on his calculators having this little reel of paper that comes out with the calculation. It's insane, but this is how people were used to getting output from computers."
Why DEL is 127 — and why that is the only value it could be

This is in the course notes rather than the slides, and it is the best single story about why encodings look the way they do.

Data was stored on punch cards. Punching a hole makes a physical, permanent change to the card. So deleting was not possible — you cannot un-punch a hole.

The workaround: define a special character that means "ignore this", and give it the bit pattern with every bit set:

DEL = 0b1111111 = 127 = 0x7F   // all seven bits on

To delete a character you punch out all seven columns. Whatever was there before becomes unrecoverable, because every hole that could exist now does. DEL is at the very top of the table because 127 is the only value that is a superset of every other value. It is not a choice about ordering — it is forced.

Why ^C interrupts a program

You press it every day. The reason it is C and not, say, K for "kill" is pure 1963 hardware.

1On a teletype, Ctrl cleared the high bits — so ^@, ^A, ^B, ^C typed control codes 0, 1, 2, 3. It makes sense on a typewriter, where the keys are in alphabetical order.
2So ^C is the fourth control character (index 3).
3Control character 3 is ETX — End of Text.
4ETX told the teletype to stop receiving data. Which, when the thing sending the data is your program, means: stop the program.

Modern terminals turn it into SIGINT, and a well-behaved program dies. The keystroke outlived the machine, the protocol and the reason — but not the number. And the same logic gives you ^D for end-of-input: control character 4 is EOT, End of Transmission.

Where you still meet control characters. '\0' terminates every C string (NUL, 0). '\n' ends lines and flushes a line-buffered stream (W7L2 §04). '\t' is still a tab stop. \a still rings. And 0x1B — ESC — is the first byte of every ANSI escape sequence, which is how the coloured terminal output in these notes is produced: it is a control character introducing a command that a device is meant to obey.
Where the lookup table becomes almost arithmetic

The patterns deliberately built into ASCII (slides 19–22 · demos ASCII_to_DEC.c, ASCII_case_insensitive.c)

ASCII is a lookup table, but it was laid out with intent, and the intent shows up as bit patterns you can exploit. This is where the section pays off in code you will actually write.

Pattern 1 — digits are 0b011 followed by their own value
'0' = 0x30 = 0b011 0000      '5' = 0x35 = 0b011 0101
'1' = 0x31 = 0b011 0001      '7' = 0x37 = 0b011 0111
'2' = 0x32 = 0b011 0010      '9' = 0x39 = 0b011 1001
                 ^^^   ^^^^
              prefix   the digit, in binary

"It wouldn't make that much sense to encode a seven without having the seven as a binary in there somewhere." Which gives you two ways to convert, and they are exactly equivalent for valid input:

arithmetic
int ascii_to_dec_sub(char c) {
    return c - '0';
}
char dec_to_ascii_add(int d) {
    return d + '0';
}
bitwise
int ascii_to_dec_bit(char c) {
    return c & 0x0F;   // keep low nibble
}
char dec_to_ascii_bit(int d) {
    return d | 0x30;   // add the prefix
}

Watch the constant. The lecturer talked himself into and out of two wrong values live — "we just want to or it with 20. Sorry — we want to or it with three. I know why I said 20. No, we want to or it with 3F… Oh, we don't want to do F, we want to do a zero. Three zero." The reasoning is worth following: OR-ing with 0x3F would set the low four bits too and turn every digit into '?'; you want 0x30, because OR with 0 leaves a bit alone and you only want to add the prefix. "So whatever is the x, we just want it to carry through."

Pattern 2 — upper and lower case differ by exactly one bit
'A' = 65 = 0b1000001        'a' = 97 = 0b1100001
'B' = 66 = 0b1000010        'b' = 98 = 0b1100010
'Z' = 90 = 0b1011010        'z' =122 = 0b1111010
              ^                        ^
        this bit — value 32 = 0x20 — and nothing else

That single bit is worth 32, which is why 'A' + 32 == 'a'. But addition is the fragile way to say it, because it only works in one direction. The robust forms:

OperationEffectSafe?
c | 0x20force lowercaseIdempotent — already-lowercase stays put. The right tool for case-insensitive comparison.
c & ~0x20force uppercaseAlso idempotent.
c ^ 0x20toggle the caseBoth directions in one operation — but applying it to something already in the target case flips it the wrong way.
c + 32upper → lowerone direction only, and silently wrong on anything that is not a letter

The demo used XOR, and explained why. "If I XOR zero with a zero then I get a zero, and if I XOR with a one then I get a one… so I'm going to be flipping this fifth bit by doing that." And the case-insensitive compare used OR instead: "because that fifth bit is set… it means that's always going to be one. So then all the other letters, if they're going to be equal, then this isn't going to be thrown." Forcing both sides to lowercase and comparing is exactly strcasecmp.

The range check is not optional. Both demos guard the letter range first — "we're making sure that the string exists between A and Z, otherwise you're getting into other things in the ASCII table and I cannot tell you what will happen." He is right to be nervous. '[' ^ 0x20 is '{'. '@' | 0x20 is '`'. '5' ^ 0x20 is 0x15, a control character. The trick works only on A–Z and a–z, and produces plausible-looking garbage everywhere else. In real code use <ctype.h>: toupper, tolower, isalpha.
"Fifth bit" or "sixth bit"? The slides say the fifth, the course notes say the sixth, and both are describing the same bit — the one worth 32 = 0x20. Counting from 0 at the least significant end (the convention this course uses everywhere else, and the one that makes 1 << n work) it is bit 5. Counting from 1, as the 1963 chart does, it is the sixth. Quote the value, not the index, and you will never be wrong: 0x20.
Pattern 3 — and the places the pattern gives up

Slide 20 ends with a short list of near-misses. The course notes are blunter about it and add a heading: "what could have been", followed by WHY!?!

PairCodesResult
< >60, 62'<' + 2 == '>' ✓
[ ]91, 93'[' + 2 == ']' ✓
{ }123, 125'{' + 2 == '}' ✓
( )40, 41'(' + 2 == '*' ✗

Three of the four bracket pairs are two apart. The round brackets — the ones you type most — are one apart, so the same code that closes the other three produces an asterisk. There is no reason. Somebody laid out the table by hand and this is what came out, which is the entire point of §06: it is a lookup table, and lookup tables have accidents in them.

ASCII_to_DEC.c & ASCII_case_insensitive.c

One spare bit, a hundred incompatible answers

Where ASCII runs out — and the code page explosion (slides 23–24)

ASCII works for American English. It "is fairly decent for British English — unless you use the pound sign". For anything else it ranges from awkward to useless, and the fix everybody reached for was the same, which is precisely why it failed.

The obvious fix

ASCII is 7 bits. Bytes are 8. There are 128 unused values sitting right there, 0x80–0xFF. "The solution for other European languages at least was to use the eighth bit to extend the encoding."

"So you can kind of imagine everyone going: yeah, this ASCII thing is good, but I can't represent accents over Latin letters. If I add an extra bit, then I should be able to add that." Which is a perfectly sensible thought, and everyone had it independently.

The failure is in one sentence: EASCII was never standardised. There is no such thing as "Extended ASCII" — there are hundreds of mutually incompatible things all legitimately called that. Wikipedia lists hundreds of code pages.
Code pageForWhat 0xE9 means in it
ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1)Western Europeané
KOI8-RRussian (Cyrillic)и
Code page 899DOS mathematical symbolsa mathematical glyph
Windows-1252Western European, DOS/Windows lineageé (mostly Latin-1, differs in 0x80–0x9F)

The bottom 128 always agree; the top 128 never do. So a file is readable right up until it uses a character above 0x7F, and then the same bytes mean different things depending on who opens them. "There was different sort of Windows — well, back in those days it was DOS — different ways of representing things on DOS versus Linux. Everyone was playing by their own rules."

And there is a second, subtler problem the notes point out: a file does not say which code page it uses. The encoding is not in the bytes. It travels separately — in a filename convention, a locale setting, an HTTP header, or nothing at all — and when it goes missing, the reader guesses. That is the setup for §11.

文字化け — "character transformation"

Mojibake, and the encoding that tried to fix it (slides 25–26 · course notes 28–31)

The word is Japanese and it is now the standard technical term in English. It names the exact failure mode that a world of unlabelled code pages guarantees.

Two ways to produce it
1A byte string is decoded using the wrong character encoding. The bytes are intact; the table applied to them is wrong.
2Two byte strings encoded in different encodings are concatenated. Now no single table is right for the whole thing, so any reader garbles at least half.

Nothing is corrupted. That is what makes it insidious — and reversible, if you can work out what happened. Every byte survives the trip. The information that was lost was never in the file: it was the name of the encoding.

The Harry Potter story (course notes 29)

The course notes tell it as a sequence, and it is worth reading as one:

1A Russian student emailed her French friend asking for a Harry Potter book.
2The French friend posted the book to the address in the email.
3But her mail client did not understand the encoding of the Cyrillic characters — so the address arrived as garbage and was copied onto the parcel as garbage.
4The Russian postal service worked out the mojibake and delivered it anyway.

Which is the whole lesson in one anecdote: the mapping is deterministic, so a sufficiently determined reader can invert it. That is also how the lab below works — and how you fix a mangled CSV in practice, by figuring out which pair of encodings was applied and undoing it.

How common is it, really? "It's easy to find garbled garbledness — it happens on my computer all the time, and that's just because different assumptions have been made in the decoding of the files." The canonical sighting is a web page where every apostrophe has become â€™ — UTF-8 bytes for ‘’’ being read one byte at a time as Windows-1252.
mojibake — encode with one table, decode with another

EBCDIC — the other 1963 (course notes 30–31)

Not on the lecture slides beyond the timeline, but on it twice, and worth thirty seconds because it is the counter-example that shows ASCII's design choices were choices.

whatExtended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code — IBM's alternative, descended from punch-card column codes rather than from telegraphy.
whereWidely used for decades on IBM's very successful mainframes. Still alive on z/OS today; use slowly disappearing.
why it hurtsThe letters are not contiguous. There is a gap between I and J, and another between R and S. So for (c = 'A'; c <= 'Z'; c++) — perfectly reasonable C — walks through characters that are not letters. Every §09 trick fails.

The lecture's description of it: "a different code that was kind of supposed to sort out the problems with extended ASCII — probably didn't do the finest job, but these things are a work in progress, always." (The course notes describe it as 6-bit; EBCDIC proper is 8-bit, descended from the 6-bit BCDIC that came before it.) The reason it matters to you is negative: ASCII's contiguous alphabet is not a law of nature, and code that assumes it is portable only because ASCII won.

"The answer to problems with lots of standards is more standards." The lecture's own summary of the situation entering the 1980s — delivered dryly — "and often that leads to just another standard." Followed by advice that generalises well beyond encodings: "If you can make something simple that people want to adopt — lower the bar to adoption. If you require everyone to learn a new thing, then that's not going to get adopted. A good encoding scheme has to be something that is easy for everybody to adopt… that's the problem with a lot of standards: they might be really clever, they might be efficient, but if they're not easy to adopt, then people aren't going to do it." Keep that in mind for §18, because UTF-8's single most important property is that it is easy to adopt — existing ASCII files are already valid UTF-8, so half the world had migrated before it noticed.
One table to end the argument

Unicode: the codespace (slides 27–28 · course notes 32–37)

The goal of Unicode is a single encoding that can represent all of the characters in all of the languages in the world. Proposed 1987, maintained by the Unicode Consortium, and — unusually for this story — it more or less worked.

THE ONE DEFINITION TO REMEMBER

The Unicode Standard defines a codespace — the range of numbers available — and each value in it is a code point, which identifies one character.

range0x0000 … 0x10FFFF
total1,114,112 code points
check17 × 65,536 = 1,114,112 — seventeen 16-bit blocks
assigned293,168 — about a quarter
THE NOTATION

U+ followed by hex, at least four digits:

U+0041A
U+20AC€
U+5B57字
U+1F600😀

A code point is a number, not a byte pattern. How it becomes bytes is a separate decision — §13 onwards. Confusing the two is the single most common Unicode misunderstanding.

Two different counts in the course materials, and they are counting different things. The slides say 293,168 assigned; the course notes say 149,251 characters. Both can be true at once, because "assigned code point" is broader than "character": the codespace also designates 137,468 private-use code points (which are permanently reserved but deliberately have no assigned meaning), 2,048 surrogates (see §18), 66 noncharacters, and the control codes. The two figures also come from different Unicode versions — the standard grows every year. The number to actually remember is the structural one, because it never changes: 1,114,112 = 17 × 65,536, roughly a quarter of it spoken for.
Categories — and one number that explains the whole design (course notes 37)

Every Unicode character carries a major and a minor category. The major ones: Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator, Other.

The largest single category is Letter — other, holding 131,612 of 149,251 characters — almost 90%. Essentially all of it is CJK: Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters, which have no case and no alphabet, so they land in the catch-all bucket and there are simply an enormous number of them compared with anything else.

That is why the BMP is nearly full, why planes 2 and 3 exist and are also mostly CJK, and why an encoding optimised for "the common case" has to decide whose common case. UTF-8 answers "ASCII", which costs CJK text an extra byte per character — a real and much-argued-about trade-off.

The lecture's own verdict, which is more sceptical than the slide's. "Given how many times I get decoding errors, I would say that it's not really the answer. It's the best we have right now, but still things get mixed up, get garbled out sometimes." And on the 75% of the codespace still unassigned: "There is some wiggle room for more emojis, which obviously we need more… I suspect the next 75% will just be emojis, for sure."
The obvious answer, and why it is not used

Storing a code point: UTF-32 (slides 29–32)

A code point is a number up to 0x10FFFF. Numbers are what this course does. So: pick a width that fits and store it. That is UTF-32, and it is both completely correct and almost never used.

The reasoning, in three steps
1Code points run 0x0000–0x10FFFF, so we need at least 21 bits.
2Machines are comfortable with 8, 16, 32, 64. The smallest that holds 21 is 32.
3So: take the code point and store it in 32 bits. That is the entire specification. UTF-32 is a fixed width encoding.

And fixed width is genuinely valuable. "Having fixed width is super useful for doing bitwise computations, super useful for defining the amount of memory that you might need… because otherwise it makes it really difficult to know how much space, how much memory, we need to assign." With UTF-32, character n is at byte 4n, strlen in characters is bytes / 4, and reversing a string is a loop over an array. Every one of those becomes work in UTF-8.

The examples, from the slide (slide 30)
A  → U+0041  → 0b00000000000000000000000001000001
€  → U+20AC  → 0b00000000000000000010000010101100
字  → U+5B57  → 0b00000000000000000101101101010111
😀 → U+1F600 → 0b00000000000000011111011000000000

Read the greyed-out part. "One thing you probably have noticed here is how crazy this zero-land is. There's so many zeros — and that is obviously not efficient. You're wasting a lot of memory. You've got to write those bits as well." The course notes add a fifth example, U+E0032 (TAG DIGIT TWO), which is the one that needs four bytes even in UTF-8; it is a preset in Lab 6.

The worked cost — "Hello 思语" (slides 32, 42)
UTF-32 — eight characters
0x00000068   H
0x00000065   e
0x0000006c   l
0x0000006c   l
0x0000006f   o
0x00000020   (space)
0x0000601D   思
0x00008BED   语

8 × 4 = 32 bytes. "Look at all those leading zeros!" Twenty of those thirty-two bytes are zero.

a small correction, in passing

The lecture writes "Hello 思语" and reads the two characters aloud as "see you, I think… is this some — this is a dating app, right?" They are U+601D (思, sī, "think") and U+8BED (语, yǔ, "language"). The pairing is closer to "thoughts, expressed" than to "see you" — but the byte counts, which are what the slide is about, are exactly right.

The H is 0x68 on the slide, which is lowercase h. The string is written "Hello" with a capital; 'H' is 0x48. It makes no difference to the count — both are one byte in UTF-8 and four in UTF-32 — but if you are checking the arithmetic by hand, that is why your first byte disagrees.

Hold that 32. §17 does the same string in UTF-8 and gets 12.

Taking the lesson from Morse code

UTF-8: variable width, and how it knows where characters end (slides 33–37)

The goal is stated plainly: waste fewer bits. "Why use four bytes for every character if we don't have to? The most common characters should use less bits." Which is Morse's insight from §06 — and it inherits Morse's problem too, so watch how the layout solves it.

What the layout buys you (slide 36)
ASCII is freeEvery ASCII character fits in 1 byte with zero wasted bits — the 7-bit form is 0xxxxxxx, which is literally the ASCII byte unchanged. An existing ASCII file is already a valid UTF-8 file. Nothing to convert.
the BMP is 3Everything in plane 0 fits in 3 bytes — 8 bits better than UTF-32 for the characters that make up almost all real text.
worst case tiesThe full codespace fits in 4 bytes — "which is the same as UTF-32 in the worst case." UTF-8 is never worse than UTF-32, and usually much better.
1 to 4"A single UTF-8 character can be anywhere from one to four bytes long. You can see that that can be problematic at the kind of machine level where we started this course at."
Self-synchronising — the property nobody advertises and everybody relies on. Because continuation bytes always start 10 and lead bytes never do, you can drop into the middle of a UTF-8 stream at a random byte and find the start of a character by walking backwards at most three bytes until you hit one that does not begin 10. Nothing else in this lecture can do that: a corrupted byte damages one character, not the rest of the file. It is also what makes a plain memchr for '/' or '\0' safe — see §18.
Four steps, done by hand

Converting a code point to UTF-8 (slides 38–41 · worked live)

This is the exam-shaped part of the lecture, done twice on the board — once for € on the slide and once for 字 from scratch. The procedure never changes.

The procedure
StepDo this
1Write the code point as raw binary (this is its UTF-32 form).
2Remove the leading zeros. What is left is the number of bits you actually need.
3Split into 6-bit chunks, from the right. The leftmost chunk will usually be short.
4Match the template for that length, drop the bits into the x slots, and pad the first byte with zeros if the leading chunk does not fill it.

Then group the result into fours and read it off as hex. "It's really just a matter of converting this into its bit pattern, starting at the right and chunking things up, and then adding the appropriate appended start parts to each byte."

€ — U+20AC, the slide's worked example (slides 38–39)
1. UTF-32:      0b00000000000000000010000010101100
2. strip zeros:              0b10000010101100        // 14 bits
3. 6-bit chunks:             0b10 000010 101100
4. 3 bytes, so:               1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx
                                      10     000010   101100
   fill (pad with 0):        0b11100010 10000010 10101100
   as hex:                     E  2    8  2     A  C
                             0xE282AC   // 3 bytes, not 4 — we saved one 😀

Note step 4's padding. The leading chunk is 10 — two bits — and the first byte's template has four x slots. So it becomes 0010: "replace the x values with the appropriate bits (0 if none)."

字 — U+5B57, done from nothing (slides 40–41)

Exercise on the slide, worked on the board. Start by writing each hex digit as four bits — 5, B, 5, 7:

1. 5    B    5    7
   0101 1011 0101 0111

2. strip the leading zero:   0b101101101010111       // 15 bits
3. 6-bit chunks:             0b101 101101 010111
4. 3 chunks → 3 bytes:      1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx
                                  101    101101   010111
                             0b11100101 10101101 10010111
                             0xE5AD97

Same shape, same length. A CJK character is 3 bytes in UTF-8 — one more than in UTF-16, one less than in UTF-32.

The chunk-counting shortcut is not actually reliable — and the slides show why. "Split into 6-bit chunks and count them" works for € and 字, but it is a proxy for the real rule, and the proxy breaks at two boundaries. Look at the emoji on slide 41: the chunks are written 11111 011000 000000 — that is three groups — but the answer uses the four-byte template. Why? Because the leading group is 5 bits and the 3-byte template's first byte only has 4 free slots. It does not fit, so you go up one.

Decide by payload bits, not by chunk count. This table is the actual rule and is worth memorising in this form:

Bits neededCode point rangeBytesPayload capacity
≤ 7U+0000 – U+007F17
≤ 11U+0080 – U+07FF25 + 6 = 11
≤ 16U+0800 – U+FFFF34 + 6 + 6 = 16
≤ 21U+10000 – U+10FFFF43 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21

The other boundary that trips the shortcut is 12 bits (U+0800–U+0FFF): exactly two 6-bit chunks, so chunk-counting says 2 bytes — but 12 bits will not fit in 11, so the answer is 3. U+0800 is E0 A0 80. Both failures are in the same direction, so the safe habit is: chunk it, then check the leading chunk fits the first byte's slots, and go up a size if it doesn't.

All four, side by side (slide 41)
A  → U+0041  → 0b01000001                              → 0x41        1 byte
€  → U+20AC  → 0b10 000010 101100
                → 0b11100010 10000010 10101100          → 0xE282AC    3 bytes
字  → U+5B57  → 0b101 101101 010111
                → 0b11100101 10101101 10010111          → 0xE5AD97    3 bytes
😀 → U+1F600 → 0b11111 011000 000000
                → 0b11110000 10011111 10011000 10000000 → 0xF09F9880  4 bytes

The A is the whole argument for UTF-8 in one line. 0x41 — identical to its ASCII byte, no prefix, no overhead, nothing to convert. "The A is nice and easy because it's our old ASCII friend… you can see we kind of go from using a little bit of space for our originally-ASCII codes to a lot of space for our emojis."

A transcription slip on slide 38. The € walkthrough writes the UTF-32 form as 0b0000000000000000010000010101100 — count them and there are 31 bits, one zero short of a 32-bit word. Slide 30 has the same value written correctly with 32. It changes nothing (the leading zeros are about to be thrown away in step 2, which is the point of the step) but if you are checking the arithmetic digit by digit, that is the discrepancy.

The exercise on slide 37

Reading UTF-8 back: where does each character end? (slide 37)

Encoding is the mechanical direction. Decoding is the one that tests whether you understood the layout, because the byte string arrives with no separators in it at all.

The question
How many UTF-8 encoded characters would this represent?

11010111 10101111 11101110 10111100 10001011 01001101

Read only the first byte of each character and count the leading ones. Everything else follows.

Lead byteLeading 1sMeansConsumes
1101011122-byte character11010111 10101111
1110111033-byte character11101110 10111100 10001011
0100110101-byte character — plain ASCII01001101

Three characters, in six bytes. "So these string of ones and zeros actually represent just three characters." And notice you never had to know which characters they were to answer the question — the lengths are readable without decoding anything.

And what they actually are, if you finish the job
// character 1 — 2 bytes
11010111 10101111   → 0b10111 101111       = 0x05EF  → U+05EF
                            (HEBREW YOD TRIANGLE)

// character 2 — 3 bytes
11101110 10111100 10001011
                     → 0b1110 111100 001011 = 0xEF0B  → U+EF0B
                            (Private Use Area — no assigned meaning)

// character 3 — 1 byte
01001101            → 0b1001101            = 0x4D    → 'M'

Strip the template bits, concatenate the payload, read as one number. That is the whole decode. The third one lands in the Private Use Area — a legal code point that the standard deliberately leaves undefined, so what it looks like depends entirely on the font.

The decoder, as C
// how many bytes does the character starting at b occupy?
int utf8_len(unsigned char b) {
    if ((b & 0x80) == 0x00) return 1;   // 0xxxxxxx
    if ((b & 0xE0) == 0xC0) return 2;   // 110xxxxx
    if ((b & 0xF0) == 0xE0) return 3;   // 1110xxxx
    if ((b & 0xF8) == 0xF0) return 4;   // 11110xxx
    return -1;                            // 10xxxxxx — a continuation byte, not a start
}

Each test masks off enough leading bits to make the pattern unambiguous, then compares. This is Week 4 Lecture 2's masking, applied to something that finally justifies it.

utf8_decode — segmenting a byte stream

Overlong encodings — a security bug, not a curiosity. Try the C0 AF preset. Mechanically it decodes to 0x2F, which is '/' — but '/' needs only 7 bits, so its only legal encoding is the single byte 0x2F. A two-byte form of it is forbidden, and a decoder that accepts it anyway is exploitable: a path-traversal filter scanning for the byte 0x2F sees nothing, and then the decoder helpfully produces a / further down the stack. Real CVEs have been written about exactly this. Every code point has exactly one valid UTF-8 encoding, and a conforming decoder rejects the others.
The payoff, and the demos

"Hello 思语" in twelve bytes — and writing C that uses Unicode (slides 42–44 · hello_unicode.c, unicode_strings.c, utf8_strlen.c)

The same string as §13, encoded the other way. Then three small programs that show what changes in C, and one that shows what it costs you.

The comparison the whole second half was building to (slide 43)
UTF-32 — 32 bytes
0x00000068  0x00000065
0x0000006c  0x0000006c
0x0000006f  0x00000020
0x0000601D  0x00008BED
UTF-8 — 12 bytes
0x68  0x65  0x6c  0x6c
0x6f  0x20
0xE6809D
0xE8AFAD

Six ASCII characters at 1 byte each, two CJK characters at 3 bytes each — 6 + 6 = 12. "12 bytes only — and no more leading zeros." A 62.5% saving on a string that is only a quarter non-ASCII; on pure English text the saving is 75%, and even in the worst case — a string of nothing but 4-byte emoji — it is 0% rather than negative. UTF-8 is never larger than UTF-32. That is why it won the web.

hello_unicode.c — four ways to print one emoji (slide 44)

All four produce 😀. They differ in which representation you are writing down — and that is the distinction the whole lecture has been drawing.

// 1 — the UTF-8 bytes, as escapes. You did the encoding yourself.
printf("\xF0\x9F\x98\x80\n");

// 2 — the same bytes, one at a time. Nothing knows they belong together.
putchar(0xF0); putchar(0x9F); putchar(0x98); putchar(0x80); putchar('\n');

// 3 — the code point. The compiler does the encoding. \U takes 8 hex digits.
printf("\U0001F600\n");

// 4 — and for anything in the BMP, \u takes 4.
printf("€\n");   // €

Forms 1 and 2 are the encoded bytes; forms 3 and 4 are the code point. "These are the encoded bytes — not the U+, but the encoded ones." And on discovering form 2 while writing the lecture: "you can put down single bytes that will then combine in the text file or the standard output… we're putting each individual byte down using putchar, and then that will give us our smiley face." Which is exactly the point — stdout is a byte stream and has no idea a character happened. The terminal does the reassembly.

utf8_strlen.c — the warning that matters most

The number of bytes in a UTF-8 string is not the number of characters. strlen counts bytes, because that is all it has ever counted.

// count characters: every byte that is NOT a continuation byte starts one
size_t utf8_strlen(const char *s) {
    size_t n = 0;
    for (; *s; s++)
        if ((*s & 0xC0) != 0x80) n++;   // skip 10xxxxxx
    return n;
}

strlen("Hello 思语")      == 12   // bytes
utf8_strlen("Hello 思语") == 8    // characters

One mask, one comparison, one pass. The idea is the whole payoff of the 10 prefix: continuation bytes are recognisable in isolation, so you can count starts without decoding anything. "Remember where I was printing out little smiley faces — I had to put four bytes down. To do one character using UTF-8 is not one byte long; it can be up to four. And so that's an important point."

Everything that indexes into a string is now suspect. s[i] is a byte, not a character. Truncating a string at byte 10 can cut a character in half and produce invalid UTF-8. Reversing a byte array reverses the bytes, which scrambles every multi-byte character. toupper(s[i]) is meaningless above 0x7F. And even utf8_strlen above is only counting code points — a visible glyph like 🇫🇷 or an emoji with a skin-tone modifier is several code points, so "how many characters is this" has at least three defensible answers. Byte count, code point count, and grapheme count are three different numbers.
unicode_strings.c — two O's that are not the same O

The demo that got a reaction. Latin O is U+004F. Cyrillic О is U+041E. In most fonts they are pixel-identical.

char *latin = "hello";      // all ASCII
char *cyril = "hellо";   // last char is Cyrillic о, U+043E

strlen(latin)  == 5            // 5 one-byte characters
strlen(cyril)  == 6            // 4 one-byte + one two-byte (0xD0 0xBE)
strcmp(latin, cyril) != 0      // different — but they look identical

This is a homograph attack. "Dodgy websites and things use these different character numbers even though they kind of look the same. And so you might think that you're at the right website… and it turns out that it's not the same. So you can use string length — the string length will actually be different because their encoding is different. You can use it sort of as a test." Length is a crude detector and a real one; browsers now do something more thorough (punycode display rules), but the underlying problem is permanent: Unicode guarantees distinct code points, not distinct appearances.

Why it works with code that predates it

What UTF-8 guarantees — and the encoding that made the other choice (slide 45 · course notes 46–47)

Slide 45 is a list of properties. Read it as a list of promises to existing C code, because that is what it is, and it is why migration was possible at all.

The five guarantees
PropertyWhat it buys you
ASCII is a subsetComplete backwards compatibility. Every ASCII file is already valid UTF-8, byte for byte. No conversion, no flag day — and, per §11, this is the "easy to adopt" property that made it win.
no byte of a multi-byte character is valid ASCIIEvery byte of a multi-byte character has the high bit set (≥ 0x80). So ASCII bytes only ever mean themselves — a '/' in a UTF-8 stream is a real '/', never part of something else. You can search for ASCII substrings with plain memchr and be right.
no byte of a multi-byte character is 0Null-terminated strings still work. 0x00 appears only as the encoding of U+0000, so strlen, strcpy and every other char * function keep working unmodified. This one property saved rewriting the C standard library.
0x00 and 0x2F never appear inside multi-byte charactersThe two bytes forbidden in a Unix filename (W7L2 §10) are exactly the two that cannot be produced accidentally. So UTF-8 works for Linux/Unix filenames with no changes to the kernel at all.
treat it like ASCII — carefullyC programs can handle UTF-8 much as they handle ASCII. Beware: number of bytes ≠ number of characters — §17.

"Compact, but not minimal." The slide's own phrasing, and it is precise. UTF-8 does not achieve the information-theoretic minimum: every continuation byte spends 2 of its 8 bits on the 10 tag, and the same code point has several bit patterns that look well-formed (the overlong forms of §16) which the standard has to forbid by rule rather than by construction. That redundancy is the price of self-synchronisation, and it is a good trade.

UTF-16 — the other answer (course notes 46)

Not in the lecture, but in the course notes, and you will meet it the first time you touch Java, JavaScript or the Windows API. Described there, accurately, as "a strange hybrid of UTF-8 and UTF-32."

the unit16 bits. A BMP character is one unit — which felt like a fixed-width encoding right up until Unicode outgrew 16 bits.
surrogatesTo reach beyond the BMP, a block of the BMP itself is reserved: U+D800–U+DFFF, 2,048 code points that are permanently not characters. A pair of them — a surrogate pair — encodes one character from planes 1–16. So UTF-16 is variable width too: 1 or 2 units.
the BOMA 16-bit unit has a byte order, so a UTF-16 file needs a Byte Order Mark at the front to say which. UTF-8 has no BOM because it has no multi-byte units — §01's problem, solved by not having it.
whereWindows, Java, JavaScript. It is why JavaScript's "😀".length is 2.

The worst of both, arguably. Variable width like UTF-8, endianness-dependent like UTF-32, and not ASCII-compatible — every ASCII character costs two bytes, one of which is zero, which breaks every null-terminated string function. Its only real advantage is that it is compact for CJK text. It exists because it was standardised while 65,536 code points still looked like enough. The notes also list UTF-1, UTF-7 and UTF-EBCDIC as lesser-used encodings; you will not meet them.

Those 2,048 surrogates are the loose end from §12. They are the reason the "assigned code points" number is bigger than the "characters" number, and the reason the codespace stops at U+10FFFF rather than somewhere rounder: 16 supplementary planes is exactly what a surrogate pair can address (1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576, plus the BMP's 65,536, gives 1,114,112). Unicode's upper limit is not a technical constraint of Unicode — it is UTF-16's limit, permanently baked into the standard.
Six sets, answers folded away

Exercises

Sets 1 and 2 close out files. Sets 3 to 6 are the encoding material, and set 5 is the one most likely to appear on a test in exactly that shape — do it with a pen, not with the lab.

Set 1 — writing bytes, and finding them again
  1. uint32_t x = 0x12345678; and fwrite(&x, 4, 1, f). What four bytes land in the file on a little-endian machine, and what does fwrite return? Rewrite it so the file gets 12 34 56 78 on any machine.
  2. What is the difference between fwrite(buf, 1, 100, f) and fwrite(buf, 100, 1, f)? Both write 100 bytes — so why would you ever pick one over the other?
  3. Write, in three lines, the shortest correct way to get the size of an open FILE *f and leave the position where you found it.
  4. The middle-byte program is run on a 10-byte file. Which byte does it print — the fifth or the sixth? On a 0-byte file, what does it print and why is that not a byte value?
  5. mkdir("proj/src", 0755) returns 0, but ls -ld proj/src shows drwxr-x---. Nothing is broken. What happened?
Show the answers

1. The file gets 78 56 34 12 — least significant byte first — and fwrite returns 1, because you asked for one item. To be portable, write the bytes yourself, most significant first: fputc((x >> 24) & 0xFF, f); fputc((x >> 16) & 0xFF, f); fputc((x >> 8) & 0xFF, f); fputc(x & 0xFF, f);. Shifting and masking operate on the value, so the result does not depend on how the machine stores it.

2. Only the return value and its granularity. The first returns the number of bytes written (up to 100) and can report a partial write usefully; the second returns 1 or 0, so a short write is indistinguishable from a total failure. For a byte buffer, size = 1 is almost always the better choice.

3. long here = ftell(f); fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(f); then fseek(f, here, SEEK_SET); — four lines if you count the restore, which you should, because a function that silently moves the caller's file position is a bug waiting to happen.

4. 10 / 2 == 5, and offsets are 0-based, so it seeks to offset 5 and reads the sixth byte. For an even-length file there is no single middle byte and this picks the first of the upper half. On an empty file bytes == 0, middle == 0, and fgetc immediately returns EOF — which is -1, not a byte, and prints as 0xffffffff under %x. Check c != EOF before believing it.

5. umask. The mode argument to mkdir is a maximum; the process's file-creation mask clears bits from it. A umask of 027 turns 0755 into 0750, which is drwxr-x---. If you truly need the exact mode, call chmod afterwards. This is the same effect that turned the lecture's 0755 into a 770 directory.

Set 2 — the ASCII table
  1. Why is DEL 127 and not, say, 31 or 255? Give the physical reason.
  2. ASCII is a 7-bit code, but every ASCII character is stored in an 8-bit byte. What happened to the eighth bit historically, and what does UTF-8 use it for?
  3. Space is 0x20, the first character of stick 2, immediately after the last control character. Give two reasons that placement was deliberate.
  4. Why is ^C the interrupt key rather than ^K or ^X? Your answer should mention a number and an abbreviation.
  5. A file contains 0x48 0x69 0x0D 0x0A. How many characters is that, how many are printable, and what would a 1963 teletype have physically done with it?
Show the answers

1. Because data lived on punch cards, where a hole is permanent. Deletion had to mean "punch every column", and the only 7-bit value that is a superset of every other value is all ones — 0b1111111 = 127. Any other choice would leave some previous character recoverable. It is forced, not chosen.

2. It was free, so the 1970s used it for Extended ASCII — 128 extra characters, defined differently by every vendor and country, with no way to tell from the file which table applied. UTF-8 uses the same bit as a structural flag: high bit clear means "this byte is a complete ASCII character", high bit set means "this byte is part of a multi-byte character". Same bit, one incompatible mess versus one universal standard, and the difference is that UTF-8 assigned it a meaning that is self-describing.

3. (i) Space is both a control character and a printable one, so putting it at the boundary between the two regions is the honest placement. (ii) Sorting: because space is numerically lower than every printable character, "go home" < "gone" under a plain byte comparison, which is what people expect. The notes add that the characters just after it are commonly used as word separators, for the same reason.

4. On a teletype, Ctrl cleared the high bits, so ^@ ^A ^B ^C produced control codes 0, 1, 2, 3 — alphabetical order on the keys. Code 3 is ETX (End of Text), which told the machine to stop receiving. Stopping the sender is stopping the process, and modern terminals preserve the mapping by turning ^C into SIGINT. (Likewise ^D → code 4 → EOT → end of input.)

5. Four characters, of which two are printable: 'H', 'i', then CR and LF. The teletype would print Hi, then slam the carriage back to the left margin (CR), then roll the paper up one line (LF). Two separate mechanical actions, which is why they are two separate codes — and why Windows still writes both.

Set 3 — the bit tricks
  1. Evaluate by hand: '7' & 0x0F, 3 | 0x30, 'm' ^ 0x20, 'Q' | 0x20.
  2. Your colleague writes c = c + 32; to lowercase a character. Give two distinct inputs for which this is wrong, and say what it produces for each.
  3. Why is c | 0x20 the right operation for a case-insensitive comparison, where c ^ 0x20 is not?
  4. Write is_digit(char c) using only a bitwise test and a comparison — no <ctype.h>, no two-sided range check on c itself.
  5. The slides say the case bit is the "5th"; the course notes say the "6th". Both are correct. Explain, and give the one description that is unambiguous.
Show the answers

1. '7' & 0x0F = 0x37 & 0x0F = 7 (the integer). 3 | 0x30 = 0x33 = '3'. 'm' ^ 0x20 = 0x6D ^ 0x20 = 0x4D = 'M'. 'Q' | 0x20 = 0x51 | 0x20 = 0x71 = 'q'.

2. (i) 'a' is already lowercase: 97 + 32 = 129, which is outside ASCII entirely — on a signed char it is negative, and passing it to <ctype.h> functions is undefined behaviour. (ii) '5' is not a letter: 0x35 + 32 = 0x55 = 'U' — a digit silently becomes a letter, with no error anywhere. Any non-letter gives nonsense; the addition has no idea what it is operating on.

3. Because OR is idempotent and XOR is not. 'a' | 0x20 == 'a' and 'A' | 0x20 == 'a', so forcing both operands lowercase and comparing gives the right answer whatever case they started in. XOR toggles: 'a' ^ 0x20 == 'A', so comparing a ^ 0x20 with b ^ 0x20 only works when both sides happen to start in the same case — which is exactly the assumption a case-insensitive compare is supposed to remove.

4. return (c & 0xF0) == 0x30 && (c & 0x0F) <= 9; — the first test says "this is in stick 3", the second rules out ':' through '?', which share the 0x3 prefix but have low nibbles above 9. Both halves are needed; (c & 0xF0) == 0x30 alone accepts '='.

5. They are counting from different ends of the same bit. Zero-indexed from the least significant bit — the convention that makes 1 << n and (x >> n) & 1 work, and the one this course uses everywhere else — it is bit 5. One-indexed, as the 1963 chart numbers its columns, it is the sixth. The unambiguous description is by value: the 0x20 bit, worth 32.

Set 4 — code pages, mojibake, and lookup tables
  1. What is the single sentence that explains why "Extended ASCII" caused so much damage? It is not "there were too many characters".
  2. A file was written in UTF-8 and is being read as Latin-1. Is any information lost? Can the damage be undone? What if it had been written in Latin-1 and read as UTF-8?
  3. Why does a text file not simply record which encoding it uses, the way a PNG records its dimensions?
  4. Two's complement and ASCII are both ways of turning bits into meaning. Name the fundamental difference, and say why it means encodings need standards bodies but integer formats need less of one.
  5. EBCDIC puts a gap between I and J. Name two pieces of otherwise-reasonable C that break because of it.
Show the answers

1. It was never standardised — hundreds of mutually incompatible code pages all legitimately called "Extended ASCII", agreeing perfectly on bytes 0x00–0x7F and disagreeing completely on 0x80–0xFF. So a file looks fine until the first accented character, at which point what you see depends on which table your machine guessed.

2. UTF-8 read as Latin-1: no loss, fully reversible. Latin-1 maps every one of the 256 byte values to a character, so all the bytes survive the trip; re-encoding the garbled text back to Latin-1 recovers the original bytes exactly. This is the ordinary â€™ case, and it is fixable. Latin-1 read as UTF-8: usually lossy, because most Latin-1 high bytes are not valid UTF-8 sequences and get replaced with U+FFFD  �  — and once a byte has been replaced, the original value is gone. Mojibake in the second direction destroys; in the first it only disguises.

3. Because a text file has no header — that is what makes it a text file. Any bytes you added to declare the encoding would themselves be text, and would need an encoding to be read. The metadata therefore has to travel out of band: an HTTP Content-Type, an XML declaration, a locale, an editor setting, or a convention. When it goes missing, the reader guesses, and §11 happens. (UTF-16's BOM is an attempted in-band answer, and it causes its own problems.)

4. Two's complement is a mathematical expression — you can derive the bit pattern for any integer from the definition, and two people who have never met will derive the same one. ASCII is a lookup table — there is no derivation for why A is 65, only a decision someone wrote down. Formulas are self-standardising; tables need someone to publish and maintain them, which is exactly why ANSI, ISO and the Unicode Consortium exist for text and essentially do not for two's complement.

5. (i) for (char c = 'A'; c <= 'Z'; c++) iterates over non-letters that fall in the gaps. (ii) if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') accepts characters that are not letters at all. Also c - 'A' as an alphabet index gives wrong indices past the gap, and sorting by byte value no longer sorts alphabetically. The general point: the contiguity of the alphabet is a property of ASCII, not of character encodings, and code that relies on it is portable only because ASCII won.

Set 5 — encode these by hand (the test-shaped one)
  1. Encode U+00A3 (£) in UTF-8. Show the binary and give the hex bytes.
  2. Encode U+07FF and U+0800. They are adjacent code points. Why do they not have the same length?
  3. Encode U+10FFFF, the largest code point. How many payload bits does it use, and how many does the 4-byte form provide?
  4. Without encoding it, say how many bytes U+FFFF takes, and how many U+1F600 takes. State the rule you used.
  5. Someone proposes encoding '/' (U+002F) as C0 AF so that all characters in their format are at least 2 bytes and easier to parse. Two bugs in one sentence — what are they?
Show the answers

1. 0xA3 = 0b10100011, 8 bits → more than 7, at most 11 → 2 bytes. Chunks from the right: 10 | 100011. Template 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx → 11000010 10100011 = 11000010 10100011 = 0xC2 0xA3. (Every Latin-1 character above 0x7F is two bytes in UTF-8 — which is why a Latin-1 file read as UTF-8 breaks, and vice versa.)

2. U+07FF = 0b11111111111, 11 bits → fits the 2-byte form exactly (5 + 6 = 11): chunks 11111 | 111111 → 0xDF 0xBF. U+0800 = 0b100000000000, 12 bits → one bit too many for 2 bytes, so it takes 3: 0000 | 100000 | 000000 → 0xE0 0xA0 0x80. This is the boundary that breaks the "count the chunks" shortcut — 12 bits is exactly two 6-bit chunks, but the 2-byte template's first byte only has five free slots.

3. 0x10FFFF = 0b100001111111111111111, 21 bits. Chunks from the right: 100 | 001111 | 111111 | 111111. Template 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx → 11110100 10001111 10111111 10111111 = 0xF4 0x8F 0xBF 0xBF. The 4-byte form provides 3 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21 bits, and the largest code point needs exactly 21. That is not a coincidence: the codespace was capped to fit.

4. U+FFFF: 3 bytes (16 bits, and 3 bytes carry 16). U+1F600: 4 bytes (17 bits, which exceeds the 3-byte form's 16). The rule is bits needed vs. payload capacity — ≤7→1, ≤11→2, ≤16→3, ≤21→4 — equivalently, by range: below U+0080, U+0800, U+10000.

5. (i) It is invalid UTF-8. Every code point has exactly one legal encoding, the shortest one; C0 AF is an overlong form and a conforming decoder must reject it, so their "format" is not UTF-8 and nothing else will read it. (ii) It is a security hole. Filters that look for the byte 0x2F to block path traversal see nothing in C0 AF — and then a lenient decoder downstream turns it into / anyway. This exact bug has produced real CVEs. The premise is wrong too: fixed-width parsing is not what UTF-8 is for, and the 10 continuation prefix already makes the stream unambiguously segmentable.

Set 6 — decoding, and UTF-8 in C
  1. How many characters is E6 80 9D E8 AF AD 21? Answer without decoding any of them, then say which one is ASCII.
  2. Decode C3 A9 to a code point. What character is it, and what would those two bytes look like to a Latin-1 reader?
  3. Why does if ((*s & 0xC0) != 0x80) n++; count characters correctly? What does it count that is not quite "characters"?
  4. A network buffer ends mid-character. You have the bytes … 41 E6 80. How do you detect this, and how many bytes must you hold back?
  5. Given char *s holding valid UTF-8, is strcmp(s, t) == 0 a correct test for "these are the same text"? Give one case where it says yes correctly, and one where two strings look identical but it says no.
Show the answers

1. Count the bytes that are not continuation bytes. E6 = 1110… lead (3 bytes), 80 and 9D continuations; E8 lead (3 bytes), AF and AD continuations; 21 = 0… lead, 1 byte. Three characters in seven bytes. The ASCII one is 0x21 = '!'. (The first two are 思 and 语.)

2. C3 = 11000011 → 2-byte lead, payload 00011; A9 = 10101001 → payload 101001. Concatenate: 0b00011101001 = 0xE9 = U+00E9, é. To a Latin-1 reader those same two bytes are 0xC3 and 0xA9, which in Latin-1 are Ã and © — so café displays as cafÃ©. That is the single most commonly seen mojibake in the world.

3. 0xC0 masks off the top two bits; 0x80 is the pattern 10. So the test is "this byte does not begin 10", i.e. it is not a continuation byte, i.e. it starts a character. Every character has exactly one starting byte, so counting starts counts characters. What it actually counts is code points — which differs from what a reader would call characters whenever combining marks, emoji modifiers or flag sequences are involved: e + combining acute is two code points and one visible glyph.

4. Walk back from the end while bytes are continuations ((b & 0xC0) == 0x80), find the lead byte, read its length from the leading ones, and check whether that many bytes are actually present. Here E6 announces 3 bytes but only 2 are there, so hold back those 2 bytes and prepend them to the next read. Because a character is at most 4 bytes, you never need to hold back more than 3 — and because UTF-8 is self-synchronising, you never need to scan back more than 3 either.

5. It is a correct test for byte-identical, which is often what you want and is exactly what caught the homograph in §17: "hello" and "hellо" compare unequal, correctly, because they genuinely are different text. But it says "no" for strings that are canonically equivalent and render identically: é as the single code point U+00E9 (C3 A9) versus e followed by combining acute U+0301 (65 CC 81). Same appearance, same meaning, different bytes. Comparing those properly requires Unicode normalisation (NFC/NFD) first — well beyond this course, but worth knowing exists the first time a "identical" string fails to match.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 46–47)

The first half tidied files away. fwrite joined the toolkit, and immediately demonstrated why you should not use it for anything you intend to read on another machine — the portable move is to shift and mask the bytes out yourself. fseek plus ftell turned out to be how you ask a file how long it is. stat, mkdir, opendir, chmod, unlink, rename, chdir, getcwd, link, symlink — all of them exist as a shell command you already use and as a C function, and the man page section number tells you which one you are reading. It ended where last lecture did: everything is a file.

The second half answered the question the course had left open since Week 1. Integers get a formula; floats get a formula; text gets a lookup table, and that single structural fact generates everything else. Lookup tables have to be agreed, so they need standards bodies; when two programs disagree you get mojibake; and because 128 slots were never going to be enough, the spare eighth bit produced hundreds of incompatible code pages before anyone built a table big enough. Unicode is that table — 1,114,112 code points, about a quarter of them spoken for. UTF-32 stores a code point in the obvious way and wastes 25 bits on every letter you actually type. UTF-8 takes Morse code's lesson — common things get short codes — and adds the piece Morse was missing: it puts the length inside the first byte. That one decision buys backwards compatibility with ASCII, safety with null-terminated strings and Unix filenames, and the ability to resynchronise anywhere in a stream.

The through-line, if you want one sentence. A code point is a number that identifies a character; an encoding is a rule for turning that number into bytes; and almost every text bug you will ever debug is caused by someone treating one as the other. U+1F600 is a code point. F0 9F 98 80 is UTF-8. "😀" is a glyph a font drew. Three different things.
Coming up next (slide 47). "Next lecture we're going to start looking at processes." The thread picks up from W7L2's observation that the file descriptor table is per-process — and it is about to matter a great deal that a process can create another one, and that the two of them share a descriptor table until they don't. The parting advice on this lecture: "Unicode — fun type of encoding. It will probably mess with your brain at some point. Just remember that a character is not always a byte when it comes to Unicode encoding and you'll be fine."
TL;DR · fwrite(ptr,size,nmemb,f) returns items, not bytes — fwrite(&data,1,2,f) returns 2, fwrite(&x,2,1,f) returns 1, both write 2 bytes · writing a multi-byte object dumps memory order, so on x86 0xABCD lands as CD AB; fputc(x & 0xFF); fputc(x >> 8) is portable because shifts act on values · file size = fseek(f,0,SEEK_END) then ftell · man 1 = shell, man 2 = system call, man 3 = C library · mkdir makes one level and the mode is a maximum — umask clears bits · opendir/readdir/closedir mirror fopen/fgetc/fclose; struct dirent gives only d_ino and d_name · character encoding is a lookup table, not a formula — that is the whole difference from two's complement and IEEE 754 · Cooke & Wheatstone: 5 trits, 20 of 243 values, 8.23% efficient, no C J Q U X Z · Morse: variable length, so H (0000) and E (0) collide — you need the length as well as the value · ASCII 1963: 7 bits, 128 values, all used, 0x00–0x7F, 8 sticks of 16 · controls in sticks 0–1, space first in stick 2, digits 0x30–0x39, upper 65–90, lower 97–122 · control chars exist because the output device was a teletype; CR + LF were two physical actions · DEL = 127 = all bits set because you cannot un-punch a card · ^C = control char 3 = ETX = stop receiving · digits are 0b011 + value, so c - '0' = c & 0x0F and d + '0' = d | 0x30 · case differs by one bit worth 0x20: | 0x20 lowercases, & ~0x20 uppercases, ^ 0x20 toggles — letters only · '(' + 2 == '*', because tables have accidents · the 8th bit gave Extended ASCII, never standardised, hundreds of code pages agreeing below 0x80 and nowhere above it · mojibake = right bytes, wrong table; nothing is corrupted, and it is often reversible · EBCDIC's alphabet has gaps, so 'A'..'Z' loops break · Unicode: codespace 0x0000–0x10FFFF = 1,114,112 = 17 × 65,536 code points, ~25% assigned; U+XXXX, at least 4 hex digits, 5th digit = plane · plane 0 = BMP, plane 1 = SMP (emoji), 15–16 = private use · UTF-32 = fixed 32 bits = the code point; wastes 25 bits on ASCII, 16 on the BMP, 11 even at the top · UTF-8 = variable, 1–4 bytes: 0xxxxxxx / 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx / 1110xxxx 10… / 11110xxx 10… · capacities 7, 11, 16, 21 payload bits → boundaries U+0080, U+0800, U+10000 — decide by bits needed, not by counting chunks · encode: binary → strip leading 0s → 6-bit chunks from the right → fill the template, pad byte 1 with zeros · A = 0x41; € U+20AC = E2 82 AC; 字 U+5B57 = E5 AD 97; 😀 U+1F600 = F0 9F 98 80; U+10FFFF = F4 8F BF BF · decode by counting leading 1s in the lead byte; (b & 0xC0) != 0x80 means "starts a character" · "Hello 思语" = 32 bytes UTF-32 vs 12 bytes UTF-8 · ASCII is a subset, no multi-byte byte is valid ASCII or 0x00 or 0x2F — so null-terminated strings and Unix filenames just work · bytes ≠ characters: strlen("Hello 思语") == 12 but 8 characters · overlong encodings are invalid and a real security hole · UTF-16 uses surrogate pairs (U+D800–U+DFFF) and needs a BOM; it is why the codespace stops at U+10FFFF · next: processes.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 8 — Lecture 2

Processes: what a running program actually is, and the two ways to make another one

The first half puts last lecture's encoding theory into C. Four ways to write the same sloth in a source file; strlen quietly returning 7 for a two-character string; and three variables called total that look identical on screen, are three different identifiers to the compiler, and turn a ten-line program into chaos — the trick real attackers use to build convincing fake domains. The second half starts a new subject: a process is an instance of a program running in an environment, and the operating system's job is to start them, stop them, and hand each one a CPU it only thinks it owns. PIDs and parents, the ps/top/kill toolkit, environment variables as the settings channel every program inherits, preemption and the context switch that makes multi-tasking an illusion — then the two system calls that matter: execve, which replaces you, and fork, which duplicates you and returns twice.
