Ten minutes of Lecture 1, compressed

Recap: character, code point, encoding (slides 5–10)

Three words that get used interchangeably in conversation and must never be confused in code. Lecture 1 built all of this from scratch — this is the compressed version, and everything after §05 is new.

1 · CHARACTER

The thing you mean

🐧 — a penguin. An abstract idea, not a number and not bytes. What it looks like is a glyph, and the glyph is the font's business: "this is the penguin character, which looks different on different platforms… sometimes it's just the penguin face."

2 · CODE POINT

The number Unicode assigns

U+1F427. One integer in the range 0x0–0x10FFFF, which needs 21 bits. The U+ prefix and the hex are just how humans write it down; it is a plain number.

3 · ENCODING

The bytes on disk

F0 9F 90 A7 in UTF-8. A rule for turning that number into a byte sequence, and back. Change the rule and the same character has different bytes — which is exactly what mojibake is.

How big is Unicode now? The slide says 159,800 characters. That is the Unicode 17.0 figure (released September 2025), and the exact number is 159,801 — 4,803 characters were added in that release, including four new scripts and 4,298 CJK ideographs. Do not memorise it: it grows every September, and the number the deck quotes was already a year old when the slide was made. What is fixed is the size of the codespace: 1,114,112 code points, so about 86% of the space is still empty.

There is, as the lecture noted, a real process for adding one: "there's actually a process for submitting a Unicode character… you need to show that it's not been done before." Emoji proposals have to argue expected usage level, distinctiveness, and that the thing is not already representable. If you build the case for a magpie, the lecturer would like to hear about it.

UTF-32 — THE OBVIOUS ANSWER

Fixed width. 4 bytes. Always.

Take the code point, store it in 32 bits, done. Indexing is trivial: character i lives at byte 4i. The cost is visible the moment you write it out — here are the slide's four examples, and look at the left-hand side of each:

A → U+0041 → 00000000000000000000000001000001 € → U+20AC → 00000000000000000010000010101100 字 → U+5B57 → 00000000000000000101101101010111 😀 → U+1F600 → 00000000000000011111011000000000

"There's a lot of leading zeros, and that means you're wasting a lot of memory." For an English document you are paying 4× for nothing: 25 of every 32 bits are zero.

UTF-8 — THE ONE EVERYONE USES

Variable width. 1 to 4 bytes.

Morse code's lesson, applied: common things get short codes. The first byte tells you how many bytes the character occupies, and every byte after it is marked as a continuation, so you can always tell where you are.

bytespayload bitsbyte 1byte 2byte 3byte 4
170xxxxxxx–––
211110xxxxx10xxxxxx––
3161110xxxx10xxxxxx10xxxxxx–
42111110xxx10xxxxxx10xxxxxx10xxxxxx

Count the leading ones in the first byte and you have the length. A byte starting 10 is never a first byte, which is the property everything else depends on.

The rule that picks the length is payload bits vs capacity — 7, 11, 16, 21 — not "how many six-bit chunks did I write down". Lecture 1 worked through why: U+0800 needs 12 bits, which is two chunks' worth of payload, but 12 > 11 so it takes three bytes, not two.
Two questions off the slide, both worth doing with a pen

Reading a UTF-8 byte stream (slides 8–9)

The layout table is only useful if you can run it backwards. Both of these are exam-shaped: a wall of bits, and a question that is answered purely by looking at the first two or three bits of each byte.

Exercise A — how many characters is this?

11010111  10101111  11101110  10111100  10001011  01001101

Do not decode anything. Walk left to right and classify each byte by its prefix.

Show the walk-through

11010111 starts 110 → two-byte lead, so one continuation must follow. 10101111 starts 10 → continuation. That is character 1, two bytes. Payload 10111 101111 = U+05EF, the Hebrew yod triangle.

11101110 starts 1110 → three-byte lead, two continuations expected. 10111100 and 10001011 both start 10. That is character 2, three bytes. Payload 1110 111100 001011 = U+EF0B — which lands in the Private Use Area, so what it draws depends entirely on your font.

01001101 starts 0 → a one-byte character, and because the top bit is clear it is plain ASCII: 0x4D = M. That is character 3.

Answer: 3 characters, in 6 bytes. Notice you never needed to know what any of them were.

Exercise B — is this legal UTF-8?

11101011  10101111  01001101  10111100  11111110  11110000

There are four separate things wrong with it. Find them all before you open the answer.

Show the four faults

1 · Truncated sequence. 11101011 is a three-byte lead and promises two continuations. 10101111 delivers the first. 01001101 is not a continuation — it starts with 0 — so the character is cut short. "And so we're missing another byte."

2 · Stray continuation. 01001101 on its own is a perfectly legal M. But the byte after it, 10111100, starts 10 with no lead byte in front of it. A continuation byte that continues nothing is always an error.

3 · A byte that can never appear. 11111110 is 0xFE. It has seven leading ones; the longest legal lead is four (11110xxx). 0xFE and 0xFF do not occur anywhere in valid UTF-8, at any position — which incidentally is how file-format detectors spot a byte-order mark.

4 · Truncated at the end. 11110000 is a four-byte lead and needs three continuations. The stream ends. "None of this is legal encoding."

Encoding 🦥 by hand (slides 11–12 · worked on the board)

The sloth is U+1F9A5. The procedure has four steps and no cleverness, but there is exactly one place it goes wrong, and the lecture went wrong in that place on camera — which makes it the best possible worked example.

THE PROCEDURE

Four steps

  1. Code point to binary. 0x1F9A5 → 1 1111 1001 1010 0101. One hex digit is four bits, so this is mechanical.
  2. Count the bits you actually need. Drop leading zeros. Here: 17 bits.
  3. Pick the length from capacity. 17 > 16, so three bytes is not enough → four bytes, capacity 21.
  4. Chunk from the right in sixes, pad the front, apply the templates. Four bytes means 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx.
THE WORKING

21 payload bits, split 3–6–6–6

U+1F9A5 = 1 1111 1001 1010 0101 (17 bits) pad to 21: 0000 1 1111 1001 1010 0101 chunk 3-6-6-6: 000 011111 100110 100101 apply templates: 11110000 10011111 10100110 10100101 0xF0 0x9F 0xA6 0xA5
Correction — the first byte on the board was wrong. The working on screen led with 0xE0, which is 11100000: the three-byte lead. A four-byte character leads with 11110xxx = 0xF0. The lecture caught that something was off ("Oh, I got this wrong, didn't I?") but the spoken correction landed on the wrong digit. The answer is F0 9F A6 A5. And the slip is worse than a typo: E0 9F A6 A5 is not merely a different character, it is invalid UTF-8 — E0 9F A6 decodes to U+07E6, which is below U+0800 and therefore an overlong three-byte form that a conforming decoder must reject, and the trailing A5 is then a stray continuation byte. Run both through Lab 1 and watch it happen.

Slide 13, and the reason Week 4 Lecture 2 existed

Given one byte, what kind of byte is it? (slide 13)

This is where the bitwise operators finally earn their keep. Every question below is one & and one ==, and together they are the whole of a UTF-8 decoder's front end.

The question on the slide: "Suppose I have char c, which is a UTF-8 byte — how can I tell if it is the first byte of a 1-byte character? the first byte of a 4-byte character? how can I tell if it is a continuing byte?" The technique is always the same: mask off the bits you do not care about, then compare against the pattern. Use the Week 4 Lecture 2 masks, and note that the mask always has a 1 for every bit of the prefix and a 0 for every payload bit.

questionprefixmasktest
1-byte character?0xxxxxxx0x80(c & 0x80) == 0x00
continuation byte?10xxxxxx0xC0(c & 0xC0) == 0x80
2-byte lead?110xxxxx0xE0(c & 0xE0) == 0xC0
3-byte lead?1110xxxx0xF0(c & 0xF0) == 0xE0
4-byte lead?11110xxx0xF8(c & 0xF8) == 0xF0
Why the tests must be in this order — or use these exact masks. A four-byte lead like 0xF0 also passes a careless "is the top bit set" check. The masks above are mutually exclusive because each one pins down the whole prefix, including its terminating zero. Testing (c & 0xE0) == 0xC0 for a two-byte lead will not accidentally match 0xF0, because 0xF0 & 0xE0 is 0xE0, not 0xC0.
Use unsigned char, not char. The slide says char c. On x86 Linux plain char is signed, so any byte with the top bit set — that is, every byte of every multi-byte character — is a negative number. Comparisons and any promotion to int sign-extend it: 0xF0 becomes 0xFFFFFFF0, and (c & 0xF8) == 0xF0 quietly becomes false. Declare it unsigned char, or mask with & 0xFF first. This bug is a rite of passage.
one byte, five questions

Lab 3 · The byte classifier

Drag the slider or type a byte. Every one of the five tests is evaluated live with its actual mask arithmetic shown, and the 256-cell map underneath colours the whole byte space so you can see how it partitions: 128 ASCII, 64 continuations, 30 usable leads, and the ones that are never legal.

byte 0x 240
the whole byte space — click any cell
0x00–0x7F ASCII, 1 byte 0x80–0xBF continuation 0xC2–0xF4 lead never legal
The red cells are worth a second look. 0xC0 and 0xC1 are structurally valid two-byte leads, but every value they could encode fits in one byte — they can only ever produce an overlong form, so they are banned outright. 0xF5–0xF7 would encode code points above U+10FFFF, which do not exist. 0xF8–0xFD are the five- and six-byte leads from the original 1992 design, removed when the codespace was capped. 0xFE and 0xFF were never assigned at all.
Demo · unicode_recap.c

Writing Unicode in a C source file (slide 14 · live demo)

The reassuring answer first: "in C we use Unicode — you can plop these characters in like they're any other character and it will print fine and it'll completely work." Nothing special is required, because printf never looks at your bytes. It copies them to stdout, and your terminal does the decoding.

That is the whole trick. A C string is a byte array; UTF-8 is bytes; %s copies bytes until it hits a zero, and no byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 character is ever zero. So the entire stack — string literals, strcpy, fputs, file I/O — passes UTF-8 through untouched without knowing it exists. There are four ways to get the character into the file, and they compile to identical bytes:

unicode_recap.c — four spellings, one sloth

Lab 4 · Four ways to write a sloth

Pick a spelling. The panel shows what the compiler puts in the string literal, whether it builds, and what lands on stdout. Two of the six choices are traps — one of them is the exact syntax error the lecture hit live.

source
what the compiler stores
literal:
Two traps in one escape sequence. The lecture's build failed because the escape was written without its x: "I worked out where my syntax error was — there we go, x to indicate hex." \F0 is not a hex escape; \0 through \7 start an octal escape and everything else is an unknown escape. The second trap is nastier because it compiles: \x in C is greedy and eats every hex digit that follows it, so "\xF09FA6A5" is one escape with a value far too large for a byte — not four bytes. You must break it up: "\xF0" "\x9F" "\xA6" "\xA5", or write "\xF0\x9F\xA6\xA5", where each \x restarts the scan.
On emoji variable names. The demo does it, and warns you off it in the same breath: "please don't do this, this will definitely get you bad style marks… kind of an insane thing to do." Beyond style, it is not as portable as it looks. C's identifier rules are defined by Unicode's identifier properties (XID_Start / XID_Continue), and emoji are not in them — a compiler that accepts 😀 as a variable name is being generous, not standard. Letters from other scripts, on the other hand, are legal identifiers everywhere, which is the whole basis of §07.

The three escape forms are worth separating clearly, because they operate at different levels. 字 and \U0001F9A5 are universal character names: you give the code point and the compiler encodes it for you in the execution character set — four hex digits after \u, exactly eight after \U, no more and no fewer. \xF0 is a raw byte: you are doing the encoding yourself and the compiler stores what you said. The first is what you want when you know the character; the second is what you want when you are demonstrating the encoding, which is precisely why the lecture wrote the sloth both ways side by side.

Demo · utf8_strlen.c

strlen counts bytes, and it will not warn you (slide 15 · live demo)

The single most consequential sentence of the whole encoding topic: the number of bytes in a UTF-8 string is not the number of characters in it. Everything that goes wrong with text in production goes wrong here.

The demo prints a two-character string — a sloth and a Chinese character — and asks for its length. The answer is 7. "It makes sense because we know we're using seven bytes, but it's indicating to you that you have to be careful when counting characters… you probably wanted to know the length of the string in characters, which is actually two." The sloth is four bytes, 字 is three.

Why strlen is not broken. It is doing exactly its documented job: walk forward until you find a zero byte, return the distance. It has no idea what an encoding is, and it must not — that is what makes it work for every encoding at once. In ASCII, one byte was one character, so the two numbers coincided and a generation of programmers stopped distinguishing them. UTF-8 separates them again, and both numbers are useful: bytes for malloc and buffer bounds, characters for display width, cursor movement and truncation.
COUNTING CHARACTERS

The one-line version

Every character has exactly one lead byte and zero or more continuation bytes. So counting characters is counting the bytes that are not continuations:

size_t utf8_strlen(const char *s) { size_t n = 0; for (const char *p = s; *p; p++) if ((*p & 0xC0) != 0x80) n++; // not a continuation return n; }

Four bytes in, one non-continuation, one character. It never decodes anything, so it is as fast as strlen — but it trusts its input.

THE VERSION THE DEMO WRITES

Decode, then count

The lecture's version does more: "it works out each individual byte… checks if we've got a valid string of encodings, and if we do have a valid string then it counts that whole encoding as one character."

while (*p) { int len; if ((*p & 0x80) == 0x00) len = 1; else if ((*p & 0xE0) == 0xC0) len = 2; else if ((*p & 0xF0) == 0xE0) len = 3; else if ((*p & 0xF8) == 0xF0) len = 4; else return -1; // not a lead byte for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) if ((p[i] & 0xC0) != 0x80) return -1; p += len; n++; }

Slower, but it can say "this is not UTF-8" — and being able to reject bad input is usually worth more than the speed.

strlen vs utf8_strlen

Lab 5 · Two lengths for the same string

Type anything — emoji, accents, other scripts, all of it. The byte strip is what strlen walks; the character boxes are what a human counts. The gap between the two numbers is where the bugs live.

Where this bites in real code. char buf[10]; strncpy(buf, name, 9); can cut a four-byte character in half and leave you with an invalid string that a strict decoder will reject and a terminal will render as �. A "20 characters maximum" check written with strlen rejects a perfectly reasonable name in Greek. And reversing a string byte-by-byte does not reverse it, it destroys it. If you slice UTF-8, slice on lead-byte boundaries — the test is the same (c & 0xC0) != 0x80.
Demo · trojan3.c — the security half of Unicode

Three variables called total, and none of them are the same (live demo)

Unicode's promise is that every writing system fits in one table. The consequence nobody advertises is that the table now contains many characters that draw the same shape — and a compiler compares code points, while you compare pixels.

Latin o is U+006F. Cyrillic о is U+043E. Greek omicron ο is U+03BF. Armenian օ is U+0585. In most fonts they are pixel-identical or near enough that no one would ever look twice. To a compiler they are four completely unrelated identifiers — and all four are legal in identifiers, because they are letters.

trojan3.c — run it and watch

Lab 6 · The homograph trap

The program declares three variables that look identical, assigns to them, prints them, and produces output that makes no sense at all. Reveal re-renders the source the way your compiler reads it — and the way an editor with Unicode highlighting turned on shows it to you.

highlighting: off
trojan3.c
the three identifiers
The editor setting the lecture demonstrated. VS Code ships with Unicode highlighting on: it draws a box around characters that look like ASCII but are not, invisible characters, and non-ASCII outside your configured locale. The lecture turned it off to make the point — adding "editor.unicodeHighlight.ambiguousCharacters": false and friends to settings.json — and the three totals instantly became indistinguishable: "all of a sudden it's not telling me about differences here… so all these look exactly the same to me." Then, wisely, put it back: "it might be an issue for me next time I teach this course." Leave yours on.
THE ATTACK THIS ENABLES — 1

Homograph domains

Register аpple.com with a Cyrillic а (U+0430) and it renders identically to apple.com in a proportional font. "This is actually the way that sometimes people create false websites — they can use these weird looking characters and it looks the same and you don't realise it."

Browsers defend against this with punycode: a domain mixing scripts gets displayed as xn--pple-43d.com instead of the pretty form. That is not decoration — it is the mitigation.

THE ATTACK THIS ENABLES — 2

Trojan Source

A sharper relative, disclosed in 2021 as CVE-2021-42574. Instead of look-alike letters it uses Unicode's bidirectional override controls, which are invisible and reorder the display of the text around them. The result is source code whose rendered order — what a human reviewer reads, in the diff, in the browser — differs from the token order the compiler sees.

A comment can be made to swallow live code, or an if can appear to guard a branch it does not. Most compilers now warn on bidi controls in source; most code hosts now flag them.

And the defence you already have. Because these characters are multi-byte and the ones they imitate are ASCII, the byte count changes even though the picture does not. That is §06 turned into a security tool: "you can use the fact that strlen counts bytes instead of characters to find out whether something nefarious might be happening." If a string looks like five ASCII characters and strlen says six, something in it is not what it appears to be. It is a crude check — it says only "not pure ASCII" — but it costs nothing and it catches the naive version of the attack.
Slide 15 — the properties, and why each one matters

Summary: what UTF-8 actually guarantees (slide 15)

Not "compact and clever" — the slide's own phrase is compact but not minimal. UTF-8 gives up a few bits of density in exchange for four properties that let it be dropped into forty years of existing C code without changing any of it.

guaranteewhat it buys
ASCII is a subsetEvery ASCII file is already a valid UTF-8 file, unchanged, byte for byte. No conversion, no flag day. This is the reason UTF-8 won.
no byte of a multi-byte character is valid ASCIIEvery byte of a multi-byte sequence has its top bit set, so ASCII-scanning code can never mistake part of a character for a delimiter it recognises.
no byte is 0x00UTF-8 lives happily in null-terminated C strings. strlen, strcpy, fputs all keep working — they just count bytes.
0x2F (/) cannot appear inside a characterA path parser can split on / byte-wise without decoding, so UTF-8 is safe for Unix filenames. Same argument for ., :, \n and every other ASCII delimiter.
All four are the same fact. Bytes 0x00–0x7F mean exactly one thing — a one-byte ASCII character — and no multi-byte sequence contains any of them. The prefix design reserves the entire top half of the byte space for multi-byte use, and never borrows back. Lecture 1 proves this by sweeping the whole codespace; Lab 3 shows it as a picture.

Which leaves the one caveat the slide ends on, and it is the caveat: "C programs can treat UTF-8 similarly to ASCII — beware: number of bytes in UTF-8 string != number of characters." Everything is compatible except the arithmetic. And with that, the lecture changed subject entirely.

Second half — a new subject

A process is a program running in an environment (slides 16–19)

You have written programs since Week 1 of your first course. This is the lecture that asks what one is once it starts running — and the answer is not "the code". The code is a file on disk, identical every time. The process is everything else.

The lecture framed it as the last rung of a ladder the course has been climbing: "we really played early on with the machine code and coding at that machine level… we looked at system calls and the interaction with the operating system… and now we're looking at what we've been doing the whole time, which is writing programs which create processes." Week 1 was the CPU. Week 5 was the system call. This is the object on the other side of the system call — the thing the operating system is actually managing.

DEFINITION

An instance of an executing program

The word doing the work is instance. One program, one file on disk, can be running as fifty processes at once — fifty of your classmates running the same a.out, or one of you running it fifty times. Each one is separate, with its own everything.

The operating system manages them: creating, finishing, and pre-empting. That verb list is the whole rest of the lecture.

EXECUTION STATE

Three things, and that is all

registersCurrent values of every CPU register — including the program counter, so where you are is part of the state.
memoryCurrent contents of its address space: code, globals, heap, stack.
open filesThe file descriptor table, and other results of system calls — cwd, umask, signal handlers.

Save those three and you can freeze a process; restore them and it resumes with no idea anything happened. That is exactly what a context switch does.

The environment a Unix process runs in — slide 18
Everything on the left is inherited, and that is the point. A process does not go looking for its environment variables or its standard input — they are handed to it at birth by whoever started it. Which means the parent controls all of it, and that is how the shell works: ./prog < in.txt > out.txt is the shell setting up fd 0 and fd 1 before your main ever runs. You will build exactly that mechanism in the next lecture.
Identity and family

PIDs, parents and children (slides 20–23)

Every process gets a number, and every process has exactly one parent. Those two facts turn "the set of things running" into a tree, which is what makes it manageable at all.

THE NUMBER

pid_t

A unique positive integer, type pid_t, declared in <unistd.h>. It is an integer typedef, so %d works in practice — but the type exists so the kernel can widen it without breaking your code.

THE SPECIAL ONES

1, and 0

PID 1 is init — the first user process, started at boot, ancestor of everything. On most Linux systems today that binary is systemd. PID 0 is not a real process; many Unix-like systems use it for the kernel scheduler itself.

THE CAVEAT

They get recycled

Low numbers are usually system processes started at boot — but PIDs wrap around and get reused, "just like with our file descriptors, we take the nearest number that's available". So a low PID is a hint, never a guarantee.

TWO SYSTEM CALLS

Who am I, and who made me

pid_t getpid()The PID of the calling process. Cannot fail.
pid_t getppid()The PID of its parent. Also cannot fail — but the answer can change underneath you, if the parent dies.

Both want <unistd.h>, and the slides also list <sys/types.h> for pid_t. There is a third, getpgid() for process groups, explicitly not used in this course. Full details: man 2 getpid — and section 2 is the tell that these are system calls, not library functions.

THE MINIMAL PROGRAM — SLIDE 23

Six lines

#include <stdio.h> #include <unistd.h> #include <sys/types.h> int main(void) { printf("My PID is (%d)\n", getpid()); printf("My parent's PID is (%d)\n", getppid()); return 0; }

Run it twice and you get two different PIDs — same program, different processes. Run it from your shell and the parent PID is your shell, every time.

getpid · getppid · the chain above you

Lab 7 · Where you sit in the tree

Run the six-line program and watch its PID change every time while its parent stays put. Then kill the shell out from under it and watch the orphan get adopted — the one case where getppid() returns something different on the second call than it did on the first.

the ancestry, root at the top
getpid()
—

—

Orphans, and who adopts them. "If a process' parent terminates, its parent becomes init (PID 1)." A process is never left parentless, because the exit status has to go somewhere — and init is the one process guaranteed to accept it. That is also why init can never exit. On modern Linux the adopter may be a nearer "subreaper" (your session manager) rather than PID 1 itself, but the principle is unchanged: somebody always inherits you.
The commands, before the system calls

Looking at processes from the shell (slide 24)

Everything the next four sections do from C, you can already do from the command line. Learn these first — when your program misbehaves, these are how you find out what it did.

commandwhat it does
shCreates processes by name — the shell's entire job is fork, exec, wait, repeat.
psA snapshot of processes. Bare ps shows only your terminal's; ps aux or ps -ef shows everything. "I know I run this set of flags when I want to see everything that's running."
wPer-user: who is logged in, from where, and what they are running right now.
topLive, sorted by CPU. htop is the friendlier one. Watch it for ten seconds and you can see the scheduler working.
killSends a signal to a process — despite the name, most signals do not kill anything.
kill -9 — "kill without prejudice, my favourite directive of all time in Unix." Plain kill sends SIGTERM, which is a request: the process can catch it, flush its buffers, remove its lock files and exit cleanly. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, blocked or ignored — the kernel simply stops scheduling the process and tears it down. Nothing is flushed. Nothing is cleaned up. It is the right tool when a process is wedged, and the wrong first choice for anything else. Try kill first; escalate if it does not work.
a shell with a process table behind it

Lab 8 · ps, top, w, kill

A simulated machine with a real process table. Type commands or use the buttons. top re-sorts by CPU each time you run it, kill is polite and can be refused, kill -9 never is. Try killing PID 1.

$
The settings channel nobody designed and everybody uses

Environment variables (slides 25–28)

A per-process set of name=value strings, inherited by every child. There is no registry, no config service, no daemon — just an array of strings that gets copied down the process tree, and it has outlasted every system built to replace it.

HOW THEY PROPAGATE

Set once, inherited forever

You set them in a shell, or more usually in a startup file — .profile, .bashrc — so they are set for every shell you open. "Then passed to any programs they run. Almost all programs pass the environment variables they are given to any programs they run", sometimes adding or editing one on the way through.

Type env to see all of yours. That inheritance is the whole mechanism: settings flow downhill, and a child can never change its parent's.

WHAT THEY CARRY

Four you already depend on

PATHDirectories searched for programs. This is how the shell finds ls.
HOMEYour home directory — what ~ expands to.
LANGPreferred language and character encoding.
TZTimezone. Set it and date answers differently.
The shape of the data. "An array of strings of the form name=value, terminated with NULL." Every part of that sentence matters: it is an array of pointers, not a hash table, so lookup is a linear scan; the = is just a character in the string, so the split is yours to do; and the terminator is a NULL pointer, exactly like argv. It is the same convention you have already used twice.
environ.c — walking the array

Lab 9 · The environ walker

The four-line loop from slide 27, stepped one iteration at a time. Watch the loop condition on the last row: environ[i] != NULL is the only thing that stops it, which is why the NULL must be there.

// print all environment variables extern char **environ; for (int i = 0; environ[i] != NULL; i++) { printf("%s\n", environ[i]); }
i = —
char **environ
The third parameter to main, and why not to use it. Many C implementations accept int main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[]). The slide's verdict is one line long: "This will not always work." It is not in the C standard and not in POSIX — POSIX specifies environ instead. "You'll see this around, you might see it in some legacy code flying around." Read it, do not write it. Use extern char **environ;, or better, getenv.
Demos · get_env.c, get_status.c

getenv and setenv (slides 29–30)

You almost never want to walk the array. You want one variable by name, and the library does the linear scan for you.

READING
#include <stdlib.h> char *getenv(const char *name);

Searches for name= and returns a pointer to the value part — not to a copy. Returns NULL if the name is not there. printf("%s", getenv("HOME")); prints your home directory.

WRITING
#include <stdlib.h> int setenv(const char *name, const char *value, int overwrite);

Adds name=value. If name already exists, it is changed only if overwrite is non-zero. Returns 0 on success, -1 on error with errno set.

The bug hiding in the get_status.c demo. The program does char *value = getenv("STATUS"); printf("Environment variable 'STATUS' has value '%s'\n", value); and, with STATUS unset, printed (null). That looks like a feature. It is not: passing NULL to %s is undefined behaviour. glibc happens to print (null) as a courtesy; other C libraries segfault, and dcc will call it out. Always check: if (value == NULL) value = "<unset>";. Getting (null) on the screen means you got lucky, not that you were right.
STATUS=okay ./get_status

Lab 10 · The getenv workbench

The demo, reproducible: check STATUS from the shell, set it, run the program, watch the answer change. The setenv panel lets you try overwrite = 0 against a name that already exists — the silent no-op that catches everyone.

$
setenv("STATUS", value, overwrite)
What environment variables are really for. "Most of the time, for me at least, environment variables have been paths to very specific places… paths to programs, or to places where something is defined so I can use it generally." That is the honest summary. They are a way to tell a program something without changing the program — which is why every deployment system on earth still configures software this way.
The illusion, and what it costs to maintain

Multi-tasking, preemption and the scheduler (slides 31–36)

Open top and there are three hundred processes. You have maybe eight cores. Every process is written as if it owns the machine, and the operating system's job is to make that lie hold.

THE ABSTRACTION

A virtual machine each

The OS provides a virtual machine to each process: it executes as if it were the only thing running, with its own address space of N bytes addressed 0..N-1. "A process just thinks, well, I'm the only one in the world."

This is not politeness, it is what makes programming possible: "you don't want to create a program, run it, and then have to know about everything else that might be happening at the same time." Your main has never once had to think about the browser running next to it.

THE MECHANISM

Take turns, very fast

A process uses the CPU until it is preempted or exits; then another does; eventually the first gets another run. Two things cause preemption:

  • it ran long enough — its time slice expired and the OS gave the CPU to someone waiting;
  • it needs to wait for input, output, or some other operation — "your process sitting at traffic lights".

The second is free: the process could not use the CPU anyway. The first is the one with a cost.

The context switch, and why it is expensive. On preemption the entire state of the process is saved and the next process's state is restored — every register, the program counter, the memory mappings. That is the §09 list, written out and read back. "Context switches are very expensive!" The register copying is the cheap part; the real cost is that the new process's data is not in cache, so it runs slowly until the caches refill. A good scheduler is largely a machine for not doing this too often.
one CPU, three processes, sixty ticks

Lab 11 · The scheduler

Slide 33 made animate-able. One CPU runs three processes in slices; the top track is what actually happens, and the strip underneath is what the user perceives. Shrink the time slice for smoother response and watch the context-switch counter climb — that is the entire trade-off, in one control.

time slice 4 ticks
what you see

What the scheduler is trying to do — four goals, in tension. Fairly share the CPUs between competing processes; minimise response delays so interactive users do not feel lag; meet real-time requirements where they exist ("if you're about to run into the back of a car, that's very high priority — don't schedule that task away"); and minimise the number of expensive context switches. Goals two and four pull in opposite directions, which is why scheduling is a research area and not a formula. As the lecture put it: "this is like a whole course in itself."
The whole toolkit on one page

Process-related system calls (slides 37–38)

Four verbs: make one, replace yourself, end, and watch. Today's lecture covers the two in bold; the rest arrive next time, and are listed here so the shape is visible from the start.

whatcallnotes
createfork()Today. Duplicates the current process. Simple to call, easy to get subtly wrong.
posix_spawn()Next lecture. The modern, standard way to start a new program.
system()Runs a command via /bin/sh. Convenient; a major security risk.
popen()Same, with a pipe attached. Same warning.
replaceexecve()Today. Runs a different program in place of the current one. Does not create anything.
destroyexit()Terminate: run atexit handlers, flush stdio, close files, return status to the parent.
_exit()Terminate immediately — no atexit, no stdio flush. Your buffered output is simply lost.
kill()Send a signal to a process, from C rather than from the shell.
monitorwaitpid()Next lecture. Wait for a child to change state, and collect its exit status.
Why system() and popen() are dangerous, concretely. Both hand a string to a shell. If any part of that string came from a user, the shell's metacharacters are now the user's to control: system("rm report.txt") is fine until the filename is report.txt; rm -rf ~. "These are convenient but they've got real security risks and so we would advise everyone not to use these." execve, fork and posix_spawn take an array of arguments — no shell, no parsing, no injection. Use them for anything that touches input you did not write.
A disagreement between your two sources, worth knowing about. The course notes label fork() OBSOLETE — "do not use in new code, use posix_spawn() instead… fork() appears simple, but is prone to subtle bugs". The lecture is warmer on it and reserves its warnings for system and popen. Both positions are defensible and neither is wrong: posix_spawn is the right call in production, because fork in a large or multi-threaded program duplicates state you did not think about — buffers, locks, threads that do not come across. But fork is the one that shows you what a process is, it is what you will be examined on, and it is still what the shell effectively does. Learn fork; reach for posix_spawn.
Demos · exec.c, exec2.c

execve — replace yourself (slides 39–41)

The first surprise of the topic: exec does not start a new process. It throws away the program you are running and starts a different one in the same process — same PID, same parent, same open files, completely different code.

#include <unistd.h> int execve(const char *file, char *const argv[], char *const envp[]);
fileThe executable to run — either a binary, or a script starting with #!. A path, not a command name: execve does not search PATH.
argvNULL-terminated array of arguments for the new program. By convention argv[0] is the program's own name, which is why the demo repeats "/bin/echo" as the first element.
envpNULL-terminated array of environment variables to hand over. Pass environ to give it yours — or pass something else and the new program's whole world changes.
WHAT SURVIVES

Three things

PIDUnchanged. To everyone outside, it is still the same process.
parentUnchanged — so getppid() gives the same answer as before.
open fdsSurvive. "stdin and stdout remain the same." This is how redirection works.
WHAT DOES NOT

Everything else

"Most of the current process is re-initialised — a new address space is created, all variables lost." Code, globals, heap, stack: gone, replaced by the new program's. "Once you run this, that's it. Everything gets dismantled."

Which explains the strangest property: on success, execve does not return. "Where would it return to?" — the return address was on a stack that no longer exists. On failure it returns -1 and sets errno, so any line after execve is error-handling code by definition.

One process, before and after execve
exec.c — five steps to obliteration

Lab 12 · The execve stepper

Step through the demo. Watch the address space get replaced while the identity panel does not move, and watch the perror line stay unreachable — until you point execve at something that does not exist, and it is suddenly the only line that runs.

target
address space
identity
The exec family, decoded. There are seven of them and the suffix letters tell you everything. l = arguments as a list in the call, execl("/bin/echo", "echo", "hi", NULL). v = arguments as a vector (an array), which is what you want when the count is not known at compile time. p = search PATH, so you can say "echo" instead of "/bin/echo". e = you supply the environment explicitly. Only execve is an actual system call — the other six are library functions that rearrange your arguments and call it. The course notes use execv/execvp, which pass your current environ along implicitly; the slides use execve, which makes that step visible. Same mechanism.
The exec2.c demo, and the point of it. Print your PID and parent PID; then execve a different program that prints its PID and parent PID. Both print the same two numbers. "It's taken the ID away from it… the process ID stays the same, the parent stays the same. But anything that happens afterwards in this program doesn't happen, because this process has been completely overridden." That is the sharpest way to see that a process and a program are different things: the process persisted, the program did not.
Demos · fork.c, fork2.c, fork_ex1.c

fork — clone yourself (slides 42–43)

The other half of the pair, and the one that bends people's brains: a function you call once and that returns twice, in two different processes, with two different values.

#include <sys/types.h> #include <unistd.h> pid_t fork(void);

It creates a new process by duplicating the calling process. The new one is the child; the caller is the parent. The child gets copies of the parent's address space, its open file descriptors, its environment — everything. Both then continue from the same line, the line after fork.

So how do you tell them apart? By the only thing that differs — the return value.
0You are the child. (A child can always find its own PID with getpid(), so the return value is free to mean something else.)
> 0You are the parent, and the value is the child's PID — which you need, because you will want to waitpid on it.
-1The call failed — no child exists. Check this first, always.
// fork creates 2 identical copies of program // only return value is different pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid == -1) { perror("fork"); // print why the fork failed } else if (pid == 0) { printf("I am the child because fork() returned %d.\n", pid); } else { printf("I am the parent because fork() returned %d.\n", pid); }
Three forks in a loop — why the last line runs eight times
fork2.c — add a line, double the output

Lab 13 · The fork tree

The demo that got everyone: two forks printed four goodbyes, and adding one more line printed eight. Set the count, step through, and watch which process is which. Shuffle re-orders the output the way the scheduler would — "they executed at a different time".

forks 2
processes
1
children made
0
lines printed
0
The buffering bug that makes fork lie to you. The child gets a copy of the parent's memory — and that includes stdout's unflushed buffer. When output goes to a terminal, stdio is line-buffered and each printf leaves nothing behind. Redirect to a file or a pipe and it becomes fully buffered, so text you "already printed" is still sitting in memory when fork copies it — and now two processes will flush the same bytes. The same program prints one line to your screen and two into a file. Fix it by calling fflush(stdout) immediately before fork. Try it: ./a.out then ./a.out | cat.
Why anyone would want this. Someone asked at the end — "real examples of when fork is useful" — and it is the right question, because on its own fork just gives you two copies of the same program. The answer is that it is half of a pair: the child immediately execs something else. fork to get a process you can afford to lose, then exec to make it into the program you actually wanted. That is what your shell does for every command you type, and between the two calls it has a moment where it is still your code — which is precisely where it sets up redirection and pipes. Next lecture makes that concrete.
Slide 44, in capital letters

The fork bomb (slide 44 · DO NOT RUN)

Doubling is fine at three. It is not fine at thirty. This is the one program in the course with a comment in shouting case, and it earned it.

#include <stdio.h> #include <unistd.h> // DO NOT RUN CODE LIKE THIS!!!!! // creates 2 ** 10 = 1024 processes int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { printf("Fork Bomb: %d forked %d\n", getpid(), fork()); sleep(1); } return 0; }

The arithmetic is the same as §17, just run further. Every process reaching iteration i forks, so the population doubles ten times: 210 = 1024 processes, all descended from one. Change the 10 to a 20 and it is a million. "You just add one more line and you've completely doubled how many processes are run… it gets big really, really quickly."

It happened in an exam. "Apparently someone threw a fork bomb during the exam and just completely killed it off… it was actually really crappy for the people sitting the exam, because they started to freak out — was there going to be more time, how long would it take to get the system up." A shared machine has one process table. Fill it and nobody can start a process — not you, not the other students, and not the administrator trying to log in and fix it, because logging in requires forking a shell. That is why it is a denial of service rather than a prank.
contained — this is arithmetic, not a fork

Lab 14 · The bomb, defused

Nothing here creates a process; it is a counter and a limit. Set the loop count and run it against a process limit like the one a shared system imposes, and watch where it stops being survivable.

iterations 10 ulimit -u
processes
—
limit hit at
—
total forks
—
RAM if 2 MB each
—
What actually stops one. Systems defend themselves with a per-user process limit — ulimit -u, or RLIMIT_NPROC from C, and on modern Linux the cgroup pids controller. Once you are at the cap, fork() stops creating processes and starts returning -1 with errno = EAGAIN. Which is the practical reason the very first thing you do with a fork is check for -1: on a busy or hostile machine it will fail, and a program that ignores that failure will merrily run the child's branch as the parent.
Six sets, answers folded away

Exercises

Sets 1 to 3 close out encoding — set 2 is the one most likely to appear on a test in exactly that shape, so do it with a pen. Sets 4 to 6 are processes, and set 6 is pure tracing: the sort of question where the answer is a number and there is no partial credit.

Set 1 — reading a byte stream
  1. How many characters is 11000010 10100011, and what is the code point? Do it without a table.
  2. Someone tells you 11100010 10000010 is a euro sign. They are wrong twice over — what is wrong, and what are the correct bytes?
  3. You are handed a pointer into the middle of a UTF-8 string. Explain why you never have to scan back more than three bytes to find the start of the character you are inside.
  4. Which of 0x80, 0xC0, 0xE0, 0xF0, 0xFF can legally begin a character?
  5. A file is exactly 100 bytes and contains valid UTF-8. What is the largest number of characters it can hold, and the smallest?
Show the answers

1. 110 prefix → two-byte lead, one continuation follows and does start 10. So one character, two bytes. Payload 00010 + 100011 = 000 1010 0011 = 0xA3 → U+00A3, the pound sign £.

2. 11100010 is a three-byte lead, so it promises two continuations and only one is present — the sequence is truncated. That is fault one; fault two is that even the bytes given are only two-thirds of the answer. The euro is U+20AC → E2 82 AC.

3. Continuation bytes are exactly the bytes matching 10xxxxxx, and a character is at most four bytes long, so at most three continuations can precede a lead byte. Scan backwards while (c & 0xC0) == 0x80 and you are guaranteed to stop within three steps. This is the self-synchronising property, and it is why a corrupted UTF-8 stream loses one character rather than everything after the damage.

4. Only 0xE0 and 0xF0. 0x80 is a continuation byte. 0xC0 is structurally a two-byte lead but is banned — every value it could encode fits in one byte, so it can only ever produce an overlong form. 0xFF never appears in UTF-8 at all.

5. Largest is 100 — all ASCII, one byte each. Smallest is 25 — all four-byte characters, and 100 divides exactly. If the file were 101 bytes the smallest would be 26, since the leftover byte must still belong to some character.

Set 2 — encoding, and the bit tests
  1. Encode U+00E9 (é) into UTF-8, showing the four steps.
  2. U+0800 needs 12 payload bits. Two bytes give you eleven. Encode it and say how many bytes it takes.
  3. Write the one-line C test for "is this byte the first byte of a three-byte character".
  4. Your classifier works for ASCII and fails for everything else. You declared the byte as char. Explain the bug in one sentence, and give two fixes.
  5. Decode F0 9F A6 A5 back to a code point by hand.
Show the answers

1. 0xE9 = 1110 1001, which is 8 bits. 8 > 7, so one byte is not enough → two bytes, capacity 11. Pad to 11: 000 1110 1001, chunk 5–6: 00011 101001. Templates: 110+00011 = 11000011 = 0xC3; 10+101001 = 10101001 = 0xA9. Answer: C3 A9.

2. Three bytes, capacity 16. 0x800 = 1000 0000 0000, padded to 16 = 0000 100000 000000. Templates give 11100000 10100000 10000000 = E0 A0 80. This is the case that breaks the "count the six-bit chunks" shortcut: two chunks, three bytes.

3. (c & 0xF0) == 0xE0. The mask has a 1 for each of the four prefix bits — including the prefix's terminating zero, which is what stops it matching a four-byte lead.

4. Plain char is signed on x86 Linux, so every byte with the top bit set — that is, every byte of every non-ASCII character — is negative and gets sign-extended when promoted to int, turning 0xE0 into 0xFFFFFFE0. Fix it by declaring the byte unsigned char, or by masking: (c & 0xFF) before the test.

5. F0 = 11110+000 → four bytes, payload 000. Then 9F→011111, A6→100110, A5→100101. Concatenate: 000 011111 100110 100101 = 1 1111 1001 1010 0101 = 0x1F9A5 → U+1F9A5, the sloth.

Set 3 — bytes, characters, and identical-looking strings
  1. What does strlen("héllo") return, in a UTF-8 source file? Why is that not a bug in strlen?
  2. Two strings render identically on screen but strcmp says they differ. Give two completely different explanations.
  3. Why is strlen(s) != utf8_strlen(s) a free but weak security check? What does it actually tell you?
  4. You truncate a UTF-8 name to fit a 16-byte column with strncpy(buf, name, 15). Describe the two ways this can go wrong.
  5. Why can a compiler accept three variables that all look like total and treat them as three different variables — and what does that have to do with fake websites?
Show the answers

1. 6 — é is C3 A9, two bytes. Not a bug: strlen is specified to count bytes up to the terminating zero and it does exactly that. It is encoding-agnostic on purpose, which is the only reason UTF-8 could be adopted without rewriting the C library.

2. (a) Homographs — different code points that draw the same shape, like Latin o U+006F and Cyrillic о U+043E. (b) Normalisation — the same character written two legal ways: é as the single code point U+00E9, or as e followed by combining acute U+0301. Both render identically and neither is wrong; comparing them requires normalising first.

3. It costs one extra pass and tells you exactly one thing: the string is not pure ASCII. That is not the same as "this string is an attack" — a legitimate name in Greek fails it too — and an attack made entirely of ASCII (rn for m) passes it. Useful as a cheap flag, useless as a decision.

4. First, you can slice a multi-byte character in half, leaving a truncated sequence that a strict decoder rejects and a terminal draws as �. Second, 15 bytes may be only four or five characters, so a perfectly short name gets mangled for no reason. Truncate on lead-byte boundaries: back off while (c & 0xC0) == 0x80.

5. Identifiers are compared by code point, and the letters of most scripts are legal in identifiers, so totаl with a Cyrillic а is a genuinely different name that happens to draw the same pixels. The same substitution in a domain name gives you аpple.com — identical to the eye, a different registration entirely. Browsers mitigate it by displaying mixed-script domains as punycode.

Set 4 — processes and their environment
  1. You run the same a.out three times from one shell. What changes between the runs, and what does not?
  2. getppid() returns 1. What happened, and when did it happen?
  3. Your program calls setenv("EDITOR", "vi", 1) and exits. You type echo $EDITOR and get nothing. Why is that correct behaviour?
  4. setenv("PATH", "/tmp", 0) returns 0, but PATH is unchanged. No error occurred. Explain.
  5. Give one good reason to use getenv instead of walking environ, and one situation where you must walk environ anyway.
  6. Why does a process ID being small suggest — but not prove — that it is a system process?
Show the answers

1. The PID changes every time — each run is a new process. The parent PID does not: all three were started by the same shell. Same program, three instances; that distinction is the whole definition.

2. Your parent exited before you did, so you were orphaned and re-parented to init. Note the timing: it did not return 1 at the start, so the answer to getppid() is one of the few things that can change under a running process without it doing anything.

3. Environment variables are per-process and inherited downwards only. Your program modified its own copy; the shell is its parent and never sees it. There is no mechanism for a child to write into a parent's environment — which is exactly why cd has to be a shell builtin rather than a program.

4. overwrite is 0 and PATH already exists, so setenv does nothing and reports success — it did what you asked. The return value tells you the call succeeded, not that the value changed. This is the standard "set a default only if unset" idiom, used deliberately far more often than it is hit accidentally.

5. Use getenv because it is one line and does the name= matching correctly — naive scanning matches PATHEXT when you wanted PATH. You must walk environ when you want all of them: printing the whole environment, or passing it to execve as envp.

6. Low-numbered processes are handed out first, at boot, so system daemons tend to have them. But PIDs are recycled — once the counter wraps, the kernel reuses the lowest free number, so an ordinary program can end up with a low PID. It is a heuristic, never an identity check.

Set 5 — exec versus fork
  1. After a successful execve, what is the value of a global variable you set on the line before? The question contains a trap — name it.
  2. Why does execve not return on success? Answer in terms of the stack.
  3. Name three things that survive an execve and two that do not.
  4. Explain, in one sentence each, what fork and execve do — without using the word "process" more than once.
  5. Why must the pid == -1 check come before the pid == 0 check?
  6. Your shell runs ls > out.txt. Between which two system calls does the redirection get set up, and why can it only happen there?
Show the answers

1. The trap is that the question is meaningless. There is no "line before" any more — your code, your globals and your stack were all discarded when the new program was loaded. Nothing of yours is running to observe the value. Asking about it is like asking what a demolished building's front door is doing now.

2. Returning means popping a return address off the stack and jumping to it. execve replaces the entire address space, including that stack. The return address does not exist any more, and the code it pointed at does not either. There is nowhere to go, so it does not go anywhere.

3. Survive: the PID, the parent, open file descriptors (also the working directory, umask, and process group). Do not survive: the code, and everything in memory — globals, heap, stack, and any signal handlers you installed.

4. fork gives you a second, identical copy of the running program that differs only in what fork returned to it. execve throws away the program currently running and loads a different one in its place. One makes a copy; the other performs a transplant.

5. Because -1 is not 0, so an else chain that tests pid == 0 first will fall through to the else branch on failure and run the parent's code with no child in existence. If that branch calls waitpid(pid, ...) with pid = -1, you are now waiting on any child — which is a hang, not a crash, and much harder to find.

6. Between the fork and the exec, in the child. It has to be there because that is the only moment when the shell's own code is running inside the process that will become ls: it can open out.txt and point fd 1 at it, and then exec keeps the file descriptors while replacing everything else. Before the fork it would redirect the shell itself; after the exec its code no longer exists.

Set 6 — trace the output

Assume every call succeeds, and that output goes to a terminal unless stated otherwise.

  1. printf("A\n"); fork(); printf("B\n"); fork(); printf("C\n"); — how many of each letter?
  2. The same program, run as ./a.out > out.txt. Why might out.txt contain more than one A?
  3. for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork(); printf("x\n"); — how many x?
  4. pid_t p = fork(); if (p == 0) execve("/bin/echo", echo_argv, environ); printf("done\n"); — how many times does done print, and can it appear before echo's output?
  5. In the fork bomb, change the 10 to a 4. How many processes exist at the end, and how many fork() calls executed in total?
Show the answers

1. One A, two B, four C. A is printed before any fork exists. The first fork gives two processes, both of which print B. Each of those forks again, giving four, all of which print C. The order of the Bs and Cs is not determined — that is the scheduler's business.

2. Because a file is fully buffered, not line-buffered. A is still sitting in stdout's buffer when fork runs, so the child inherits a copy of the buffer with A in it, and both processes eventually flush it. Same program, same code, different output — purely because of where the output was going. fflush(stdout) before forking fixes it.

3. Eight. Each of the three forks doubles the population: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8, and all eight reach the printf. This is the demo that surprised the room — adding a single line doubles the output.

4. Once, from the parent. The child's execve succeeds, so the child never reaches the printf — that code is gone. And yes, done can absolutely appear first: the parent is not waiting for anything, so the two processes race. Without a waitpid you have no control over the order at all.

5. 16 processes (24), and 15 fork calls succeeded — every process except the 16th generation's members made children, and the count of children created is always 2n − 1. The original process is the one that was never created by a fork.

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 45–46)

The first half took last lecture's theory and made it something you can type. Four ways to spell a sloth in a C file, all producing the same four bytes; strlen reporting 7 for two characters and being right to; a utf8_strlen that is one if inside one loop, because counting characters is counting the bytes that are not continuations. And then the uncomfortable part: three variables that look like total, are three different identifiers, and turn a trivial program into nonsense — the same mechanism that turns аpple.com into a phishing page, with your editor's Unicode highlighting as the only thing standing between you and it.

The second half opened the last major topic of the course. A process is an instance of a running program, and its state is three things: registers, memory, open files. It has a PID, exactly one parent, and a place in a tree rooted at init. It inherits an environment — an array of name=value strings ending in NULL — from whoever started it, and it can never push a change back up. It shares the CPU by being preempted, and every preemption costs a context switch: the whole of that three-item state written out and read back, which is why schedulers work as hard at avoiding switches as at being fair.

And then two system calls that between them are how every program on the machine got started. execve replaces the program inside the process you already have — same PID, same parent, same open files, everything else gone, and no return, because there is nothing left to return to. fork duplicates the process — one call, two returns, 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent, which is the only way they can tell each other apart. Neither is much use alone. Together they are a shell.

The through-line, if you want one sentence. A program is a file; a process is a program plus a state, an identity and a parent. exec changes the program and keeps the process. fork keeps the program and makes another process. Every command you have ever typed is one of each.
Next lecture — now written up at Week 9 Lecture 1. The three things this one deliberately left dangling: waitpid — how a parent collects a child's exit status, and why a child that is never waited for becomes a zombie; posix_spawn — the modern, standard replacement for the fork-then-exec dance; and pipes, which is where the file descriptor work from Week 7 and this lecture's process work finally meet: two processes, one byte stream, no file on disk. The lecturer also promised to bring a real-world example of what fork is actually good for.

Where this page corrects or supplements its sources

1 · The sloth's first byte. The board working led with 0xE0, the three-byte lead, for a four-byte character. The correct first byte is 0xF0 and the answer is F0 9F A6 A5. The spoken correction did not land on the right digit either. Worse than a typo: E0 9F A6 is an overlong encoding of U+07E6 and must be rejected by any conforming decoder. Flagged in §03; both versions are runnable in Lab 1.

2 · The Unicode character count. Slide 5 says 159,800. The Unicode 17.0 figure (September 2025) is 159,801. Noted in §01 along with the reason the number is a moving target and the codespace size is not.

3 · char versus unsigned char. Slide 13 writes char c for the bit tests. On x86 Linux that is signed, and sign extension silently breaks every one of the tests for exactly the bytes they exist to detect. Added in §04.

4 · printf("%s", NULL). The get_status.c demo prints (null) when STATUS is unset. That is undefined behaviour that glibc happens to handle; it is not portable and dcc flags it. Added in §13.

5 · execve versus execv. The slides use execve with an explicit envp; the course notes use execv/execvp, which pass environ implicitly. Neither is wrong — the whole family is explained in §16, including which one is the actual system call.

6 · fork's status. The course notes mark fork() OBSOLETE and direct you to posix_spawn(); the lecture presents it as the main mechanism and reserves its warnings for system and popen. Both positions are given, with the reasoning, in §15.

7 · The stdio buffer and fork. Not mentioned in either source, but it is the first bug most people hit — the fork bomb slide has a printf inside the loop, which makes it live. Added as a pitfall in §17 and question 2 of exercise set 6.

8 · Escape-sequence traps. The lecture's live syntax error (a missing x) and the greedy-\x trap that compiles but is wrong are both reproducible in Lab 4, from §05.

9 · Emoji as identifiers. The demo does it and the lecture warns it is bad style. It is also not standard — C's identifier rules exclude emoji, though letters from other scripts are legal, which is what makes §07 possible. Noted in §05.

10 · Trojan Source. The homograph demo has a sharper relative using invisible bidirectional controls (CVE-2021-42574). Added as context in §07.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 9 — Lecture 1

Processes and pipes: collecting a child, spawning safely, and wiring two programs together

Last lecture ended with two calls that make a process: execve replaces you, fork duplicates you. Neither is any use until a parent can collect what its child did — so this lecture starts with waitpid, the status word that is not the exit code, exit versus _exit, and the zombies you get when nobody reaps. Then the three ways to start a program ranked by how badly they can go wrong: fork+exec, system — "there's no layer of protection between running this function and access to the shell" — and posix_spawn, the standard one. The second half is the machinery the shell is built from: dup2, which makes stdout point somewhere else, and pipe, which is a byte stream with a file descriptor at each end. Put all four together and you have ls | wc -l.

Ten minutes of Lecture 2, compressed

Where Week 8 Lecture 2 left off (slides 4–13)

The first third of this lecture is a re-run. Week 8 Lecture 2 built all of it from scratch — processes, PIDs, execve, fork, the fork bomb — so here is the compressed version. Everything from §02 onwards is new.

A PROCESS

Program + state + identity

An instance of an executing program. Its execution state is exactly three things: CPU registers, memory contents, open files. It has a unique pid_t PID, exactly one parent, and possibly children. PID 1 is init.

execve

Replace yourself

A new address space is built and every variable is gone. Open file descriptors survive — stdin and stdout still point where they pointed. The PID does not change. On success it does not return; there is nothing to return to.

fork

Duplicate yourself

One call, two returns: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, -1 on failure. The child gets copies of the address space and the open file descriptors. That return value is the only way the two can tell each other apart.

The lecturer's image for exec, which is better than the textbook one. "It's kind of like getting plastic surgery… your PID is unchanged but your face looks completely different." And when a process execs something that prints getpid() and getppid(), the numbers are unchanged: "it's like a doppelgänger that stole your life and your parents as well, and nobody noticed."
SLIDE 5 · THE SIGNATURE

Three arguments, all NULL-terminated where it matters

#include <unistd.h> int execve(const char *file, char *const argv[], char *const envp[]);

file is an executable — a binary, or a script starting with #!. argv is the argument array and envp the environment, and both must end in NULL: "that's when it knows that you've got to the end." On error it returns -1 and sets errno.

SLIDE 8 · THE FAMILY

One system call, six wrappers

Only execve is the actual system call. The rest are libc convenience functions around it, and the letters after exec tell you exactly what changes:

lettermeans
larguments as a list: execl(path, "a", "b", NULL)
varguments as a vector: execv(path, argv)
psearch $PATH for the name
eyou supply the environment

So execvp("ls", argv) searches PATH; execv("/bin/ls", argv) does not. "They're usually all fine to use. Just be careful in the assignment as some of them are explicitly not allowed."

A wrinkle in slide 7. The slide is titled execve(2) and then the code calls execv — two-argument, no envp. Both work here, because execv passes the current environ for you. But they are not interchangeable in general, and the difference matters again in §10 when we deliberately hand a child a different environment. The course notes use execv/execvp throughout; the slides use execve. Pick one and know which you picked.
The fork exercise, if you want to check yourself. Slide 11's program prints Hello, then fork() three times, then prints Goodbye. Three forks means 2³ = 8 processes at the end, so 8 Goodbyes. "You can see that it exponentially gets bigger. If you add another line then we should be expecting 16, and then 32, and it gets big real quick." How many Hellos reach the screen is a much more interesting question, and it is §04.
Slide 14 — the missing half of fork

waitpid — wait for a child to change state (slide 14 · fork_wait.c)

A parent that forks and walks away has no idea what happened. waitpid is how it finds out, and it is also how the child's last resources get released. It does two jobs at once, and the second one is the one people forget.

THE SIGNATURE
#include <sys/types.h> #include <sys/wait.h> pid_t waitpid(pid_t pid, int *wstatus, int options);

It pauses the calling process until the process pid changes state — finishing, stopping, restarting. It returns the PID it reaped, or -1 on error. And critically: it releases the child's remaining resources. Without that call, the corpse stays in the process table. That is §05.

WHICH CHILD?

The pid argument has three special ranges

valuewaits for
> 0that specific child
-1any child
0any child in the same process group

Which is why the older, simpler call is just an alias:

pid_t wait(int *wstatus); // exactly equivalent to: waitpid(-1, &wstatus, 0);
THE options ARGUMENT

Zero is the one you will use

optionbehaviour
0block until the child terminates
WNOHANGreturn immediately if no child has exited — returns 0 rather than blocking
WCONTINUEDalso report a stopped child that has been restarted

WNOHANG is how a program polls: do some work, check on the children, do more work. "So you can actually keep track of your children." For more: man 2 waitpid.

THE PATTERN

Always check the return, always decode the status

int status; if (waitpid(pid, &status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); exit(1); } // status is NOT the exit code -- decode it: if (WIFEXITED(status)) { printf("exited with %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status)); }

That second half is the part every example in this lecture gets wrong. It is important enough to have its own section, which is the next one.

What the demo actually showed. fork_wait.c puts a sleep in the child so you can watch the ordering: the child prints, the parent sits in waitpid, then the parent prints. Asked why the sleep is there, the lecturer was direct — "mainly to simulate something else happening… in real life you wouldn't have the sleep. It's just to simulate the sequence of events." The sleep is scaffolding, not technique.
The bug that is in every example on the slides

The status word is not the exit code (slide 14 · correction)

Slide 20 waits for a child and then prints exit_status directly. Slide 26 does the same. Slide 22 does it with system. The course notes do it too. In all four places the number printed is not the exit status — it is a packed 16-bit word with the exit status in the high byte, and it only looks right because the demo child exits with 0.

What the slide prints. printf("/bin/date exit status was %d\n", exit_status); after waitpid(pid, &exit_status, 0). If /bin/date succeeds you see 0 and nothing looks wrong. Change the child to exit(1) and the same line prints 256. Change it to exit(42) and it prints 10752. The lecture ran it, got two zeros, and moved on: "the exit status from this waitpid and the exit status itself was zero — everything happens the way that it was supposed to." It did, for that one input.
THE LAYOUT (LINUX)

Two bytes, three cases

The kernel packs "how did it end" and "with what" into one int. On Linux the low seven bits hold the terminating signal, bit 7 is the core-dump flag, and the next eight bits hold the exit status.

endingbitsexample
exited normallystatus << 8exit(42) → 10752
killed by signalsignal numberSIGKILL → 9
killed + coresignal | 0x80SIGSEGV → 139

Never write that arithmetic yourself. The layout is not portable; the macros are.

THE MACROS

Ask the question, then read the answer

macrowhat it tells you
WIFEXITEDtrue if the child called exit or returned from main
WEXITSTATUSthe actual exit code — only valid if WIFEXITED
WIFSIGNALEDtrue if a signal killed it
WTERMSIGwhich signal — only valid if WIFSIGNALED
WCOREDUMPtrue if it dumped core (not in POSIX; glibc has it)
WIFSTOPPEDtrue if merely stopped, e.g. by ^Z

The guard clauses are not optional: WEXITSTATUS of a signalled child is meaningless garbage.

// the fix, in full int status; if (waitpid(pid, &status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); exit(1); } if (WIFEXITED(status)) { printf("exit status was %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status)); } else if (WIFSIGNALED(status)) { printf("killed by signal %d%s\n", WTERMSIG(status), WCOREDUMP(status) ? " (core dumped)" : ""); }
one int, unpacked

Lab 1 · The status word

Pick how the child ended, or type a raw number. The bit strip shows where the information physically sits, every macro is evaluated live, and the last line is what slide 20's printf would put on your screen.

raw status word 0x0000
bit 15 → bit 0
exit status (bits 8–15) signal number (bits 0–6) core flag (bit 7)
Where 127 comes from. It is a convention, not a rule: a shell that cannot find the command exits 127, and one that found it but could not run it exits 126. So system("nosuchcmd") returns 32512 — which is 127 << 8. If you ever see 32512 out of a status word you have not decoded, that is what it is telling you.
Slides 15–16 · two functions, one letter apart

exit and _exit — terminate yourself (slides 15–16)

Both end the process. The difference is what happens to everything the C library was holding on your behalf — and after fork, "everything the C library was holding" includes a copy of output you thought you had already printed.

exit(status) — THE TIDY ONE

Five things, in order

  1. runs every function registered with atexit()
  2. flushes the stdio buffers and closes open FILE *s
  3. terminates the process
  4. sends SIGCHLD to the parent
  5. hands status to the parent, retrievable through waitpid

Any children it still had are inherited by init (PID 1). Returning from main does the same thing: return 0; is exit(0).

_exit(status) — THE ABRUPT ONE

Same, minus the cleanup

No atexit handlers. No buffer flush. Anything sitting in the stdio buffer is discarded, unwritten.

That sounds like pure loss, until you remember what fork did: the child got a copy of the parent's buffer, including anything the parent had printed but not yet flushed. If the child exits with exit, that copy is written out too — and the line appears twice.

"Sometimes used by children of fork() when exiting." That is the reason, in full.

fork_gotcha.c, explained. The lecture ran this demo and walked through the output without saying why it looks like that:
printf("about to fork getpid() = %d... ", getpid()); // no \n ! pid_t fork_return = fork(); printf("fork() = %d, getpid() = %d...\n", fork_return, getpid());
When stdout is a terminal it is line buffered, so the first printf — which has no newline — is still sitting in the buffer when fork runs. fork copies the buffer. Both processes then flush it. The about to fork line appears twice, even though it was printed once, by one process, before the fork existed. Put an fflush(stdout) before the fork and it appears once.
the buffer that got copied

The same program, three destinations. Buffering mode is chosen by the C library based on where stdout points — and that choice silently changes how many lines your program produces. Every count here is the real one; they were produced by compiling and running the code.

The number that should bother you. Slide 12's fork bomb puts the printf inside the loop. Run it with output going to a terminal and you get 2,046 lines — 2 + 4 + 8 + … + 1024, because each round of processes prints once and there are 2i of them in round i. Redirect that same binary into a pipe and you get 10,240, because now nothing flushes until exit, and each of the 1,024 final processes is carrying a private copy of all ten lines its ancestors printed. Same program, same machine, five times the output, and the only thing that changed was what was on the other end of a |.
Slides 17–18 · "this is a horrifying picture, so I'm going to go to the next one"

Zombies and orphans (slides 17–18)

Two words for two different situations, and people mix them up constantly. One is about a dead child with a live parent. The other is about a live child with a dead parent. Only one of them is a problem.

ZOMBIE — DEAD CHILD, LIVE PARENT

Waiting to be collected

A process cannot fully disappear until its parent has been told how it ended. So when it terminates, the kernel frees its memory and its file descriptors but keeps its entry in the process table: the PID, and the status word. That entry is the zombie.

It goes away the moment the parent calls wait or waitpid — reaping it. Until then it holds a PID and a table slot and nothing else.

"This can be a problem for long-running processes that don't reap their children… zombies that hang around waste system resources."

ORPHAN — LIVE CHILD, DEAD PARENT

Adopted, immediately

If a parent exits first, its children are not killed. They are reparented to init (PID 1) and carry on running. Their getppid() changes to 1 mid-execution.

This is why orphans are harmless: "init always accepts notifications of child terminations." init's entire job description includes reaping whatever lands on it, so an orphan that later exits is reaped instantly.

Which gives the useful corollary: a zombie whose parent dies stops being a problem, because it gets reparented to init, which reaps it on the spot.

Why you should care, from someone who does. "I use a program that often crashes and then leaves zombies all over the place. So I'm often sort of running these commands… looking for whatever processes I've left behind, and then I have to go find which process and I have to kill it." The command was ps ... | grep ... — which is also, conveniently, this lecture's other half. A real zombie cannot be killed, incidentally: it is already dead. kill -9 on a zombie does nothing. You have to make its parent reap it, or kill the parent so init inherits the job.
a process table you can leak
