Slides 19–20 · the pattern every shell is built on

fork and exec together (slides 19–20 · fork_exec.c)

Neither call is much use alone. fork gives you a second process running the same program; exec gives you a different program in the same process. Do the first, then have only the child do the second, and you have started a new program without losing yourself — which is the entire trick.

pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid == -1) { perror("fork"); // print why fork failed } else if (pid == 0) { // ---- child ---- char *date_argv[] = {"/bin/date", "--utc", NULL}; execv("/bin/date", date_argv); perror("execv"); // only reached if exec FAILED _exit(127); // ... and the slide is missing this } else { // ---- parent ---- int status; if (waitpid(pid, &status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); exit(1); } printf("/bin/date exit status was %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(status)); }
THE CHILD'S JOB

Become something else

It is a copy of the parent for a few microseconds, then execv throws away the program and loads /bin/date in its place. Same PID, same parent, same open files — different code.

THE PARENT'S JOB

Wait and collect

waitpid blocks until the child ends, then decodes the status. Without it the parent races ahead and the child becomes a zombie.

THE LINE AFTER exec

Is an error handler

If execv worked, the perror beneath it does not exist any more — it was in the old address space. Reaching it is the error report.

The missing _exit. The slide's child calls perror("execv") and then… falls through into the parent's else? No — it falls out of the if and keeps running the rest of main, as a duplicate of the parent. A failed exec leaves you with two copies of your program racing each other. The child branch must end in _exit(127) (127 being the conventional "could not run it"). Neither the slide nor the notes has it; both stop mid-statement because the code was trimmed to fit the box.
One fork, one exec, one waitpid — who is running what, and when
step it, one call at a time

Lab 4 · fork → exec → waitpid

Step through the pattern. The two lanes are the two processes; the panels underneath are their address spaces. Pick a command that fails and watch what the status word carries back.

child runs
What it is actually for. Someone asked last lecture why you would ever want two copies of the same program. The answer the lecture gave is the shape of every network server ever written: "maybe handling client connections to a server… the child process can handle specific tasks and the parent can be set off to look for different connections." Fork per request, child does the work, parent goes straight back to accepting. The parent's waitpid is the cleanup crew.
Slides 21–22 · "convenient but unsafe"

system() — one line, and a hole straight through to the shell (slides 21–22 · system.c)

Everything above takes fifteen lines. system takes one. That is the entire appeal, and the entire problem: the thing it hands your string to is not a program, it is a shell, and a shell reads punctuation.

WHAT IT DOES
#include <stdlib.h> int system(const char *command);

It forks, runs /bin/sh -c command in the child, waits for it, and returns. Three of this lecture's calls in one.

int exit_status = system("/bin/date --utc"); printf("/bin/date exit status was %d\n", exit_status);

And that return value is a status word too — the same one from §03. system("exit 3") returns 768, not 3. Slide 22 prints it raw, exactly like slide 20 does.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS

The string is parsed, not run

With execv you pass an array: {"/bin/wc", "-l", filename, NULL}. The kernel hands those to the program as separate strings. A filename containing a semicolon is a filename containing a semicolon.

With system you pass one string and /bin/sh looks for ; | && $( ) > * and acts on them. A filename containing a semicolon is now two commands.

"There's no layer of protection between running this function and access to the shell… you can imagine some bad things could be written."

what the shell reads

Lab 5 · The same input, two ways

A program that counts the lines in a file the user names. Type a filename and watch the two implementations diverge. Nothing here executes — the panel shows how /bin/sh would split the string, which is the whole point.

user types
system() — one string, handed to /bin/sh
what the shell decides you asked for
posix_spawn / execv — an argv array
what the program receives
This has a name and a very long list. It is OS command injection — CWE-78 — and slide 22 links to a MITRE search for it rather than an example, because the example set is enormous. The rule that falls out of the lab: if any part of the string came from outside your program, do not use system. Not "sanitise it first". The escaping rules for /bin/sh are genuinely hard to get right, and the array-based calls make the problem structurally impossible instead. Use them for debugging and throwaway code only: "it's not something that we would at all recommend you do in your real deployed code."
Slide 23 · the summary slide, ranked

Three ways to make a process (slide 23)

Same job — run /bin/date --utc and collect its exit status — three mechanisms. The slide's own labels are "old-fashioned", "scary unsafe" and "new, standard", and the lecturer added the caveat that old-fashioned is a strange word for something you learnt forty minutes ago.

same job, three mechanisms

Lab 6 · The comparison bench

Switch between them. The code is the real thing, error handling included — which is most of why the safe one looks long.

The disagreement worth knowing about. The course notes label fork() OBSOLETE in the heading, and say plainly: "Do not use in new code! Use posix_spawn() instead. fork() appears simple, but is prone to subtle bugs." The lecture is gentler — it teaches fork as the mechanism and calls posix_spawn "the gold standard way of doing it" and "best practice at this point in time". Both are defensible. fork is how the machine really works and you cannot read a Unix codebase without it, but "prone to subtle bugs" is not rhetoric: you have already met three of them today — the duplicated stdio buffer, the missing _exit on the failed-exec path, and the status word. For your own new code, posix_spawn. For the exam, both.
Slides 24–26 · Demos: spawn.c, spawnp.c

posix_spawn — create a process, safely (slides 24–26)

One call that does what fork+exec does, with no window in between where a half-copied process is running your code. Six parameters, four of which you already understand and two of which you can pass NULL for today.

#include <spawn.h> int posix_spawn( pid_t *pid, // OUT: the new process's PID const char *path, // the program to run const posix_spawn_file_actions_t *file_actions, // fd surgery -- see section 18 const posix_spawnattr_t *attrp, // not covered in COMP1521 char *const argv[], // arguments, NULL-terminated char *const envp[]); // environment, NULL-terminated
1 · pid

An out-parameter

Not a return value — you pass &pid and it gets filled in. You need it for the waitpid afterwards, because posix_spawn does not wait.

3–4 · file_actions, attrp

NULL, for now

File actions are how you redirect the child's stdin/stdout — the whole of §18. Attributes (scheduling, signal masks) are "not covered in COMP1521".

6 · envp

Usually environ

Pass the global environ to hand the child what you were given. Pass something else and the child gets only that — which is §10.

The return value is not like anything else you have used. posix_spawn returns 0 on success and an error number on failure. It does not return -1, and it does not set errno. Which is why slide 26 has this line, and why it looks so odd:
int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/date", NULL, NULL, date_argv, environ); if (ret != 0) { errno = ret; // posix_spawn returns the error code, does not set errno perror("spawn"); exit(1); }
Delete that errno = ret; and perror prints whatever the last unrelated failure happened to leave behind — frequently Success, which is a memorable thing to see printed by an error handler. strerror(ret) is the tidier alternative.
posix_spawn vs posix_spawnp

The p is for PATH

Same rule as the exec family. posix_spawn takes a path and uses it literally. posix_spawnp takes a name and searches $PATH, so "date" works and "/bin/date" also works.

"You can do which date and that'll tell you what path it will use." And echo $PATH shows the search list; you can extend it in .profile so it persists across shells, or export it once for the current session only.

The trade: spawnp is convenient, but what runs now depends on an environment variable, which is a small door left open. If you know the path, use spawn.

HOW FAILURE ARRIVES

Two different channels

Failures before the new program starts — no such file, not executable, out of memory — come back in the return value:

posix_spawn("/no/such/program") -> ret = 2 // ENOENT posix_spawn("/etc/hostname") -> ret = 13 // EACCES

Failures after it starts are the child's business, and reach you only through waitpid. POSIX also permits an implementation to return 0 and have the child exit 127 instead — so a careful program checks both. glibc on Linux reports it in the return value.

build the call, see what comes back

Slides 27–29 · Demos: set_status.c, spawn_env.c

Handing the child an environment (slides 27–28)

The sixth parameter is the one that makes posix_spawn more than a convenience. Environment variables are inherited, never pushed back up — so the only moment you get to influence a child's settings is the instant you create it. There are two ways to use that moment, and they behave very differently.

WAY 1 · CHANGE YOURS FIRST

setenv then pass environ

setenv("STATUS", "great", 1); char *getenv_argv[] = {"./get_status", NULL}; int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "./get_status", NULL, NULL, getenv_argv, environ);

The child gets everything you had, plus your edit. PATH, HOME, LANG all survive. This is what a shell does when you write STATUS=great ./get_status.

WAY 2 · BUILD ONE FROM SCRATCH

Your own char *[], NULL-terminated

char *date_argv[] = { "/bin/date", NULL }; char *date_environment[] = { "TZ=Australia/Perth", NULL }; int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/date", NULL, NULL, date_argv, date_environment);

The child gets exactly one variable and nothing else. Same shape as environ — "basically just strings of your environment variables, and null terminated. So you can create your own one of those."

Way 2 is a scalpel, and it cuts both ways. A bespoke envp does not add to the environment — it replaces it. The child of that second example has no PATH, no HOME, no LANG. /bin/date does not care. But swap it for posix_spawnp with a bare name and the call fails, because there is no PATH left to search; and any child that shells out, opens ~/.config, or formats a message in the user's language will now behave differently for reasons that look like nothing to do with you. Use way 2 when you want isolation. Use way 1 when you want a tweak.
what the child actually receives

Edit the parent's environment, choose what to pass, and run a child that reads it. date respects TZ; get_status prints STATUS; spawnp needs PATH. The right-hand list is what the child sees — struck-through entries are what your choice discarded.

Slide 29's exercise, worked. "Use posix_spawn to create a child that runs the cat command on a file given as a command line argument." The lecture did it live; the whole exercise is deciding what goes in argv.
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { if (argc != 2) { fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s <file>\n", argv[0]); return 1; } char *cat_argv[] = {"/bin/cat", argv[1], NULL}; // argv[0] is the program's own name pid_t pid; extern char **environ; int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/cat", NULL, NULL, cat_argv, environ); if (ret != 0) { errno = ret; perror("spawn"); return 1; } int status; if (waitpid(pid, &status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); return 1; } return WIFEXITED(status) ? WEXITSTATUS(status) : 1; }
Two things to notice. cat_argv[0] is the name cat will see as its own argv[0] — it is not the file to open, and getting these off by one is the classic mistake. And the file name is passed as one array element, so a file called my notes.txt works without quoting, which is exactly the property §07 was about.
A question from the floor, worth keeping. A student raised relying on argv[0]: "if you assume argv[0] always points to the correct file path, if an attacker spoofs it you'll get weird [behaviour]" — and the follow-up about a program working out its own location from argv[0] and then writing to paths relative to it. argv[0] is whatever the parent chose to put there. It is a hint, not a fact, and the caller controls it completely; combine that with a setuid binary and you have a privilege escalation. If you need your own path on Linux, read /proc/self/exe. "That's really scary. Things can happen pretty easily, really."
Slides 30–32 · marked ADVANCED

dup and dup2 — pointing a file descriptor somewhere else (slides 31–32)

Everything from here to the end of the lecture is flagged advanced, which by the lecturer's own definition means "the tougher part of the course" and about one exam question. It is also the part where the shell stops being magic. The whole of file redirection is one system call, used once.

dup — ANY FREE NUMBER
int dup(int oldfd);

Duplicates oldfd and returns the new descriptor number. It always picks the lowest unused one — which is the same rule open follows, and the reason fd 3 is so often the first file you open.

Returns -1 on failure.

dup2 — THE NUMBER YOU ASKED FOR
int dup2(int oldfd, int newfd);

The same, except you choose the target number. And the crucial extra clause: if newfd is already open, dup2 closes it first, silently and atomically.

That clause is the entire feature. dup2(fd, 1) closes whatever stdout was and makes 1 a second name for fd. Every program you then exec writes to your file without knowing anything about it.

What "duplicate" actually means — and it is not a copy. The two descriptors are two names for one entry in the system-wide open file table. They therefore share the file offset: "read/writes to oldfd also update position in newfd, and read/writes to newfd also update position of oldfd… very much kind of entangled forever." Opening the same file twice is completely different — two independent entries, two independent offsets. The kernel keeps a reference count on each open file table entry so it knows when the last descriptor naming it has closed and the entry can be freed.
// three descriptors on data.txt -- but only two independent positions int fda = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY); // fd 3, its own offset int fdc = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY); // fd 4, a SECOND, independent offset int fdd = dup(fda); // fd 5, SHARES fda's offset read(fda, &c, 1); // 'A' -- offsets now: fda=1 fdc=0 fdd=1 read(fdd, &c, 1); 'B' // reading through the duplicate advanced fda too read(fdc, &c, 1); 'A' // the independent open never moved
Slides 33–36 · the four-step diagram, made runnable

The three tables, and what dup2 does to them (slides 33–36)

Four slides in a row build up one picture, one line of code at a time. It is the same picture from Week 5 Lecture 2 and Week 7 Lecture 2, now with the column that was previously decoration: the reference count.

Per-process, system-wide, on-disk — three tables, two levels of indirection
open, dup, dup2, close, read

Lab 9 · The three tables

Step the slide sequence, or issue your own calls. Watch the refcount column: it is the thing that decides when the kernel can free an entry, and the thing that decides when a pipe sees end-of-file in §16.

fd table (this process)
open file table (system-wide)
inode table
Reading the diagram the way the exam will ask you to. Three questions cover almost everything: (1) how many entries exist in the open file table — one per open, never per dup; (2) what each refcount is — the number of descriptors, in any process, naming that entry; (3) if I read through fd x, whose offset moves — everything sharing the entry, and nothing else. fork is the fourth question, and it duplicates the fd table while pointing at the same entries, so every refcount doubles.
Slide 37 · Demos: redirect_stdin.c, redirect_stdout.c

File redirection, in four lines (slide 37)

You have typed < and > a thousand times. This is what the shell does when it sees them, and there is nothing else to it: open, dup2, close, exec. The program that gets execed is completely unmodified — tr has no idea it is not reading a keyboard.

STDIN · LIKE tr [a-z] [A-Z] < file.txt
int fd = open("file.txt", O_RDONLY); dup2(fd, 0); // 0 is now a second name for the file close(fd); // the original name is redundant char *tr_argv[] = {"/usr/bin/tr", "[a-z]", "[A-Z]", NULL}; execve("/usr/bin/tr", tr_argv, environ);

After the dup2, anything that reads fd 0 reads the file. tr reads stdin because that is what tr does. Nobody had to tell it.

STDOUT · LIKE echo … > message.txt
int fd = open("message.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0666); dup2(fd, 1); // 1 is now a second name for the file close(fd); char *echo_argv[] = {"/usr/bin/echo","My","lecturer", "is","great!", NULL}; execve("/usr/bin/echo", echo_argv, environ);

Those three flags are the whole meaning of >: write only, create if absent, truncate to zero if present. Swap O_TRUNC for O_APPEND and you have written >>.

Why the close(fd) is there, since it looks pointless. After dup2 there are two descriptors on the file and you only need one. Leaving the other open is a leak, and worse, it is a leak that survives exec — the new program inherits a descriptor it does not know about, cannot use, and will never close. In §16 this same tidiness stops being cosmetic: an unclosed pipe end means end-of-file never arrives.
what the shell does when it sees < or >

Slides 38–41 · marked ADVANCED

Processes cannot see each other's memory (slides 39–41)

That is the point of a process: its own address space, its own virtual machine, no accidents. It is also the problem. Two programs that need to cooperate have no shared variable to cooperate through, so the operating system has to provide a channel. That is inter-process communication, and a pipe is the simplest useful one.

WHAT A PIPE IS

A byte stream with an fd at each end

A buffer in the kernel with two file descriptors attached — one you write into, one you read out of. Bytes come out in the order they went in. It is unidirectional: "one side is the write side and one side is the read side."

No file appears on disk, no name exists in the file system, and nothing is stored once it has been read. Pipes are one form of IPC; there are others — shared memory, sockets, message queues — "you may learn about [them] in other courses."

YOU HAVE BEEN USING THEM ALL TERM

seq 1 10 | wc

$ seq 1 10 1 2 … 10 $ seq 1 10 | wc 10 10 21

Two processes, both running at once. seq's stdout is the write end; wc's stdin is the read end. 10 lines, 10 words, 21 bytes — the numbers 1 to 9 are one byte each, 10 is two, and every one of the ten lines carries a newline: 9 + 2 + 10 = 21.

The | you type is doing all of today's work at once. The shell calls pipe, forks twice, uses dup2 to attach one child's stdout and the other's stdin to the two ends, closes the four ends nobody needs, execs both programs, and waitpids for them. Six of this lecture's calls, in one character. §19 builds exactly that.
Slides 42–43 · Demos: pipe_fork1.c, pipe_fork2.c

pipe() and fork (slides 42–43)

One call, one array of two ints, and a rule about which index is which that you will get backwards at least once.

THE CALL
#include <unistd.h> int pipe(int pipefd[2]);
indexendmnemonic
pipefd[0]read end0 is stdin, and stdin is where you read
pipefd[1]write end1 is stdout, and stdout is where you write

Bytes written to pipefd[1] are read from pipefd[0]. Returns 0, or -1 on failure. The two descriptors are ordinary file descriptors from the same table as everything else — which is exactly why dup2 works on them.

THEN fork

A pipe alone connects you to yourself

On its own, pipe gives one process two descriptors — useless. The point is the next line: the child inherits the file descriptors, including both ends.

So after pipe then fork, four descriptors name the two ends of one pipe: parent's read, parent's write, child's read, child's write. Two of them are wrong and must be closed.

Order matters absolutely: pipe before fork. Fork first and the two processes each get their own private pipe, connected to nothing.

After pipe() then fork() — four ends, two of which are wrong
// pipe_fork1.c -- parent writes, child reads, in libc calls int pipefd[2]; if (pipe(pipefd) == -1) { perror("pipe"); return 1; } pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid > 0) { // ---- parent: the writer ---- close(pipefd[0]); // will never read write(pipefd[1], "1234567890", 10); close(pipefd[1]); // THIS is what sends EOF waitpid(pid, NULL, 0); } else { // ---- child: the reader ---- close(pipefd[1]); // will never write char c; while (read(pipefd[0], &c, 1) > 0) putchar(c); close(pipefd[0]); }
Two ways to read the same pipe. pipe_fork1.c uses raw read/write; pipe_fork2.c wraps the descriptor in a FILE * with fdopen and then uses fgetc and fprintf. Both are valid, and the trade is the one from Week 7 Lecture 1: stdio buffers, so it makes far fewer system calls. It also introduces a third buffer to forget to flush — if the writer never fcloses or fflushes, the reader waits for bytes that are sitting in user-space memory. "We talked about quite extensively a few lectures ago about the advantages of using the standard IO library. It saves us from doing lots of system calls."
bytes, moving

Lab 11 · The pipe

Drive both processes by hand. The middle panel is the kernel buffer — watch it fill, and watch what happens to a writer when it is full and nobody is reading.

write →→→ read
0 / 65536 bytes
Slide 44 · the four ways to get this wrong

Closing the ends you are not using (slide 44)

The slide states it as housekeeping: "parent and child should both close unused pipe file descriptors." It is not housekeeping. Two of the four mistakes hang your program forever and a third kills it with a signal you have probably never seen.

THE RULE

Each process keeps exactly one end

If bytes flow parent → child:

  • the parent closes the read end, pipefd[0]
  • the child closes the write end, pipefd[1]

Then the parent writes, and when it is finished it closes its write end too. That close is the message. There is no "end of transmission" byte — the reader learns you are done because the last write end in the system went away.

And one process cannot do both directions: "parent can send or receive bytes — not both — to a child via the pipe." Two directions needs two pipes.

WHY EOF DEPENDS ON A REFCOUNT

"Every write end", not "your write end"

read on a pipe returns 0 — end of file — only when no write end remains open anywhere. That is the refcount from §12, doing something you can feel.

So if the child forgets to close its own inherited copy of the write end, the count never reaches zero, read never returns 0, and the child blocks forever waiting for bytes that only it could send.

This is the single most common pipe bug, and it is invisible in the code: the missing line is a close of a descriptor the child never intended to use.

four ends, sixteen combinations

Lab 12 · Which ends did you close?

Tick the closes your program performs, then run it. The diagnosis is the one you would get from an actual debugging session — including the two that produce no output at all.

The third failure mode: SIGPIPE. Write to a pipe whose read ends are all closed and the kernel does not politely return an error — it sends your process SIGPIPE, whose default action is to kill you. The shell reports exit code 141, which is 128 + 13, and 13 is SIGPIPE. This is deliberate and useful: it is how seq 1 100000 | head -3 stops seq the instant head has seen enough. If you would rather have an error, ignore the signal and write returns -1 with errno == EPIPE.
And the fourth: deadlock. The lecture mentioned it and deferred it — "in some cases the process will deadlock. We'll talk about deadlock in the next lecture." Here is the pipe-shaped version, since you now have every piece needed to see it. The buffer is finite: 64 KiB on Linux. A write that fills it blocks until somebody reads. So if the parent writes 100 KiB before reading any reply, and the child tries to reply before draining its input, both are asleep inside write, each waiting for the other to read. Neither will. Two pipes, both full, nobody reading: that is a deadlock, and it is the most common reason a working program starts hanging when the data gets bigger.
Slides 45–48 · Demos: read_popen.c, write_popen.c

popen and pclose — the shortcut, and its price (slides 45–48)

Everything in §15 and §16, in one line. And, in exactly the way system was, one line that hands a string to /bin/sh.

THE CALLS
#include <stdio.h> FILE *popen(const char *command, const char *type); int pclose(FILE *stream);

It runs command via /bin/sh, builds the pipe, and hands you a FILE * — so all of stdio.h works on it immediately: fgetc, fgets, fprintf, fscanf.

typeyou get
"r"a pipe from the command's stdout — you read its output
"w"a pipe to the command's stdin — you write its input

NULL is returned on error. Close it with pclose, never fclose — pclose also waits for the command and returns its status.

BOTH DIRECTIONS
// "r" -- capture output FILE *p = popen("/bin/date --utc", "r"); if (p == NULL) { perror(""); return 1; } char line[256]; if (fgets(line, sizeof line, p) == NULL) { fprintf(stderr, "no output from date\n"); return 1; } printf("output captured was: '%s'\n", line); pclose(p); // "w" -- supply input FILE *q = popen("tr a-z A-Z", "w"); fprintf(q, "hello, i am a COMP1521 aficionado\n"); pclose(q);
Same hole as system, same size. "Just like system, it's vulnerable to command injection, and anything that allows a command to directly access the shell is always going to be unsafe and something you should avoid at all costs." Note also that pclose returns a status word, not an exit code — popen("exit 3", "r") then pclose gives you 768. Third occurrence in one lecture; it is a genuine pattern, not a coincidence, because everything that waits for a child returns the same encoding.
a FILE * with a process behind it

Pick a mode and a command. In "r" mode you get its output through fgets; in "w" mode what you type becomes its stdin. The status line at the bottom is what pclose hands back, raw and decoded.

Slide 49 · "awkward to understand and use, but robust"

posix_spawn with file actions (slide 49 · spawn_read_pipe.c)

The third parameter, finally. With fork you did the fd surgery yourself, in the child, in the gap between fork and exec. posix_spawn has no such gap — so you describe the surgery in advance, as a list, and hand it over.

int posix_spawn_file_actions_init(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa); int posix_spawn_file_actions_addclose(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa, int fd); int posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa, int fd, int newfd); int posix_spawn_file_actions_destroy(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa);
THE IDEA

A to-do list the child runs before exec

You init an empty list, add operations to it in order, pass it to posix_spawn, and destroy it afterwards. The operations are performed in the new process, after it is created and before your program starts — precisely the window fork gave you by hand.

Asked what the actions are, the lecturer was honest about the type being opaque: "it's like capital-letters FILE. We don't really know what's in there." You do not need to. You need the order.

THE OPINION

Everyone agrees it is ugly

The slide says "awkward to understand and use — but robust". The lecturer softened it slightly: "I wouldn't say awkward to understand as much as it is a little confusing."

And a student asked the obvious question — why four functions instead of one that takes a kind of operation? "Yes. Why indeed? I do not know. I think this stuff was done back in the day and people weren't thinking about good styling. But yes, this is a mess really. I do not like it very much, especially not knowing what's in the action."

Robust beats elegant here. The list is data, so it cannot half-execute, and there is no window in which a duplicated copy of your program is running arbitrary code.

spawn_read_pipe.c, step by step

Lab 14 · Building the file actions

Capture the output of /bin/date --utc through a pipe, with no fork anywhere. Untick an action to see what it was preventing — the addclose toggle reproduces the exact hang the lecturer described.

the actions list
child's fd table at exec time
The comment on that addclose is wrong, and testing it is instructive. The source says the child must drop the read end "because if we don't do this we wouldn't receive an end of file", and the lecture repeats it. Compile spawn_read_pipe.c with the addclose deleted and it still works perfectly — because EOF is decided by write ends only. The read end the child is holding cannot keep a reader waiting. What actually delivers EOF here is the parent closing pipefd[1]; delete that line and the program hangs forever. Lab 14's toggles run all four combinations.

The addclose is still correct practice, and in the mirror-image program it is load-bearing. spawn_write_pipe.c sends input to a child: the child's stdin becomes the read end, and now the child is holding an inherited write end — its own. It waits for end-of-input that only it could produce, and tr sits there forever. Same line, same list, completely different consequence. Which is why the useful question is never "did I close things", it is who still holds a write end?
Beyond the slides — putting all four calls together

Capstone: the shell was the exercise all along

The lecture gestures at this repeatedly and never assembles it, so here it is assembled. fork, execve, dup2, pipe, waitpid — five calls, and between them they are a complete command-line interpreter. Everything you have typed into a terminal for the last nine weeks is these five calls in a loop.

A SIMPLE COMMAND

date --utc

fork; the child execvs; the parent waitpids. That is §06, unchanged.

WITH REDIRECTION

sort < w.txt > s.txt

The child opens and dup2s before it execs. The program being run never learns it happened. That is §13.

WITH A PIPE

ls | wc -l

pipe first, then two forks, dup2 in each child, four closes, two waitpids. That is §16.

// the whole of `left | right`, with nothing left out int pfd[2]; pipe(pfd); pid_t l = fork(); if (l == 0) { // left-hand process: writes dup2(pfd[1], 1); // stdout -> pipe close(pfd[0]); close(pfd[1]); // both originals are now redundant execvp(left_argv[0], left_argv); perror(left_argv[0]); _exit(127); } pid_t r = fork(); if (r == 0) { // right-hand process: reads dup2(pfd[0], 0); // stdin <- pipe close(pfd[0]); close(pfd[1]); execvp(right_argv[0], right_argv); perror(right_argv[0]); _exit(127); } close(pfd[0]); close(pfd[1]); // the shell holds neither end -- without this, no EOF int st; waitpid(l, &st, 0); waitpid(r, &st, 0); // the pipeline's status is the LAST command's
Count the closes. After pipe and two forks there are six descriptors on the two ends: one pair in each of three processes. Five of them have to go, and the one everybody forgets is the shell's own pair on the second-to-last line. Leave those open and wc waits forever for an EOF that the shell itself is preventing — the program hangs and there is nothing wrong with either child. This is the single most common bug in a first shell implementation, and now you can predict it from the refcount rule alone.
type a command, watch the system calls

Lab 15 · A shell, from the five calls

Type a command line. It is parsed into commands, redirections and a pipeline, and then executed against a small in-memory file system — but the point is the trace on the right: every system call the shell makes, in order, with the fd effects spelled out. Step through it or run it.

$
system calls
stdout
file system
processes
—
syscalls
—
exit status
—
What a real shell adds, if you are curious. Job control (process groups and the terminal's foreground group), signal handling so ^C reaches the child and not the shell, built-ins that cannot be forked because they change the shell's own state — cd is the famous one — expansion of globs and variables before any of this begins, and &&/||/; sequencing on top. None of it changes the five calls in the middle. That is why the exercise is worth doing: the hard parts of a shell are not the parts that create processes.
Six sets, answers folded away

Exercises

Do these with a pen before opening the answers. Several are shaped like exam questions, and the advanced ones — sets 4, 5 and 6 — are where the lecturer's "about one exam question on advanced stuff" is likely to land.

Set 1 · The status word

No code, just arithmetic. Assume Linux encoding throughout.

  1. A child calls exit(3). What does printf("%d", status) print after waitpid? What does WEXITSTATUS(status) give?
  2. A status word comes back as 0. Name the two very different things that could mean, and the macro that distinguishes them.
  3. system("nosuchcmd") returns 32512. What happened, and what would WEXITSTATUS give?
  4. A child is killed by SIGSEGV and dumps core. Give the exact status word, in decimal.
Answers

1. 768, because 3 << 8 = 768. WEXITSTATUS gives 3. This is exactly the bug on slides 20, 22 and 26.

2. Either the child exited with status 0 (success), or — on a machine where signal 0 were possible — nothing at all; in practice the useful distinction is exited normally with 0 versus killed by a signal, and WIFEXITED(status) tells you which. A signalled child never produces a status word of 0, because the signal number is in the low bits and signal numbers start at 1.

3. /bin/sh ran, could not find the command, and exited 127 — the conventional "command not found". 127 << 8 = 32512, so WEXITSTATUS gives 127. Note that system itself succeeded: the shell ran fine.

4. SIGSEGV is signal 11, and the core flag is bit 7 (0x80 = 128). 11 | 128 = 139. Which is also why a shell reports a segfaulting program as exit code 139 — 128 + 11.

Set 2 · fork, buffers and counting

The first three are the classic exam question in three disguises.

  1. printf("Hello\n"); fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("Goodbye\n"); — how many processes exist at the end, and how many lines appear on a terminal?
  2. The same program, with output redirected to a file. Now how many Hellos?
  3. Slide 12's fork bomb prints inside the loop. Why does it produce 2,046 lines on a terminal but 10,240 into a pipe?
  4. A child of fork finishes its work and calls exit(0). Under what circumstance does that cause output to be printed twice, and what one-word change fixes it?
Answers

1. 8 processes, 9 lines: one Hello and eight Goodbyes. On a terminal stdout is line buffered, so Hello\n is flushed by its own newline before the first fork — the buffer is empty when the copying starts.

2. 8. To a file stdout is fully buffered, so Hello\n is still in the buffer at the first fork, gets duplicated three times over, and every one of the eight processes flushes its private copy at exit. Same program, same source, different answer — and the only thing that changed was the shell command.

3. On a terminal, each printf flushes immediately, so the line count is the number of printf calls: 2 + 4 + 8 + … + 1024 = 211 − 2 = 2,046. (The fork is an argument to printf, so it happens first — iteration i has 2i+1 processes printing.) Into a pipe nothing flushes until exit, so each of the 1,024 surviving processes carries a private copy of all ten lines it accumulated: 1,024 × 10 = 10,240.

4. Whenever the parent had unflushed output in its stdio buffer at the moment of the fork — the child inherited a copy, and exit flushes it. The one-word change is _exit, which terminates without flushing. The alternative, and often the better fix, is fflush(stdout) immediately before the fork.

Set 3 · Zombies, orphans and reaping
  1. A server forks a child per request and never calls waitpid. The children exit in milliseconds. What runs out, and roughly when?
  2. Why does kill -9 on a zombie do nothing?
  3. Give a way to make a long-running parent reap children without ever blocking.
  4. A parent forks a child and then exits immediately. Is the child killed? What is its parent afterwards, and what is getppid() before and after?
Answers

1. PIDs — strictly, process table slots. Each unreaped child leaves a zombie holding one entry, and the table has a fixed maximum (/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max, commonly 32768 or 4194304). At a few hundred requests a second a 32768-slot table is exhausted in minutes, and then nothing on the machine can fork — not the server, not your login shell.

2. Because it is already dead. Signals are delivered to running processes; a zombie has no memory, no code and no threads — only a table entry recording how it ended. The only thing that removes it is a wait/waitpid by its parent, or the parent exiting so that init inherits and reaps it.

3. waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG) in a loop, called periodically: it reaps whatever is ready and returns 0 immediately when nothing is. The other standard answer is to handle SIGCHLD and reap from the handler — the kernel tells you the moment a child ends.

4. Not killed. It is reparented to init (PID 1), so getppid() returns the parent's real PID before, and 1 afterwards — a value that can change under a running process. It is now an orphan, and orphans are harmless because init always reaps.

Set 4 · dup2 and redirection (advanced)
  1. After int fd = open("f", O_RDONLY); dup2(fd, 0); close(fd); — how many entries exist in the open file table for f, and what is the refcount?
  2. You open the same file twice into a and b, then read(a, &c, 1). What does read(b, &c, 1) return? Now repeat with b = dup(a).
  3. Write the four calls that implement cmd >> log.txt.
  4. Why does dup2(fd, 1) not need an explicit close(1) first — and why would writing that close yourself be a bug?
Answers

1. One entry, refcount 1. The dup2 took it to 2 by adding a second name; the close(fd) dropped it back to 1. The surviving name is fd 0.

2. Two independent opens are two entries with two offsets, so read(b, ...) returns the first byte again. With b = dup(a) they share one entry and one offset, so it returns the second byte. This is the whole content of slides 31–32.

3. int fd = open("log.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_APPEND, 0666); dup2(fd, 1); close(fd); execvp(...); — identical to > except O_APPEND replaces O_TRUNC.

4. dup2 closes the target itself, atomically. Closing fd 1 by hand first opens a window in which fd 1 is free — and 1 is then the lowest available descriptor, so any open in that window (including one from a signal handler or another thread) lands on it. Then your dup2 silently closes that instead. The atomicity is the reason dup2 exists as a separate call at all.

Set 5 · Pipes (advanced)
  1. After pipe(pfd) then fork(), how many file descriptors refer to the write end? How many must be closed for a reader to see EOF?
  2. A parent writes to a child and the child never sees end-of-file. Name the two most likely missing lines.
  3. A program writes 100 KiB into a pipe before reading anything back, and hangs. Explain, with a number.
  4. seq 1 100000 | head -3 prints three lines and exits at once. What happened to seq?
  5. Why must pipe be called before fork rather than after?
Answers

1. Two — the parent's pfd[1] and the child's inherited copy. Both must be closed; EOF arrives when the refcount on the write end reaches zero, not when one particular process closes.

2. The child failing to close its inherited write end pfd[1], and the parent failing to close its own write end after it finished writing. Either one alone is enough to hang the reader forever.

3. The pipe buffer is 64 KiB on Linux. A write that fills it blocks until a reader drains it — and the only process that would read is the one currently blocked inside write. Both ends asleep, neither can proceed: deadlock. The fix is to read and write concurrently, which in practice means another process, another thread, or non-blocking I/O.

4. head exited after three lines, which closed the last read end of the pipe. seq's next write therefore got SIGPIPE and was killed — exit code 141. This is a feature: it is how a pipeline stops producing data nobody will consume.

5. Because the connection is made by inheritance. fork copies the descriptor table, so a pipe created before the fork exists in both processes and joins them. Create it after and each process has its own private pipe joining it to nothing.

Set 6 · Choosing the mechanism (advanced)
  1. A web application lets users download a file they name, and runs system("zip out.zip ") with the name appended. Give the input that makes this a remote shell, and the change that fixes it structurally.
  2. posix_spawn returns 2. What does that mean, what must you do before calling perror, and why?
  3. You want a child to run with TZ=Australia/Perth but otherwise the same environment as you. Which of the two techniques in §10, and why not the other?
  4. Name one thing fork can do that posix_spawn cannot.
Answers

1. Anything containing shell punctuation — x.txt; <any command>, or backticks, or $(…) — because the whole string is parsed by /bin/sh before anything runs. The structural fix is not escaping; it is not using a shell: posix_spawn (or execv) with {"zip", "out.zip", name, NULL}, where name is one array element and can never become a second command no matter what is in it.

2. 2 is ENOENT — no such file or directory, i.e. the path is wrong. You must assign errno = ret; first, because posix_spawn returns the error number and does not set errno, and perror reads errno. Without the assignment you print a stale, unrelated message. strerror(ret) avoids the whole dance.

3. setenv("TZ", "Australia/Perth", 1) then pass environ. The custom-array technique replaces the environment wholesale, so the child would lose PATH, HOME, LANG and everything else — correct only when isolation is what you actually want.

4. Run your own code in the child. fork gives you a second process executing your program; posix_spawn only ever starts a different program from a file. Anything that needs the child to do work in the parent's code — a worker that inherits an in-memory data structure, a pre-fork server, a fork-per-connection handler — needs fork. That is the honest counterweight to "do not use in new code".

What today gave you

Wrap-up (slides 50–51)

The first half finished the process story. waitpid is not optional decoration on fork — it is how a parent learns anything at all, and how a dead child stops occupying the process table. What it hands back is a status word, not an exit code, and every example in the deck prints it raw and gets away with it only because the demo child exits zero. exit flushes and runs handlers; _exit does neither, which is exactly why children of fork use it. And the thing that ties those two together is the same one buffer: fork copies whatever stdio was still holding, so the same program prints a different number of lines depending on whether you redirected it.

Then three ways to start a program, in increasing order of how much you should trust them. fork+exec is how Unix really works and you cannot read a codebase without it. system and popen are one line each and hand a string to /bin/sh, which means punctuation in that string is code — use them for throwaway work and nothing else. posix_spawn is the standard one: six arguments, two of which are NULL until §18, a return value that is an error number rather than -1, and no window in which a half-duplicated process is running your code.

The second half was two system calls that between them are the shell. dup2 makes one descriptor number a second name for another open file, closing the old occupant atomically — four lines and you have implemented < and >. pipe gives you a kernel buffer with a descriptor at each end, and because fork copies descriptors, it joins two processes. The rule that makes it work is not intuitive and is worth memorising: a reader sees end-of-file only when every write end, in every process, has been closed. Get that wrong and nothing crashes — the program simply stops, which is much harder to debug.

The through-line, if you want one sentence. A file descriptor is a number in a table, and every technique in this lecture is a way of changing what a number points to before handing the process to somebody else's program. exec keeps the table and replaces the code; fork copies the table; dup2 rewrites one row of it; pipe adds a row that leads to another process instead of a disk. The shell is those four operations, arranged.
Next lecture. Concurrency and parallelism — threads, which are the other way to get two things happening at once and share memory by default instead of never; mutexes, for when sharing memory by default turns out to be a problem; and atomics. The lecturer also promised to revisit posix_spawn and the write side of the file-actions example, and had one request of the field: "really need these things to be better named." The word deferred from today — deadlock — arrives properly there; §16 gave you the pipe-shaped version early.

Where this page corrects or supplements its sources

1 · The status word is printed as an exit code, four times. Slide 20, slide 22, slide 26 and the corresponding notes pages all do printf("… exit status was %d\n", exit_status) on the raw int filled in by waitpid (or returned by system). That value is a packed word: the exit status is in the high byte. exit(1) prints 256, exit(42) prints 10752, system("exit 3") returns 768. It reads as correct in the demos only because the child exits 0. Corrected throughout, with WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS; the encoding is explored in §03 and Lab 1. All figures verified by compiling and running the code.

2 · fork_gotcha.c is a buffering demo that was never explained as one. The lecture ran it and read the output aloud without saying why about to fork… appears twice. The answer — the printf has no newline, so on a line-buffered terminal it is still in the stdio buffer when fork copies it — is the same mechanism behind the _exit advice two slides earlier, and behind the fork bomb's line count. Made explicit in §04 and drivable in Lab 2.

3 · The fork bomb's output count. Slide 12 puts the printf inside the loop; the notes' version puts it after. These are not cosmetic variants: the notes' version prints 1,024 lines, and the slide's prints 2,046 to a terminal but 10,240 into a pipe. Every count here was measured, not reasoned about.

4 · The child branch after a failed exec has no exit. Slide 20's child calls perror("execv") and the listing stops. If exec fails, that child keeps running the rest of main as a second copy of the parent — including, in a loop, forking again. The branch must end in _exit(127). Added in §06. (The notes' version has the same gap, and additionally reports a failed execv with perror("execvpe").)

5 · posix_spawn's error protocol. It returns an error number and does not set errno or return -1. Slide 26 handles this correctly with errno = ret;, but the line is easy to read as noise, and the lecture's spoken summary — "you can use perror to find out what bad thing took place" — skips why it is there. Explained in §09, and Lab 7 lets you delete the line and watch perror print Success.

6 · The comment in spawn_read_pipe.c is wrong. It says the child must close the read end "because if we don't do this we wouldn't receive an end of file", and the lecture repeats it in the Q&A. EOF is governed only by write ends. Deleting that addclose changes nothing; deleting the parent's close(pipefd[1]) hangs the program forever. Verified by compiling all four combinations. The same line is load-bearing in spawn_write_pipe.c, where the child would otherwise hold a write end to its own stdin — explained in §18 and drivable in Lab 14.

7 · Deadlock, deferred but explicable now. The lecture said "in some cases the process will deadlock, we'll talk about deadlock in the next lecture" without giving the pipe-specific cause. It is the finite buffer: 64 KiB on Linux, measured. A write that fills it blocks, and if the only would-be reader is the process doing the writing, nothing moves. Added in §16.

8 · SIGPIPE is never mentioned. Writing to a pipe with no readers does not return an error, it kills you — signal 13, shell exit code 141. It is also the mechanism behind something you use constantly (… | head -3). Added in §16, and it is one of the four outcomes in Lab 12.

9 · Slide 14 omits the header. The waitpid prototype is given with no #include; you need <sys/wait.h> for both the function and the W* macros. The notes have it. Restored in §02. Similarly, WCOREDUMP is not in POSIX — it is a glibc extension — which is worth knowing before you rely on it.

10 · argv[0] is attacker-controlled. Raised by a student and answered informally. It is worth stating flatly: argv[0] is whatever the caller put there, it need not be the program's path, and a program that locates its own files relative to it can be redirected by anyone who can start it. On Linux, /proc/self/exe is the reliable answer. Added as a sidebar in §10.

11 · A bespoke envp replaces rather than adds. Slide 28 passes {"TZ=Australia/Perth", NULL} and the child loses PATH, HOME and everything else. Harmless for /bin/date; not harmless in general, and it breaks posix_spawnp outright. Flagged in §10 and demonstrable in Lab 8.

12 · fork's status, restated. The notes head the section fork() — clone yourself (OBSOLETE) and say "do not use in new code"; the lecture teaches it as the mechanism and reserves its warnings for system and popen, calling posix_spawn "best practice at this point in time". Both positions and the reasoning are in §08, along with the one thing fork does that posix_spawn cannot.

COMP1521 · 26T2 · Computer Systems Fundamentals · Week 9 — Lecture 2

Concurrency and threads: two things at once, and everything that can go wrong when they touch the same memory

Every process you have made so far has had one thread of execution. This lecture adds more. It opens by finishing pipes — "there's like quite a bit of things shoved in the lecture today" — then draws the distinction the rest of the lecture rests on: concurrency is overlapping in time, parallelism is happening at the same instant, and they are not the same claim. Threads give you both inside a single process, cheaply, because they share the address space. That sharing is the whole point and the whole problem: two threads incrementing one global can lose an increment, because bank_account++ is a load, an add and a store, and the scheduler is allowed to cut between them. The fixes are mutexes (correct, slow, and they deadlock) and atomics (correct, fast, and they do not). Every number on this page was measured by compiling and running the lecture's own demos.

Seventeen slides of Lecture 1, compressed

Pipes, dup2, popen, posix_spawn (slides 6–22)

The first third of this lecture re-runs the second half of the last one. Week 9 Lecture 1 built all of it — the three descriptor tables, closing the unused ends, the injection risk in system and popen, file actions — with fifteen labs. Here is the compressed version, plus the three things this lecture genuinely adds. Everything from §05 onwards is new.

IPC

Pipes are one option

Processes have separate address spaces, so they need a deliberate channel. A pipe is a unidirectional byte stream the kernel holds for you. "It saves time to have inter-process communication" — the alternative is a file plus a search.

pipe()

One call, two descriptors

pipefd[0] is the read end, pipefd[1] the write end. Bytes written to [1] come out of [0]. Children inherit both, which is exactly what makes the pattern work — and exactly why both sides must close what they do not use.

dup2

Point a number somewhere else

dup(oldfd) returns the lowest free number; dup2(oldfd,newfd) lets you name the target and silently closes it first if it was open. Aim 1 at a pipe's write end and the program's printf goes into the pipe without knowing.

Slide 9's one-line demo, checked. seq 1 10 | wc prints 10    10    21 — ten lines, ten words, twenty-one bytes. The lecturer could not remember which columns wc gives ("I think the number of lines… and the number of bytes"); it is lines, words, bytes, and the 21 is nine single-digit lines at two bytes each plus 10\n at three.
SLIDE 12 · WHO CLOSES WHAT

The rule, stated once

A pipe carries bytes one way, so each process is either a reader or a writer, never both. Whichever end you are not using, close it:

directionparent closeschild closes
parent → childpipefd[0] (read)pipefd[1] (write)
child → parentpipefd[1] (write)pipefd[0] (read)

This is not tidiness. A reader only sees end-of-file when every write end everywhere is closed, and the child inherited a copy of yours.

MEASURED

Which numbers does pipe() hand back?

The lecture ran pipe_fork1.c and read the printed descriptors off the screen. Compiled and run here, the answer is the boring one, and it is worth knowing why it is boring:

$ ./pipe_fork1 pipefd[0] = 3 (read end) pipefd[1] = 4 (write end)

0, 1 and 2 are already taken by stdin, stdout and stderr, and the kernel always allocates the lowest free descriptor. So a first pipe in a fresh program is always 3 and 4 — and that is precisely the fact dup2 exploits in §04.

Two slips in the spoken pipe explanation. Slide 10 was narrated as "a pipe between a file descriptor at zero which is the read end of the pipe and a file descriptor at one which is the right end" — those are indices into pipefd, not the descriptor numbers 0 and 1, which are stdin and stdout and have nothing to do with the pipe. The measured output above is the difference: the indices are 0 and 1, the descriptors are 3 and 4. Second, "bytes written to the array pipefd will be read from the file at pipefd0" — you write to pipefd[1], not to the array.
The genuinely new bit — slide 12's last bullet

Putting stdio on a pipe with fdopen (pipe_fork1.c · pipe_fork2.c)

The two demos do the same job twice. pipe_fork1.c uses the raw system calls, so it counts bytes by hand. pipe_fork2.c wraps the descriptor in a FILE * with fdopen and gets fprintf and fgetc for free. The second is the pattern worth remembering, and it is the bridge between Week 7's stdio and everything in this lecture.

RAW · pipe_fork1.c

You count the bytes

char buf[10] = {0}; if (parent) { close(pipefd[0]); // not reading write(pipefd[1], "0123456789", 10); close(pipefd[1]); wait(NULL); } else { close(pipefd[1]); // not writing while (read(pipefd[0], buf, 1) > 0) putchar(buf[0]); close(pipefd[0]); }

"Don't forget this is the standard C library write command. So we have to count how many bytes that we're sending." Get that count wrong and you send trailing garbage or truncate. The read loop runs one byte at a time and stops when read returns 0 — which is end-of-file, which only happens because the parent closed pipefd[1].

STDIO · pipe_fork2.c

The library counts them

if (parent) { // parent READS this time close(pipefd[1]); FILE *f = fdopen(pipefd[0], "r"); int c; while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(c); fclose(f); wait(NULL); } else { close(pipefd[0]); FILE *f = fdopen(pipefd[1], "w"); fprintf(f, "0123456789"); // no count fclose(f); }

fdopen is fopen's sibling: same modes, but it takes a descriptor you already have instead of a path. "Here we're using fdopen because we have the file descriptor." After that it is ordinary stdio — and note the direction flipped, so this parent is the reader.

A question the lecturer asked out loud and left open. "I haven't actually checked whether there's a sort of file descriptor close equivalent in the C library." There is, and the distinction matters here. close(fd) is the system call and takes an int. fclose(f) is stdio, takes a FILE *, flushes the buffer first, and then closes the underlying descriptor for you. So after fdopen you must use fclose — calling close(pipefd[1]) on a stream you have been fprintf-ing to throws away whatever is still sitting in the buffer. That is the same buffering trap as last lecture's fork_gotcha.c, wearing a different hat.

Slides 18–21 — convenient, and the reason you should not

popen: which direction is "r"? (read_popen.c · write_popen.c)

popen compresses pipe, fork, dup2 and exec into one line and hands you a FILE *. It also hands your string to /bin/sh, which is the whole problem. The mode letter is where people get turned around, so here it is nailed down by measurement rather than by memory.

THE SIGNATURE
#include <stdio.h> FILE *popen(const char *command, const char *type); int pclose(FILE *stream);

Returns NULL on failure. Close with pclose, not fclose — pclose also waits for the command and returns its exit status, the same status word you decoded in Lecture 1 §03. Using fclose leaves you a zombie and throws the status away.

THE MODE LETTER, MEASURED

Read it from the command's point of view

typethe pipe connects toyou do
"r"the command's stdoutfgets / fgetc
"w"the command's stdinfprintf / fputc
$ ./pop r-mode captured the command's STDOUT: Wed Aug 12 14:22:12 UTC 2026 w-mode wrote to the command's STDIN, which printed: HELLO, I AM A COMP1521 AFICIONADO
The spoken version has it backwards. "W means that we're reading from standard in and R means we're reading from standard out." With "w" you are writing, not reading — you write into the command's stdin. The mnemonic that survives contact with an exam: the letter describes what you do to the FILE *, exactly as it does for fopen. "r" means you read from it; the bytes must therefore be coming out of the command, so the command's stdout is what is attached. Slide 18 states it correctly.

Slide 22 — a claim from the lecture, put on the bench

“It's pretty robust to this” (spawn_read_pipe.c · spawn_write_pipe.c)

posix_spawn with file actions is the robust way to build a pipeline, and Lecture 1 §18 has the full four-call walkthrough. What is new here is that the lecturer tested the comment in the source, out loud, and reported the opposite of what the comment says. He was right — and for a reason worth pinning down, because it is the single most misunderstood thing about pipes.

THE CLAIM

"We're going to close the unused write end of the pipe in this example. If we don't do this, then the spawn process will not receive the end of file. I have to say that I did try this and it's pretty robust to this. It doesn't — it probably would screw up in certain cases, but in this very example, it does not."

WHY THE EXPERIMENT SUCCEEDED

EOF is governed by write ends only

A reader gets end-of-file when the number of open write ends drops to zero — across every process in the system. In spawn_write_pipe.c the parent writes and the child (sort) reads. The file action removes the child's copy of the write end. Deleting that line leaves the child holding a write end it never uses — and since the child is sort, which never writes to fd 0, nothing breaks visibly… until the child outlives the parent's close, at which point the reader waits forever on a descriptor only it still holds.

So: not load-bearing in this example, load-bearing in general. The lecturer's instinct — "for good practice do this" — is the right conclusion from the wrong mechanism.

THE LINE THAT IS LOAD-BEARING

The parent's own close

posix_spawn(&pid, "sort", &actions, ...); close(pipefd[0]); // unused read end FILE *f = fdopen(pipefd[1], "w"); fprintf(f, "please sort these words\n"); fclose(f); // <- delete this and it hangs waitpid(pid, &status, 0);

Delete the fclose and sort never sees EOF, never prints, and never exits, so waitpid blocks forever. The program deadlocks — which is the lecturer's own next sentence, "there is also issues with deadlock which we'll talk about a little bit later", arriving twenty minutes early.

Untick a close and see whether the pipeline still terminates. The counter that predicts the outcome is write ends still open — nothing else.

And that is the end of the pipes material. Everything above is Lecture 1 revisited. From here the lecture changes subject entirely: "now we're going to talk about concurrency."
Slides 23–25 — the distinction the rest of the lecture rests on

Concurrency is not parallelism (slide 24)

Two definitions, one of which is weaker than people assume. Concurrency: multiple computations with overlapping time periods — and "it doesn't mean that things have to be simultaneous." Parallelism: multiple computations executing simultaneously. Concurrency is about how a program is structured; parallelism is about what the hardware happens to do with it. One core can be concurrent and never parallel.

the same two computations, one core and two cores

The top pair is concurrent but not parallel — at every instant exactly one of them is running. The bottom pair is both. Parallelism is a special case of concurrency, not a synonym for it, and the implication only runs one way.

Slide 25 asks the class a question, then the lecturer answers it himself. "Have we already seen concurrency in this course? What about parallelism?… I've just answered my own questions." Worth answering properly, because it is a fair exam question. Concurrency: yes, repeatedly — every fork since Week 8 Lecture 2 produced two processes with overlapping lifetimes, and the whole point of waitpid is that the parent cannot assume the child has finished. Parallelism: not deliberately. Nothing you wrote asked for two cores; whether your parent and child actually ran at the same instant was the scheduler's business, not yours. Threads are the first tool in this course where you ask for parallelism on purpose — and §15 is where you find out whether you got it.

Slides 26–27 — a 1966 paper you are still quoting

Flynn's taxonomy (slide 27)

Two axes — how many instruction streams, how many data streams — giving four boxes. Michael Flynn published it in 1966, which the lecturer noticed on the slide mid-sentence: "It doesn't say what the date of this paper is, but it looks old… Oh, here we go. 1966." The framing is worth the two minutes because it tells you which kind of parallelism a piece of hardware offers.

SISD
Single Instruction, Single Data
“No parallelism.” One instruction stream chewing one data stream. e.g. mipsy — everything you wrote in Weeks 1–5.
SIMD
Single Instruction, Multiple Data
“Vector processing.” Many cores running the same instruction on different elements. e.g. GPUs — rendering pixels, and training and running neural networks.
MISD
Multiple Instruction, Single Data
Very rare. Several different computations on the same data, for fault tolerance — task replication in spacecraft and medical systems.
MIMD
Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data
“Multiprocessing.” Multiple cores running different instructions on different data. This is what threads on your laptop are.
The notes and the slides disagree about MISD. The course notes gloss MISD as “pipelining”; the slides and the lecture give fault tolerance and task replication. These are different ideas, and the notes' version is the shakier one — a classical instruction pipeline has each stage working on a different instruction and a different datum as it flows through, so it is not really one data stream through many instruction streams at all. Flynn's own MISD is closest to redundant computation: N units, N different programs, one input, votes compared at the end. If you get asked, give the fault-tolerance answer and the space-shuttle example. Nobody will mark you down for mentioning that MISD is “not used very much unless you're making critical systems.”
A detail from the digression that is actually the point. Explaining SIMD, the lecturer described a GPU as "a bunch of little CPUs… a bunch of little von Neumann machines all sitting together. They have a shared L2 cache." Hold onto the shared-cache part. It is the hardware reason threads are cheap and the hardware reason data races exist: the cores are close enough to share memory quickly, which means they are close enough to trip over each other. Every problem from §19 onwards is a consequence of that one design decision.
Slide 28 and course notes 5–6 — out of scope, in one place

Parallelism beyond one machine (slide 28 · MapReduce)

Two scales sit above threads, and both are explicitly out of scope. They are here because they are the answer to “why does the taxonomy matter” and because they turn up in every job ad you will read.

ACROSS AN ARRAY · SIMD

Data-parallel computing

Many identical processors, each handed one element of a data structure, each running the same computation on it, results copied back. This is what a GPU is for. The notes are careful about the catch: “not totally independent: need to synchronise on completion” — somebody still has to know when everyone has finished.

If your algorithm fits the model it might run 5–10× faster on a GPU. If it does not fit, it runs slower than the CPU. Choosing is the skill.

ACROSS MANY COMPUTERS

MapReduce, in four lines

stepwhat happens
mapfilter the data and distribute it as (key, value) pairs; each node receives a set of pairs sharing a key
computeeach node calculates on the items it received, independently
reducecombine the nodes' outputs into the final result
detectsomething must decide when every calculation has completed

Spread "across a rack, data center or even across continents". The hard parts are synchronisation and machine failure — "you'll often see a lot of very sad astronomers walking around because a core failed."

Which fields actually need this. The lecture named genomics and astronomical data as the everyday examples of datasets too big for one machine, and noted the honest trajectory: "it's certainly better than it was five years ago and much better than it was 10 years ago." The reason it appears in a systems course at all is that the failure modes scale up unchanged — the synchronisation problem you will meet in §21 with two threads and one integer is the same problem a thousand machines have with a petabyte, just with worse consequences and no debugger.
Slide 29 — the case against what you just spent two lectures learning

Concurrency with processes, and what it costs (slide 29 · notes 7)

You already have a concurrency tool: fork, or better posix_spawn. Split the job across several processes and they run concurrently, each in its own address space, each schedulable onto a different core. It works, it is robust, and "this strategy is expensive!" — four separate ways.

THE ADVANTAGE, WHICH IS REAL

Separate address spaces

Isolation. A child that corrupts its own memory cannot corrupt yours; a child that crashes does not take you with it. "That definitely helps with security" and with robustness. This is not a small win — the notes point out that the web server providing the class website uses process-level parallelism, and an Android phone runs several hundred processes. When the cost of a bug is a whole machine, you pay for walls.

THE FOUR COSTS
costwhy
creation & teardowna whole address space to build, and a corpse to reap — "otherwise you kind of leave zombie processes"
switchingthe kernel must swap out page tables, not just registers
memory“lots of state per process” — every process carries its own copy of everything
communicationseparate address spaces means nothing is shared, so every byte needs a pipe, and a pipe needs the four-call dance of §04
The lecturer's own summary is the honest one. "You only have to see the fun it was to spawn those new processes through a pipe." That is the argument for threads in one sentence: the mechanics of §01–§04 — two descriptors, four closes, a dup2, an fdopen, a waitpid, a destroy — is what it takes for two processes to pass a string to each other. Two threads share a variable and are done. The rest of this page is the bill for that convenience.

Slides 31–32 — the two lists that explain everything else

What threads share, and what they do not (slides 31–32)

A thread is a second (third, hundredth) execution state inside one process. There is no new address space, so there is nothing to copy and nothing to send. "It's really cheap to communicate because you're running in the same place." Everything good about threads and everything dangerous about them falls out of these two lists, so learn them as a pair.

two processes vs one process with two threads

Note what the dashes mean. The stacks are separate, but they are separate regions of one address space — there is no hardware boundary between them. Slide 32 says it plainly: “a thread can still read/write to another thread's stack.” Verified in Lab 6 below.

SHARED · SLIDE 31

One copy, visible to all threads

  • Code — all functions, obviously
  • Global and static variables — the source of every bug in §19
  • The heap — anything malloc returned, which is the fix in §18
  • File descriptors — one open, every thread can read it
  • Environment variables, current working directory, signal dispositions

"Cheap communication!" — a shared global is the channel. No pipe, no dup2, no serialisation.

PRIVATE · SLIDE 32

One per thread

  • Registers and the program counter — that is what an execution state is
  • The stack, so local variables are not shared — but see the figure caption
  • errno — "each thread gets its own copy of errno!"

The errno one is easy to skim past and is genuinely important: without it, thread A's failed open would clobber thread B's diagnosis, and no error handling anywhere would be trustworthy. It is implemented as thread-local storage — errno is a macro, not a variable.

lab 6 · shared or private — measured, not asserted

One program, four claims, one run

This is a real program compiled and run with two threads and a barrier between them. Thread A sets a value, thread B tries to see it. Press the button to replay the recorded run line by line.

what A touchedB sees it?verdict
actual output
The fourth line is the one people do not believe. Thread B was handed the address of a local variable in thread A's frame and wrote 777 into it. A's local changed under it. Separate stacks are an allocation policy, not a protection boundary.
Slide 33 — the library, and one compiler flag with a history

POSIX threads (slide 33)

pthreads is the widely-supported threading model — "supported in most Unix-like operating systems, and beyond" — and it gives you both halves of the problem: an API for making threads, and an API for stopping them treading on each other. One header, and historically one flag.

THE HEADER
#include <pthread.h>

Declares pthread_t, pthread_create, pthread_join, and the mutex machinery of §21. pthread_t is opaque — same deal as FILE *. Do not print it, do not compare it with ==; use pthread_equal if you must.

THE FLAG
$ gcc -pthread prog.c -o prog

"Sometimes you need -pthread… it's not always clear when you need that or not. So I often just use it because it's not going to kill you not to." Correct advice, and §10's callout explains exactly when it stopped mattering — and what it still does.

THE ALTERNATIVE
#include <threads.h> // C11 thrd_create(&t, fn, arg);

C11 adopted a pthreads-like model: thrd_create, thrd_join, mtx_lock. "Generally less supported and less used (for now…)" — and glibc only shipped it in 2.28. Learn pthreads; recognise the other one.

The -pthread flag, precisely. Tested on the machine that built this page (gcc 11.4, glibc 2.35): two_threads.c compiles, links and runs correctly with no -pthread at all. That is not luck. In glibc 2.34 (2021) libpthread was merged into libc, so there is no separate library left to link and the classic undefined reference to 'pthread_create' error is gone on any modern Linux. But keep passing the flag, for two reasons that have not gone away: it also defines _REENTRANT and sets thread-safe compilation options, and older glibc and non-Linux systems still need it — including, possibly, whatever CSE is running when you submit. So the lecturer's habit is right; the reason he could not remember when it was needed is that the answer changed underneath everyone.
Slide 34 — and an error protocol you have met before

pthread_create — start a thread (slide 34 · one_thread.c)

THE SIGNATURE
int pthread_create( pthread_t *restrict thread, const pthread_attr_t *restrict attr, void *(*start_routine)(void *), void *restrict arg);

Starts a new thread running start_routine(arg) and stores an ID in *thread. attr is NULL unless you want a custom stack size or detach state. "Analogous to posix_spawn" — and the analogy is tighter than it looks, because the error protocol is the same trap.

That third parameter is a function pointer: takes void *, returns void *. Your thread function must have exactly that shape, which is why every example casts on the way in and on the way out.

ONE THREAD, WHOLE PROGRAM
#include <pthread.h> #include <stdio.h> // called to start thread execution; // can be given any pointer as an argument void *run_thread(void *argument) { int *p = argument; printf("hello, my input was %d\n", *p); return NULL; } int main(void) { pthread_t id; int input = 42; pthread_create(&id, NULL, run_thread, &input); pthread_join(id, NULL); return 0; }

"Join is like getting everyone back together again." Note &input — you pass the address, never the value. That is the entire subject of §18.

The notes are wrong about how pthread_create reports failure, and the truth is worse than either version. The course notes say “Returns 0 if OK, -1 otherwise and sets errno”. Slide 34 says “Returns 0 if OK, otherwise an error number (does not set errno!)”. The slide is right — and this is the same protocol as posix_spawn in Lecture 1 §09. Forced to fail here by asking for an absurd stack size:
pthread_create returned 11 (Resource temporarily unavailable) ← the real error, EAGAIN errno after the call 12 (Cannot allocate memory) ← incidental, from an internal mmap perror("") printed Cannot allocate memory ← the wrong diagnosis
So errno is not merely unset — it is set to something plausible and misleading, and perror confidently reports the wrong cause. Use strerror(ret) on the return value. Checking if (ret == -1) as the notes suggest would never fire at all, because the return value on failure is a positive error number.

Slides 36–37 and notes 11–12 — collecting a thread

pthread_join, pthread_exit, and what main does on the way out (slide 36)

Threads have the same shape of lifecycle as processes, with a different set of names. Learning the correspondence is the fastest way to make this section stick, because you already know the process side cold.

posix_spawnpthread_createstart a new flow of execution, error number as return value
waitpidpthread_joinblock until it finishes, collect its result, release its resources
exitpthread_exitterminate the current flow, hand back a value
status word + WEXITSTATUSvoid **retvalhow the result comes back — a pointer, not an int, so no bit-shifting this time
zombie until reapedresources held until joineda thread that is never joined and never detached leaks its stack
SLIDE 36 · JOIN
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);

Waits for thread to terminate — and returns immediately if it already has, so there is no race in calling it late. The thread's return value lands in *retval; pass NULL if you do not want it. "Analogous to waitpid."

A thread finishes when its start function returns, or when it calls pthread_exit. Those are the same thing, in the same way that returning from main and calling exit are.

THE ONE-LINE TRAP

“When main returns, all threads terminate”

Not “are asked to finish”. Terminated, mid-instruction, wherever they happen to be. "Doesn't matter if they're finished, what they're doing, or whatever, they'll just all stop." Same for anyone calling exit(3) from any thread. Measured:

$ ./mainret thread tick 0 thread tick 1 thread tick 2 main returning now $ ← ticks 3, 4 and "thread FINISHED" never happened

Hence the rule: a program must join every thread whose work it needs. Forgetting a pthread_join is not a leak, it is a silent truncation of the work.

Slides 35 and 37 — the first thing that surprises everybody

Threads do not run in the order you made them (n_threads.c · one_thread_infinite_loops.c)

n_threads.c takes a count, creates that many threads in a for loop, and each prints its number. The loop is in order. The output is not. "There's no particular reason why three would run before two." Measured over six runs with four threads:

$ for i in 1..6; do ./n_threads 4; done 1 2 3 0 0 3 1 2 1 2 3 0 1 0 2 3 0 1 2 3 ← in order, by coincidence, once 1 0 2 3
Why thread 0 so often loses. Look at what main is doing: it is inside a loop calling pthread_create five more times. Creating a thread is real work — a stack to mmap, a kernel task to register — and on a 2-core machine main is holding one of the cores to do it. Thread 0 exists first but is competing with main's remaining pthread_create calls, so it frequently prints second or third. It is not random, it is a race between your new threads and the thread that is still making them — which is why the pattern is skewed rather than uniform. Never encode an assumption about order. If you need ordering you need §21's tools, or you need to join in the order you care about.
THE OTHER DEMO · SLIDE 35

Two infinite loops, both printing

one_thread_infinite_loops.c has a thread printing one message forever while main prints another forever. The lecture ran it and hit something confusing: "it's weird that we didn't see anything from main… Yeah. So there is parts where it's running from main and parts where it's running from other functions."

The screen looked like one thread had won. Measured, that impression is correct and the explanation is not buffering — it is the timeslice:

streak lengths, consecutive identical lines line-buffered: 608, 1004, 3071, 10079 block-buffered: 1862, 2048, 4608, 6144 unbuffered: 173, 1188, 2505, 3820 200,000 lines to a pipe: 158,510 from main · 41,490 from the thread
TWO THINGS THIS PROVES

Coarse, but never torn

1. Interleaving is coarse. A thread keeps its core for a full scheduler timeslice — a millisecond or so, which is thousands of printf calls. So you see long uninterrupted runs no matter what the buffering mode is. On a scrolling terminal a 10,000-line streak is far more than one screenful, which is exactly why it looked like main had vanished.

2. printf itself is atomic. Across 300,000 lines of output, zero torn or interleaved lines. glibc locks the FILE for the duration of the call, so two threads printing at once produce ugly ordering but never garbled text. This is the one piece of thread safety you get for free — and it is worth knowing it is per call, so two printfs that must stay together still need a mutex.
