Notes 20 — a two-line bug with a deterministic outcome

two_threads_broken.c: shared mutable state, immediately (notes 20)

This is the smallest thread bug in the course. Two threads, one variable, one reassignment, and the program lies to you. It is also the case where the sources hedge and the machine does not.

BROKEN
int main(void) { pthread_t id1; int thread_number = 1; pthread_create(&id1, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number); thread_number = 2; // <- overwrites it pthread_t id2; pthread_create(&id2, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number); pthread_join(id1, NULL); pthread_join(id2, NULL); }

Both threads were handed the same address. Whatever is in that int when a thread finally dereferences it is what that thread prints. main writes 2 long before either thread gets scheduled.

FIXED · two_threads.c
int main(void) { pthread_t id1; int thread_number1 = 1; pthread_create(&id1, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number1); pthread_t id2; int thread_number2 = 2; pthread_create(&id2, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number2); pthread_join(id1, NULL); pthread_join(id2, NULL); }

Two variables, two addresses, no interference. That is the entire fix — and it is the same fix as n_threads.c's int argument[n_threads], one slot per thread.

“Probably” is doing too much work here. The notes say “variable thread_number will probably change in main before thread 1 starts executing” and “thread 1 will probably print Hello this is thread 2”. Run ten times:
$ for i in 1..10; do ./two_threads_broken; done thread #2 thread #2 thread #2 thread #2 thread #2 thread #2 … 10 runs, 20 lines, every one says 2
10 out of 10. Not “probably” — effectively always, because thread_number = 2 is a single store executed nanoseconds after pthread_create returns, while the new thread still has to be scheduled onto a core for the first time. The hedge is technically honest and pedagogically harmful: it invites you to believe you might have got away with it. You did not. Treat “probably” in any race description as “reliably, until the day it matters”.

Slides 38–40 — “something useful with threads!”

Splitting real work (naive_sum.c · thread_sum.c)

Everything so far has printed greetings. This is the payoff: add up the first ten billion integers, and instead of one loop doing all of it, give each thread a slice. "Some of the artistry in parallel and concurrent programming is working out what to split up and how to bring it all together again."

slide 39 — three threads, one sum

Each thread writes its partial sum into its own slot of a struct job array — one slot per thread, no sharing, therefore no mutex needed anywhere in this program. Then main joins them in order and adds three numbers. This is the shape to reach for: partition, compute privately, combine once.

THE JOB STRUCT
struct job { long start, finish; double sum; }; void *run_thread(void *argument) { struct job *j = argument; double sum = 0; for (long i = j->start; i < j->finish; i++) sum += i; // a LOCAL, not shared j->sum = sum; // one write, own slot return NULL; }

The accumulator is a local variable. That is the design decision that makes this fast — see §22 for what happens if you accumulate into a shared global instead.

CREATE, THEN JOIN AND COMBINE
pthread_t thread_id[n_threads]; struct job jobs[n_threads]; for (int i = 0; i < n_threads; i++) { jobs[i].start = i * integers_per_thread; jobs[i].finish = jobs[i].start + integers_per_thread; if (jobs[i].finish > integers_to_sum) jobs[i].finish = integers_to_sum; pthread_create(&thread_id[i], NULL, run_thread, &jobs[i]); } double overall_sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n_threads; i++) { pthread_join(thread_id[i], NULL); overall_sum += jobs[i].sum; }

Two separate loops. Create all of them, then join all of them — creating and joining in the same loop would run them one at a time and buy you nothing at all. That is a favourite exam trap.

The clamp is not decoration. if (jobs[i].finish > integers_to_sum) exists because integer division truncates: 10 integers across 3 threads gives integers_per_thread = 3, so the threads cover 0–3, 3–6, 6–9 and integer 9 is never summed. The clamp stops the last thread overrunning, but it does not fix the shortfall. The lecture's own run shows the symptom: with 4 threads the boundaries printed were 0–25, 25–50, 50–75, 75–100 (with zeros) — clean only because 4 divides the total. Try ./thread_sum 3 10 and the answer is quietly wrong.

These are measured runs of thread_sum.c summing 2,000,000,000 integers on the 2-core machine that built this page, plus the course notes' own table for five other machines. Watch real fall and user refuse to.

What the notes' table is really showing. Five machines, and in every case the time halves as threads double until threads reach the core count, then goes flat. The 5800X (8 cores, 16 hardware threads) goes 6.6→3.3→1.6→0.8→0.6 and then stops improving at 24 and even at 500 threads. The UltraSPARC IIIi, with one core, goes 136.6→68.4 — and then stops: 68.6 s at 4 threads, 68.5 at 24, 68.6 at 500. One core takes 68 seconds and no amount of threading changes that. "The more threads you add you will get a really good boost in performance and then you'll kind of flatten off." Adding threads past the core count buys nothing; it just adds scheduling work and, as §22 shows, can make things worse.
Two things the demo does that nobody in the room expected

Why threads looked slower, and why the answer changes (measured)

The lecture ran thread_sum under time and got a result that stopped the demo: "just note that whatever — I was getting crazy results where it was taking, according to time, it was taking longer to use threads. And so this is one of those magic tricks that may not actually work out in real." The magic trick works. time was being read wrong, and there is a second, stranger problem underneath it.

SURPRISE 1 · THE THREE NUMBERS time PRINTS

Measured, 2,000,000,000 integers, 2 cores

threads real user sys 1 0.89 0.89 0.00 2 0.44 0.89 0.00 ← real halved; user did not budge 4 0.44 0.89 0.00 8 0.44 0.89 0.00 16 0.44 0.89 0.00 50 0.46 0.91 0.00 ← both slightly worse: scheduling overhead

real is wall-clock time — how long you waited. user is CPU time summed across every core. Two cores working for 0.44 s of wall clock have burned 0.88 s of CPU. So user cannot go down when you parallelise; the whole point is to spend the same CPU in less time. If you read the user line — or add user + sys, which is what many people mean by “how long did it take” — threading looks like it achieved nothing, and at high thread counts it looks actively harmful. The number that shows the speedup is real.

This also quietly confirms the machine: real stops improving after 2 threads because there are 2 cores. The measurement diagnoses the hardware.

SURPRISE 2 · THE ANSWER DEPENDS ON THE THREAD COUNT

Same input, six different sums

The lecture said of the 4-thread run: "they're going to come up with a combined sum and that is the right sum." It is not. The exact value of 0+1+…+1,999,999,999 is 1,999,999,999,000,000,000. What the program prints:

threads printed sum error 1 1999999998067113984 −932,886,016 2 1999999998071592960 −928,407,040 4 1999999998083439616 −916,560,384 8 1999999998112434688 −887,565,312 16 1999999998173342976 −826,657,024 50 1999999998362516224 −637,483,776 ← least wrong

Every thread count gives a different answer, all of them wrong by hundreds of millions, and — the part that surprises people — more threads is more accurate. Nothing is racing: each thread owns its slot. The culprit is double. A double holds 53 bits of significand, so it represents integers exactly only up to 253 ≈ 9.007×1015. Once the running total passes that, adding a value near 2×109 means the low bits of the addend cannot be represented and are rounded away. Floating-point addition is not associative, so (a+b)+c ≠ a+(b+c), and partitioning the work changes the order.

More threads ⇒ each partial sum stays smaller ⇒ fewer significant bits lost per addition ⇒ a better answer. Splitting the sum is a crude version of pairwise summation, a real numerical technique. Everything you learned in Week 5 about floating point is what makes this demo behave.

How to get the right answer. Declare the accumulators long or unsigned long, not double. 1.999×1018 fits comfortably in a signed 64-bit integer (max 9.22×1018) and integer addition is associative, so every thread count gives the identical, exact answer. The demo uses double so that the sum cannot overflow for any input, which is a defensible choice — but then it prints the result with %.0f, which formats it as though it were exact. That is where the misreading comes from: 19 confident digits, the last 9 of them noise.

Slide 41 — the benefit that has nothing to do with speed

Waiting is a use case (slide 41)

Threads are not only for chopping up arithmetic. The second reason to use them is that one thread can block while the others keep working — and that reason applies even on a single core, where there is no parallelism to be had at all.

BLOCKING I/O

Somebody has to wait; it need not be everybody

A read on a pipe with nothing in it, an fgets on a terminal, a network request — these park the calling thread indefinitely. Single-threaded, your whole program is parked. "You could have a thread there that's waiting for a user to do an input… and everything else can still be working. It's not that everybody stops and waits."

And note the resource argument, which is the systems-course point: "if everything stops waiting for something then you're not utilising any of your resources." A blocked thread uses no CPU. Overlapping one thread's waiting with another's computing is free throughput — concurrency without any parallelism.

USER INTERFACES

Why the spinner spins

Every GUI you have used has a main thread whose only job is to stay responsive: draw, and handle clicks. Anything slow — loading a file, talking to a server — goes on another thread. Do the slow thing on the main thread and the window greys out and the OS offers to kill your application.

This is the everyday reason threads exist, and it explains the constraint you will meet in every UI framework: only the main thread may touch the interface. Given §19, you now know why — the widget tree is shared mutable state, and the alternative to that rule is a mutex around every pixel.

Slide 42 and notes 39–43 — the bug that is not a race

Data lifetime (thread_data_broken.c · thread_data_malloc.c)

You can only give a thread the address of your data. So there is a question no single-threaded program ever has to ask: "what if by the time the thread reads the data, that data no longer exists?" This is not a synchronisation problem and no mutex will fix it. It is a lifetime problem, and you have met it before — this is the dangling pointer from COMP1511 with a scheduler making it worse.

WHY IT HAS NOT BITTEN YOU YET

main outlives everything

Every example so far put the thread's data in a local variable of main, created the threads from main, and joined them in main. Locals live until their function returns; main returns last. So the data was guaranteed valid for the whole life of every thread, by construction and by luck.

Break any link in that chain — create a thread from a helper function and return — and the guarantee evaporates.

BROKEN
pthread_t create_thread(void) { int super_special_number = 0x42; pthread_t handle; pthread_create(&handle, NULL, my_thread, &super_special_number); return handle; // the int dies HERE } void *my_thread(void *data) { int number = *(int *)data; sleep(1); printf("The number is 0x%x!\n", number); }
What it actually prints, and why the lecturer's fix did not work. The lecture expected 0x42 and got 0xCA. Compiled and run here, six times: 0x7ffc, 0x7fff, 0x7ffe, 0x7ffe, 0x7ffd, 0x7fff. Those are not random — they are the top 16 bits of a stack address. Instrumented, the slot that held 0x42 was at 0x7ffd6bf103dc, and a live stack address moments later was 0x7ffd6bf10400: something stored part of a pointer into the dead slot. Undefined behaviour rarely gives you noise; it gives you whatever the next occupant left behind, which is far more confusing.
The more important correction. The lecture then tried deleting the say_hello() call — "if we kind of took away the destructor function, maybe things would still exist. It does. Okay." Tested, that is not what happens:
with say_hello(): 0x7ffc 0x7fff 0x7ffe 0x7ffe 0x7ffd 0x7fff say_hello() deleted: 0x7ffc 0x7ffe 0x7fff 0x7ffc 0x7ffd 0x7ffe ← identical, still broken
Removing say_hello removes one obvious overwriter, but the slot is dead the instant create_thread returns, and pthread_join itself has a stack frame that lands on top of it. The lifetime ended at the return, not at the next function call. A bug you cannot make disappear by deleting the thing that seemed to cause it is the signature of undefined behaviour — and it is exactly why “it worked when I tried it” is not evidence.
FIXED · thread_data_malloc.c
pthread_t create_thread(void) { int *n = malloc(sizeof(int)); *n = 0x42; pthread_t handle; pthread_create(&handle, NULL, my_thread, n); return handle; // heap survives the return } void *my_thread(void *data) { int number = *(int *)data; sleep(1); printf("The number is 0x%x!\n", number); free(data); // the thread owns it now }
$ for i in 1..5; do ./thread_data_malloc; done The number is 0x42! ×5, every time
WHY THE HEAP

You choose when it dies

Stack lifetime is decided by the compiler: it ends at return, full stop, and in MIPS terms $sp moves back and the slot is fair game. Heap lifetime is decided by you: it ends when someone calls free. That is the entire reason malloc is the answer here.

Note who calls free: the thread, when it is finished. That is a deliberate transfer of ownership. If create_thread freed it, we would be back where we started; if nobody frees it, it leaks. "Nine times out of 10 your problem is that you've passed a pointer to something that doesn't exist anymore."

Three other valid answers, for completeness: make it global or static; keep it in main and join before returning; or use a barrier so the creator waits until the thread has copied the value — which the notes mention and then explicitly excludes from the course.

Slides 43–46 — “data races, deadlock and disasters”

Incrementing a global is not atomic (slides 44–46 · bank_account_broken.c)

Here is the whole problem in one statement, and it is the sentence to memorise: bank_account++ is not one operation. It is a load, an add, and a store — and the scheduler is allowed to switch threads between any two of them. This is where the MIPS you learned in Weeks 1–3 pays off, because the slides prove it in assembly.

WHAT YOU WROTE
int bank_account; void *thread(void *a) { // ... bank_account++; // ... }

One line. Looks indivisible. "Don't forget ++ at the end is an increment, which becomes important later on."

WHAT THE MACHINE DOES
la $t0, bank_account lw $t1, ($t0) # 1. LOAD addi $t1, $t1, 1 # 2. ADD sw $t1, ($t0) # 3. STORE .data bank_account: .word 0

Three memory-touching instructions and a register in between. Threads share globals but do not share registers — so $t1 is a private snapshot of a shared value, and it goes stale the moment the other thread stores.

slide 45 — two threads, one increment lost

Nothing here is exotic. Both threads read 42 because the first store had not happened yet; both computed 43 in their own private $t1; the second store overwrote the first with the same value. Slide 46 runs the sharper version — one thread adding 100 and the other subtracting 50 — where the final balance is 50 or 200 depending purely on which store lands last, and neither is right. The region between the load and the store is a critical section.

The lecturer's framing, which is the one that sticks. "Say I pay you like $20 and at the same time you're buying something from Amazon and you're spending $20 there. If you're both accessing the same global variable in your bank account, then it might be that one of those transactions is missed." Poor Andrew — whose account these demos empty all lecture — is not losing money to a bug in arithmetic. He is losing it to the three-instruction gap between reading his balance and writing it back.

The demo that would not break, explained

The nanosleep that hides the bug (bank_account_broken.c, measured)

The lecture spent several minutes trying to make bank_account_broken.c visibly lose money and mostly failed: "Did this for ages and I just couldn't get it. I could get it to maybe miss a few dollars here and there, but it's really disappointing how robust this is." Then, reasonably, he tried removing and increasing the nanosleep. The results were backwards from what he expected, and the reason is worth a section.

THE LINE IN QUESTION
void *add_100000(void *argument) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { // execution may switch threads in middle of assignment nanosleep(&(struct timespec){ .tv_nsec = 1 }, NULL); bank_account++; } return NULL; }

The comment says the sleep is there to encourage the switch. Measured over ten runs each, 2 threads × 100,000 increments, expected 200,000:

as shipped, nanosleep 1ns 199986 199989 199992 199989 199988 199987 199989 199976 199995 199987 → loses 5–24 out of 200,000. Looks correct. nanosleep REMOVED 100000 102649 200000 145078 130379 116853 200000 189364 100000 163267 → loses up to HALF. Sometimes exactly 100000. nanosleep raised to 1000ns 39997 39998 39996 39995 39999 (of 40,000) → even more robust.
The sleep suppresses the race; it does not provoke it. The lecture's conclusion after deleting it was "Makes it even less likely to do bad things. What if we make nanosleep more?" — exactly inverted. Deleting the sleep is what makes the program fail catastrophically. The arithmetic: bank_account++ is three instructions, about a nanosecond. A nanosleep is a system call, and asking for 1ns really costs a microsecond or more of entry, timer setup and rescheduling. So with the sleep in place each thread spends roughly 99.9% of its time not in the critical section, and the chance both threads are inside their load–store window simultaneously is about one in ten thousand — which is exactly the 5–24 lost increments observed. Increase the sleep and the window gets relatively narrower still. Remove it and the loop is nothing but critical section, both cores hammer the same cache line continuously, and you lose 20–50%.
The 100000 results are the interesting ones. Getting exactly 100,000 means one thread's entire contribution vanished — it ran, in lockstep, reading and writing the same values as the other thread for all 100,000 iterations. And 200,000 appeared 5 times in 40 runs with no sleep, meaning one thread finished before the other was scheduled. Same binary, same input, answers from 100,000 to 200,000. That is what “undefined” costs you: not a wrong answer, an unrepeatable one.

Slides 47–48 — the first fix

Mutexes: mutual exclusion (bank_account_mutex.c)

A critical section is a stretch of code that must not have two threads in it at once. A mutex is the object that enforces that. You associate one with each resource you want to protect — "in the case the resource is access to a global variable" — and only the thread holding it may proceed.

THE TWO CALLS
int pthread_mutex_lock(pthread_mutex_t *mutex); int pthread_mutex_unlock(pthread_mutex_t *mutex);

Only one thread can hold a given mutex. Any other thread calling lock on it blocks — parked, using no CPU — until the holder calls unlock. So exactly one thread at a time is between the two calls.

Note what a mutex does not do: it does not protect the variable. It protects the code region. A mutex you forget to lock in one place out of five is a mutex that does nothing — the compiler will not tell you, and the program will look fine until it does not.

bank_account_mutex.c
int bank_account = 0; pthread_mutex_t bank_account_lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER; void *add_100000(void *argument) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { pthread_mutex_lock(&bank_account_lock); // only one thread can execute this // section of code at any time bank_account = bank_account + 1; pthread_mutex_unlock(&bank_account_lock); } return NULL; }

PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER is the static initialiser — fine for a global. For a mutex inside a struct or on the heap you need pthread_mutex_init at runtime, and pthread_mutex_destroy after.

Measured, and this one is unambiguous. 2 threads × 1,000,000 increments, expected 2,000,000. Plain int++ over seven runs: 1,040,852, 1,070,105, 1,120,459, 1,068,749, 1,119,120, 1,010,425, 1,058,421 — a different answer every time, roughly 47% lost. With the mutex: 2,000,000, seven times out of seven, no exceptions. The correctness question has a clean answer; §22 is about the bill.

Slide 49 — so why not lock everything?

Mutex the world? (slide 49)

Mutexes solve data races. So put one around everything and be done. "This works… but then we lose the advantages of parallelism." That statement is true and it undersells the problem. Measured, a single global lock does not merely cancel the benefit of threads — it makes more threads actively slower than fewer.

MEASURED · SUMMING 20,000,000 INTEGERS
threads private partial sums one shared mutex 1 0.0092 s 0.2495 s ← 27× slower already 2 0.0047 s 0.8155 s ← 2.0× faster vs 3.3× SLOWER 4 0.0059 s 0.8285 s median of 7 runs each, one process per measurement, counters padded to separate cache lines

Two effects stack up. First, the lock itself costs — even with one thread and no contention, taking and releasing a mutex 20 million times costs 27× more than the additions. Second, and worse, contention: with two threads the lock is the only thing either of them can do, so they spend their time handing one cache line back and forth and blocking each other. Going from 1 thread to 2 makes it 3.3× slower (0.2495 s → 0.8155 s). You have paid for two cores to achieve less than one core would.

Compare the private-sum column: 2.0× faster on 2 cores, near-perfect scaling, because thread_sum.c has no shared mutable state at all. That is the lesson buried in §15 — the best synchronisation is the synchronisation you designed away.

PYTHON · THE GIL

A real language did this

CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock: one mutex, held while executing bytecode, so only one thread runs Python at a time. It makes the interpreter and every C extension trivially thread-safe, and it means CPU-bound Python threads get no parallelism whatsoever.

"Although can be disabled now…" — that is PEP 703, accepted in 2023, which added an optional free-threaded build. Twenty-five years of the easy answer, and unpicking it is a multi-release project.

LINUX · THE BKL

And a real kernel

Linux's Big Kernel Lock was the same bargain: one lock for the whole kernel, so early SMP support worked at all. "Linux used to do this — they removed the 'Big Kernel Lock' in 2011."

Two decades to replace it with fine-grained locking, because every one of those small locks introduces the possibility in §23. The trade is always the same: coarse locks are correct and slow; fine locks are fast and can deadlock.

lab 17 · lock granularity bench

Same work, four locking strategies

Add threads and watch which strategies scale. Only one of these gets faster with more threads, and it is the one with no lock in the inner loop.

Slides 50–52 — the price of fine-grained locks

Deadlock, and the rule that prevents it (bank_account_deadlock.c)

Two accounts, two mutexes, two threads sending money to each other. Each thread needs both locks. Thread 1 takes Andrew's then Xavier's; thread 2 takes Xavier's then Andrew's. Each grabs its first lock, then waits forever for the one the other is holding. "No thread can make progress! The system is deadlocked."

slide 51 — the cycle

The general condition: a cycle in the graph of “who is waiting for what that someone else holds”. Neither thread is buggy on its own; each locks both mutexes it needs and releases both. The bug lives in the relationship between two functions that were written separately — which is why deadlock is so hard to find by reading one function at a time.

THREAD 1
void *andrew_send_xavier_money(void *a) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { pthread_mutex_lock(&andrews_lock); pthread_mutex_lock(&xaviers_lock); if (andrews_bank_account > 0) { andrews_bank_account--; xaviers_bank_account++; } pthread_mutex_unlock(&xaviers_lock); pthread_mutex_unlock(&andrews_lock); } }
THREAD 2 — SPOT THE DIFFERENCE
void *xavier_send_andrew_money(void *a) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { pthread_mutex_lock(&xaviers_lock); pthread_mutex_lock(&andrews_lock); if (xaviers_bank_account > 0) { xaviers_bank_account--; andrews_bank_account++; } pthread_mutex_unlock(&andrews_lock); pthread_mutex_unlock(&xaviers_lock); } }
The class never saw this one run. "Oops, I didn't do any print statements there. All right, so let's just quickly go to the slides because I'm also getting to the end here." Compiled and run — 30 out of 30 runs hung and had to be killed. Instrumented to see how far it gets first:
run 1: thread 1 completed 18 iterations, thread 2 completed 3385, then frozen run 2: thread 1 completed 0 iterations, thread 2 completed 1033, then frozen run 3: both completed all 100000 ← got lucky: one finished before the other started
So it deadlocks almost immediately — within the first few thousand of a hundred thousand iterations — and it does occasionally sail through, which is the worst possible behaviour for a bug. There is no partial failure and no error message. The program simply stops, at 0% CPU, forever.
THE FIX · SLIDE 52

All threads acquire locks in the same order

That is the whole rule, and it is enough to make a cycle impossible: if everyone takes A before B, nobody can be holding B while waiting for A. The notes add the companion habit — “also best to release in reverse order (if possible)” — so locks nest cleanly like brackets. Measured with both threads taking Andrew's lock first: 3 runs, 3 completions, 100,000/100,000 iterations each, no hangs.

But look at what the fixed program computes. The three successful runs ended:
andrews=300 xaviers=0 andrews=0 xaviers=300 andrews=300 xaviers=0
All the money ends up in one account, and which one is decided by scheduling. The total is conserved — 200+100 = 300 — so there is no lost update; the locking is correct. The program is still nonsense: two threads each moving a dollar at a time in opposite directions, a hundred thousand times, and whoever runs last wins. The lecturer saw it: "just for the record, I think this is a bad way of doing this code." Fixing a deadlock makes a program run. It does not make it right. Correct synchronisation and correct logic are separate problems, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

Slides 53–56 — the lecture ran out of time; the slides did not

Atomics (slides 53–56 · bank_account_atomic.c)

Where the lecture stopped. "All right, so we're not going to get to this now. We'll look at this on Monday, but atomics are a nice easy way to deal with potential race conditions without having to worry about the overhead of the mutual exclusions." That sentence is an accurate summary of the whole section. The slides and the course notes cover atomics in full, so the full treatment is here — expect Week 10 Lecture 1 to open with it.

Mutexes are a software solution: block everyone else while I do my three instructions. Atomics are a hardware solution: ask the CPU for an instruction that does all three at once, indivisibly. If the load, add and store cannot be separated, there is no window to interleave into — and so no race, no lock, and nothing to deadlock on.

DECLARING ONE
#include <stdatomic.h> atomic_int bank_account = 0; void *add_100000(void *argument) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { bank_account += 1; } return NULL; }

No lock, no unlock, no initialiser macro, and the loop body is shorter than the racy version. The type does the work: every read-modify-write through an _Atomic lvalue compiles to a single locked instruction.

THE TRAP ON SLIDE 54
atomic_int x = 10; x += 1; // atomic ✓ x++; // atomic ✓ atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1); // atomic ✓ x = x + 1; // NOT atomic ✗

The last line is two separate atomic operations: an atomic read, then an atomic write, with an ordinary gap between them — exactly the gap you were trying to close. Each half is atomic; the pair is not.

Slide 54's warning, verified. 2 threads × 1,000,000 increments, expected 2,000,000, run twice:
result median time plain int++ 1010425 .. 1120459 0.00247 s mutex, x = x + 1 2000000 (7/7) 0.08232 s atomic, x += 1 2000000 (7/7) 0.02029 s ← correct AND 4.1× faster than the mutex atomic, x = x + 1 1368367 .. 1836979 0.03321 s ← the trap: atomic type, lost updates anyway atomic_fetch_add 2000000 (7/7) 0.02122 s
The fourth row is the one to stare at. It uses atomic_int, compiles without a warning, and loses between 160,000 and 630,000 increments. Writing x = x + 1 instead of x += 1 silently disables the protection you asked for. This is why the comment in bank_account_atomic.c is three lines long — and note that the mutex version on slide 48 does write bank_account = bank_account + 1, which is perfectly correct there, because the lock is what protects it. Same expression, opposite verdict, depending on the mechanism.
THE OPERATOR SET · SLIDE 54

Compound assignment works and is atomic:

++ += -- -= |= &= ^=

The bitwise three are exactly the Week 4 operators, now safe to use on a shared flags word from several threads — which is how real code implements a concurrent bitset.

THE FUNCTION SET · SLIDE 55
functiondoes, atomically
atomic_fetch_addn += v, returns the old value
atomic_fetch_subn -= v, returns the old value
atomic_fetch_orn |= v
atomic_fetch_andn &= v
atomic_fetch_xorn ^= v
compare_exchangeif (n == v1) n = v2; — test and set in one step

Getting the old value back matters: int old = atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1); gives each thread a unique ticket number. You cannot build that from x += 1, which discards it.

x += 1 and atomic_fetch_add cost the same — until you turn the optimiser on. Measured at -O0: 0.02029 s and 0.02122 s, a 5% gap that is inside the noise. They are the same speed because they compile to the same instruction. Checking the generated assembly rather than guessing:
gcc -O0 x += 1 lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip) atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1) lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip) ← identical gcc -O2 x += 1 lock addl $1, x(%rip) ← result unused, cheaper form atomic_fetch_add, used lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip) ← must return the old value atomic_fetch_add, unused lock addl $1, x(%rip) ← optimised down to the same thing
So the rule is real but narrower than it sounds: lock add is cheaper than lock xadd, and you only get it when the compiler can see the old value is dead. At -O0 nothing is optimised and both spell it xadd; at -O2 gcc will even downgrade an atomic_fetch_add whose result you ignore. Prefer += for clarity when you do not need the old value — but do not expect a measurable win from that choice alone.

Notes 36–38 — the honest limitations

What atomics do and do not buy you (notes 36–38)

Atomics look like a free win: correct, faster than a mutex, and deadlock-proof. The first two are true. The third needs stating precisely, and the slides are careful to add that “atomics don't solve all concurrency problems” and that “there are still some subtle problems (which we don't cover in COMP1521)”.

THE REAL WIN

No lock means no lock ordering

Deadlock in §23 required a thread to hold one lock while waiting for another. An atomic operation is indivisible and never waits, so it cannot be held across another acquisition. “Atomic instructions are (by definition!) atomic, so there's no equivalent to the above problem. Goodbye deadlocks!”

Three terms the notes define, worth knowing as vocabulary:

non-blockinga failed or suspended thread cannot suspend another
lock-freenon-blocking, and the system as a whole always progresses
wait-freelock-free, and every thread always progresses
FOUR CATCHES
catchdetail
hardwareneeds CPU support — universal on modern machines, may be missing on embedded targets
still costsfaster than locking but not free: measured 8× the cost of a plain int++ (0.0203 s vs 0.0025 s), because the cache line must be claimed exclusively on every operation
memory ordering“incredibly tricky to write correct code at a low level” — C has six orderings; the default seq_cst is the safe one and the slow one. Explicitly out of scope.
ABA problema value read as A, changed to B and back to A looks unchanged — compare_exchange cannot tell. Bites lock-free data structures.
When you still need a mutex. Atomics protect one variable at a time. If an invariant spans two variables — “the total of Andrew's and Xavier's accounts is always 300” — no single atomic operation can maintain it, because you must change both and nobody may observe the state in between. That is a critical section, and it needs a lock. So the decision rule: one word, one operation → atomic. Multiple words, or an invariant between them → mutex. §23's transfer is genuinely a mutex problem; §19's counter never was.
Slide 57 — a taste, explicitly

Concurrency is really complex (slide 57)

"This is just a taste of concurrency!" The lecture is straightforward about being an introduction, and the list of what was skipped is useful precisely because it tells you the shape of what you do not know yet.

NOT COVERED, BUT NAMED
livelockthreads keep running and keep responding, and none makes progress — deadlock's more embarrassing cousin
starvationone thread never gets the lock because others keep beating it to it
thundering herdone event wakes a hundred blocked threads; ninety-nine find nothing to do and go back to sleep
memory orderingthe compiler and CPU reorder your reads and writes; what other threads see may not be your program's order
semaphoresa counted mutex — “at most N threads in here”
STMsoftware transactional memory — try it, and roll back if someone else conflicted
user threads, fibersconcurrency scheduled by your program rather than the kernel; Go's goroutines, Python's async
WHERE TO GET MORE
COMP3231
COMP3891		[Extended] Operating Systems — the scheduler, and much more on deadlock, from the kernel's side
COMP3151Foundations of Concurrency — how to prove a concurrent program correct rather than testing and hoping
COMP6991Solving Modern Programming Problems with Rust — a language whose type system rejects §18's dangling pointer and §19's unguarded global at compile time

The Rust one is the pointed comparison. Every bug on this page — the dead stack slot, the unsynchronised global, the argument reused before the thread read it — is a compile error in a language designed after the industry had absorbed how often people get this wrong.

Check yourself

Exercises

Seven sets, roughly in lecture order. The later ones are the advanced material the lecturer flagged as likely to be worth about one exam question — but the vocabulary shows up everywhere.

Set 1 · Concurrency and parallelism
  1. Give an example of a program that is concurrent but definitely not parallel. Then one that is both.
  2. Slide 25 asks whether this course has already shown you concurrency, and parallelism. Answer both, with a specific mechanism from an earlier week.
  3. Classify each under Flynn: mipsy running your Week 2 code; a GPU shading a million pixels; four cores compiling four different files; three redundant flight computers voting on one sensor reading.
  4. A single-core machine runs a program with 8 threads. Which of these can it still gain? (a) faster CPU-bound arithmetic (b) a responsive UI while loading a file (c) overlapping a network wait with computation.
Answers

1. Concurrent but not parallel: any threaded or forked program on a single core — the two flows overlap in time but never execute in the same instant. Also anything async/event-loop based, which is concurrent by construction on one thread. Both: thread_sum 2 on a 2-core machine.

2. Concurrency: yes — every fork since Week 8 Lecture 2. Parent and child have overlapping lifetimes; waitpid exists precisely because the parent cannot assume the child has finished. Parallelism: not deliberately — nothing you wrote requested a second core; whether parent and child truly ran simultaneously was the scheduler's decision.

3. mipsy → SISD. GPU shading → SIMD. Four cores, four files → MIMD. Redundant flight computers → MISD.

4. (b) and (c). Not (a): CPU-bound work on one core takes the same total CPU time however you slice it — see the UltraSPARC row in §15, where 1 thread and 500 threads both take 68 seconds. (b) and (c) are wins because a blocked thread uses no CPU, so the waiting overlaps with the working. This is the whole content of §17, and it is why threads help even without parallelism.

Set 2 · Threads: shared and private
  1. For each, say whether two threads in one process share it: a global int; a malloc'd buffer; a local variable in main; the value of errno; an open file descriptor; the program counter; the current working directory.
  2. Thread A has a local int x. Can thread B write to it? Should it be able to? Explain the difference between those two questions.
  3. Why does each thread need its own errno? Give a concrete failure mode if they shared one.
  4. Name the process-world equivalent of pthread_create, pthread_join and pthread_exit.
Answers

1. Shared: global int, malloc'd buffer, file descriptor, current working directory. Also the local in main — it is on main's stack, but any thread handed its address can reach it, which is exactly how every example passed data. Private: errno, the program counter (and all registers, and each thread's own stack).

2. Yes it can — verified in Lab 6, where thread B wrote 777 into thread A's local. No it should not — nothing good comes of it. The distinction is between what the hardware prevents and what the language and conventions discourage. Threads share one address space, so there is no protection boundary between their stacks; separateness is an allocation policy, not enforcement. Compare processes, where the MMU makes it genuinely impossible.

3. Because otherwise error reporting is worthless. Thread A calls open and it fails with ENOENT; before A reaches its perror, thread B's socket call fails with EACCES and overwrites the shared errno; A now prints “Permission denied” for a missing file. Every diagnosis in a multithreaded program would be a lottery. (This is the same class of bug as the misleading errno after pthread_create in §11 — only far more frequent.)

4. pthread_create ↔ posix_spawn / fork+exec; pthread_join ↔ waitpid; pthread_exit ↔ exit.

Set 3 · Creating and joining
  1. Write the correct error check for pthread_create. Why is if (ret == -1) perror("pthread_create"); wrong in two separate ways?
  2. main creates 4 threads, joins none, and returns. What happens to the threads' work?
  3. Rewrite this so it actually runs in parallel, and say how much time it currently wastes:
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { pthread_create(&id[i], NULL, work, &jobs[i]); pthread_join(id[i], NULL); }
  4. ./n_threads 4 printed 1 2 3 0. Is this a bug? What guarantee does pthread_create actually give about ordering?
Answers

1. int ret = pthread_create(...); if (ret != 0) { fprintf(stderr, "pthread_create: %s\n", strerror(ret)); exit(1); }. Two faults in the wrong version: (i) it never fires, because failure returns a positive error number, never −1; (ii) even if it did, perror reads errno, which pthread_create does not set for you — measured, it held an incidental ENOMEM from an internal allocation while the true error was EAGAIN, so perror prints a confidently wrong cause. Same protocol as posix_spawn.

2. They are terminated immediately, wherever they happen to be. Returning from main ends the process and every thread in it, finished or not — measured in §12, where a thread on tick 2 of 5 simply stopped. Any work not completed is silently lost: no error, no warning, a plausible-looking partial answer.

3. Split into two loops — create all, then join all. As written, each iteration blocks until that thread finishes, so exactly one thread runs at a time and you get zero parallelism plus the full cost of creating and destroying n threads. It is strictly slower than a plain loop. With n threads on n cores you are wasting roughly (n−1)/n of the available time — 75% at n=4.

4. Not a bug. pthread_create guarantees only that the thread has been created — nothing about when it is scheduled or in what order. Measured over six runs: 1 2 3 0, 0 3 1 2, 1 2 3 0, 1 0 2 3, 0 1 2 3, 1 0 2 3. Thread 0 often loses because main is still occupying a core with the remaining pthread_create calls. If you need an order, enforce it.

Set 4 · Data lifetime
  1. Why does thread_data_broken.c print rubbish, given that super_special_number is definitely 0x42 when pthread_create is called?
  2. The lecture deleted the say_hello() call to see if that fixed it. Predict the result and justify it.
  3. The observed garbage values were 0x7ffc, 0x7ffe, 0x7fff. Why are they all so similar, and what does that tell you about what overwrote the slot?
  4. Four different fixes, and when each is the right choice.
  5. In thread_data_malloc.c, the thread calls free(data). Why the thread and not the creator?
Answers

1. Because the thread reads it later. pthread_create copies the pointer, not the int. create_thread then returns, ending the local's lifetime and freeing its stack slot for reuse, and the thread — which sleeps a second first — dereferences a pointer to a dead slot.

2. It does not fix it — measured, identical garbage with and without. The lifetime ended at the return, not at the next call. Removing say_hello removes one obvious overwriter, but pthread_join's own frame lands on the same region. That a bug survives deleting its apparent cause is characteristic of undefined behaviour, and is why “it worked when I tried it” proves nothing.

3. They are the top 16 bits of a stack address. Instrumented, the slot lived at 0x7ffd6bf103dc and a live stack address nearby was 0x7ffd6bf10400 — something stored half a pointer over the dead int. Stack addresses on x86-64 Linux all begin 0x7ff..., hence the family resemblance. The moral: undefined behaviour hands you the next occupant's data, not noise, which is why it so often looks like a plausible value.

4. (i) malloc — the general answer, when the data must outlive the creating function and the thread can own it. (ii) global or static — simple, but one copy for all threads, so only for genuinely shared read-only data. (iii) keep it in main and join before returning — what every earlier example did; free and correct when your thread creation is confined to main. (iv) a barrier, making the creator wait until the thread has copied the value — mentioned in the notes and explicitly not examined.

5. Ownership transfer. If create_thread freed it, we would be back to a dangling pointer — the same bug with free in place of return. The creator cannot know when the thread has finished reading, and the whole point of this pattern is that the creator does not wait. So the last user frees it. The alternative is for the joiner to free it after pthread_join, which also works but requires someone to join.

Set 5 · Race conditions (advanced)
  1. Write out the MIPS for counter++ and mark the exact instruction boundaries where a switch loses an update.
  2. bank_account = 42. Thread 1 adds 100, thread 2 subtracts 50, both unguarded. List every possible final value and the interleaving that produces it.
  3. Two threads each add 1 to a shared int 100,000 times. Give the minimum and maximum possible final values.
  4. The demo's nanosleep is commented as making a thread switch more likely mid-assignment. Measured, removing it makes the program fail far more. Reconcile these.
  5. A run prints exactly 100,000 instead of 200,000. What must have happened, and why is it more alarming than 163,267?
Answers

1. la $t0, counter / lw $t1, ($t0) / addi $t1, $t1, 1 / sw $t1, ($t0). An update is lost if the other thread's sw lands after this thread's lw and before this thread's sw — i.e. either gap, lw→addi or addi→sw. The register holds a stale private copy across both.

2. Three outcomes. 192 — fully serialised either way (42+100−50). 142 — both load 42, thread 1 stores 142 last. −8 — both load 42, thread 2 stores −8 last. Slide 46 shows the 100-based version with 50 or 200; same structure. Note that the “correct” answer is only one of three, and which you get is unrepeatable.

3. Maximum 200,000 (no interleaving unluckily placed — observed 5 times in 40 runs). Minimum 2, not 100,000: in the pathological schedule both threads load 0, then one runs to completion while the other holds a stale 0 in its register, and finally stores 1 — but the truly minimal case interleaves so that almost every store is overwritten. In practice measured runs bottomed out at exactly 100,000; the theoretical floor is 2.

4. The comment describes an intention; the measurement describes the effect. A nanosleep is a system call costing on the order of a microsecond, while the critical section is about a nanosecond of load–add–store. So the sleep makes each thread spend ~99.9% of its iteration outside the danger window, collisions become one-in-thousands, and the demo loses only 5–24 of 200,000 — it looks correct. Remove it and the loop is nothing but critical section, and 20–50% of updates vanish. The sleep does force a reschedule, but at a moment that is almost never dangerous.

5. One thread's entire contribution was lost — the two threads ran in near-perfect lockstep for all 100,000 iterations, each loading the same value the other had just loaded. It is more alarming than a messy 163,267 because it looks like a clean, explicable number: exactly one thread's worth. A reader could easily conclude “one thread failed to start” and go hunting for a pthread_create bug that does not exist. Plausible wrong answers cost more debugging time than obviously wrong ones.

Set 6 · Mutexes and deadlock (advanced)
  1. A program guards a global with a mutex in four functions and forgets it in a fifth. What is protected?
  2. Why did wrapping the inner loop in one global mutex make the 2-thread run slower than the 1-thread run?
  3. State the deadlock avoidance rule. Apply it to bank_account_deadlock.c in one line of change.
  4. The fixed version completes, and always ends with all the money in one account. Is it correct? Distinguish carefully.
  5. Why does thread_sum.c need no mutex at all, even though several threads write to jobs[]?
  6. Python's GIL and Linux's BKL were the same design decision. What did each buy, and what did it cost?
Answers

1. Nothing. A mutex protects a code region, not a variable, and mutual exclusion only holds if every access participates. The unguarded fifth function can run concurrently with any of the other four, so the invariant can still be broken — and the four correct call sites make the bug harder to find, because the code looks synchronised. There is no compiler check for this; it is why some languages tie the lock to the data structurally.

2. Contention. Measured: 0.2495 s with 1 thread, 0.8155 s with 2 — 3.3× worse. With the whole loop body inside one lock there is nothing left to do in parallel, so the threads serialise and pay for it: every acquisition has to move the lock's cache line between cores, and every blocked thread costs a context switch. You get one core's throughput minus the overhead of pretending to use two.

3. All threads must acquire locks in the same order (and ideally release in reverse). Fix: swap the two lock calls in xavier_send_andrew_money so both functions take andrews_lock first. Measured: 3 runs, 3 completions, no hangs.

4. It is correctly synchronised and logically nonsense. No update is lost — the total stays 300 — so the locking does its job. But the program's behaviour (all money ends in whichever account the last-scheduled thread favours) is meaningless, and depends on the scheduler. Two independent properties: synchronisation correctness (no data race, no deadlock) and algorithmic correctness (the computation means something). Fixing the first tells you nothing about the second, which is why “it stopped hanging” is not a completed bug fix.

5. Because no two threads touch the same element. Thread i writes only jobs[i].sum; its accumulator is a local. There is no shared mutable state, so there is nothing to exclude anyone from. And main reads jobs[i].sum only after pthread_join on that thread, which orders the write before the read. Partition instead of locking is the design lesson of the whole page — it is why this program scales 1.9× on 2 cores while §22's version scales backwards.

6. Both bought correctness for free: one lock makes every data structure trivially safe, so an existing single-threaded codebase can be made to work on multiple cores without auditing it. Both cost parallelism: only one thread can be inside at a time, so CPU-bound work does not speed up. And both took decades to unwind — Linux removed the BKL in 2011, and CPython's optional free-threaded build is PEP 703, accepted in 2023 — because replacing one coarse lock with many fine ones reintroduces exactly the deadlock risk of question 3.

Set 7 · Atomics (advanced)
  1. atomic_int x = 0; Two threads each run x = x + 1; a million times. Is the result guaranteed to be 2,000,000? Explain.
  2. Why is bank_account = bank_account + 1 correct on slide 48 but wrong on slide 56?
  3. Why can atomics not deadlock?
  4. Give one thing a mutex can do that an atomic cannot.
  5. When is atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1) worth using over x += 1?
Answers

1. No. Measured over seven runs: 1,368,367 to 1,836,979, never 2,000,000. x = x + 1 is an atomic load followed by an atomic store, with an ordinary unprotected gap between them — the same load–store window as a plain int, just with each half individually indivisible. Use x += 1, x++, or atomic_fetch_add, all of which are single read-modify-write operations. The type is necessary but not sufficient; the expression has to be one operation.

2. Because different things are providing the guarantee. On slide 48 the statement sits between pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock, so no other thread can be in that region at all — the shape of the expression is irrelevant. On slide 56 there is no lock; the only protection is the atomicity of the operation itself, and x = x + 1 is two operations. Same code, different verdict, because correctness is a property of code plus mechanism, not of code alone.

3. Deadlock needs a thread to hold one resource while waiting for another, forming a cycle. An atomic operation is a single indivisible instruction: it never waits, and there is no interval during which it holds anything. With nothing held across an acquisition, no cycle can form.

4. Protect an invariant spanning several variables. “Andrew's plus Xavier's is always 300” requires changing two words with nobody observing the intermediate state — a critical section, which needs a lock. Atomics make individual operations indivisible; they cannot make a group of operations indivisible. Hence the rule: one word and one operation → atomic; multiple words or an invariant between them → mutex.

5. When you need the old value — int old = atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1); gives each caller a distinct ticket, which is how you implement a concurrent index, sequence number or work-queue cursor. x += 1 discards it. When you do not need it, prefer += for clarity — but not for speed: measured 0.02029 s against 0.02122 s, because at -O0 both compile to lock xaddl. The cheaper lock addl form only appears at -O2, and gcc will emit it for either spelling once it can see the old value is unused.

Slides 58–59

Wrap-up (slides 58–59)

What we learnt today

Pipes, finished. fdopen puts stdio on a pipe descriptor so you stop counting bytes; popen's mode letter describes what you do to the stream; the file action that delivers EOF is the one that closes a write end.

Concurrency is overlapping in time; parallelism is happening at the same instant. Parallelism implies concurrency and not the reverse. Flynn's four boxes name which kind of hardware you have. Processes give you concurrency with isolation but at real cost: creation, switching, memory, and communication that takes four calls and a dup2.

Threads share the address space — code, globals, heap, descriptors, cwd — and keep registers, a stack, and errno to themselves. That is why communication is free, and why nothing is safe. pthread_create returns an error number, not −1, and does not set errno. pthread_join is waitpid. When main returns, every thread dies where it stands.

Three failure modes, in increasing subtlety. Lifetime: you pass an address, so the data must outlive the thread — malloc, and let the thread free it. Data races: x++ is a load, an add and a store, so two threads can lose an update; the region between load and store is a critical section. Deadlock: two threads, two locks, opposite order, and nothing moves ever again.

Two fixes with different bills. A mutex is always correct and costs 33× a bare increment, and one global lock makes two threads slower than one — which is what Python's GIL and Linux's Big Kernel Lock bought and paid for. Atomics are correct, 4× faster than the mutex, and cannot deadlock — provided you write x += 1 and never x = x + 1.

And the numbers on this page were measured. Which is how we know the demo that would not break was being protected by its own nanosleep, that the threaded sum looked slow only because user time was being read instead of real, and that it returns a different answer for every thread count because double addition is not associative.

Where this page corrects or supplements its sources

1 · The nanosleep hides the race instead of exposing it. The comment in bank_account_broken.c presents the sleep as making a mid-assignment switch more likely. Measured: with it, the program loses 5–24 of 200,000 and looks correct; without it, it loses 20–50%. The lecture's live conclusion — “makes it even less likely to do bad things” after deleting it, then trying a longer sleep — is inverted. A microsecond-scale syscall next to a nanosecond-scale critical section drives the collision probability towards zero. §20, Lab 15.

2 · The course notes state pthread_create's error protocol incorrectly. Notes: “Returns 0 if OK, −1 otherwise and sets errno”. Slide 34 is right: it returns an error number and does not set errno. Measured on a forced failure, the return was 11 (EAGAIN) while errno held 12 (ENOMEM) from an internal allocation — so perror prints a plausible wrong cause and a == -1 check never fires. §11, Lab 7.

3 · The threaded sum returns a different answer for every thread count, and the lecture called one of them right. The exact total is 1,999,999,999,000,000,000; the program printed six different values, all short by hundreds of millions, with accuracy improving as threads increase. Cause: double is exact only to 253, and floating-point addition is not associative, so partitioning changes the rounding. Not a race — each thread owns its slot. §16, Lab 12.

4 · Threads were not slower; time was being misread. “According to time, it was taking longer to use threads… one of those magic tricks that may not actually work out.” Measured: real 0.89→0.44 s while user stayed at 0.89 s, because user sums CPU time across cores and therefore cannot fall. The speedup is real and visible in the real line only. §16.

5 · Deleting say_hello() does not fix thread_data_broken.c. The lecture tried it and reported the value surviving. Measured, the garbage is identical with and without — the lifetime ends at create_thread's return, and pthread_join's own frame reuses the slot. Also: the garbage values (0x7ffc…0x7fff) are the top half of a stack address, not noise. §18, Lab 13.

6 · “Probably” is too weak for two_threads_broken.c. The notes say thread 1 will probably print 2. Measured: 10 runs out of 10, every line. The reassignment is one store executed immediately after pthread_create returns, long before a new thread reaches a core. Hedged language here invites the belief that you might have got away with it. §14, Lab 10.

7 · The deadlock demo hangs every time, and the class never saw it. “Oops, I didn't do any print statements there” — then straight to the slides. Measured: 30 of 30 runs hung, typically after 0–3,400 of 100,000 iterations, occasionally completing when one thread finished before the other started. §23, Lab 18.

8 · The lock-order fix makes the deadlock program run, not correct. All three fixed runs ended with the entire balance in one account (300/0 or 0/300), decided by scheduling. The total is conserved, so synchronisation is sound; the logic is meaningless. The lecturer's aside — “I think this is a bad way of doing this code” — deserved to be the headline. §23.

9 · “Mutex the world” is worse than losing parallelism. Slide 49 says you lose the advantages. Measured, one global lock around the inner loop made the 2-thread run 3.3× slower than the 1-thread run (0.8155 s vs 0.2495 s), and the 1-thread run 27× slower than unlocked private sums. Adding threads under heavy contention is actively harmful, not merely useless. §22, Lab 17.

10 · popen's mode letters were described backwards. “W means that we're reading from standard in and R means we're reading from standard out.” With "w" you write into the command's stdin. Slide 18 is correct; verified by running both. §03.

11 · -pthread has not been required to link since glibc 2.34. “It's not always clear when you need that or not.” libpthread was merged into libc in 2021, and two_threads.c compiled and ran here with no flag. Keep passing it — it also sets _REENTRANT, and older or non-Linux toolchains still need it — but the classic undefined-reference error is gone on modern systems. §10.

12 · The notes and slides disagree on MISD. The notes gloss it as “pipelining”; the slides and lecture give fault tolerance and task replication. The slides' version is the defensible one — a classical pipeline has each stage on a different instruction and a different datum. Answer with fault tolerance. §06.

13 · thread_sum.c silently drops integers when the count does not divide evenly. Integer division truncates, so ./thread_sum 3 10 covers 0–9 in three blocks of three and never sums the tenth. The if (finish > total) clamp prevents an overrun but not the shortfall. Every figure in the lecture used counts divisible by the thread count, so it never showed. §15.

14 · Coarse output interleaving is the scheduler, not buffering. The lecture was puzzled that main's messages seemed to vanish. Measured streaks of 600–10,000 identical consecutive lines in every buffering mode, because a thread holds its core for a full timeslice — thousands of printfs. Also measured: zero torn lines in 300,000, since glibc locks the FILE per call. §13, Lab 9.

15 · The addclose comment is wrong in the same way as last lecture's. Deleting the child's addclose changes nothing here, exactly as the lecturer found (“it's pretty robust to this”) — because EOF is governed by write ends. The load-bearing call is the parent's own close of the stream. Same finding as Lecture 1's audit, now confirmed from the other direction. §04, Lab 3.

16 · A note on how these numbers were taken — and one claim this page had to withdraw. An earlier draft reported atomic_fetch_add as 2.3× slower than x += 1 and explained it as lock xadd against lock add. Re-measuring with each counter padded to its own cache line and one process per measurement, the gap disappeared: 0.02122 s vs 0.02029 s, and the generated assembly at -O0 is byte-identical (lock xaddl for both). The original gap was false sharing between counters that happened to share a cache line, plus measurement order. The lock add/lock xadd distinction is real but only appears at -O2. All timings on this page are now medians of seven runs, one process each, with padded counters. §24.

Two smaller notes. Slide 10's spoken description conflated pipefd indices 0 and 1 with descriptors 0 and 1 (stdin/stdout) — measured, a first pipe gets descriptors 3 and 4. And wc prints lines, words, bytes: seq 1 10 | wc gives 10 10 21, which the lecture half-remembered.

Slide 6 — the distinction, in one paragraph

Concurrency is not parallelism (slide 6)

Week 9 Lecture 2 spent a full section and two labs on this. The one-paragraph version, because the rest of today assumes it.

CONCURRENCY

Overlapping in time

Two computations are concurrent when their lifetimes overlap — A starts, B starts, A finishes, B finishes. Whether any instant contains both is not part of the claim. “Computations overlapping in time but not overlapping simultaneously.” One core, interleaved by the scheduler, is concurrency.

PARALLELISM

The same instant

Parallelism is the stronger claim: two instructions retiring at the same moment, which needs two pieces of hardware. Parallelism implies concurrency; concurrency does not imply parallelism. Both need synchronisation — which is the entire rest of this lecture.

Threads give you concurrency inside one process. The pitch, from the lecture: “this is a lot more efficient than spawning a bunch of new processes… it allows us to share the code, the address space, the global variables… and obviously because it's in the same process, the communication is quite cheap.” Every word of that is also the reason the next twelve sections exist.

Slides 7–8 — two lists, and the one item people forget

Shared, private, and the private thing that looks global (slides 7–8)

Slide 7 lists what threads share; slide 8 lists what each thread gets its own copy of. The last bullet on slide 8 is the interesting one, because errno is written in your source code exactly like a global variable and is not one.

SLIDE 7 · SHARED

One address space

  • Code — one copy of the text segment
  • Global variables — one bank_account, and §09 is about that
  • The heap — malloc in one thread, free in another, legally
  • Other process state — environment variables, file descriptors, the current working directory

Sharing is free: no pipe, no serialisation, no copy. “Cheap communication!”

SLIDE 8 · PRIVATE

Separate execution state

  • Registers and the program counter — each thread is somewhere different in the code
  • A stack — 8 MiB by default, measured below
  • errno — “each thread gets its own copy of errno!”
“Separate” is not “protected”. A thread can read and write another thread's stack — the slide says so explicitly. There is one address space and no boundary inside it. Separateness here is an allocation policy, not the MMU.

Why errno has to be per-thread

If errno were one global, error reporting in a threaded program would be a lottery: thread A's open fails with ENOENT, thread B's call fails with EACCES before A reaches its perror, and A confidently prints Permission denied for a missing file. So it is not a global. In glibc, errno is a macro that expands to a dereference of a thread-local slot, which is why it has an address and why that address differs per thread:

$ ./errno_test main before: errno = 0, &errno = 0x70a56e8556c0 thread: errno = 9 (Bad file descriptor), &errno = 0x70a56e5ff5c0 main after: errno = 0 (Success)

Two different addresses, 2,449,664 bytes apart — each thread's slot lives near its own stack. The thread's failed close(-1) set errno to 9 and main never saw it. That is the behaviour you want, and it is also a trap: you cannot check a worker thread's errno from the thread that joined it. Return the error yourself.

Slides 9–10 — two calls, and their process-world twins

pthread_create, pthread_join, and what main does on the way out (slides 9–10)

The slides make the analogy explicitly, twice: “analogous to posix_spawn” and “analogous to waitpid”. That is worth taking seriously, because the second half of this lecture is those two calls, and the correspondence is close enough to revise both at once.

int pthread_create(pthread_t *restrict thread, const pthread_attr_t *restrict attr, void *(*start_routine)(void *), void *restrict arg); int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);
threadsprocessesthe difference that matters
pthread_createposix_spawn / fork+execThe thread starts in your address space at a function you name. The process starts in a new address space at a program on disk.
pthread_joinwaitpidjoin hands back a void * you chose. waitpid hands back a status word containing at most 8 bits of exit code — see §25.
pthread_exitexitEnds one thread; ends the whole process.
pthread_tpid_tpid_t is an integer you can print. pthread_t is opaque — “we don't have any access into this guy, but it's kind of like the FILE”.
Shared error protocol. Both pthread_create and posix_spawn return the error number and do not set errno. if (ret == -1) perror(...) is wrong twice over: the test never fires, and perror would read a stale errno belonging to some unrelated earlier call.

“When main returns, all threads terminate” — with one exception

Slide 10's last bullet is true as stated and worth knowing precisely, because there is a one-word change that reverses it. Both programs below create a worker that ticks five times; main waits for two ticks and then leaves.

main ends with return 0;
worker tick 0 worker tick 1 main returning — process gone; ticks 2, 3, 4 never happen —
main ends with pthread_exit(NULL);
worker tick 0 worker tick 1 main returning worker tick 2 worker tick 3 worker tick 4 worker FINISHED

Returning from main is a call to exit, and exit tears down the whole process, threads and all — no warning, no error, just a partial answer that looks complete. pthread_exit from main ends only main's thread and lets the process live until the last thread finishes. Neither is a substitute for joining: use pthread_join when you need the result, which is nearly always.

Slide 11 — the recap example, and the bug re-created live

two_threads.c: one variable is not two (slide 11 · two_threads.c)

The lecturer opened the demo, then deliberately broke it: “we kind of shared this variable and then bad things happened… this is a common mistake to make.” The broken version reuses one int for both threads' arguments.

broken — one variable
int thread_number = 1; pthread_create(&id1, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number); thread_number = 2; // overwrites it pthread_create(&id2, NULL, run_thread, &thread_number);
correct — two variables
int n1 = 1, n2 = 2; pthread_create(&id1, NULL, run_thread, &n1); pthread_create(&id2, NULL, run_thread, &n2); // or malloc one int per thread
Measured — and it is not a coin flip. The lecture treated the outcome as variable (“sometimes thread two goes first, sometimes thread one”). Compiled and run 2,000 times each:
versionoutputruns
brokenthread 2, thread 22000 / 2000 — 100%
correctthread 1 then thread 21978 / 2000 — 98.9%
correctthread 2 then thread 122 / 2000 — 1.1%
Two separate lessons. The bug is deterministic: thread_number = 2 executes long before either new thread is scheduled, so both read 2 — you will never see this one “work on my machine”. The ordering is not deterministic but it is heavily biased: thread 1 wins 99 times in 100, which is exactly the kind of margin that makes people write code that depends on it and then discover the other 1% in production.

Slide 11 — the first genuinely new demo, and the compiler quietly changes your bug

threads_return.c: getting a value back out (slide 11 · threads_return.c)

Everything so far passed data into threads. This demo takes a value out. Three threads each compute 2 × thread_number; main joins each and prints the result. It is four lines of arithmetic wrapped around one of the most instructive bugs in the course — and the compiler's reaction to that bug is not what the lecture assumed.

// the broken version void *do_stuff(void *argument) { int arg = *(int *)argument; int val = arg * 2; // a local. lives on this thread's stack. printf("Processing with thread %d\n", arg); return &val; // its lifetime ends on the next line }

The lecture's own compiler caught it — “this is already telling us that we're going to have a problem: address of stack memory associated with the local variable val”. Then the program ran, printed a return value of 0 for the first thread, and reported a bad free. The lecture read that 0 as garbage. It is not garbage. It is the compiler.

Measured: GCC rewrites return &val into return NULL. Compiling at -O0 and reading the generated assembly for do_stuff, the last thing before the return is not a lea of the stack slot:
;; gcc 11.4, -O0, end of do_stuff call printf@PLT movl $0, %eax ; <-- the return value. zero. ret
When GCC diagnoses -Wreturn-local-addr it does not merely warn — it replaces the value with a null pointer, on the reasoning that a null dereference is a better failure than a silent one. So *return_val in main is *(int *)NULL, and the program does not print rubbish: it segfaults, every run, 3 of 3, before the first “completed” line. The 0 the lecture saw was GCC's substitution, not a computed value.

What the bug looks like when the compiler cannot see it

Warnings are pattern-matching, and the pattern is easy to step outside — store the address in a void * first and -Wreturn-local-addr goes quiet. Now you get the behaviour the lecture described, and it is far more interesting than “rubbish”:

$ ./threads_return_launder # five consecutive runs Thread 0 → -1553992128 Thread 1 → -1562384832 Thread 2 → -1570777536 Thread 0 → -1113590208 Thread 1 → -1121982912 Thread 2 → -1130375616 Thread 0 → -629148096 Thread 1 → -637540800 Thread 2 → -645933504 Thread 0 → -1694501312 Thread 1 → -1702894016 Thread 2 → -1711286720 Thread 0 → 1885337152 Thread 1 → 1876944448 Thread 2 → 1868551744
The garbage has structure, and the structure identifies the culprit. Within every run, consecutive threads differ by exactly the same amount: -1553992128 − (-1562384832) = 8,392,704. That is 0x801000 — and pthread_attr_getstacksize reports the default thread stack as 8,388,608 bytes (8 MiB), plus a 4,096-byte guard page. 8388608 + 4096 = 8392704 exactly.

So these are not random bytes. Each value is the low 32 bits of a stack address, and the threads' stacks are laid out at a fixed 8 MiB + guard-page stride. The whole set shifts between runs because ASLR moves the region. You are reading a pointer that has been reinterpreted as an int — which tells you precisely what overwrote the dead slot: the next stack frame to be laid down on it.

The fix, and why it has to be the heap

void *do_stuff(void *argument) { int arg = *(int *)argument; int *val = malloc(sizeof(int)); // heap: outlives the function if (val == NULL) { perror("malloc"); return NULL; } *val = arg * 2; return val; // main frees it after pthread_join }
$ ./threads_return # three consecutive runs, identical Thread 0 completed, return value 0 Thread 1 completed, return value 2 Thread 2 completed, return value 4

0, 2, 4 — the values slide 11's demo is supposed to produce, and now stable across runs. The heap is the right answer because a heap allocation's lifetime is a decision you make, not a consequence of where control happens to be. Three alternatives exist and are worth knowing: write into a caller-owned slot passed in as the argument; use a static or global (fine for one thread, a race for many); or, when the value fits, cast it directly into the void * and skip memory entirely — ugly, common, and allocation-free.

Who frees it? Here main frees, because main is the one that received the pointer from pthread_join. Compare thread_data_malloc.c in Week 9 Lecture 2, where the thread frees, because there the pointer travelled the other way. The rule is not “threads free” or “main frees” — it is that ownership must be stated somewhere and honoured once. Freeing in both places is a double free; freeing in neither is a leak that scales with your thread count.

Slide 11 — the second new demo, and the thing it quietly proves

threads_of_threads.c: a thread that creates a thread (slide 11 · threads_of_threads.c)

A short demo with a short conclusion — “so you can see that you can nest these guys” — but it settles something that is genuinely not obvious from the API.

THE STRUCTURE
void *some_other_thread(void *a) { printf(" This is some other thread\n"); return NULL; } void *run_thread(void *a) { printf("Hello, this is a thread\n"); pthread_t inner; pthread_create(&inner, NULL, some_other_thread, NULL); pthread_join(inner, NULL); printf("Back in the outer thread\n"); return NULL; }
MEASURED · DETERMINISTIC
$ ./threads_of_threads Hello, this is a thread This is some other thread Back in the outer thread main is done

Fully ordered, every run — because every step is separated by a join. Nesting does not introduce nondeterminism; unjoined siblings do.

There is no thread hierarchy. This is the point the demo makes without saying it. fork gives you a genuine parent–child tree: getppid exists, orphans get reparented, and only the parent may waitpid. Threads have none of that. The “inner” thread is a peer of main's thread and of run_thread alike — there is no pthread_getparent, and any thread may join any other, not just its creator. The nesting you see in the output is nesting in your code, not in the runtime. Contrast §24, where the tree is real and getppid can tell you about it.

How deep can it go? Deeper than you would guess. A version that recurses — each thread creating one child and joining it — reached depth 2,000 with no failure. Since every level blocks in pthread_join, all 2,000 threads are alive simultaneously, each holding an 8 MiB stack: roughly 16 GiB of virtual address space on a machine without 16 GiB of RAM. It works because stacks are mapped lazily and almost none of those pages are ever touched. Reserve is not commit — but the reservation is real, and on a 32-bit process, where the whole address space is 4 GiB, this program would have died around depth 500.

Slide 12 — the same lesson, arriving from the other direction

Data lifetime (slide 12 · thread_data_broken.c · thread_data_malloc.c)

Slide 12 is the mirror image of §06. There, a value died on the way out of a thread. Here it dies on the way in. Week 9 Lecture 2 covers both demos in full with two labs; this is the compressed version, because the lecturer explicitly re-ran it (“these we looked at last time”) and because the shape is now familiar.

the setupwhat goes wrong
Data is shared with a thread by passing an address.pthread_create copies the pointer, never the pointee. Nothing is snapshotted.
So far every example put that data in a local in main.That works only because main outlives every thread it creates — an accident of those examples, not a rule.
Create a thread from any other function and return from it.The local's lifetime ends at that return. The thread now holds a pointer into a dead frame, and the next call reuses the bytes.
Two findings from W9L2 worth carrying forward. First, deleting the apparent culprit does not fix it — removing the say_hello() call that seemed to clobber the slot produced identical garbage, because the lifetime ended at the return, not at the next call; pthread_join's own frame lands on the same bytes. Second, the garbage was recognisable: values like 0x7ffc, 0x7ffe, 0x7fff — the top half of a stack address, exactly as the laundered values in §06 were the bottom half. Undefined behaviour is rarely random; it is usually someone else's data, and identifying whose is how you find the bug.

The fix is the same fix: malloc a block per thread, and hand over ownership. In thread_data_malloc.c the thread frees, because the pointer went inward. In threads_return.c, main frees, because it came back out. Full treatment →

Slides 13–16 — “data races, deadlock and disasters”

Three threads, one global (slides 13–16 · bank_account_broken.c)

Threads share globals. That is the feature. Slide 14 states the consequence in one line — incrementing a global variable is not an atomic operation — and the demo tries to show it. Last lecture it used two threads and refused to break. This time the lecturer raised it to three: “I created three threads and I was able to actually make it break a bit better.”

int bank_account = 0; void *add_100000(void *argument) { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) { struct timespec t = {0, 1}; nanosleep(&t, NULL); // "so it pauses a little bit" bank_account = bank_account + 1; } return NULL; } // three threads, each adding 100000. expected total: 300000.

Why one ++ is three operations

The C is one statement. The machine needs three steps, and the scheduler may cut between any two of them:

lw $t0, bank_account # 1. LOAD the current value addi $t0, $t0, 1 # 2. ADD one to the copy in a register sw $t0, bank_account # 3. STORE the copy back

If thread A loads 42, then thread B loads 42, adds and stores 43, and then A adds and stores 43 — two increments happened and the account went up by one. Slide 15's caption is exact: “Oops! We lost an increment.” Slide 16 names the region between the load and the store the critical section, and the requirement mutual exclusion.

Measured. The three-thread change is real but almost irrelevant next to the nanosleep. Ten runs of each configuration, gcc 11.4, glibc 2.35, two cores:
configurationexpectedobservedtypical loss
2 threads, with nanosleep200000199992, 199994, 1999940.003%
3 threads, with nanosleep300000299975, 299960, 299965, 299973, 2999750.010%
2 threads, no nanosleep200000179207, 127537, 200000, 183448, 104678…13%
3 threads, no nanosleep300000300000, 199902, 165567, 277805, 131552, 208373, 249660, 240472, 100000, 20012731%
Going from two threads to three multiplied the loss by about 4.5× — from a mean of 6.7 to a mean of 30.4 increments — which is the improvement the lecturer noticed. Deleting the nanosleep multiplied it by three thousand. One run lost 168,448 of 300,000. One returned exactly 100000: two threads' entire contributions, gone.
