The demo that would not break, explained with arithmetic

The nanosleep is why it looked fine (measured)

The lecture spent two weeks trying to make this program misbehave — “I still didn't have any luck in getting this thing really working very well. It's quite robust” — and reached for more threads. The line that was suppressing the bug was three lines above the bug.

A data race needs two threads inside the same three-instruction window at the same time. The nanosleep asks the kernel to sleep for one nanosecond, but a sleep is a syscall plus a timer, and the smallest one that actually happens is on the order of tens of microseconds. So each loop iteration is overwhelmingly sleep and barely at all increment:

measured wall time, 3 threads × 100,000 iterations, with nanosleep = 7.19 s ⇒ one iteration = 71,900 ns measured same loop with the nanosleep removed = 3.84 ns per iteration duty cycle inside the critical section = 3.84 / 71,900 = 1 in 18,700

With three threads, the chance that some other thread is inside the window when you enter it is roughly 2 × 1/18,700, so over 300,000 increments you would expect to lose on the order of 30. Measured losses across five runs: 25, 40, 35, 27, 25. The model and the machine agree, which is the strongest evidence that the mechanism is understood: the sleep does not fix anything, it just makes the threads take turns.

Sleeps do not reduce races — they move the window. Put a sleep outside the critical section and the threads spend their lives not-colliding, so the bug hides. Put one inside — between the load and the store — and the same program fails almost every iteration. You will see the second version in §13, where a sleep(1) placed between two lock acquisitions turns a 1.5%-of-the-time deadlock into a 100%-of-the-time deadlock. Same tool, opposite result, entirely because of placement. This is also why “I ran it and it was fine” is not evidence about concurrent code: you tested one scheduling out of astronomically many, and timing changes which one you get.

Slides 17–18 — the first fix

Mutexes: only one thread in the room (slides 17–18 · bank_account_mutex.c)

Slide 17's phrasing: associate each shared resource with a mutex; only one thread can hold it; anyone else attempting to lock it waits. So only one thread is ever executing between the lock and the unlock.

int bank_account = 0; pthread_mutex_t bank_account_lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER; void *add_100000(void *argument) { for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) { pthread_mutex_lock(&bank_account_lock); // only one thread can execute this // section of code at any time bank_account = bank_account + 1; pthread_mutex_unlock(&bank_account_lock); } return NULL; }
MEASURED

It is exact, not just better

$ ./bank_account_mutex # 3 threads, 10 runs 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000 300000

10 / 10 exact. Compare the unsleeping unlocked version, which was wrong in 9 of 10 runs. This is the difference between a bug made rare and a bug made impossible.

THREE THINGS TO GET RIGHT
  • Initialise it. PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER for a static, pthread_mutex_init otherwise. The lecturer noticed the omission live: “you'll note that I didn't actually do that here — it's probably good practice.”
  • Lock the smallest region that is still correct. Everything inside is serial. §12 measures what that costs.
  • Every path unlocks. An early return or a break that skips the unlock leaves the mutex held forever and every other thread blocked. There is no scope guard in C.

The mutex protects the resource, not the code. Two functions that both touch bank_account must take the same lock; a second mutex around the second function protects nothing at all. And the mutex has no idea what it is guarding — the association exists only in your head and in your comments, which is why naming it bank_account_lock rather than lock1 is a correctness measure and not a style preference.

Slide 19 — so why not lock everything?

Mutex the world? (slide 19)

Slide 19 asks the obvious question and answers it in four bullets: this works, but you lose the advantages of parallelism, and mutexes have overhead. Two famous systems did exactly this, and both regretted it in public.

CPython · THE GIL

One lock for the interpreter

The Global Interpreter Lock means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, whatever your core count. It makes the interpreter and every C extension trivially thread-safe, and it makes CPU-bound Python threading pointless. The slide's parenthesis — “although can be disabled now…” — refers to the free-threaded build: experimental in 3.13, and officially supported in 3.14 under PEP 779, though still not the default. Reported speed-ups reach about 3.5× on four cores, against a single-threaded penalty of roughly 5–10%.

LINUX · THE BKL

One lock for the kernel

The Big Kernel Lock did the same job for Linux: any thread in kernel mode held it. It was introduced to make SMP work at all in 1996, and then took fifteen years to remove — the last of it went in 2.6.39, in 2011. Replacing one giant lock with many small correct ones is not a refactor; it is a decade-long project, and it is why the decision matters at design time.

What the overhead actually is

Slide 19 asserts the cost without quantifying it. Three threads, five million increments each, -O0, one process per measurement, median of seven runs:

no lock (wrong)
19.2 ms
atomic_fetch_add
138.3 ms  7.2×
atomic +=
149.4 ms  7.8×
mutex
656.4 ms  34.2×

Correctness costs 7× if you take the cheap route and 34× if you take the general one — and the mutex is 4.4× slower than the atomic doing the identical job. That is the trade the slide is describing, with numbers on it. Note what the first bar is not: it is not a faster program, it is a wrong one, and a wrong answer can always be computed arbitrarily quickly.

The deeper cost is not the instruction, it is the serialisation. A mutex around a whole loop body means your n-thread program has an n-times-contended one-thread critical path, plus context switches. Under heavy contention, adding threads makes it slower — measured in W9L2, where one global lock made the two-thread run 3.3× slower than the one-thread run. The fix is not a faster lock. It is locking less: give each thread private state and combine at the end.

Slide 20 — the third new demo, written because the old one would not cooperate

deadlock.c: a deadlock you can rely on (slide 20 · deadlock.c)

Last lecture's deadlock demo would not deadlock on demand — “occasionally it deadlocked, but most of the time it did not”. So a new one was written: “I did make a new one that definitely deadlocks.” It does, and the reason it does is worth more than the deadlock itself.

task_one
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a); sleep(1); pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b); // ... work ... pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b); pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a);
task_two — the opposite order
pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_b); sleep(1); pthread_mutex_lock(&lock_a); // ... work ... pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_a); pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock_b);

Both threads hold one lock and want the other. Neither will release what it has until it gets what it wants. Nobody is spinning, nobody is using CPU, nobody is at fault, and nobody will ever finish. The lecturer's summary on seeing it hang: “one of them has something locked and the other one is trying to lock something and so they're both stuck.”

$ ./deadlock # typical run, then nothing, forever thread 2: attempting lock B thread 2: locked B thread 1: attempting lock A thread 1: locked A thread 1: attempting lock B <-- blocked; thread 2 holds it thread 2: attempting lock A <-- blocked; thread 1 holds it ^C
Measured: the sleep(1) is the entire difference between a demo and a lottery.
versionrunsdeadlocked
as written, with sleep(1) between the two locks55 — 100%
identical, with the sleeps deleted2003 — 1.5%
Deadlock needs both threads to hold their first lock before either asks for its second. Without the sleep, each thread takes both locks in a few nanoseconds and is almost always finished before the other starts — the window is real but vanishingly narrow. The sleep holds the window open for a full second, so the interleaving that was one-in-seventy becomes certain. Nothing about the bug changed. Only the odds of observing it.
Which is the lesson. A concurrency bug that appears 1.5% of the time is not 1.5% of a problem — at a thousand requests a second it is fifteen hangs a second. It also cannot be found by running the program, which is what the lecturer discovered across two lectures of trying. Concurrency bugs are found by reading the lock order, not by testing. The same program also ran pthread_mutex_init and pthread_mutex_destroy properly, which the bank account demo skipped — a static PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER is fine, but anything with a lifetime should be initialised and destroyed explicitly.

Slide 20 — and the question the lecture left open

Is Xavier getting ripped off? (slide 20 · bank_account_deadlock.c)

Two threads, two accounts, money moving both ways: Andrew pays Xavier, Xavier pays Andrew. Each thread locks two mutexes — and in the broken version, in opposite orders. After fixing the order live, the lecturer checked the balances, was not sure what to make of them, and set homework: “check that out at home. See if Xavier is getting ripped off here.” Here is the answer.

$ ./bank_account_deadlock # original lock order, 10 runs, 2s timeout DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK DEADLOCK 10 / 10 $ ./bank_account_deadlock_fixed # both threads lock andrew, then xavier andrew 100, xavier 100, total 200 × 10 runs, identical 0 / 10 deadlocked
Nobody is ripped off, and it is not luck. Both accounts return to exactly 100 in every run, total exactly 200. Two independent reasons, and it is worth separating them:
  • The total is conserved because every transfer debits and credits while holding both locks. No other thread can observe or interleave with the half-done transfer, so money is never created or destroyed. This would hold no matter how the transfers were distributed.
  • The individual balances return to 100 because the two threads perform exactly 100 transfers of $1 in opposite directions. That is arithmetic, not synchronisation — change one thread's loop bound and the balances differ, correctly.
The interesting failure would be a version that locked only its own account. That still avoids deadlock — one lock each, no cycle — and it still loses money, because the two halves of a transfer become separately racy. Correct locking is not the same as enough locking.

A note on the demo's design. Both threads want both accounts every iteration, so the mutexes are contended essentially 100% of the time and no work happens in parallel at all. The program is a deadlock exhibit rather than a bank. A real implementation locks the two accounts in a canonical order — by account number, say — so that any pair of transfers between any two accounts agrees on the order without anyone coordinating. That is the generalisation of §15's rule, and it is what makes it usable when you have a million accounts instead of two.

Slides 21–22 — one rule, and why it is sufficient

All threads acquire locks in the same order (slides 21–22)

Slide 22 gives the rule in two lines: all threads must acquire locks in the same order, and it is also good to release them in reverse order where possible. The rule looks like a convention. It is closer to a theorem.

WHY IT WORKS

Deadlock needs a cycle

A deadlock is a cycle in the “thread T holds lock X and waits for lock Y” graph. Give every lock a number and require that threads only ever acquire in increasing order. Then every waiting edge points from a lower number to a higher one — and a graph whose edges all increase cannot contain a cycle. No cycle, no deadlock. Ever, on any schedule, with any number of threads.

That is why this rule is worth more than the testing that never found the bug: it is a property you can check by reading, and it holds for schedules you will never run.

WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX
  • Forgetting to unlock. Ordering says nothing about release.
  • Holding a lock across a blocking call — a read, a join, a sleep. Not a deadlock; just everyone waiting.
  • Livelock: threads that keep releasing and retrying politely, making no progress. Nothing is blocked, nothing advances.
  • Starvation: a thread that is always last in the queue. The system progresses; that thread does not.

Slide 27 names livelock and starvation as things this course does not cover. It is worth knowing they are separate failures with separate fixes.

Reverse-order release, and why it is only “also good”. Releasing B then A cannot itself deadlock — unlock never blocks. The lecturer's caution (“if you unlock A first, then you can still deadlock on acquiring lock B… you'd have to have a lot of threads”) points at something real but different: unlocking out of order widens the window in which a thread holds a subset of the locks, which multiplies the interleavings and invites the next person to acquire in the wrong order. It is hygiene that keeps the invariant easy to check, which is why slide 22 puts it in brackets.
Slides 23–26 — the hardware fix, and the demo the lecture could not break

Atomics, and why x = x + 1 is not one (slides 23–26 · bank_account_atomic.c)

Slide 23's pitch: with hardware support you can avoid data races without locks — no mutex overhead, and since there are no locks, no deadlock is possible. Slide 24 then delivers the strangest-looking rule in the course, and the lecturer flagged it as such: “one of the interesting and I dare say somewhat crazy parts of this…”

#include <stdatomic.h> atomic_int x = 10; x += 1; // atomic x++; // atomic atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1); // atomic x = x + 1; // NOT atomic. same type, same result, different guarantee.

Slide 24 lists the operators that carry the guarantee — ++, +=, --, -=, |=, &=, ^= — and slide 25 the function forms: atomic_fetch_add, atomic_fetch_sub, atomic_fetch_or, atomic_fetch_xor, atomic_fetch_and. The fetch functions return the old value, which is what makes them composable into counters and reference counts.

The rule is not arbitrary — read the assembly

The lecture explained the distinction as “because this is implemented in the hardware” and moved on. The actual reason is visible in four lines of generated code. Same variable, same -O0, same compiler:

Cx86-64 at -O0atomic?
x += 1lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip)yes — one locked instruction
x++lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip)yes — identical code
atomic_fetch_add(&x,1)lock addl $1, x(%rip)yes — and cheaper still, because the unused return lets GCC drop the exchange
x = x + 1movl x(%rip), %eax
xchgl x(%rip), %eax		no — two instructions with a gap between them

The last row is the whole lesson. Each of those two instructions is individually atomic — the load cannot see a torn value, and xchg is implicitly locked on x86. What is not atomic is the pair. Between the movl and the xchgl your thread is holding a stale copy in a register, and any number of other threads may load, add and store. This is the exact three-step race from §09, unchanged: declaring the variable atomic_int made each step safe and did nothing about the gap. An assignment expression is a read and a write, and no type can fuse those two into one instruction; a compound assignment is one operation, so the compiler can emit one instruction for it.

The lecture could not break it. Measured, it breaks 8 times in 10. Faced with the non-atomic version, the lecturer hedged — “I'm not sure if I'm going to break it doing this… I'm not going to waste time with that” — and predicted it would need more threads. It needs three, and no nanosleep. Ten runs each, expected 300000:
incrementresults
bank_account += 1300000 × 10 — 10/10 exact
bank_account++300000 × 10 — 10/10 exact
atomic_fetch_add(&bank_account, 1)300000 × 10 — 10/10 exact
bank_account = bank_account + 1255824, 215202, 190753, 280319, 253711, 111077, 237461, 205465, 300000, 300000 — 8/10 wrong, worst case lost 63%
The two runs that came out right are the point, not the exception: this is a bug that produces the correct answer 20% of the time. The lecturer's instinct — “if I played this enough, there might be a case where it slightly doesn't work” — had the direction right and the magnitude wrong: not a rare slight discrepancy, but the usual outcome, and often a catastrophic one. The demo on the day used two threads with the nanosleep still in the loop, which is the configuration §10 showed hides the race almost perfectly.
Atomics do not solve concurrency. Slide 23 says so twice, and it is not modesty. An atomic makes one operation indivisible. It says nothing about two atomics needing to happen together — if (x > 0) x -= 1; is a race no matter how atomic x is, because the test and the decrement are separate. It says nothing about invariants across two variables. And the memory ordering question — which other writes a thread is guaranteed to see — is a genuinely hard topic that C exposes and this course does not cover. Slide 23's “there are still some subtle problems” is doing a great deal of work.

Slide 27 — explicitly a taste

Concurrency is really complex (slide 27)

“This is just a taste of concurrency… we don't go into this very deeply at all, just to say that it exists. So in the future when you're out there in the wild you'll go, ah, atomics, I have seen that before.” Slide 27's list of what was left out, with one line each so the words are not new when you meet them:

termwhat it is
livelockThreads keep changing state to be polite and none progresses. Nothing is blocked, which is what makes it harder to spot than deadlock.
starvationThe system makes progress; one particular thread never does, because it always loses the race for the lock.
thundering herdOne event wakes a thousand waiters, all of which run, and 999 of which discover there was nothing for them and go back to sleep.
memory orderingWhich of another thread's writes you are guaranteed to see, and in what order. CPUs and compilers both reorder. The reason stdatomic.h has a memory_order parameter you have never passed.
semaphoresA counter with atomic wait/post. A mutex is roughly a semaphore that only counts to one; semaphores also express “at most N at a time” and producer/consumer.
software transactional memoryMark a region as a transaction; the runtime detects conflicts and retries. Composable in a way locks are not.
user threads / fibersThreads scheduled by a library rather than the kernel. Far cheaper to create and switch; they cannot use two cores by themselves. Go's goroutines and Rust's async tasks are the modern examples.

Where it continues at UNSW, from slide 27: COMP3231 / COMP3891 ([Extended] Operating Systems) for scheduling, synchronisation primitives and deadlock in the kernel, and COMP6991 (Solving Modern Programming Problems with Rust) for a language whose type system rejects data races at compile time — the same problems from this lecture, made unrepresentable rather than merely detectable.

Part two · slide 28

Revision

“I'll start off backwards. I'll just look at threads backwardsly… and then we'll do some revision exercises with processes.” The second half of the lecture walks Weeks 8 and 9 in reverse, from posix_spawn back to getpid. Reordered here into the shape you would want the night before an exam, ending at posix_grep.c — the one exercise slide 28 names.

Slide 28 — what is being revised, and what is coming

The revision half (slide 28)

Slide 28 lists processes revision exercises — posix_grep.c and threads revision. Slide 29 lists files as well; that is Wednesday, not today — the lecturer corrected the slide out loud. What follows is the process material from Week 8 Lecture 2 and Week 9 Lecture 1, compressed to what is worth carrying into an exam, with the claims re-measured.

EXAM SIGNAL

What the lecturer flagged

File actions, dup2 redirection and pipes were repeatedly called advanced: “where the lecture notes say advanced it means this stuff is not going to feature prominently in the exam — maybe sort of the last question, or something which is purposefully supposed to break you.” The core — fork, exec, waitpid, status decoding, posix_spawn — is not advanced.

THE ONE SKILL

Man pages, unaided

The practice exam exists partly to test whether you can navigate man without the course website. man 2 waitpid has the status macros; man 3 posix_spawn has the file actions; man 7 environ has the variable list. Knowing which section is most of the skill.

THE ONE DIAGRAM

Who replaces whom

exec replaces you and keeps your pid. fork duplicates you and gives the copy a new pid. posix_spawn is both at once, in the child. system is posix_spawn of a shell, with the arguments concatenated into a string an attacker can steer. Everything else is detail.

Threads revision — “the kind of regular stuff”

Threads, backwards (one_thread.c · one_thread_infinite_loops.c · two_threads.c)

The lecturer's separation is a good one for revision: “this stuff with mutual exclusives and deadlocks, that's kind of all the advanced stuff. The regular stuff is just how do you start a thread.” Three programs, three facts.

programthe one thing it teaches
one_thread.cThe mechanics with nothing else in the way: declare a pthread_t, call pthread_create with a function and an argument, pthread_join. Passing 42 to a thread that prints it — “pretty straightforward”.
one_thread_infinite_loops.cConcurrency you can see: main loops forever printing, the thread loops forever printing, and the output alternates. “It just keeps on jumping forever… you can see it flicking between other function and main.”
two_threads.cThe argument-lifetime rule from §05: two threads need two variables, or two mallocs. One variable reused is one bug.
Measured — the “flicking” is coarser than it looks. The alternation in one_thread_infinite_loops is not per-line. A thread keeps its core for a whole timeslice, which at printf speed is hundreds to thousands of consecutive lines from one thread before the other gets a turn (measured in W9L2: streaks of 600–10,000). Also measured there: zero torn lines in 300,000, because glibc locks the FILE for the duration of each printf. Interleaving happens between calls, never inside one — which is a guarantee stdio gives you and your own shared data structures do not.

The compile flag. -pthread, and the honest answer to “you may or may not need to put in this… depending on your compiler”: since glibc 2.34 (2021) libpthread has been merged into libc, so on a current Linux box the link succeeds without it — verified here. Keep passing it anyway. It also defines _REENTRANT, it is portable, and it costs nothing.

Processes revision — back to Week 8

What a process is, and how to see one (week 8 lecture 2 · process_example.c)

A process is a program executing in an environment. The operating system starts them, stops them, tracks their memory, and gives each an integer name. “These are our processes existing in the space of our operating system, and these are the ways in which they can grab things outside of the process.”

WHAT CROSSES THE BOUNDARY
stdin, stdout, stderrdescriptors 0, 1, 2 — inherited, and redirectable by whoever starts you
argc, argvarguments, chosen by the parent
environenvironment variables — §21
exit status8 bits back to the parent — §25
getpid(), getppid()who you are, who started you — both return pid_t, both declared in <unistd.h>
MEASURED
$ ./process_example ./process_example: pid=18 ppid=5

Every process except init has a parent, so the pids form a tree rooted at pid 1. The tools: ps for a snapshot, top for a live view sorted by CPU, kill to send a signal. The lecture's top demo found a runaway Python process at 200% CPU — “that is some serious Python… if this is your computer, you can go, well, this is doing something crazy, let's kill that.” 200% means two cores fully occupied; top counts per-core.

Measured — and this one contradicts the demo. The lecture ran fork and pointed out that the child's getppid() matched the parent's getpid(): “so you can see how they're related, you can see how you can keep track of them.” Run 30 times here, with no wait in the parent:
child's getppid() 26 runs → 1 <-- not the parent 1 run → 35 1 run → 38 1 run → 47 1 run → 50 same program, parent calls wait() first 30 runs → the parent's pid, every time
In 87% of runs the parent had already exited, the child was reparented to init, and getppid() returned 1. The relationship the demo displays is real but transient: getppid() tells you who your parent is right now, and a parent that finishes first is gone before you ask. This is the same mechanism as orphans and zombies from Week 9 Lecture 1, showing up in the simplest possible program. If you want the answer the slide implies, the parent must still be alive — which means it must wait.

Week 8 — the other thing a process inherits

Environment variables (environ · getenv · setenv)

A null-terminated array of NAME=value strings handed to every program at startup. The lecturer's example was a debugging afternoon lost to one: “I was having all kinds of problems with my environment variables because my PATH didn't have the thing that I wanted to run.”

the raw array
extern char **environ; for (int i = 0; environ[i] != NULL; i++) printf("%s\n", environ[i]);

Measured: 39 entries in a plain shell here. Terminated by a NULL pointer, exactly like argv.

the interface you should use
char *p = getenv("PATH"); // NULL if absent setenv("COMP1521", "great", 1); // 1 = overwrite
environ has 39 entries; PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin... after setenv: COMP1521=great getenv of something absent: (nil)
Why this matters for the process calls. Every one of execve, posix_spawn and posix_spawnp takes the child's environment as an explicit argument. Pass environ and the child inherits yours; pass your own array and it gets exactly what you list and nothing else. That is not a detail — PATH lives there, so an empty environment means posix_spawnp cannot find anything, and TZ lives there, which is the demo in §26. system and popen give you no say at all: the child gets your environment, whatever it contains.

Shell versus program. export PATH=$PATH:. changes the shell's own environment, which every later child inherits — the lecturer used exactly this to run a.out without ./. It lasts until the terminal closes; putting it in .bashrc makes every new shell run it. Neither reaches backwards into a process that has already started: an environment is copied at exec time, never shared.

The decision, on one screen

Four ways to start a program, and which to reach for (weeks 8–9)

The lecture walked these in creation order: exec, then system and popen (“convenient but unsafe”), then fork, then “the kind of new standard way of doing things”, posix_spawn. Here they are as a decision.

callwhat happens to younew pid?use it when
execveReplaced. New address space, all variables gone. Open descriptors and the pid survive.no — same pidYou are the child already and want to become the target program.
forkDuplicated. Two processes return from one call, distinguished by the return value.yesYou want a copy of yourself — or you are about to exec in the copy.
systemRuns /bin/sh -c "your string" and waits. The string is parsed by a shell.yes (two: shell + program)Never, in new code. “We told you about it but don't use it… the main reason for us to tell you about it is you might see it in other code.”
posix_spawnFork and exec in one call, with file actions and attributes.yesDefault choice. Arguments are passed as an array, so nothing is ever parsed by a shell.
Why system is the dangerous one, in one line. It builds a command string, and a shell splits strings on spaces, ;, |, $() and backticks. Concatenate anything a user typed into that string and they can append their own command — the lecturer's illustration was rm -9 *-flavoured obliteration. posix_spawn takes char *argv[], so a filename containing ; rm -rf ~ is a filename with an unusual name and nothing more. popen has the identical hole for the identical reason. This is the whole argument, and it is worth being able to state it in one sentence in an exam.

Week 8 — the call that does not return

exec: same process, different program (exec.c · exec_example.c)

The lecturer's image is the right one: “some kind of spawning into a new kind of creature — you still kind of look like you, but it's not your brain anymore.” The pid, the open descriptors and the parent stay. Everything you had written down is gone.

int execve(const char *pathname, char *const argv[], char *const envp[]); // returns only on failure: -1, and errno is set.
SURVIVES
  • the process id — and the parent's
  • open file descriptors, so stdin/stdout redirection set up before the exec still applies afterwards
  • the current working directory, the umask, signal dispositions set to default
DESTROYED
  • the entire address space — code, globals, heap, stack
  • every variable, every malloc, every buffered byte of stdout that was not flushed
  • all threads but the calling one
$ ./exec_example hello, my pid is 18 ./process_example: pid=18 ppid=5 — "goodbye" is never printed, because there is nobody left to print it —

Measured: the pid is identical across the exec — 18 before, 18 after — and the line after execve never runs. That is the diagnostic: any code after a successful exec is unreachable, so the idiom is to follow it immediately with perror and an exit, because reaching that line is the error. The lecture's version printed “goodbye” there deliberately: “if we get to goodbye, then something bad happened.”

The buffer trap, in the same three lines. printf writes into a buffer, and execve destroys the address space — buffer included. If stdout is a pipe or a file rather than a terminal, the buffer is not flushed at each newline, so “hello” disappears entirely. Call fflush(stdout) before every exec. The same buffer, in the other direction, is what makes §24's output duplicate rather than vanish.

Week 8 — the call that returns twice

fork: the tree, and the output the demo hides (fork.c · forks.c)

fork duplicates the calling process. The child is a copy of the parent's address space, open files and all. One call, two returns, and the return value is the only thing that differs.

fork returnsyou are
0the child — ask getpid() if you want your own number
a positive pid_tthe parent, and the value is your child's pid — which you need for waitpid
-1nobody forked; check errno

Three forks make eight processes

The lecture's caution demo: “if we fork three times, we're going to actually run through this program eight times… if I put just one more line of forks, then it's going to be twice as long.” Each fork doubles the population, so n forks in a row give 2n processes — and the fork bomb from Week 8 is the same fact with the forks in a loop.

Measured — and the demo's output depends on where you point it. The program prints one line before the forks and one after:
printf("hello world\n"); fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("goodbye\n");
stdout is…“hello world”“goodbye”
a terminal (line buffered)18
a pipe — ./forks | sort88
a file — ./forks > out.txt88
On a terminal, stdout is line-buffered, so “hello world” is already written out before the first fork — which is what the lecture saw. Redirect it and stdout becomes block-buffered: the line is still sitting in the buffer when fork copies the address space, so every one of the eight children inherits a copy of it and prints it at exit. The program did not change. The buffering mode did. Anyone who has ever redirected a forking program's output to a log and found duplicated lines has met this, and the fix is fflush(stdout) before forking.

Week 9 — the most exam-shaped thing in the revision half

waitpid and the status word (sys/wait.h)

The lecturer pointed straight at the man page: “all these guys are defined in there — what the return values mean and then all the flags… you can see what all those guys mean in there.” The single most important fact is that the integer waitpid fills in is not the exit status. It is a packed word, and the macros unpack it.

int exit_status; if (waitpid(pid, &exit_status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); return 1; } if (WIFEXITED(exit_status)) // did it exit normally? printf("exit code %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(exit_status)); // low 8 bits else if (WIFSIGNALED(exit_status)) // killed by a signal? printf("signal %d\n", WTERMSIG(exit_status));
Measured — the decode table. Six children, each ending differently, with the raw word printed in hex:
child doesraw statusWIFEXITEDWEXITSTATUSWIFSIGNALEDWTERMSIG
exit(0)0x0000100—
exit(1)0x0100110—
exit(42)0x2a001420—
raise(SIGSEGV)0x008b0—111
exit(256)0x0000100—
exit(-1)0xff0012550—
Read the two red rows carefully. Only 8 bits survive. exit(256) reports success, because 256 & 0xff is 0 — a program that returns a count, or a negative error code, will lie to its parent. exit(-1) arrives as 255. And note that 0x2a00 is 10752, not 42: printing the raw word is the classic mistake, and WEXITSTATUS is just (status >> 8) & 0xff.

Where the shell's $? gets its numbers. 128 + signal is a shell convention for “killed by a signal” — 139 for a segfault is 128 + 11, and it is why echo $? after a crash prints 139. The kernel's word encodes it differently, in the low seven bits, which is what 0x008b shows. Also worth knowing: grep returns 0 when it matched, 1 when it did not, and 2 on an error — all three measured, and all three needed in §27.

Week 9 — the one to actually use

posix_spawn, and the p that changes everything (spawn.c · spawnp.c)

“It's a little bit more complex, but not like it's not going to hurt your brain too much. And I think after looking at threads, this should at least make a little bit more sense to you.” The comparison is apt — six arguments, and the same error protocol as pthread_create.

int posix_spawn(pid_t *pid, // out: the child's pid const char *path, // the program const posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa, // NULL, or fd surgery (advanced) const posix_spawnattr_t *attr, // NULL in this course char *const argv[], // argv[0] onwards, NULL-terminated char *const envp[]); // the child's environment
Same error protocol as pthread_create. It returns the error number and does not set errno. The course idiom is to assign it yourself so perror works: if ((ret = posix_spawn(...)) != 0) { errno = ret; perror("spawn"); }. And note what “success” means: 0 means the child was created, not that the program ran. A child that cannot exec exits with 127, and you only find that out from waitpid.

posix_spawn vs posix_spawnp

One letter, and it is the difference between working and not. posix_spawn takes a path; posix_spawnp searches PATH. Measured with the identical argument:

$ ./spawnp posix_spawn("date") → ret=2 (No such file or directory) // there is no ./date posix_spawnp("date") → ret=0 // found /bin/date via PATH

The lecturer's take on choosing — “it's all about code portability at the end of the day… date may not exist here as well” — is the right instinct: /bin/date is not /bin/date everywhere, so hard-coding a path is fragile across systems, while trusting PATH is fragile against whatever PATH happens to contain. For a fixed system utility, prefer the explicit path; for something the user is expected to have installed, use spawnp. What you must not do is let a caller choose the string and use spawnp.

Choosing the child's environment

Passing your own envp instead of environ means the child sees exactly what you list. The lecture's demo sets one variable and gets time travel:

$ ./spawn_env # same binary, same instant, two environments TZ=Australia/Perth → Thu Aug 13 03:33:05 AWST 2026 TZ=UTC → Wed Aug 12 19:33:05 UTC 2026

“We've gone back in time and we're actually not even time for the lecture yet.” Same moment, two renderings — date reads TZ out of the environment it was handed. The general lesson is bigger than time zones: the environment is part of the interface to a child process, as much as argv is, and it is the part people forget to control. An empty envp is a legitimate choice and a good default for anything security-sensitive; just remember it takes PATH with it.

Slide 28 — the named revision exercise

posix_grep.c (slide 28 · posix_grep.c)

The one program slide 28 names. It takes a pattern and a list of files, spawns grep once per file, and counts how many files matched — which means it has to read exit statuses, and that is the point of it. Everything in the revision half meets here.

extern char **environ; int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { if (argc < 3) { fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s <pattern> <file>...\n", argv[0]); return 1; } int n_matched = 0; for (int i = 2; i < argc; i++) { char *grep_argv[] = {"grep", argv[1], argv[i], NULL}; pid_t pid; int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/grep", NULL, NULL, grep_argv, environ); if (ret != 0) { errno = ret; perror("posix_spawn"); return 1; } int exit_status; if (waitpid(pid, &exit_status, 0) == -1) { perror("waitpid"); return 1; } if (WIFEXITED(exit_status) && WEXITSTATUS(exit_status) == 0) n_matched++; } printf("%d file(s) matched\n", n_matched); return 0; }
$ ./posix_grep at f1.txt f2.txt kitkat.txt the cat sat at the mat no match here look at that at the start 2 file(s) matched
Four things this program is quietly teaching.
  • Exit status as data. grep returns 0 for matched, 1 for not matched, 2 for error — all three measured. The count is built entirely out of WEXITSTATUS, which is why the status macros are not trivia.
  • The child writes straight to your stdout. Nobody redirected anything, so grep inherits descriptor 1 and its output appears inline with yours. To capture it instead you would need file actions and a pipe — the advanced material.
  • WIFEXITED first, always. WEXITSTATUS is meaningless if the child was killed by a signal. Checking both is the habit; && here is not defensive padding.
  • argv[0] is a convention, not a lookup. The program run is /bin/grep, from the second argument; the "grep" inside the array is only the name the child sees in its own argv[0]. They can differ, and in some programs deliberately do.

A detail worth catching: the output above matched no match here, because at occurs inside match. grep matches substrings, not words — grep -w if you meant words. Two of three files matched, and running it against a missing file gives grep: nosuchfile.txt: No such file or directory on stderr, exit status 2, and correctly no increment.

Advanced — named, not re-taught

Redirection and pipes, compressed (dup2 · pipe · popen · file actions)

The lecture closed the revision by listing these and pointing at the examples — “pipes are one of the super really awesome parts of Linux… I do it all the time” — while repeating that they are advanced. Week 9 Lecture 1 builds all of it with fifteen labs; Week 9 Lecture 2 adds fdopen and tests the addclose claim. The five facts to keep:

factwhy
pipe(pipefd) gives you 3 and 40, 1, 2 are taken and the kernel always allocates the lowest free descriptor. pipefd[0] reads, pipefd[1] writes.
dup2(old, new) silently closes new firstWhich is exactly what makes redirection a one-liner: dup2(fd, 1) and every printf goes to fd.
Close the ends you do not useA reader sees end-of-file only when every write end everywhere is closed — and the child inherited a copy of yours. This is the number-one cause of a pipe program that hangs.
popen is system with a streamSame shell, same injection hole. "r" reads the command's stdout; "w" writes to its stdin. “It accesses directly the shell just like system. So we try not to use that anywhere.”
File actions are the safe versionposix_spawn_file_actions_addclose / adddup2 describe the descriptor surgery declaratively, and posix_spawn performs it in the child between fork and exec — no shell anywhere.

The lecture's spawn_read_pipe.c walkthrough is the assembly of all five: create a pipe, build file actions that close the read end in the child and dup2 the write end onto descriptor 1, spawn date, close your own write end, wrap the read end in a FILE * with fdopen, and read a line. “So everything happened as it should.” Full treatment →

Check yourself

Exercises

Eight sets. The first four are the concurrency half, the last four are revision — and the revision ones are deliberately shaped like exam questions, because that is what the second half of this lecture was for.

Set 1 · Shared, private, and the API
  1. Two threads in one process. Which of these does thread B see when thread A changes it: a global int; a malloc'd buffer; errno; the current working directory; a local in A's function; the program counter?
  2. errno is written in source exactly like a global. Explain how it can be per-thread, and give a concrete bug that would occur if it were not.
  3. Give the process-world equivalent of pthread_create, pthread_join, pthread_exit and pthread_t. For each pair, name one way the thread version differs.
  4. Write the correct error check for pthread_create. Why is if (ret == -1) perror("pthread_create"); wrong in two independent ways?
  5. main creates four threads, joins none, and returns. What happens? Change one line so the threads finish, without adding a join.
Answers

1. Shared: global int, malloc'd buffer, working directory — and also the local in A's function, if B was given its address. There is one address space and no barrier inside it; slide 8 says explicitly that a thread can read and write another thread's stack. Private: errno and the program counter (with all registers and each thread's own stack region).

2. errno is a macro, not a variable — it expands to a dereference of a thread-local slot, which is why &errno is legal and differs per thread (measured: 0x70a56e8556c0 in main, 0x70a56e5ff5c0 in the thread). Bug if shared: A's open fails with ENOENT; before A reaches perror, B's call fails with EACCES; A prints “Permission denied” for a missing file. Every diagnosis becomes a lottery.

3. pthread_create ↔ posix_spawn/fork+exec (the thread starts inside your address space at a function; the process starts in a new one at a program on disk). pthread_join ↔ waitpid (join returns a void * you chose; waitpid returns a packed status word with 8 usable bits). pthread_exit ↔ exit (one thread vs the whole process). pthread_t ↔ pid_t (opaque vs a printable integer).

4. int ret = pthread_create(...); if (ret != 0) { fprintf(stderr, "pthread_create: %s\n", strerror(ret)); exit(1); }. The wrong version (i) never fires, because failure returns a positive error number and never −1; and (ii) even if it did, perror reads errno, which pthread_create does not set. Identical protocol to posix_spawn — which is worth remembering as one fact rather than two.

5. All four are killed immediately, wherever they are: returning from main calls exit, which ends the process. The one-line change is pthread_exit(NULL); instead of return 0; — measured, the worker then completes all five of its ticks instead of stopping at two. This is not a substitute for joining, because you still get no return values and no ordering.

Set 2 · Lifetime, in and out
  1. do_stuff ends with return &val; where val is a local int. Compiled with GCC at -O0, what does the caller actually receive, and what does the program do? Why is your first guess wrong?
  2. The laundered version printed -1553992128, -1562384832, -1570777536. What is the difference between consecutive values, and what does that number identify?
  3. Four ways to get an int out of a thread. Give all four and one situation where each is the best choice.
  4. In threads_return.c, main frees. In thread_data_malloc.c, the thread frees. State the rule that covers both.
  5. A colleague fixes a data-lifetime bug by making the variable static. When does this work, and when does it silently replace one bug with a worse one?
Answers

1. The caller receives NULL, and the program segfaults (measured: 3 of 3 runs, before the first “completed” line). The natural guess is “a dangling pointer to reused stack, so garbage values” — wrong, because when GCC diagnoses -Wreturn-local-addr it rewrites the return value to a null pointer: the emitted code is movl $0, %eax. The lecture saw “return value 0” and read it as garbage; it was the compiler.

2. Exactly 8,392,704 both times — 0x801000, which is 8 MiB (the default thread stack, confirmed by pthread_attr_getstacksize) plus a 4,096-byte guard page. So the values are the low 32 bits of stack addresses, one per thread, laid out at a fixed stride. They differ between runs because ASLR relocates the region. Garbage with a constant stride is not garbage.

3. (i) malloc in the thread, caller frees — the general answer, and the one the demo uses. (ii) Write into a caller-owned slot passed in as the argument — best when the caller already has somewhere to put it and you want no allocation. (iii) A static or global — only when there is exactly one such thread, ever. (iv) Cast the value into the void * itself — allocation-free, fine for small integers, and genuinely common; ugly, and limited to things that fit in a pointer.

4. Ownership follows the pointer, and is discharged exactly once. Whoever ends up holding the last copy frees it. In threads_return.c the pointer travels outward via pthread_join, so main frees; in thread_data_malloc.c it travels inward via the argument, so the thread frees. There is no rule about threads or about main — only about direction. Both ends freeing is a double free; neither is a leak that scales with thread count.

5. It works if there will only ever be one thread using that function at a time — the storage now outlives the call, which was the actual problem. It is a disaster with several threads, because they all now share one slot: you have converted a lifetime bug into a data race, which is harder to see, harder to reproduce, and no longer produces an obvious crash. This is the two_threads_broken.c bug wearing a different hat.

Set 3 · Races, mutexes, deadlock
  1. Three threads each add 100,000 to a global. The program prints 299,975. Explain where the 25 went, in terms of instructions.
  2. The demo has a nanosleep in the loop and loses about 30 of 300,000. Delete it and the loss jumps to about 90,000. Explain the direction of that change — most people predict the opposite.
  3. The lecturer raised the thread count from two to three to make the bug more visible. Was that a good idea? Quantify.
  4. deadlock.c hangs 100% of the time as written and 1.5% of the time with the sleeps removed. Which version has the bug?
  5. State the lock-ordering rule and prove it prevents deadlock. Then name two failures it does not prevent.
  6. A transfer function locks only the account it is debiting. Can it deadlock? Can it lose money?
Answers

1. bank_account = bank_account + 1 is load, add, store. On 25 occasions two threads loaded the same value before either stored: both computed v+1, both wrote it, and two increments produced one. Nothing is corrupted and no instruction failed — the update was simply based on a value that was stale by the time it was written back.

2. The sleep does not protect the critical section — it is outside it. It makes each iteration take about 71,900 ns of which about 3.84 ns is the increment, a duty cycle of roughly 1 in 18,700. Threads are therefore almost never inside the window at the same time. Predicted loss over 300,000 increments: about 30; measured 25–40. Remove the sleep and the duty cycle becomes 1, so collisions become routine. Sleeps do not reduce races; they change which interleavings you sample.

3. It worked, and it was the smaller of the two available levers. Two threads with the sleep lost a mean of 6.7; three lost 30.4 — a genuine 4.5×. Deleting the nanosleep instead takes the mean loss to 92,654, roughly 3,000× larger. Correct diagnosis, wrong knob.

4. Both. It is the same program with the same lock-ordering fault; the sleep only changes the probability of observing it. That is the entire lesson: a bug that appears 1.5% of the time is not 1.5% of a bug — at a thousand requests per second it is fifteen hangs a second — and it cannot be found by running the program, which is what two lectures of trying demonstrated. It is found by reading the lock order.

5. Rule: every thread acquires locks in the same order (and, where possible, releases in reverse). Proof: number the locks and require acquisition in increasing order. A deadlock is a cycle in the holds-and-waits graph; every edge of that graph now points from a lower number to a higher one, and a graph whose edges strictly increase cannot contain a cycle. Not prevented: livelock (threads politely retrying forever, nothing blocked, nothing progressing) and starvation (the system advances, one thread never does). Also not prevented: forgetting to unlock, or holding a lock across a blocking call.

6. It cannot deadlock — each thread holds at most one lock, so there is no cycle. It absolutely loses money, because the debit and the credit are no longer one indivisible operation: another thread can observe or interleave with the half-completed transfer, and the credit side is unprotected. This is the trap in the question — “no deadlock” is not evidence of “correctly locked”. Measured version of this in Lab 12.

Set 4 · Atomics
  1. atomic_int x = 0;. Which of these are atomic: x += 1; x++; x = x + 1; atomic_fetch_add(&x, 1); x |= 4; x = x * 2?
  2. Explain the difference between x += 1 and x = x + 1 in terms of generated instructions. Both compile without warnings and both produce the same answer single-threaded.
  3. Is each individual instruction in the x = x + 1 version atomic? If so, why is the statement not?
  4. Rank by cost: unlocked int, mutex, atomic +=, atomic_fetch_add. Then say why the fastest is not the answer.
  5. atomic_int available; and a thread doing if (available > 0) available -= 1;. Both operations are atomic. Is the code correct?
Answers

1. Atomic: x += 1, x++, atomic_fetch_add(&x,1), x |= 4. Not atomic: x = x + 1, and x = x * 2 — both are assignments, and there is no *= in slide 24's list anyway (the guaranteed set is ++ += -- -= |= &= ^=). The pattern: a compound assignment is one operation the compiler can emit as one instruction; a plain assignment is a read and a separate write.

2. Measured at -O0: x += 1 becomes a single lock xaddl %eax, x(%rip). x = x + 1 becomes two instructions — movl x(%rip), %eax then xchgl x(%rip), %eax. One instruction cannot be interrupted part-way; two can be interrupted between them. (atomic_fetch_add with an unused result compiles to lock addl $1, cheaper still, because nothing needs the old value.)

3. Yes, individually atomic — the load cannot observe a torn value and xchg is implicitly locked on x86. The pair is not. Between them your thread holds a stale copy in a register while any number of other threads load, add and store; your xchgl then overwrites all of their work with a value computed from the old one. Atomicity does not compose: two atomic operations are not an atomic operation.

4. Measured (3 threads × 5,000,000, -O0, median of 7): unlocked 19.2 ms, atomic_fetch_add 138.3 ms (7.2×), atomic += 149.4 ms (7.8×), mutex 656.4 ms (34.2×). The fastest is not the answer because it is wrong — the same runs lost up to 31% of the increments. A wrong answer can be computed arbitrarily quickly; the meaningful comparison is 4.4× between the two correct options.

5. No. The test and the decrement are two separate atomic operations with a gap between them, so two threads can both read available == 1 and both decrement, leaving −1. This is the check-then-act race, and it is the standard demonstration that atomics protect operations rather than invariants. Fixes: a mutex around both, or a compare-and-swap loop (atomic_compare_exchange_weak), or a semaphore, which exists precisely for this shape of problem.

Set 5 · Processes: who is who
  1. After pid_t p = fork();, what are the three possible values of p and what does each mean?
  2. A child prints getppid() and gets 1. The parent definitely existed. Explain, and give the one-line change that fixes it.
  3. A program calls fork() five times in a row (not in a loop). How many processes exist at the end, and how many were created?
  4. What survives an execve, and what does not? Why is code after a successful execve unreachable?
  5. Why must you fflush(stdout) before exec, and also before fork? Are these the same problem?
Answers

1. 0 → you are the child. A positive value → you are the parent, and the value is your child's pid (which you need for waitpid). -1 → the fork failed, no child exists, and errno says why.

2. The parent exited before the child asked, so the child was reparented to init (pid 1). Measured: without a wait, this happened in 26 of 30 runs. The fix is one line in the parent — wait(NULL); before returning — after which the child read the true parent pid in 30 of 30. getppid() reports who your parent is at the moment you call it, which is a different question from who created you.

3. Each fork doubles the population, so 25 = 32 processes exist, of which 31 were created (the original was already there). This is the fork-bomb arithmetic; the lecture's three-fork version produced eight processes and eight “goodbye” lines.

4. Survives: the pid, the parent, open file descriptors (which is what makes pre-exec redirection work), the working directory, the umask. Destroyed: the entire address space — code, globals, heap, stack, every variable, all other threads. Code after a successful execve is unreachable because there is no longer a program containing that code; reaching it is the error report, which is why the idiom is execve(...); perror("execve"); exit(1);.

5. Same buffer, opposite symptom. Before exec: the buffer is destroyed with the address space, so unflushed output vanishes. Before fork: the buffer is copied into every child, so unflushed output is duplicated — measured, 8 copies of “hello world” when stdout is a file or pipe, 1 when it is a terminal, from the identical binary. Line buffering on a terminal is what hides both, which is why these bugs appear the first time someone redirects to a log.

Set 6 · Status words
  1. waitpid filled in 0x2a00. What happened to the child?
  2. A child calls exit(256). What does the parent see, and why?
  3. A child segfaults. Give WIFEXITED, WIFSIGNALED, WTERMSIG, and what the shell's $? would print.
  4. Why is if (WEXITSTATUS(status) == 0) not a sufficient success test?
  5. grep exits 0, 1 and 2 in different situations. Name them, and say how posix_grep.c uses the distinction.
Answers

1. It exited normally with status 42. 0x2a00 >> 8 = 0x2a = 42. Printing the raw word would give 10752, which is the classic mistake — the exit code is in the high byte of the low 16 bits.

2. The parent sees 0 — success. Only 8 bits are transmitted, and 256 & 0xff = 0 (measured: raw word 0x0000, WEXITSTATUS 0). Any program that returns a count or a negative error code from main can therefore lie: exit(-1) arrives as 255. Exit codes are 0–255, and 0 means success.

3. Measured: raw 0x008b, WIFEXITED = 0, WIFSIGNALED = 1, WTERMSIG = 11 (SIGSEGV). The shell prints $? = 139, by the 128 + signal convention — a shell convention, not the kernel's encoding, which is why 139 does not appear in the status word.

4. Because WEXITSTATUS is only meaningful if WIFEXITED is true. A child killed by a signal never exited, so its exit status is undefined — and on Linux it reads as 0, so the test silently reports success for a program that crashed. Always WIFEXITED(st) && WEXITSTATUS(st) == 0.

5. 0 = at least one line matched, 1 = no lines matched (not an error), 2 = an actual error such as a missing file — all three measured. posix_grep.c increments n_matched only on 0, so a non-matching file and an unreadable file are both correctly excluded, and they are excluded for different reasons that the program can tell apart if it wants to.

Set 7 · Choosing a call
  1. A web handler runs system(cmd) where cmd was built by concatenating a user-supplied filename. Show the attack in one line, then fix the code.
  2. posix_spawn returns 0. Has the program run successfully? What must you still check?
  3. When does posix_spawn("date", ...) fail where posix_spawnp("date", ...) succeeds? Give the errno.
  4. You need a child that reads from a file instead of the terminal. Which mechanism, and which two calls?
  5. You want the child to see only TZ=UTC and nothing else. How, and what breaks?
Answers

1. Filename report.txt; rm -rf ~ — the shell sees ; as a command separator and runs both. Fix: char *argv[] = {"wc", "-l", filename, NULL}; posix_spawn(&pid, "/usr/bin/wc", NULL, NULL, argv, environ);. No shell parses anything, so the filename is a filename with an unusual name. Quoting the string is not the fix; removing the shell is.

2. No. 0 means the child was successfully created. Whether the program existed, was executable, or ran correctly is reported through waitpid — a child that cannot exec exits with 127. Always waitpid, then WIFEXITED and WEXITSTATUS.

3. Whenever date is not the literal path to an executable — i.e. there is no ./date — because posix_spawn does no PATH search. Measured: ret = 2, ENOENT, “No such file or directory”, while posix_spawnp returned 0 and ran /bin/date. Remember it as: the p is for PATH.

4. File actions: build a posix_spawn_file_actions_t, add posix_spawn_file_actions_addopen (or addopen plus adddup2) targeting descriptor 0, and pass it to posix_spawn. The spawn performs the surgery in the child between fork and exec. The fork-based equivalent is open then dup2(fd, 0) in the child before exec — same idea, more lines, one more thing to get wrong.

5. char *envp[] = {"TZ=UTC", NULL}; and pass envp instead of environ. What breaks: PATH is gone, so posix_spawnp can no longer find anything and you must use a full path. Also gone: HOME, LANG (so message and number formatting may change), and anything the child's libraries read. A minimal environment is a good default for anything security-sensitive, provided you know what you removed.

Set 8 · Reading posix_grep.c
  1. Why does the loop start at i = 2?
  2. grep_argv[0] is "grep" but the path is "/bin/grep". Could they differ? Which one decides what runs?
  3. The program never redirects anything, yet grep's output appears. Where does it go, and how would you capture it instead?
  4. Rewrite the loop to spawn all the greps first and wait afterwards. What do you gain, and what do you now have to be careful about?
  5. ./posix_grep at f1.txt printed a line containing “no match here”. Is that a bug?
Answers

1. argv[0] is the program's own name and argv[1] is the pattern, so the filenames start at index 2. Hence also the argc < 3 usage check: you need at least a name, a pattern and one file.

2. Yes, they can differ, and nothing enforces a relationship. The path decides which program is executed; argv[0] is merely the string the child sees as its own name — it is what grep would print in its error messages. Some programs deliberately exploit this (busybox dispatches entirely on argv[0]); the convention is to match, and breaking it silently is a good way to write confusing error output.

3. The child inherits descriptor 1, which is still your terminal — nobody changed it, so grep writes directly to your stdout, interleaved with your own output. To capture it: create a pipe, build file actions that adddup2 the write end onto 1 and addclose the read end in the child, spawn, close your own write end, and read. That is spawn_read_pipe.c from Week 9 Lecture 1, and it is the advanced material.

4. You gain parallelism — N greps running at once instead of one at a time, a real win over many files. You now have to: store every pid in an array (they are the only handle you have); still call waitpid on each, or you accumulate zombies; and accept that the output is now interleaved unpredictably, since several children share descriptor 1 with no coordination. The count stays correct, because it depends only on statuses.

5. Not a bug. grep matches substrings, and “match” contains “at”. If you meant whole words, that is grep -w, or the pattern \bat\b. Worth noticing because it is the same class of mistake as searching for a short flag name in a config file and matching half your keys.

Slides 29–33

Wrap-up (slides 29–33)

What we learnt today

Concurrency, finished

  • Threads share code, globals, the heap and descriptors; each has its own registers, stack and errno.
  • Getting a value out of a thread has the same lifetime problem as getting one in — and GCC's response to return &local is to return NULL, not to let you find out.
  • Threads can create threads. There is no thread hierarchy; any thread may join any other.
  • A data race is a load–add–store split across two threads. A mutex makes it impossible and costs 34×; an atomic makes it impossible and costs 7×.
  • Deadlock needs two locks in two orders. One rule — a consistent global acquisition order — makes it impossible, provably.
  • x += 1 is one instruction; x = x + 1 is two, and the gap between them is where the race lives.

Revision: processes

  • exec replaces you and keeps your pid; fork duplicates you and returns twice; posix_spawn does both at once and is the default choice.
  • system and popen hand a string to a shell. That is the whole objection, and it is enough.
  • The status word is not the exit code. WIFEXITED first, then WEXITSTATUS — and only 8 bits survive.
  • The environment is part of a child's interface: PATH decides whether spawnp finds anything, TZ decides what date prints.
  • posix_grep.c is the whole revision half in twenty lines: spawn, wait, decode, count.
  • Buffered output is copied by fork and destroyed by exec. fflush before both.

Corrections and additions — 17 items, all measured

Everything below was produced by compiling and running the lecture's own programs on gcc 11.4.0, glibc 2.35, Linux 6.8, two cores. Timings are medians of seven runs, one process per run. Where a claim contradicts the lecture, the measurement is quoted rather than the reasoning.

1 · return &val does not return a dangling pointer — GCC replaces it with NULL. The lecture read the resulting “return value was zero” as garbage from a reused stack slot. It is not: at -O0 the emitted code for do_stuff ends movl $0, %eax, because diagnosing -Wreturn-local-addr makes GCC substitute a null pointer. The program then segfaults on *return_val in 3 of 3 runs, before printing anything. §06.

2 · The real dangling-pointer values are stack addresses with an 8 MiB stride. Hiding the return behind a void * defeats the warning and produces the behaviour the lecture described. Consecutive threads' values differ by exactly 8,392,704 every time — 0x801000, the default 8 MiB thread stack (confirmed via pthread_attr_getstacksize) plus one 4,096-byte guard page. Not noise: the low 32 bits of a stack address. §06, Lab 5.

3 · two_threads_broken.c is not intermittent. It fails 2000 times out of 2000. The lecture treated the outcome as scheduling-dependent. thread_number = 2 runs long before either new thread is scheduled, so both print 2, always. Separately, the correct version's ordering is not a coin flip either — 1978 runs printed 1-then-2 and 22 printed 2-then-1, a 98.9% / 1.1% split, which is exactly the kind of margin that hides an ordering assumption until production. §05.

4 · The nanosleep is what kept bank_account_broken.c “quite robust”. Two lectures were spent trying to make the program fail, and the suppressing line was inside the loop. With it, 3 threads lose 25–40 of 300,000. Without it: 0, 100098, 134433, 22195, 168448, 91627, 50340, 59528, 200000, 99873 lost across ten runs — up to 56%, and one run returned exactly 100000, two threads' contributions entirely gone. §10.

5 · Raising the thread count from two to three helped by 4.5×; deleting the sleep would have helped by 3,000×. The lecturer's diagnosis was right and the lever was the smaller one. Measured mean loss: 2 threads with sleep 6.7, 3 threads with sleep 30.4, 3 threads without 92,654. §09.

6 · The duty-cycle model predicts the measurement. With the sleep, one iteration takes 71,900 ns of which the increment is 3.84 ns — a 1-in-18,700 window. Over 300,000 increments with three threads that predicts ~30 lost; measured 25, 40, 35, 27, 25. Agreement at this level is what justifies calling the mechanism understood rather than guessed. §10, Lab 8.

7 · deadlock.c's sleep(1) converts a 1.5% bug into a 100% bug, and changes nothing else. As written: 5 of 5 runs hung. With the sleeps deleted: 3 of 200. Both versions contain the identical lock-ordering fault. This is the counterpart to item 4 — a sleep outside a critical section hides a race, a sleep between two acquisitions exposes a deadlock. Placement is everything. §13.

8 · Xavier is not being ripped off. The lecture set this as homework and was unsure of the answer. Measured, the original lock order deadlocked 10 of 10 runs; with both threads locking Andrew then Xavier, 10 of 10 completed with andrew 100, xavier 100, total 200 — identical every run. The total is conserved structurally, because both accounts are mutated while holding both locks; the individual balances return to 100 because the loops are equal and opposite. Neither is luck. §14.

9 · The non-atomic increment does break, 8 times in 10. The lecture could not make it fail and moved on (“I'm not going to waste time with that”), predicting it would need many threads. Three threads with the nanosleep removed: 255824, 215202, 190753, 280319, 253711, 111077, 237461, 205465, 300000, 300000. Worst case lost 63%. The two correct runs are the interesting part — a bug that is right 20% of the time. §16.

10 · The atomics rule has a two-line explanation, and it is not “hardware”. At -O0: x += 1 and x++ both emit one instruction, lock xaddl; atomic_fetch_add(&x,1) emits lock addl $1 (cheaper, since the unused return lets GCC drop the exchange); x = x + 1 emits two, movl then xchgl. Each of the two is individually atomic — the failure is the gap between them, which is the same load–store gap as the plain int version. §16.

11 · A child's getppid() usually does not return the parent's pid. The lecture used the fork demo to show the relationship between the two processes. Measured over 30 runs with no wait in the parent: 26 returned 1 — the parent had already exited and the child was reparented to init. Adding wait(NULL) to the parent gave the true pid in 30 of 30. The demo works on the day because of timing, not because of a guarantee. §20.

12 · The three-fork demo prints eight “goodbye” on a terminal and eight of both lines anywhere else. The lecture saw one “hello world”. Redirect the same binary to a file or a pipe and stdout switches from line- to block-buffered, so the unflushed line is still in the buffer when fork copies the address space: 8 copies. Measured all three destinations. fflush(stdout) before forking. §24.

13 · exit(256) reports success. Only the low 8 bits of an exit code reach the parent. Measured: raw status 0x0000, WEXITSTATUS = 0. exit(-1) arrives as 255, and a segfault gives raw 0x008b with WIFSIGNALED = 1 and WTERMSIG = 11 while WEXITSTATUS reads a misleading 0. §25, Lab 20.

14 · “When main returns, all threads terminate” is true only for return. Slide 10 states it without qualification. Measured: with return 0, a worker stopped at tick 1 of 5; with pthread_exit(NULL) in the identical program, it ran to worker FINISHED. Returning from main calls exit; pthread_exit does not. §04, Lab 2.

15 · posix_spawn does no PATH search, and reports it unusually. Measured with the identical argument: posix_spawn(&pid, "date", ...) returned 2 (ENOENT) while posix_spawnp returned 0 and ran /bin/date. Note also that the 2 is the return value — errno was untouched, exactly as with pthread_create. And a return of 0 only means the child was created: a failed exec surfaces later as exit status 127. §26.

16 · Per-thread errno, confirmed by address. &errno in main was 0x70a56e8556c0; in the thread, 0x70a56e5ff5c0 — 2,449,664 bytes apart. The thread's close(-1) set its own errno to 9 (EBADF) and main's remained 0. The consequence is worth stating: you cannot inspect a worker's errno after joining it. §03, Lab 1.

17 · Slide 5 was out of date, and the poll had already moved. The lecturer flagged it live: “oops, I haven't updated this — revision files will be on Wednesday.” Today was threads and processes; files, UTF-8 and the rest are the final lecture. Also from the day: the topic poll had threads and files leading. §01.

Three smaller notes. Nested threads reached depth 2,000 with every level blocked in pthread_join — 2,000 live threads reserving roughly 16 GiB of virtual address space on a machine without it, which works only because stacks are mapped lazily. -pthread has not been required to link since glibc 2.34 (2021), when libpthread merged into libc — keep passing it anyway, for _REENTRANT and portability. And grep at matches inside “match”, which is why the posix_grep demo prints a line that appears not to contain the pattern — substrings, not words.

The practice exam, and why the room was empty

Slide 3 puts it plainly and the lecturer was blunter: “there have been a lot of empty labs. People aren't showing up probably because you don't need to get checked off. It really is worthwhile doing the practice exam if you haven't already done it — it definitely will give you a bit of confidence going into the final exam.” Three things make it worth an afternoon:

  • It is the only way to see the environment before it counts. Not your CSE account, not your editor config, no course website, no dcc-help. §08 lists what that leaves.
  • The hardware is not yours. “Maybe the keyboard's slightly different to what you're used to, or the mouse… it won't be kind of your preferred conditions.”
  • The questions are never released. They exist only in that room, so there is no version of “I'll look at them later”.

Slides 6–8 — what the last ten weeks were for

The course, in one page (slides 6–8)

Slide 6 states the goal as “transform you into a systems programmer”. Slide 7 turns that into six questions you should now be able to answer — which doubles neatly as a self-test. If a row makes you uneasy, the link is where it was covered.

Slide 7 asks…The answer, and where it lives
What's in a compiled file?Machine code — the same instructions you can write by hand in assembly, plus a data segment and symbol information. W1L1, W1L2.
How does your CPU run a compiled file? (and what if we write those instructions ourselves?)Fetch, decode, execute — load operands into registers, operate, store the result back. That is the whole of MIPS. W2L1–W3L2, and §28.
How are variables represented?As bits at an address. Integers in two's complement, reals in IEEE-754, characters in UTF-8 — three different agreements about what a pattern of bits means. W4L1, W5L1, W8L1.
What magic are the functions in stdio.h doing?Buffering, and wrapping system calls. Assignment 2 was this question. W5L2, W7L1, and §18.
Why and how do emoji even exist?Unicode assigns code points; UTF-8 encodes them in 1–4 bytes so that ASCII stays one byte and nothing else can be mistaken for it. W8L1, W8L2, and §24.
How do computers multitask?Processes with separate address spaces, threads sharing one, and a scheduler interleaving both. W8L2, W9L1, W9L2, W10L1.

Slide 8's syllabus list maps onto the same territory: MIPS assembler and how C constructs become instructions; bit-level operations and integer representation; IEEE-754; UTF-8; systems programming — file operations and processes; and an introduction to threads with pthreads. The word introduction is doing real work in that last item, and slide 35 admits it.

The framing worth keeping. “Every operation you do above it has a cost — in terms of moving memory around, in terms of power… and also thinking about security issues. Throughout the course we told you some functions that we didn't want you to use because of security issues. Hopefully this will help you think about any kind of function call that you make and whether it's going to have some inherent issues with it.” That is the actual transferable skill: gets, strcpy, system and popen were not banned as arbitrary course rules.
Slides 9–11 — five components, two caps, one piece of arithmetic

Where your marks come from (slides 9–11)

The lecturer expected this slide to start a certain kind of mental arithmetic — “so you guys can start doing the flurried math that you need to do in order to work out how much you need on the final exam to pass”. Lab 1 does the flurried math for you. First, the three slides it is built from.

SLIDE 9 · WEIGHTS
labs15
weekly tests10
assignment 115
assignment 215
final exam45

Coursework caps out at 55. The exam is worth more than everything else put together minus one mark.

SLIDE 10 · LABS

Labs in weeks 1–5 and 7–10 — 9 labs, 2 marks each, so 18 marks available for a 15-mark component. Within each lab, 1.6 is split across the regular exercises and 0.4 across the challenges.

Full marks on every regular exercise all term gives 9 × 1.6 = 14.4 — “very close to 15!” Challenges are the top-up, not the requirement.

“Most students usually get 12+/15.”

SLIDE 11 · TESTS

Max 1.7 per week. Best 6 of 8 summed, then capped to give a mark out of 10.

6 × 1.7 = 10.2, capped to 10 — so a perfect six is a hair more than you need, and two zero weeks cost nothing if the other six are perfect.

“Most people usually get 7+/10.”

Both coursework components are deliberately over-provisioned. Labs offer 18 marks for a 15-mark slot; tests offer 10.2 for a 10-mark slot. That is not generosity for its own sake — it is what makes a bad week survivable without a special consideration application. It also means that by Week 10 your coursework mark is essentially fixed, and the only variable left is the exam.

Slide 9 — the sentence people misread

Two hurdles, not one (slide 9)

Slide 9 states the pass condition as two bullets, and then gives a worked example specifically because the two are independent:

To pass, you must: • score 50/100 overall • score 18/45 (40%) on the final exam component (For example, 55/100 overall, 17/45 on final exam would result in 55 UF, not 55 PS)

That example is the whole point. 55 is a comfortable pass and it is not a pass, because 17 is one mark under the exam hurdle. The lecturer returned to it later, unprompted: “if you've got a friend that's like, well, I've already passed the course — shake them and say to them, no, you have not passed the course. You need to go to the exam and you need to get over 40%.”

The non-obvious consequence

Work out, for a given coursework total, which of the two conditions is harder to satisfy. Coursework is out of 55; the exam is out of 45. To reach 50 overall you need 50 − banked on the exam. The hurdle needs 18 regardless. Those cross at 32 out of 55:

banked (of 55)needed for 50 overallneeded for the hurdlewhich one actually binds
262418the 50% total
302018the 50% total
321818they coincide exactly
381218the hurdle — by 6 marks
44618the hurdle — by 12 marks
55−5 (none)18the hurdle, and only the hurdle
Above 32/55, the pass mark stops being the target. The lecture's own “most students” figures — 12+/15 on labs, 7+/10 on tests — put you at 19 before either assignment is counted. Any pair of assignment marks summing to 13 or more (out of 30) crosses the line. For most of the cohort the arithmetic that matters is not “how much do I need to pass”; it is “can I get 18 out of 45”, and slide 30 says that is what the first eight questions are for.

The overlap, and what it costs you

Slide 15 is the one people do not expect. The afternoon session starts before the morning session finishes. The reason is containment: afternoon students are corralled so that they cannot talk to morning students. Two consequences follow directly, and both are practical:

Slides 16–18 — what you bring, and what starting the exam commits you to

The rules, and fit-to-sit (slides 16–18)

SLIDE 16 · BRING / DO NOT BRING
  • Student card. If lost or expired, get a new one before the 20th. A passport or Australian driver's licence is acceptable — physical, not on your phone.
  • Phone, watches, other electronics: switched off, in your bag. You will be asked about smartwatches.
  • Water bottle: allowed if completely clear. “I would advise to bring one — it is a long time to go without water.”
  • No keyboard, mouse or other hardware of your own.

Deliberate violation is treated as serious misconduct and may go to the Student Conduct and Integrity Unit. “This is very scary when this happens — it can mean expulsion. So just don't do it.”

SLIDES 17–18 · FIT TO SIT

The exam is covered by UNSW's fit-to-sit policy. Stated exactly: “by starting the exam, you are saying ‘I am well enough to finish the exam’.”

  • Unwell before? See a doctor, apply for special consideration, and do not attend.
  • Unwell during? Tell a supervisor as soon as you start feeling unwell — not afterwards.
Retrospective certificates do not work. “I cannot tell you how many emails come through after you've sat the exam — oh, I wasn't feeling well, and have a retrospective doctor's certificate. The fit-to-sit policy is that you came, you sat down, that's you saying you're good to go.” And remember you cannot leave early: “if you get sick during, it's hard to say what will happen there.”
On cheating, said unprompted. “Last term we had an incident where someone was found to be cheating during the exam. That caused chaos and was not a great situation for anyone… you will be found, and it does not end well for you, but also it's really bad for everybody else.” If you see something during the exam, tell a supervisor — the point made was that you should not be disadvantaged by someone else's decision.

Closed book. A restricted environment — not your CSE account. Learn man properly, this week

With no internet and no course website, man is the entire reference. It came up four separate times in the revision half — for write, for open, for fopen, and for error returns. The section numbers are the part people never learn:

commandwhat it gets you
man -k keywordSearch every page's description. The way in when you know what you want but not what it is called. man -k directory finds opendir, readdir, mkdir.
man 2 writeSection 2 — system calls. write, read, open, close, stat, lseek.
man 3 fopenSection 3 — library functions. fopen, fgetc, fgets, printf, malloc, strlen.
man 3 printf vs man 1 printfSame name, different thing. Section 1 is the shell command. Getting the wrong one wastes a minute you will not have.
the RETURN VALUE and ERRORS headingsThe two sections that answer the question you will actually have under pressure: what does this give me back when it fails? open says −1; fopen says NULL. That distinction is §20.

The format (slides 21–24)

SLIDE 21 · SHAPE
  • 10 minutes reading, then 3 hours working
