Use the reading time to read the mark allocations, not just the questions. They are the only signal you get about where the three hours should go.

SLIDE 22 · MECHANICS
  • Each question is answered in a separate file.
  • Some ask for C (a .c file), some for MIPS (a .s file). No other language is permitted.
  • Submission is via a command similar to give.
  • Questions include examples.
  • You may or may not get starter code. If not, you create the file yourself — with exactly the filename in the question.
The translation questions are named explicitly. “Sometimes you're provided with a C file and asked to reproduce it as an .s file, or vice versa. So make sure that you're able to look at the stuff we did when we were translating between the two.” That is W2L1 through W3L2, and it is §28.

Autotests are a guide, not a verdict (slide 23)

Autotests are available for all questions. Slide 23 then spends its whole body undercutting them: “passing autotests does not guarantee any marks — do your own testing. It is not sufficient to just match supplied examples.” Slide 23 also promises a demo of “bad code that may match some or all autotests but would get 0 marks”.

The demo did not happen — and the lecturer said so. Asked to give an example live: “yeah, I'm not exactly sure what an example of bad code would be, but I guess code that calls something else to do it… not in the spirit of what we wanted.” The concrete version, from the same answer and from slide 24, is the useful one: if a question says use a system call, using fopen scores zero even if every test passes; and “you won't be able to get away with being asked to do a call to give the date and you just look at the time and write down what it is and do a printf statement — we'll see that you did that.” A hardcoded answer that reproduces the sample output is the canonical case.

Restrictions are marks, not style (slide 24)

Questions may impose additional limitations. Violating one voids the question — and this is checked by a human, so passing the autotests does not protect you:

if the question says…then this is not allowedbecause
“using a system call”fopen, fprintf, fgetc — anything from stdio.hYou are being asked to demonstrate the layer below the library. See §18.
“without using the standard I/O library”printf. Use write.Same reason, one layer up.
“in MIPS”a .c file that happens to workThe .s is the answer.
The failure mode is silent. Nothing warns you. Your code compiles, the autotests pass, and the mark is zero. Re-read the restriction line after you finish each question — it costs fifteen seconds and it is the cheapest marks-per-second in the exam.
Slides 25–27 — how a partly-working answer is treated

How it is marked (slides 25–27)

SLIDE 25 · STYLE

No marks for style or comments. But a human may need to deduce what your program does, so use reasonable names and indentation — “so that we can give you the mark that you deserve”.

Comments only where they tell the marker something. Nothing identifying — you are a zID. “Don't say ‘hey, this is me from your lab on Tuesdays’.”

SLIDE 26 · AUTOMARKING

Everything goes through automatic marking. Follow the input/output format exactly. There are unseen tests beyond the ones you can run.

Answers that do not pass everything are handmarked, guided by the automarking — which is why readable code converts into marks even though style scores nothing.

SLIDE 27 · PARTIAL CREDIT

Minor errors, small penalty. A missing whitespace gets “almost full marks”.

No marks below roughly 33% progress toward a solution. No marks for generic code. Zero for submitting starter code.

The 33% floor is a strategy constraint, not a marking detail. Read it together with slide 21's warning about the hard questions: “you might bang away at it for a couple of hours and still not get anywhere near the solution, and then you won't get any marks at all even though you've put in a big effort.” Effort below the floor scores exactly the same as not attempting. That makes a half-hour of hopeless progress on Q10 strictly worse than a half-hour re-checking Q3 — which is where §13 comes from.

Slide 29 and the transcript — three hours, ten questions, one plan

Three hours, ten questions (slide 29 + transcript)

Slide 29 is four words long — eat, sleep, drink water, take all your medication — under the line “you can't perform well if your body is falling apart”. The strategy advice is all in the talking, spread across slides 21, 27 and 31. Collected:

ORDER

“It's probably best to go from top to bottom. If you start on the insanely difficult question 10 — which has been purposefully made to be mind-bogglingly difficult — you might use up all your time doing that and miss out on answering the other questions.”

The recommendation as given: knock away the first five or six, then decide where the extra time goes. With the caveat: “difficulty is subjective, and some of you might be absolutely awesome at the difficult stuff and have no idea about the easy stuff… my recommendation stands in the general case.”

THE FLOOR CHANGES THE MATH

Because nothing under ~33% progress scores, time on a question you cannot start is worth zero, while the same time spent verifying an early answer converts directly into marks — and every early question is one you have already shown you can do.

Corollary: if you are stuck at 20% on Q9 with forty minutes left, going back to re-test Q1–Q6 against edge cases is the higher-expected-value move. Autotests are a guide; unseen tests are not.

Slide 39 · threads — one rule, two ways to obey it

Threads: the data has to outlive the function (transcript)

The lecturer picked one thing out of the whole threads topic, and it is the right one: “that's the really important thing about threads — you need to make sure that you have memory allocated for variables that exist only within functions.” The pair of programs is thread_data_broken.c and thread_data_malloc.c.

thread_data_broken.c
pthread_t function_creates_thread(void) { int super_special_number = 0x42; // on this function's stack pthread_t thread_handle; pthread_create(&thread_handle, NULL, my_thread, &super_special_number); return thread_handle; // <-- the stack frame dies HERE }
thread_data_malloc.c
pthread_t function_creates_thread(void) { int *super_special_number = malloc(sizeof(int)); *super_special_number = 0x42; // on the heap pthread_t thread_handle; pthread_create(&thread_handle, NULL, my_thread, super_special_number); return thread_handle; // heap outlives the frame }

The consumer differs by one line — the malloc version's thread calls free(data) when it is done. That is the second half of the rule: the programmer controls the lifetime, so the programmer has to end it.

What the broken one actually prints

The notes' comment says “should print 0x42, probably won't”. Probably understates it. Measured over 120 runs:

The number is 0x7ffd! x 33 The number is 0x7ffe! x 32 The number is 0x7ffc! x 31 The number is 0x7fff! x 22 The number is 0x42! x 2 <-- accidentally correct 118 of 120 wrong (98.3%); 2 of 120 right, for no reason you control.

The wrong values are not random. 0x7ffc–0x7fff is the top half of a stack address — user-space stacks on x86-64 Linux sit at 0x00007fff…, and the four bytes that used to hold 0x42 now hold part of a pointer that some later call left there. So the bug does not print garbage; it prints a fragment of the machinery that overwrote it, which is a much better clue than noise if you ever see it in your own output.

The 2-in-120 is the dangerous part, not the 118. A bug that is right 1.7% of the time is a bug you cannot reproduce on demand, and it is exactly the shape of failure that passes an autotest run once and fails the unseen one. This is also why W9L2's say_hello() exists in the demo — it makes the overwrite happen reliably, converting an intermittent bug into a deterministic one so you can see it at all.

The other place to put the malloc

The lecturer flagged a second, equally valid arrangement: “the other way of doing it is to carve out the memory allocation within the thread that takes as an argument that data… it depends on where you want to put it. But in either case, you need to allocate memory.” The three arrangements, and when each is right:

where the data liveswho frees ituse when
creator's stacknobody — it is goneNever, unless the creator joins before returning. If the creating function outlives the thread, a local is fine — the bug is specifically that this one returns.
heap, allocated by the creatorthe thread, at the endThe default. One allocation per thread, each thread owns its own argument. This is thread_data_malloc.c.
heap or globals, one block, indexed per threadthe creator, after joinMany threads over one array — each gets &results[i]. Fewer allocations, and the creator can read every result after joining. Watch out for false sharing if the entries are adjacent and hot — see W9L2.
creator's stack, same variable reused in a loop—The classic loop bug. for (i…) pthread_create(&t[i], NULL, f, &i); passes one address to every thread, and they all read whatever i is when they get scheduled. Not a lifetime bug — a sharing bug — but it looks identical from the output.

Slide 39 · processes — the one distinction the lecture drew

fork+exec versus posix_spawn (transcript)

“Really the big thing for us in the processes was the difference between fork and spawning — spawn being the more modern way. I think we used the words ‘old-fashioned’ last time for fork and execute.” The revision-level summary, with the exam-relevant details attached. Full treatment is W9L1 and W10L1 §22–§26.

fork + execposix_spawn
callstwo, plus waitpidone, plus waitpid
returnsfork returns twice — 0 in the child, the child's pid in the parent, −1 on failureonce; the pid comes back through the first argument
errorsfork sets errno the usual wayreturns the error number and does not set errno. if (ret == -1) perror(...) is wrong twice over
address spaceduplicated, then thrown away by execnever duplicated
redirectiondone between the two calls, with ordinary close/dup2 in the child — easy to readdone in advance, via a posix_spawn_file_actions_t — §17
path searchexecvp searches PATH; execv does notposix_spawnp searches PATH; posix_spawn does not — measured, posix_spawn(&pid, "date", …) returns 2 (ENOENT)

The lecture's assessment of where the difficulty is, and it doubles as an exam hint: “it's not really that much more difficult if we're not doing any of those file actions. So the file actions is where it becomes complex, and that's why that's considered challenge topics. Otherwise it's returning the process ID, you're telling it what function to run, you're passing arguments and you're passing environment variables.”

// the whole of the non-challenge version, from the notes char *date_argv[] = {"date", "-u", NULL}; pid_t pid; int ret = posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/date", NULL, NULL, date_argv, environ); // ^ file_actions ^ attrp if (ret != 0) { errno = ret; perror("posix_spawn"); return 1; } int status; waitpid(pid, &status, 0);

Five arguments after the pid: path, file actions, attributes, argv, environment. The course never uses the attributes — “in this course we didn't look at the attributes at all” — so in every non-challenge question, argument three is NULL and argument four is NULL. Learn that shape; it is most of the marks.

On argv[0], since it looks redundant. The path decides what runs; argv[0] is only the name the child sees for itself. They conventionally match, and nothing enforces it. date_argv[] must be NULL-terminated — forgetting that is a segfault inside exec, not a compile error.
Linux commands are fair game, and the terminal is right there. “During the exam you obviously have a terminal. So if a Linux command is mentioned within the question, you might want to look at its man page, type it, see how it works on the command line so you understand what the output for that should be.” If a question spawns sort or grep or date, run it first and look at exactly what it prints — including whether it ends with a newline.
The question that was actually asked — and the answer, checked

posix_spawn_file_actions, and the two pipe programs (transcript)

This is the only student question in the lecture, and it got about ten minutes. “As I said during the lectures, we don't actually know what's inside this type — but how we use it.” That is the right framing: it is an opaque handle, like FILE and pthread_t, and the only thing you can do is build it up from four functions.

int posix_spawn_file_actions_init (posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa); int posix_spawn_file_actions_addclose(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa, int fd); int posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2 (posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa, int fd, int newfd); int posix_spawn_file_actions_destroy(posix_spawn_file_actions_t *fa);

The mental model that makes it click: a file actions object is a recorded to-do list. You are not closing or duplicating anything when you call addclose — you are writing down “when you make the child, before you run the program, do this”. The kernel replays the list inside the new process, between creation and exec. That is precisely the window that fork+exec gives you for free, and which posix_spawn otherwise takes away.

Why any of it is needed at all, stated well in the lecture: “the spawned process has access to all the file descriptors of the parent process. And so the actions structure allows us to close those within the spawned process without closing those in the parent process.” Descriptors are inherited; the to-do list is how you un-inherit selectively.

The two programs, side by side

spawn_read_pipe.c — capture a child's output
int fd[2]; pipe(fd); // fd[0] read, fd[1] write posix_spawn_file_actions_t actions; posix_spawn_file_actions_init(&actions); posix_spawn_file_actions_addclose(&actions, fd[0]); posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2(&actions, fd[1], 1); // write end becomes the child's stdout posix_spawn(&pid, "/bin/date", &actions, NULL, argv, environ); close(fd[1]); // PARENT closes its write end FILE *f = fdopen(fd[0], "r"); while (fgets(line, sizeof line, f)) printf("captured: %s", line);
spawn_write_pipe.c — feed a child's input
int fd[2]; pipe(fd); posix_spawn_file_actions_t actions; posix_spawn_file_actions_init(&actions); posix_spawn_file_actions_addclose(&actions, fd[1]); posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2(&actions, fd[0], 0); // read end becomes the child's stdin posix_spawn(&pid, "/usr/bin/sort", &actions, NULL, argv, environ); close(fd[0]); // parent closes its read end FILE *f = fdopen(fd[1], "w"); fprintf(f, "pear\napple\nbanana\n"); fclose(f); // this is the EOF the child waits for
$ ./spawn_read_pipe captured: Thu Aug 13 03:36:48 UTC 2026 child exited with 0 $ ./spawn_write_pipe apple banana pear child exited with 0

Which close is load-bearing? — the lecture's reasoning, measured

The explanation given for the addclose was: “make sure your spawned process doesn't have access to the read end of the pipe that you've just opened… because it may not get an end-of-file signal from the write end. So you close the read end.” The principle underneath that is exactly right and worth memorising:

A reader sees EOF only when every write-end descriptor, in every process, is closed. That is the rule. Everything else is bookkeeping about who is holding what.

But applied to spawn_read_pipe.c, the specific instance points at the wrong descriptor. Each variant below was compiled and run under a 5-second timeout:

variantresultwhy
spawn_read_pipe.c as writtenworks — captures the date, exits 0—
…with the child's addclose(fd[0]) deletedstill works, identicallyThe child holding a spare read end cannot stop the parent from seeing EOF. EOF depends on write ends only.
…with the parent's close(fd[1]) deletedhangs — killed at 5sThis is the one that matters. The parent is itself a writer. date exits, but the pipe still has a write end open — the parent's own — so fgets waits forever.
spawn_write_pipe.c with addclose(fd[1]) deletedhangs — killed at 5sHere the addclose is load-bearing. The child inherits a write end; the parent's fclose no longer closes the last one, so sort never sees EOF and never prints.
The correction, precisely. In the read direction the essential close is the parent's plain close(fd[1]) — which is not a file action at all. In the write direction the essential close is the child's addclose(fd[1]) — which is. The lecture's rule of thumb (“close what you don't use”) produces correct programs either way; it is the explanation that was attached to the wrong end. Both directions follow from the single sentence in the tip above, which is the thing to take into the exam.

Slide 39 · files — three layers, and which one a question is asking for

Three ways to write a string (transcript)

The lecture opened files by putting the three layers next to each other, and the reason is entirely exam-driven: “in your questions make sure that you're clear on — is it asking for the standard I/O library way of doing things, so things like printf? Is it asking for the standard C library way of doing things, like write? Or is it asking for a system call? Those are all different things.”

// 1. stdio -- buffered, formatted, portable printf("via stdio: printf\n"); // 2. libc wrapper -- unbuffered, you count the bytes yourself char *m = "via libc: write\n"; write(1, m, strlen(m)); // ^ file descriptor 1 == stdout // 3. the raw system call -- no wrapper at all char *s = "via syscall: syscall(SYS_write)\n"; syscall(SYS_write, 1, s, strlen(s)); // ^ syscall number 1 ^ file descriptor 1 -- two different 1s

The two 1s in the last call trip people up, and the lecture called it correctly: “the one means we're doing a write, the next one means that we're writing to standard output.” On x86-64 Linux SYS_write really is 1 — checked — and file descriptor 1 really is stdout. They are unrelated numbers that happen to coincide.

Running it proves which layer buffers

The three lines are written in the order stdio, libc, syscall. Measured, they do not come out in that order — and the order depends on where stdout is pointing:

stdout is a terminal — line buffered
via stdio: printf via libc: write via syscall: syscall(SYS_write) source order preserved: the \n flushes
stdout is a file or a pipe — block buffered
via libc: write via syscall: syscall(SYS_write) via stdio: printf printf is last: flushed at exit
This is the same mechanism as the fork duplication bug. printf puts bytes in a buffer in your address space; only a flush turns them into a write. Redirecting changes when that happens, which is why ./prog and ./prog > out can differ, why unflushed output gets duplicated by fork, and why it gets destroyed by exec. fflush(stdout) before you fork, exec, or crash. See W10L1 §24.
layerheaderman sectionfails by returningbuffered?
printf, fopen, fgetc, fgetsstdio.hman 3NULL / EOF / negativeyes
write, read, open, closeunistd.h, fcntl.hman 2−1, and sets errnono
syscall(SYS_…)sys/syscall.hman 2 syscall−1, and sets errnono
The middle row is what a question means by “a system call”. Nobody expects the third row in an answer — it was shown to make the point that write is itself only a thin wrapper.

Slide 39 · files — the same job, two vocabularies

open versus fopen (transcript)

“We did a lot of comparing this sort of thing.” Both open a file. One gives you an int; the other gives you a FILE *. Everything else follows from that.

C LIBRARY / SYSTEM CALL
#include <fcntl.h> int fd = open(argv[1], O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666); if (fd < 0) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; } char c; while (read(fd, &c, 1) == 1) { /* ... */ } close(fd);

Returns a small integer — an index into the kernel's table for your process. Flags are OR-ed together; the third argument is the permission mode, and is only used when O_CREAT actually creates the file.

STANDARD I/O LIBRARY
#include <stdio.h> FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "w"); if (f == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; } int c; while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF) { /* ... */ } fclose(f);

Returns a pointer to an opaque struct — “we don't exactly know what's in it, but there's definitely file descriptor information and such”. The mode string replaces the flags, and the permissions are chosen for you.

The translation table

These are the same set of intentions in two notations, and the exam will ask for one of them by name. The lecturer specifically called out truncation: “truncate means if the file exists, we're going to go to the beginning of the file and we're going to write over everything. Make sure you know the difference between truncation and appending.”

fopen modeequivalent open flagsexists?missing?starts at
"r"O_RDONLYread itfailsthe beginning
"r+"O_RDWRread and writefailsthe beginning
"w"O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNCtruncated to zerocreatedthe beginning
"w+"O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_TRUNCtruncated to zerocreatedthe beginning
"a"O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_APPENDkeptcreatedthe end, always
"a+"O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_APPENDkeptcreatedreads at the start, writes at the end
b — as in "rb", "r+b" — means binary. On Linux it does nothing at all; on Windows it stops newline translation. Write it anyway when the data is not text: it costs nothing and it documents intent.
0666 is not the permissions the file gets. The mode argument is masked by your umask, typically 022, so 0666 produces rw-r--r-- and not rw-rw-rw-. Also note it is octal — the leading zero is load-bearing. Writing 666 asks for mode 0o1232, which is not what anyone wants. The lecture read the bits out in the right order: “read-write for the owner, read-write for the owner's group, and read-write for everyone.”

Slide 39 · files — a test that is wrong, and the man page that says so

Error checking, and the fd < 1 bug (transcript)

The lecture is right that error checking gets marks: “you might be asked an exam question about making sure you put error checking.” And right about how to look it up under pressure: “if you don't remember during the exam, be calm, go to the man page, see what it says about error — they're usually quite extensive.” The test it quotes, though, is off by one.

As described in the lecture: if (fd < 1) { /* error */ } <-- rejects a valid descriptor What the man page says: RETURN VALUE open() returns the new file descriptor, or -1 if an error occurred.

0 is a perfectly good file descriptor. It is normally stdin, but if stdin has been closed, open hands out 0 — the kernel always returns the lowest available number. Demonstrated:

close(0); // stdin gone: 0 is now the lowest free descriptor int fd = open("hello.txt", O_RDONLY);
open returned fd = 0 test (fd < 1) says: ERROR test (fd < 0) says: ok test (fd == -1) says: ok and it reads fine: the file really is readable

So the < 1 version reports failure on a descriptor that works. It is not hypothetical: any program that closes stdin, or that is run with 0<&-, or a child spawned after an addclose(0) — which is exactly what §17 does — can land on descriptor 0.

callcorrect failure testthen
open, creat, dupif (fd == -1) — or < 0perror(name); errno is set
read, writeif (n == -1)note 0 from read means end of file, not an error
fopen, fdopenif (f == NULL)perror(name); errno is set
fgetcif (c == EOF)ambiguous — feof() vs ferror() distinguishes them. Store it in an int, never a char
fgetsif (s == NULL)same ambiguity, same resolution
posix_spawn, pthread_createif (ret != 0)the return value is the error number; errno is untouched. Set errno = ret before perror
Why fgetc must go in an int. It returns 257 distinct values: 0–255 plus EOF (which is −1). A char holds 256. Assign to a char and the byte 0xFF in a binary file becomes indistinguishable from EOF, and your loop stops early on exactly the files where it matters. Same family of bug as §23.

Slide 39 · files — the one the lecture called a likely exam question

Seeking, ftell, and fuzz.c (transcript)

This got the most explicit exam flag in the whole hour: “a likely exam question would be something like… fuzz.c tells us about opening a file, working out how many bytes the file has, determining a particular place within the file, going to that byte, changing a bit within that byte, and then writing it back again. So this kind of file manipulation is something you could see in the exam.”

int fseek(FILE *stream, long offset, int whence); // whence: SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, SEEK_END long ftell(FILE *stream); // current position, in bytes from the start

Three moves cover everything the lecture demonstrated on a 1024-byte file whose byte i holds the value i mod 256:

fseek(f, -1, SEEK_END); fgetc(f) → last byte = 255 (offset 1023) fseek(f, 0, SEEK_SET); fgetc(f) → first byte = 0 fseek(f, 41, SEEK_SET); fgetc(f) → the 42nd byte = 41 fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END); ftell(f) → size = 1024 bytes
The size idiom, and the off-by-one. fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END) then ftell(f) gives the size, because the end is size bytes from the start. The last byte is therefore at offset size - 1, which is what SEEK_END with -1 reaches. The nth byte counting from one is at offset n − 1 — the 42nd byte is at 41, which is why that number appears in the lecture.

fuzz.c, and the two things that make it work

FILE *f = fopen(argv[1], "r+b"); // read AND write, no truncation if (f == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; } fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(f); // how many bytes are there? if (target >= size) { /* past the end */ } fseek(f, target, SEEK_SET); int before = fgetc(f); // read the byte (position is now target+1) int after = before ^ (1 << bit); // flip one bit fseek(f, target, SEEK_SET); // GO BACK -- both necessary and required fputc(after, f); fclose(f);
$ ./fuzz data.bin 100 0 file is 1024 bytes byte 100: 100 (0x64) -> 101 (0x65) bit 0 flipped on disk afterwards: byte 100 is now 101, size still 1024

Two details carry the whole program, and both are the kind of thing that costs a mark:

1 · THE MODE MUST BE "r+b"

"rb" cannot write. "wb" truncates the file to zero bytes the moment you open it — your ftell then reports a size of 0 and there is nothing left to modify. "r+b" is the only mode that opens an existing file for both reading and writing without destroying it. See the table in §19.

2 · THE SECOND fseek IS NOT OPTIONAL

After fgetc the position is target + 1. Writing without seeking back writes to the wrong byte. C also requires a positioning call between a read and a write on an update stream — so leaving it out is undefined behaviour, not merely a logic slip.

Measured, with the second fseek deleted — and this is the reason it is worth showing rather than describing:

byte 100: 101 (0x65) -> 100 (0x64) bit 0 flipped <-- what the program says bytes that actually changed on disk: [101] <-- byte 101, not 100
The program corrupts a different byte from the one it reports. No crash, no warning, no diagnostic — and its own output confirms the operation it did not perform. If a question asks you to modify byte n and an autotest checks byte n, you will fail it while your program cheerfully prints that it succeeded.

Slide 39 · files — everything is a file, including the thing files live in

Directories are files (transcript)

“One of the slides during the lectures said everything is a file. Directories are a special type of file… to the file system it's a file, but a special type of file.” The proof is in ls -l: the first character of the mode string is - for a regular file and d for a directory. Underneath, that is a few bits in the same st_mode field.

demodir mode=040755 DIRECTORY inode=43288 size=4096 demodir/alpha.txt mode=100644 regular inode=43289 size=0 data.bin mode=100644 regular inode=43269 size=1024 the high octal digits are the type; the low three are the permissions

But the API is deliberately different, because the contents are structured rather than a byte stream. You do not fread a directory:

list_dir.c
#include <dirent.h> DIR *dirp = opendir(argv[1]); if (dirp == NULL) { perror(argv[1]); return 1; } struct dirent *de; while ((de = readdir(dirp)) != NULL) printf("%10lu %s\n", de->d_ino, de->d_name); closedir(dirp);
output on a directory with three entries
43288 . 43245 .. 43289 alpha.txt 43290 beta.c 43291 sub the inode numbers match `ls -i` exactly

The lecture described the output as “the file ID — or the inode number — and the name of the files. So inside this directory are these three files plus the file itself and the parent file above it.” That is the shape to remember: . and .. are entries like any other, they come back from readdir, and a program that lists or recurses without skipping them either prints noise or loops forever.

directoriesfilesnote
opendir → DIR *fopen → FILE *Both opaque handles. Both NULL on failure.
readdir → struct dirent *fgetc → intOne entry vs one byte. Both signal the end with a distinguished value.
closedirfclose—
Order is not guaranteed. readdir returns entries in whatever order the filesystem stores them — not alphabetical, not creation order. If a question wants sorted output, you sort it. readdir also returns the pointer to a shared buffer: copy d_name if you need to keep it.
Two useful neighbours. stat (or lstat) fills a struct stat with the mode, size, inode and times — that is where the table above came from, and it is how you tell a subdirectory from a file while recursing. mkdir and rmdir create and remove them; rmdir only works on an empty directory. All are man 2.

Slide 39 · files — the trap the lecture named as an exam trip-up

cp, and why fgets silently loses bytes (transcript)

Rebuilding cp is the canonical file exercise, and the lecture used it to set up a specific warning: “that would be a place where you could get tripped up in an exam… if your solution gets tested with a binary file, it won't work. It might occasionally work, but it won't work most of the time.”

cp_fgetc.c — byte by byte
int ch; while ((ch = fgetc(in)) != EOF) fputc(ch, out);

Copies bytes. A byte is a byte; nothing in the loop cares what it means.

cp_fgets.c — line by line
char line[4096]; while (fgets(line, sizeof line, in) != NULL) fputs(line, out);

Copies C strings. Which means it stops at the first zero byte in every chunk — and binary files are full of zero bytes.

Measured on the same 1024-byte file

$ ./cp_fgetc data.bin copy_getc.bin ; cmp data.bin copy_getc.bin fgetc : IDENTICAL 1024 bytes $ ./cp_fgets data.bin copy_gets.bin ; cmp data.bin copy_gets.bin fgets : DIFFERS 980 bytes -- 44 lost, first difference at byte 1 $ ./cp_fgetc text.txt ... ; ./cp_fgets text.txt ... both IDENTICAL on a text file -- which is how the bug survives testing

The mechanism is worth working through once, because “binary breaks it” is not precise enough to reason with. fgets reads up to and including the next newline — byte value 0x0A. fputs then writes up to the first 0x00. The two functions disagree about where a chunk ends, and everything between the NUL and the newline vanishes:

chunk starting atfgets readfputs wrotelost
011 bytes0 — the very first byte is 0x0011
11256 bytes24511
267256 bytes24511
523256 bytes24511
total44 — and 1024 − 44 = 980, exactly the measured size

A byte-for-byte simulation of that rule reproduces the corrupted file exactly — same length, same contents. So the loss is not vague “binary weirdness”; it is four NUL bytes, each truncating its chunk, each costing 11 bytes.

Why this is an exam trap specifically. It passes every test you are likely to write yourself, because you will test with a text file. It fails the unseen test, because the unseen test uses a binary one. This is the concrete instance of slide 23's “it is not sufficient to just match supplied examples” — and of slide 26's “there are also unseen autotests we use in automarking”. If a question says copy a file without saying text file, copy bytes.
usewhenfails on
fgetc / fputcalways safenothing — but one byte per call is slow for large files
fread / fwrite with a bufferalways safe, and fastnothing — but you must write back exactly the count fread returned, not the buffer size
fgets / fputstext onlyany NUL byte; also any “line” longer than your buffer, which is silently split
read / writealways safe — and what a “use system calls” question meansnothing, but check the return value: a short write is legal and you must loop

Slide 39 · Unicode — decode a byte pattern by hand

UTF-8: reading the lead byte (transcript)

The lecture's framing is exactly the exam task: “if you're given a question where you're given this 32-bit representation, make sure you know how to translate that into the UTF-8.” Everything you need is in the first byte.

lead byte startstotal bytescode pointsthe rest look like
0xxxxxxx1U+0000 – U+007F — plain ASCII—
110xxxxx2U+0080 – U+07FFone 10xxxxxx
1110xxxx3U+0800 – U+FFFFtwo 10xxxxxx
11110xxx4U+10000 – U+10FFFFthree 10xxxxxx
The rule in one sentence: count the leading 1-bits of the first byte. Zero of them means one byte; otherwise the count is the number of bytes. Continuation bytes always start 10, and no lead byte ever does — which is what makes the encoding self-synchronising.

Checked against the real encoder:

U+00041 A 1 byte lead=01000001 leading 1-bits = 0 U+000E9 é 2 bytes lead=11000011 leading 1-bits = 2 + 10101001 U+02603 snowman 3 bytes lead=11100010 leading 1-bits = 3 + 10011000 10000011 U+1F9A5 sloth 4 bytes lead=11110000 leading 1-bits = 4 + 10011111 10100110 10100101

Why strlen said 7

The lecture's example: two characters, and “it says that these two characters here have a length of seven… the sloth uses four bytes and the other uses three.” Reproduced exactly:

sloth alone strlen= 4 bytes: F0 9F A6 A5 characters: 1 snowman alone strlen= 3 bytes: E2 98 83 characters: 1 sloth + snowman strlen= 7 bytes: F0 9F A6 A5 E2 98 83 characters: 2 "hello" strlen= 5 bytes: 68 65 6C 6C 6F characters: 5

strlen is not broken. It answers the question it was designed for — how many non-zero bytes are there — which was the same question as “how many characters” only while everything was ASCII. As the lecture put it: “what strlen is really doing is counting how many bytes there are. So if you actually want to count characters, you need to do something different.”

Counting characters, without any library help. Walk the bytes and count only the ones that are not continuation bytes: if ((b & 0xC0) != 0x80) n++; That single test is the whole algorithm — 0xC0 masks the top two bits, and 0x80 is the 10 pattern that every continuation byte and no lead byte has. It works for every valid UTF-8 string and needs no table.

Slide 39 · floating point — one worked decode, done properly

Floating point: decoding 10.0 (transcript)

The lecture ran explain_float_representation on the number 10 and read the answer off the screen. Every step of that reading is reproduced below and checked against the actual bits — because the arithmetic is the exam question, not the program.

10.0f → bits = 0x41200000 0 10000010 01000000000000000000000 ^ ^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ sign exponent fraction 1 bit 8 bits 23 bits
stepthe lecture saidchecked
sign“a sign of zero — remember zero means positive”0 → positive
exponent field“the exponent is 130”100000102 = 130
remove the bias“we minus the bias — don't forget the bias — we get three”130 − 127 = 3
the mantissa“everything in floating point is a 1-something”fraction 01000… gives 1.012 = 1.25. The leading 1 is implicit — it is not stored
put it together“1.01 × 23… that'll give us 10”1.25 × 23 = 1.25 × 8 = 10.0  ✓

And the negative case, which the lecture noted in passing: “negative numbers have a sign bit.” Measured, -10.0f is 0xC1200000 — identical to 10.0f except the top bit. Nothing else changes. That is what makes floating point different from two's complement, where negating rewrites every bit:

10.0f = 01000001001000000000000000000000 -10.0f = 11000001001000000000000000000000 one bit (int)10 = 00000000000000000000000000001010 (int)-10 = 11111111111111111111111111110110 everything
The exam-shaped version of this. “Make sure you understand the difference between floating point and two's complement, how to convert between the two, and what it looks like if somebody gives you a floating-point number — how do you work out what it means, how do you explain it?” The procedure is always the same four steps: split the bits 1/8/23, subtract 127, prepend the implicit 1, multiply. Getting the bias direction backwards is the single most common error — you subtract 127 when decoding and add it when encoding.
Two special cases the four steps do not cover. An exponent field of all zeros means subnormal — the implicit leading bit is 0, not 1, and the exponent is −126. All ones means infinity (fraction 0) or NaN (fraction non-zero). Both are on the notes' infinity.c and nan.c; see W5L1.

Slide 39 · integers — one representation, one reason

Two's complement, and why it needs no special cases (transcript)

“The big thing with integers is: how do you express negative numbers? The nice thing about two's complement is we can do additions, multiplication, subtraction, all the same, without making any adjustments.” That last clause is the entire justification for the representation, and it is worth being able to state why.

3 as 8 bits: 00000011 as unsigned: 3 2 as 8 bits: 00000010 as unsigned: 2 1 as 8 bits: 00000001 as unsigned: 1 0 as 8 bits: 00000000 as unsigned: 0 -1 as 8 bits: 11111111 as unsigned: 255 -2 as 8 bits: 11111110 as unsigned: 254 -3 as 8 bits: 11111101 as unsigned: 253

Read down the middle column: the bit patterns just count down through zero and keep going. There is no discontinuity, which is exactly why the hardware needs no special case — −1 is the pattern that, added to 1, carries out of the top and leaves 0. The adder does not know or care whether you meant 255 or −1.

one addition, two readings: 100 + 100 in 8 bits = -56 (signed) / 200 (unsigned) -- same bits, 0xC8 the CPU computed 0xC8. Which number that is, is your declaration's business.
factconsequence
The top bit is the sign, but is not a separate sign flagNegating is invert all bits, add 1 — not “flip the top bit”. That is floating point, and confusing the two is the classic exam error.
The range is asymmetric: −128 to +127 in 8 bitsThere is one more negative than positive, because zero occupies a positive-looking pattern. So -INT_MIN overflows and equals itself.
Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C; unsigned wrapsThe bits do the same thing either way; the compiler is allowed to assume signed overflow never happens and optimise accordingly. See W4L1.
Right-shifting a negative value shifts in 1sArithmetic shift, preserving the sign. On unsigned it shifts in 0s. -8 >> 1 is −4; (unsigned)-8 >> 1 is 2147483644. Same operator, different instruction — sra vs srl in MIPS.

Slide 39 · bitwise — one idiom, and one character that changes everything

Extracting a bit, and & versus && (transcript)

The lecture picked the archetypal operation — “things like where we want to get the nth bit from a byte… we use a shifting operation” — and then spent longer on a one-character distinction, correctly.

int get_nth_bit(uint8_t byte, int n) { return (byte >> n) & 1; }

Two steps, in this order: shift the bit you want down to position 0, then mask off everything else. Reversing them ((byte & 1) >> n) gives you bit 0 shifted into oblivion. Verified on 0xB4:

byte = 0xB4 = 10110100 bit: 76543210 10110100 get_nth_bit(0xB4, n) for n = 7 down to 0
you want toidiom
read bit n(x >> n) & 1
set bit nx |= (1 << n)
clear bit nx &= ~(1 << n)
flip bit nx ^= (1 << n) — this is fuzz.c
take the low k bitsx & ((1 << k) - 1)
test whether bit n is setif (x & (1 << n)) — note this yields 1<<n, not 1, so do not compare it to == 1

One ampersand or two

“Make sure you know the difference between them and logical. Logical AND has two ampersands; bitwise has a single one. Make sure you know what's the difference between doing a logical and a bitwise AND.” The cleanest demonstration is a pair of operands where they disagree completely:

x = 4 (0100), y = 2 (0010) x & y = 0 bitwise: no bit is set in both, so every output bit is 0 x && y = 1 logical: both operands are non-zero, so the answer is true
&, |, ^, ~&&, ||, !

the classic slipif (flags & MASK) — correctif (flags && MASK) — compiles, always true whenever flags is non-zero, wrong

Slide 39 · MIPS — the oldest material, and the one most likely to have faded

C to MIPS, one construct at a time (transcript)

The lecture ended here, with an honest warning: “it is a long time ago. We were all a lot younger back then… you might have been really solid on it during assignment one and then you forgot all about it. So make sure you look at that.” Assignment 1 was MIPS, and slide 30 says assignment topics show up in the first eight questions.

The method taught in W1L2 is worth restating because it is a procedure, not an act of invention. Translate C into simplified C first — one operation per statement, all control flow via goto and labels — and the MIPS falls out line by line. The lecture's own description: “we did that simplified C, we used that dreaded goto, which is terrifying to me, but that's how we learned how to split out a loop and replicate loops inside MIPS files. We use labels in order to create functions or to go to different places in our file.”

1 · C
int sum = 0; int i = 1; while (i <= n) { sum += i; i++; } printf("%d\n", sum);
2 · SIMPLIFIED C
sum = 0; i = 1; loop: if (i > n) goto end; sum = sum + i; i = i + 1; goto loop; end: print sum;
3 · MIPS
li $t0, 0 # sum li $t1, 1 # i loop: bgt $t1, $t2, end add $t0, $t0, $t1 addi $t1, $t1, 1 b loop end: move $a0, $t0 li $v0, 1 syscall
The one transformation that makes loops easy. A while becomes test-and-jump-out at the top, unconditional jump back at the bottom. Note the condition is inverted: C loops while i <= n; MIPS branches away when i > n. Getting that inversion wrong is the most common single error in a translation question, and it produces a loop that runs zero times or forever — both obvious the moment you run it, which is why you should.
CMIPS shapewatch for
x = y + z;add $t0, $t1, $t2destination first — the opposite order from reading it as an equation
if (a < b) { ... }bge $t0, $t1, skip … skip:branch on the negation of the C condition
while / forlabel, test-out, body, b backa for is initialiser, then exactly the while shape, with the increment at the bottom
a[i] where a is int[]sll $t1, $t1, 2 then lw $t0, a($t1)scale the index by the element size — 4 for int, 1 for char. Forgetting this reads every fourth element
calling a functionjal name, return with jr $rajal overwrites $ra — nested calls must save it on the stack. W3L1
return x;move $v0, $t0 then jr $raarguments in $a0–$a3, result in $v0

Four longer ones, worked

These four are closer to full exam questions — write the whole program, then check against the worked answer. Each is deliberately in the style slide 24 warns about: read the restriction line before you start.

Set A · bytecount.c — system calls only

Restriction: you may not use anything from stdio.h. Write a program taking one filename argument that prints the number of bytes in the file, followed by a newline. Print nothing else. On any error, print a message to stderr and exit non-zero.

$ ./bytecount data.bin 1024 $ ./bytecount nosuchfile bytecount: nosuchfile: No such file or directory
Worked answer, and the three ways to lose the marks

The trap in the restriction. No stdio.h means no printf, so you must format the number yourself and write it. That is the actual content of the question — everything else is easy. A solution that uses printf passes every autotest and scores zero under slide 24.

Getting the size. Two legitimate routes. lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) returns the new offset, which is the size — the system-call twin of the fseek/ftell idiom in §21. Or fstat(fd, &st) and read st.st_size, which is better because it does not require the file to be seekable. Either is fine; fstat is the one a marker will nod at.

Formatting without printf. Build the digits backwards into a small buffer and reverse them, or write them out from the most significant end. Do not forget the zero case — a loop of the form while (n > 0) emits nothing at all for an empty file, and empty files are exactly what an unseen test will use.

Error checking. open fails with −1, not < 1 — see §20. And perror is in stdio.h: under this restriction you must build the message and write it to descriptor 2 yourself, or use strerror(errno) from string.h and write that. Noticing this is most of the difference between a full-marks answer and a 90% one.

Set B · flipbit.c — modify a file in place

Write a program taking a filename, a byte offset and a bit index. It must flip that bit in that byte, leaving the rest of the file and its length unchanged, and print the old and new byte values. Reject offsets past the end of the file.

$ ./flipbit data.bin 100 0 byte 100: 100 -> 101 $ ./flipbit data.bin 5000 0 flipbit: offset 5000 is past the end (file is 1024 bytes)
Worked answer

The mode is the question. "r+b". Anyone who reaches for "w" has already destroyed the file before reading a byte of it, and their program then reports a size of 0 — a failure mode that looks like a bug in the offset check. See the table in §19.

The seek-back. After fgetc the stream is at offset + 1. You must fseek back before fputc, and not only for the obvious reason — C requires an intervening positioning call between a read and a write on an update stream. Measured, omitting it writes to the next byte while the program prints the offset you asked for: a corrupted file and a reassuring message. §21.

The flip itself. b ^= (1 << bit). Not | (that only ever sets), not & ~ (that only ever clears). XOR is the one that toggles.

The bounds check. Get the size with fseek(f,0,SEEK_END) then ftell, and reject offset >= size. Note >=: for a 1024-byte file the last valid offset is 1023. Off-by-one here is the difference between rejecting a valid request and silently extending the file.

Set C · utf8len.c — count characters, not bytes

Read a file and print two numbers: the number of bytes and the number of UTF-8 characters. You may not use any wide-character or locale function — work from the bytes.

$ printf 'hi \360\237\246\245\342\230\203!\n' > s.txt $ ./utf8len s.txt bytes 12 characters 7
Worked answer

The whole algorithm is one condition. Read bytes one at a time; increment the byte count always; increment the character count only when the byte is not a continuation byte: if ((b & 0xC0) != 0x80) chars++;

Why that works. Continuation bytes are exactly the ones matching 10xxxxxx. Masking with 0xC0 keeps the top two bits; comparing to 0x80 tests for 10. Every lead byte — 0xxxxxxx, 110xxxxx, 1110xxxx, 11110xxx — fails that test, and there is exactly one lead byte per character. §24.

The counting check. hi  is 3 bytes and 3 characters, the sloth is 4 bytes and 1, the snowman 3 and 1, then ! and \n are 1 each. 3+4+3+1+1 = 12 bytes; 3+1+1+1+1 = 7 characters.

Store the byte in an int. If you use fgetc into a char, the byte 0xF0 may compare as negative and your mask test still works — but c != EOF becomes unreliable, and multi-byte characters are precisely where high bytes appear. §20.

Set D · capture.c — a challenge question, in the slide-31 sense

Using posix_spawn, run /bin/date with the argument -u, capture its standard output, and print it with the prefix > . Then print the child's exit status. You may not use system, popen, or fork.

$ ./capture > Thu Aug 13 03:36:48 UTC 2026 child exited with 0
Worked answer, and the two places it hangs

Shape. pipe(fd); init a posix_spawn_file_actions_t; adddup2(fd[1], 1) so the child's stdout is the write end; addclose(fd[0]) for hygiene; spawn; close(fd[1]) in the parent; read until EOF; waitpid; destroy. Full code in §17.

Hang 1 — the one everybody hits. Forgetting the parent's close(fd[1]). The parent is itself holding a write end, so the pipe never reaches EOF and your read loop blocks forever, even though date exited long ago. Measured: killed at 5 seconds. This is the close that matters, and it is not a file action.

Hang 2 — the deadlock at scale. If the child produces more output than the pipe buffer holds (64 KiB on Linux) and you waitpid before reading, the child blocks writing and you block waiting: neither can proceed. Read first, wait second. date is far too small to show this, which is precisely why it is a good exam question — the correct order is invisible in testing and obvious in reasoning.

The status. posix_spawn returning 0 only means the child was created. A failed exec surfaces later as exit status 127. And remember to check the return value as ret != 0, not == -1: posix_spawn returns the error number and leaves errno alone. §16.

SLIDES 35–36 · THE GOOD AND THE BAD

The bad, as listed by the course itself: not enough tutorial and lab time with processes and concurrency; no time to talk about caching or virtual memory; labs a decent bit of work; assignments a lot of work.

The good: comprehensive lab exercises and test questions, the tutors, and the students.

The virtual memory admission is worth noting if you have the notes: virtual_memory_notes exists in the course notes bundle and was never lectured. It is not examinable.

What to take away

The exam

  • Two conditions, not one: 50/100 overall and 18/45 on the exam. Above 32/55 banked, the hurdle is the one you are actually fighting.
  • Thursday 20 August 2026, CSE labs, 3 hours plus 10 minutes reading. You cannot leave the morning session early and cannot be late to the afternoon one.
  • Closed book, restricted environment: no internet, no course website, no personal config. You get man, the MIPS docs, the C/Linux cheatsheet, mipsy and mipsy_web. Study against that list.
  • 10 questions, one file each, .c or .s. Restrictions in a question are worth the whole question — re-read them before you submit.
  • Autotests are a guide. Unseen tests exist, and nothing under ~33% progress scores at all — which makes verifying an early answer worth more than starting a hard one.
  • Q1–Q8 come from labs, tests and assignments; Q9–Q10 from challenges and pipes. Q10 is expected to go unfinished.

The revision sweep

  • Threads: anything a thread reads must outlive the function that created it. malloc it, and free it in the thread.
  • File actions are a recorded to-do list replayed in the child between creation and exec. A pipe reaches EOF only when every write end everywhere is closed — including the parent's.
  • Three layers: printf (buffered), write (a system call), syscall (the bare number). A question naming one of them means it.
  • open fails with −1; fopen fails with NULL. fd < 1 is not a failure test. fgetc goes in an int.
  • Seeking: "r+b" to modify in place, and seek back between the read and the write — or you corrupt the wrong byte and your program says otherwise.
  • Copy bytes, not lines. fgets/fputs lost 44 bytes of 1024 on a binary file and passed every text test.
  • UTF-8: leading 1-bits of the first byte give the length. Characters are bytes that are not 10xxxxxx.
  • Float: split 1/8/23, subtract 127, prepend the implicit 1, multiply. Two's complement: negate by inverting and adding 1 — not by flipping the top bit.
Corrections and additions — 16 items, all measured

Everything below came from compiling and running these programs on gcc 11.4.0, glibc 2.35, Linux 6.8, two cores — or, for the assessment arithmetic, from computing every figure on the slides independently. Where a claim contradicts the lecture, the measurement is quoted rather than the reasoning.

1 · In spawn_read_pipe.c, the addclose the lecture explained is not the close that matters. The explanation given was that the child must not hold the read end or it “may not get an end-of-file signal”. Measured: deleting that addclose entirely, the program still works — captures the date, exits 0. Deleting the parent's plain close(fd[1]) hangs, killed at 5 seconds. EOF depends only on write ends, and in the read direction the parent is the extra writer. The addclose is load-bearing in spawn_write_pipe.c, where the child inherits a write end — deleting it there also hangs. The underlying rule the lecture was reaching for is correct and worth memorising in the general form: a reader sees EOF only when every write-end descriptor in every process is closed. §17, Labs 9–10.

2 · thread_data_broken.c is wrong 118 times out of 120, and the wrong value is not garbage. The notes say “should print 0x42, probably won't”. Measured over 120 runs: 0x7ffd ×33, 0x7ffe ×32, 0x7ffc ×31, 0x7fff ×22, and 0x42 ×2. The values cluster in 0x7ffc–0x7fff because that is the top half of a user-space stack address — the four bytes that held 0x42 now hold part of a pointer. The two accidentally-correct runs are the dangerous part: a bug that is right 1.7% of the time. §15, Lab 8.

3 · fd < 1 is not a valid error test for open, and it is straightforward to break. The lecture described the check as “is the file descriptor less than one”. open returns −1 on failure and the lowest free descriptor on success — which is 0 if stdin is closed. Measured: after close(0), open("hello.txt", O_RDONLY) returned 0; the < 1 test reported ERROR; the file read back correctly. Not hypothetical — a child spawned after an addclose(0) lands in exactly this state. §20, Lab 13.

4 · fuzz.c without the seek-back corrupts a different byte from the one it names. Deleting the second fseek, then asking it to flip bit 0 of byte 100: the program printed byte 100: 101 -> 100 bit 0 flipped, and a byte-for-byte diff of the file showed the only changed byte was 101. No crash, no warning, and the program's own output confirms an operation it did not perform. (C also requires a positioning call between a read and a write on an update stream, so this is undefined behaviour rather than a logic slip.) §21, Lab 14.

5 · The fgets copy loses exactly 44 bytes of 1024, and the mechanism is fully determined. The lecture's warning — “it might occasionally work, but it won't work most of the time” — understates how systematic it is. Measured: cp_fgetc produced a byte-identical 1024-byte copy; cp_fgets produced 980 bytes, differing from byte 1. The file contains 4 NUL bytes; each truncates its chunk at fputs, costing 11 bytes — 4 × 11 = 44. A simulation of that exact rule reproduces the corrupted file byte for byte. Both loops are identical on a text file, which is how the bug survives your own testing. §23, Lab 16.

6 · The three-layer write demo comes out in the wrong order, and the order depends on redirection. Written as printf, write, syscall. On a pseudo-terminal the output is in source order. Redirected to a file or a pipe, printf appears last — measured both ways. stdout is line-buffered to a terminal and block-buffered to anything else, so the same binary reorders its own output depending on where you point it. Same mechanism as the fork output-duplication bug in W10L1 §24. §18, Lab 11.

7 · The two 1s in the syscall example really are unrelated, and the lecture read them correctly. “The one means we're doing a write, the next one means that we're writing to standard output.” Confirmed: SYS_write is 1 on x86-64 Linux, and file descriptor 1 is stdout. Worth stating explicitly because the coincidence makes the call look like it has a repeated argument. §18.

8 · strlen = 7 reproduced exactly, along with the character count. Sloth (U+1F9A5) is 4 bytes F0 9F A6 A5; snowman (U+2603) is 3 bytes E2 98 83; together strlen 7, characters 2. The lead-byte rule was verified against the encoder for 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-byte characters: the number of leading 1-bits equals the byte count, except that zero leading 1-bits means one byte. §24, Labs 17–18.

9 · Every step of the floating-point walkthrough checks out. 10.0f = 0x41200000; exponent field 100000102 = 130; 130 − 127 = 3; fraction 01000… gives mantissa 1.012 = 1.25; 1.25 × 23 = 10.0. Added here: -10.0f is 0xC1200000 — identical except the top bit, which is the sharpest available contrast with two's complement, where negating −10 rewrites every bit. §25, Lab 19.

10 · The assessment arithmetic, computed independently — all of it holds. Weights sum to 100. Labs in weeks 1–5 and 7–10 is 9 labs, 18 raw marks capped at 15; regular exercises alone cap at 9 × 1.6 = 14.4. Best 6 tests at 1.7 is 10.2, capped to 10. The hurdle 18/45 is exactly 40.0%. The slide's worked example fails by precisely one mark. §04, Lab 1.

11 · Above 32 out of 55 banked, the hurdle binds harder than the pass mark — and most students are above it. Not stated in the lecture, and it changes what you are optimising. Reaching 50 overall needs 50 − banked on the exam; the hurdle needs 18 regardless. They coincide at 32/55. The lecture's own “most students” figures — 12+/15 labs, 7+/10 tests — give 19 before either assignment, so any pair of assignment marks totalling 13 or more crosses it. For that student the question is never “how much do I need to pass”; it is “can I get 18 out of 45”. §05, Lab 2.

12 · 20 August 2026 is a Thursday, seven days after this lecture. Checked, because slide 12 asserts the weekday and it is the kind of thing worth not getting wrong from memory. §06.

13 · 4 & 2 is 0 and 4 && 2 is 1. The lecture stressed the distinction without giving an example. This is the cleanest one: two operands where the bitwise answer is false and the logical answer is true. Added alongside: if (flags && MASK) compiles, is true whenever flags is non-zero, and is wrong. §27, Lab 21.

14 · The two's-complement claim, made concrete. “We can do additions, multiplication, subtraction, all the same without making any adjustments.” Measured in 8 bits: 100 + 100 produces 0xC8, which reads as −56 signed and 200 unsigned. One addition, one bit pattern, two answers — the adder does not know which you meant, which is exactly the property being claimed. §26, Lab 20.

15 · The list_dir inodes are real, and the type lives in st_mode. The numbers readdir returns match ls -i exactly. Measured st_mode: a directory is 040755, a regular file 100644 — the high octal digits are the type and the low three are the permissions, which is the precise sense in which “a directory is a file, but a special type of file”. Also worth stating: readdir returns . and .. like any other entry, and its order is not sorted. §22, Lab 15.

16 · The “bad code” demo promised by slide 23 did not happen. Asked for an example live, the answer was “yeah, I'm not exactly sure what an example of bad code would be, but I guess code that calls something else to do it.” The concrete cases are elsewhere in the same answer and on slide 24, and they are collected in §09 and Lab 4: hardcoding the expected output, shelling out to the program you were asked to reimplement, and — the one most likely to actually happen — using stdio.h in a question that said system calls. §10.

Two smaller notes. Slide 4 said the first past paper was “released now”; it had not been, and the lecturer corrected it live — “I had this in anticipation that one would be released by now, but that hasn't happened yet.” And the fseek demo's numbers check out on a 1024-byte file whose byte i holds i mod 256: last byte 255, first byte 0, the 42nd byte (offset 41) 41, size via ftell 1024.

myExperience, and reaching out (slides 40–42). Feedback goes through myexperience.unsw.edu.au, and slide 40 asks specifically that you give your tutors feedback there — “it will more likely than not make their day”. Content questions go to the forum; admin questions to cs1521@cse.unsw.edu.au. Slide 43 is the full UNSW student support directory: counselling and the Mind Hub, the after-hours mental health line, Student Support advisors for financial, visa and accommodation pressures, EDI for reporting sexual misconduct, Equitable Learning Services for adjustments, Academic Language Skills, and Special Consideration — all at student.unsw.edu.au.
And that's a wrap (slide 41). “Good luck. We hope you've learnt useful things in this course. We hope you get the mark you're aiming for. You are nearly there!” The lecture's closing advice, in the order it was given: show up to the practice exam, study, sleep, eat. And — “I will be sending you all good positive thoughts. I'm sure you'll all do great.”

This is a team, project-driven course. Here's the part that actually shapes your term: where the marks are, the one hurdle that can fail you despite a passing total, and how to get help when something goes wrong.

Assessment & the exam hurdle

ComponentWeightNotes
Labs & quizzes10%Auto-marked; submitted weekly. Use lab time + lab assist for help.

The exam hurdle. You need ≥ 40% on the final exam to pass the course — a strong project total won't save you if you miss it. The exam covers everything: lectures, tutorials, labs and the project.

Computer science vs software engineering

More than just coding (process deck · slides 5–10)

You can do both at once, but they ask different questions. Computer science asks what can computers do, and how efficiently? Software engineering asks how do we build the right software, the right way, so it survives contact with real users and other people's hands?

Computer science

  • Understanding how computers work and how we make them do things.
  • What can computers do — and how efficiently?

Software engineering

  • Building software for people — the right software, with the right practices.
  • Maintainable over time, by a team.
  • An extension of computer science, not a replacement.
The key difference: “Collaboration is a key difference between computer science and software engineering.” — Rob Pike. Engineering is what coding becomes once other people, time, and scale enter the picture.

Student code

It works… probably… we think. Bugs don't matter after submission, and no one is touching it again. The classic anti-pattern: an isEven written as twenty else if branches.

Industry code

What if there are millions of users? How many devices must it support? What happens if something goes wrong in a banking app or a self-driving car? Poor engineering costs money — and sometimes lives.

Key takeaway. Good software isn't just functional — it's scalable, maintainable, and secure. That's the whole reason this course exists.
Understanding the software process

Why a structured process (process deck · slides 11–16)

You wouldn't YOLO a house — you need a plan, materials, workers and inspections. Software is the same. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is the structured path from an idea to maintained software.

The three pillars of quality & productivity

A software delivery organisation stands on three pillars — weaken one and the whole thing wobbles.

Common development models

Waterfall
Linear and structured — each phase finishes before the next begins.
Prototyping
Build something rough fast to get early feedback.
Iterative
Continuous improvement across repeated cycles.
Agile
Rapid and collaborative — the model this course's project leans toward.
The Waterfall model in full: 1 · requirements gathering → 2 · system design → 3 · implementation → 4 · testing → 5 · deployment → 6 · maintenance. Clean on paper, but each step locks in before the next — which is exactly the rigidity that iterative and agile models push back against.
A first look at JavaScript

JavaScript, starting from C (js deck · slides 2–11)

JavaScript is a quirky language — designed in 10 days in 1995 so Netscape could script its browser, then locked in and evolved live on billions of devices. It's also the most in-demand language on the web (≈99% of sites use it), and you'll need it for every lab and the project.

Same shape as C

C

int minimum(int a, int b) {
  if (a > b) {
    return b;
  } else {
    return a;
  }
}

JavaScript

function minimum(a, b) {
  if (a > b) {
    return b;
  } else {
    return a;
  }
}

Different to run

No type annotations, and function instead of a return type. You print and run differently too:

# C: compile, then run the binary
gcc -Wall -Werror compare_2.c -o runnable
./runnable
// JS: node runs the source directly
node compare_2.js

In JS you just call console.log(minimum(3, 5)); — no main(), no printf, no #include.

The everyday syntax

Variables, strings & control flow (js deck · slides 12–15)

Because you already know C, here's only what's different. Try every snippet live in the playground above.

const, let & printing

// let CAN be reassigned
let years = 5;
// const CANNOT be reassigned
const fullname = "Giraffe";
console.log(years);
// '' and "" are equivalent
console.log('Hello!');

No int/char* — the variable just holds whatever you put in it.

String interpolation

// + still concatenates
let s = 'My';
s += ' name is Pikachu';
// backticks interpolate ${ }
const name = 'Yuchao';
const age = 7;
console.log(`Hi ${name}, age ${age}`);

The backtick ` template literal is the JS answer to printf's format string.

Control structures — identical to C

if / else if / else, while and for all read exactly as you'd expect:

const number = 5;
if (number > 10) {
  console.log('Bigger than 10');
} else if (number < 2) {
  // do nothing
} else {
  console.log('Number between 2 and 9');
}

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  console.log('Hello there');
}
Data structures: collections

Sequential collections — arrays (js deck · slides 16–21)

Collections come in two flavours. Sequential collections reference values by an integer index that fixes their order — in JavaScript that's an array. (The other flavour, associative, is the next section.)

Dynamic & mixed-type

const names = ['Yuchao', 1, 1.2];
names.push('Giuliana');  // end
names.unshift('Rani');   // front
names[1] = 'Carl';       // by index
console.log(`Hi ${names}`);

There are many array methods — push, unshift, and more.

for…in vs for…of

const items = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
// in → keys/indexes: 0 1 2
for (const i in items) {
  console.log(i);
}
// of → values: a b c
for (const item of items) {
  console.log(item);
}

in gives you the index, of gives you the value. Mixing them up is a classic early bug.

Associative collections

Objects — key → value (js deck · slides 18, 22–34)

Associative collections reference values by a string key rather than a numeric index, and usually have no inherent order. In JavaScript that's an object: a bag of name: value pairs.

Create, read, extend

const student = {
  name: 'Rani',
  score: 99,
  rank: 1,
};
student.score = 100;        // dot
student['zID'] = 'z123456'; // bracket
console.log(student);

Declared with const by convention — you can still mutate its properties, just not rebind the variable.

Inspecting an object

const u = { name: 'Sally', age: 18 };
Object.keys(u);    // ['name','age']
Object.values(u);  // ['Sally', 18]
Object.entries(u); // [['name','Sally'],…]

These three are your workhorses for looping over objects. Run objects.js and array of objects in the playground to see them print.

Plot twist: arrays are objects. const arr = [1,2,3]; arr.length; arr.includes(3); — where did length and includes come from if we never set them? An object is any value with properties and methods — and arrays, strings and functions all fit that definition. Arrays are just objects with integer keys and array methods bolted on.
Feeling fast? It is — that's the point. You're not meant to memorise all of JavaScript today. Learn what you need for the problem in front of you, then practice in the labs, help sessions and the optional extra resources.
Active recall

Test yourself first

Try to answer before you flip. Each card is tagged to its deck and slide.

Glossary

Keywords at a glance

Software engineering
Building the right software with the right practices so it's scalable, maintainable & secure — coding plus people, time and scale.
SDLC
Software Development Life Cycle: requirements → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance.
3 pillars
People, process and technology — the supports under any software delivery organisation.
Waterfall / Agile
Waterfall is linear (each phase locks in); Agile is rapid & collaborative. Prototyping and iterative sit between.
NodeJS
Runs JavaScript outside the browser. Interpreted — compiles & runs in one step (convenience over raw speed).
const vs let
let can be reassigned; const cannot be rebound (its object's properties can still change).
Template literal
Backtick string with ${ } interpolation — the JS way to mix variables into text.
Array (sequential)
Dynamic, index-addressed, mixed-type collection. Loop values with for…of, indexes with for…in.
Object (associative)
Key → value pairs reached by obj.key or obj['key']. Arrays, strings & functions are objects too.
Object.keys / values / entries
Return an object's keys, its values, or its [key, value] pairs as arrays — for iterating objects.

One-screen summary

COMP1531 is a team, project-driven course: 10% labs/quizzes, 45% group project (3 iterations), 45% final exam — with a 40% exam hurdle. Software engineering extends computer science with people, time and scale: the goal is software that's scalable, maintainable and secure, built through a structured SDLC (requirements → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance) resting on people · process · technology, via models like Waterfall and Agile. The course language is JavaScript, run with Node (interpreted). Coming from C you mostly learn the differences: const/let, console.log, backtick template literals, dynamic mixed-type arrays (for…in = index, for…of = value), and objects as key→value bags — where even arrays, strings and functions are objects underneath.
