COMP1531 · 26T2 · Software Engineering Fundamentals · Week 1 — Lecture 2

Git: version control for one machine, many machines & a whole team

Once a project grows past a single file and a single person, emailing code around falls apart. This lecture builds Git up in three stages — version control on your machine, then across your machines, then across a team — and the branch → merge request → merge workflow that makes collaboration safe.

why version control add · commit · push · pull branches & merging merge requests live git sandbox
01Git sandbox 02Why not file-sharing? 03Git vs GitLab 04Solo: one machine 05status · diff · log 06Many machines 07Branches & merging 08Merge requests
Play first

The Git sandbox (solo + team decks · the live demo)

This is the whole lecture in one widget. A GitLab project already exists in the cloud with a single README.md — but nothing is on your machine yet. Type real git commands (or tap the buttons) and watch code travel across the four areas: working directory → staging → local repo → remote. Start with git clone.

bash — git_demo

Run it, watch it move

The order matters: add → commit → push. Edit a file with a button, then stage it, seal the box, and send it to GitLab. Green = new file, amber = modified.

~/git_demo (main) $
Working directoryyour machine
▲ git add │ git pull / checkout ▼
Staging areathe open box
▲ git commit
Local repoyour machine
▲ git push │ git pull ▼
Remote repoGitLab · cloud
Suggested run-through. git clone → tap edit README → git status → git add . → git status again → git commit -m "…" → git push. Then go team: git checkout -b functions → + function.js → add/commit → git push (watch it fail, then follow the hint) → git checkout main → git merge functions.

The problem

Why simple file-sharing isn't enough (solo deck · slides 2–4)

In this course you won't write one function in one file alone. You'll build a large project, across many files, in a team — sometimes editing the same file. Emailing code or dropping it in a shared folder breaks down fast: people overwrite each other, and a teammate's change can silently break yours.

What Dropbox / OneDrive / Google Docs give you

  • File syncing
  • Basic version history
  • Some collaboration features

…but for code they fall short

  • Too simple for complex software projects
  • Not designed for programming — no granular tracking of what changed where
  • Limited at large-scale collaboration (hundreds of contributors, reviews, approvals)
What we actually need. Two things together: version control — a detailed, systematic logbook (and time machine) of every change — and concurrent collaboration — letting many people work on the same files and integrate their work cleanly. That's exactly what Git is built for.
A popular solution

Git, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket (solo deck · slides 5–7)

A point of confusion worth clearing up early: Git and GitLab are not the same thing. Git is the engine; GitLab is one of several websites wrapped around it.

Git — the command-line program

Git tracks changes to files and lets teams build software together safely and efficiently. It's distributed: every user has a full backup of the whole history, and work also lives in the cloud. Think of it like gcc — the engine you drive from the terminal.

GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket — the web apps

These are websites that implement Git behind an easy-to-use GUI. The look and feel differs, but the engine underneath is the same Git. This course uses GitLab — like choosing VS Code as the IDE in front of the Node engine.

One line to remember. Git is the back end (the language & engine); GitLab is just an interface to it running in the cloud. Same commands, same concepts — only the website changes.
Stage 1 · version control on a single machine

The four areas, and the courier-box model (solo deck · slides 8–10)

Everything in the sandbox above hinges on one mental model. Your changes pass through four areas on the way to the cloud, and you move them with four core commands — always in the same order.

Setup (once)

  • SSH keys — install them per the getting-started guide so you don't log in on every push/pull.
  • git clone <repo-url> — copy the GitLab repo onto this machine. You can't run code on GitLab directly.

The everyday loop

# 1 · stage your changes
git add README.md   # one file
git add .           # everything changed
# 2 · seal the box with a message
git commit -m "Changed README"
# 3 · ship it to GitLab
git push
Commit messages are marked. Always write informative messages — “Added subtraction function”, not “stuff”. Future-you and your teammates read the log to understand what happened, and meaningful messages are part of your project mark.
Knowing where you stand

status vs diff vs log (solo deck · slides 9, 13)

Three read-only commands answer “what's going on?” — and the subtle part is what each one compares. Getting that straight saves you the classic bug where a change “won't go up” because you forgot to add it after editing again.

git status

Compares your working directory against what you've committed, and tells you whether files are modified, staged, or untracked — plus whether your branch is ahead of the remote. Your everyday “where am I?”.

git diff

Shows the actual line-level changes between your working directory and the staging area. Edit a file and it appears; git add it and git diff goes quiet again — because working and staging now match.

git log

Displays the commit history — each commit's id and message, newest first. It's how you see the trail of sealed boxes and, later, jump back to an earlier version.

# the gotcha, in two steps:
# edit README again → git status sees it, git diff shows the new line
# git add . → now diff is silent (working == staging)
# edit ONCE MORE without adding → diff picks up the new change again
The key distinction. git status roughly compares working dir ↔ last commit (am I ahead / behind / dirty?). git diff compares working dir ↔ staging area (what have I changed but not yet staged?). If diff is empty but you swear you changed something, you probably already added it — check status.
Stage 2 · across multiple of your machines

One person, many machines (solo deck · slides 11–13)

Because your work lives in the cloud, you're not tied to one laptop. Start a lab at home, push it, then walk into a CSE lab and pick up exactly where you left off — no USB stick required. The new command here is git pull.

A brand-new machine

git clone once to get the repo, then work normally. Clone is the first-time step — you grab the whole repository.

A machine that already has it

git pull brings the most recent updates down from GitLab into your local repo and working directory. Use it before you start working so you build on the latest code.

clone vs pull. clone is the one-time copy of everything onto a fresh machine. pull is the routine top-up once you already have the repo — it fetches whatever's newest and merges it in. You can't pull a single file; a pull updates the whole repo.
Sometimes pull collides. If the remote changed the same lines you did locally, the pull can't auto-combine them and you get a merge conflict to resolve by hand — covered properly with team work, below.
Stage 3 · version control across a team

Branches & merging (team deck · slides 2–8)

Git is most useful with other people — and the thing that makes that safe is branching. Each teammate develops a feature on their own branch, so the shared main branch never breaks while work is in progress. When a feature is ready and reviewed, it's merged back in.

Working with branches

# create + switch to a new branch
git checkout -b functions
# …write code on an isolated file…
# switch back (commit/stash first!)
git checkout main
# list your branches
git branch

Your local repo checks out one branch at a time. Tidy up staged/unstaged changes before swapping.

The two common merges

  1. main → your branch, regularly: pull in others' bug-fixes and improvements so you stay current and reduce big conflicts later.
  2. your branch → main, once done & reviewed: this integrates your finished feature into the project.
First push of a new branch. The branch only exists locally until you push it — your first git push errors with “no upstream branch” and helpfully prints the fix: git push --set-upstream origin functions. Run that and the branch appears on GitLab. (Try it in the sandbox.)
Reviewing before it goes live

You don't merge to main directly (team deck · slides 9–11)

In most professional teams — and in your project — you cannot merge into main from the command line. Instead you open a Merge Request (MR): a web-based workflow on GitLab that puts a review step between your branch and the protected main branch.

What a Merge Request does

  • Shows exactly what you changed (the diff)
  • Lets others review your code and discuss it
  • Runs automated tests (CI/CD)
  • Controls approval before anything merges

Why it matters

  • Protects the main branch from breakage
  • Improves code quality & shares knowledge
  • Catches bugs early
  • Encourages real collaboration
Don't approve your own work. GitLab will let you assign yourself as reviewer, but in a group project that's not acceptable practice and you'll be penalised for it. The approver must be a different teammate. And remember: once a feature is approved, the person who made it is responsible for actually merging it in.
Cheat sheet

Git commands at a glance

The full set used this term. You rarely need extra flags — the basics carry you through every lab and the project.

CommandWhat it doesExample
git cloneCopy a remote repo onto your machine (the one-time first step)git clone <repo-url>
git statusShow the state of your repo — staged, unstaged, untracked filesgit status
git logShow the commit history, newest firstgit log
git addStage changes for commit (one file, or all of them)git add .
git diffShow line-level changes between working dir and staginggit diff
git commitSeal staged changes into a snapshot with a messagegit commit -m "msg"
git pushSend local commits up to the remote/cloud repogit push origin master
git pullBring the latest from the remote down to your machinegit pull origin master
git checkoutSwitch branches, or create one with -bgit checkout -b feature
git branchList your branches (the current one is starred)git branch
git mergeBring another branch's work onto your current branchgit merge master
Active recall

Test yourself first

Try to answer before you flip. Each card is tagged to its deck and slide.

Glossary

Keywords at a glance

Version control
A systematic logbook of every change to your code over time — both a history and a time machine.
Git
A distributed command-line version-control program. Every clone is a full backup of the whole history.
GitLab
A website that wraps Git in a GUI (like GitHub/Bitbucket). The interface this course uses.
Working directory
The files as they are right now on your machine — where you actually edit.
Staging area
The “open box” you fill with git add before sealing it with a commit.
Local vs remote repo
Your machine's copy of the history vs the cloud copy on GitLab. push/pull sync them.
Commit
A sealed, labelled snapshot of staged changes — created with git commit -m "message".
Branch
A movable pointer to a commit — an isolated line of work. Make one with git checkout -b name.
Merge
Bringing two branches back onto the same commit, combining their changes.
Merge conflict
When the same lines changed two ways and Git can't auto-combine them — you resolve it by hand.
Merge request (MR)
A GitLab review workflow: show changes, review, run CI, approve — then merge into protected main.
SSH keys
A one-time setup so you can push/pull without retyping your username and password each time.

One-screen summary

Simple file-sharing (Dropbox, Drive) can't do real version control or large-scale collaboration, so we use Git — a distributed command-line engine — through GitLab, its web interface. Solo on one machine, changes flow through four areas: working dir → staging → local repo → remote, moved by add → commit → push (and clone once to set up). status shows where you stand, diff shows working-vs-staging changes, log shows history. Across your own machines, pull keeps every device current (clone is one-time, pull is routine). With a team, each feature lives on its own branch (checkout -b) so main never breaks; finished work returns via a merge — but only through a Merge Request that's reviewed and approved by someone else, protecting main and keeping quality high.

TL;DR · file-sharing ≠ version control → use Git (engine) via GitLab (interface) · 4 areas: working → staging → local → remote · add→commit→push (clone once) · status = where am I, diff = working vs staging, log = history · pull keeps your machines in sync · team = branch per feature (checkout -b), merge back · never merge to main directly — open a Merge Request, get someone else to approve.

COMP1531 · 26T2 · Software Engineering Fundamentals · Week 2 — Teamwork

How to succeed in a group project — in COMP1531 & beyond

Teamwork is one of the most important — and most under-practised — skills in software engineering. This lecture is a toolkit for the term-long group project: how to plan work, how to develop & review it, and how to handle the conflict that every team eventually meets. None of these strategies are compulsory; the point is to pick the ones that make your team better.

meetings & minutes task boards & standups code review conflict management live task board
01Live task board 02Why teamwork? 03Meetings & minutes 04Planning dependencies 05Distributing tasks 06Standups 07On-time & leadership 08Review & quality 09Conflict management 10Evaluation
Play first

The task board, live (progress at a glance · slides 20–24)

A task board (kanban) is the single best way to see your team's progress at a glance. Each card is one piece of work with a title, labels, an assignee and a status column. Move a card with the ◀ / ▶ buttons and watch it travel from To Do → Doing → In Review → Done — the course expects progression through at least 3 stages.

GitLab Issues — Development board

Drag-free kanban

Seeded with this iteration's functions. Notice the priority cards and the iter prefixes — both ways the course asks you to mark which iteration a task belongs to.

Done 0/0
What a good card needs. Assignee(s) · a brief title · a description with subtasks or implementation details · a clear iteration (a title prefix like iter1: …, a milestone, or a label) · and movement through at least three columns. The board is your status report — keep it current and nobody has to ask "how's it going?".
The why

Why teamwork? (slides 3–5)

Real software is never built alone, and "throwing smart people in a room" is not a strategy. Deliberate teamwork is what makes a good outcome better than random chance — it's a skill you practise, not a trait you're born with.

This lecture, in three parts

  • Planning — effective meetings, assigning tasks, tracking progress
  • Development & review — getting work done on time, to a high standard
  • Conflict management — planning for it, deciding as a group, handling it well

A disclaimer worth keeping

None of these strategies are compulsory. They're a menu, not a checklist. The marking criteria sets a small minimum (notes, an issues board, standups); everything else is here so you can pick and choose what actually helps your team.

Planning · running meetings

Meetings that aren't a waste of time (slides 7–10)

Most "bad team" stories are really bad-meeting stories. The difference between a great meeting and a terrible one is almost entirely about preparation and discipline, not luck.

Great meetingsTerrible meetings
Always run on timeRun overtime
Have a clear agenda and goalAimless
Encourage contribution from everyoneDominated by one person
People prepare beforehandPeople arrive unprepared
Stay on topicDrift off topic

Types of meeting you'll actually use

kick-offSet direction & roles weekly statusWhere are we? daily standupQuick progress check decisionPick between options design reviewCritique a design debriefWhat did we learn?
Meeting minutes. Every meeting should leave a record: a Meeting X header (date/time, week, attendees), an agenda table of items and their discussion/decision, action items, and questions for your tutor. A markdown template is provided, but you can use any tool — what matters is that the minutes end up timestamped on your GitLab project-backend repo. That timestamp is your proof the meeting happened.
Planning · sequencing work

Planning for dependencies (slides 11–17)

Each iteration hands you a list of functions to implement — clear, adminAuthRegister, adminUserDetails, adminQuizCreate, adminQuizList, adminQuizNameUpdate, and more. The natural question: is there an order?

No — work in parallel

Branches are independent, so several people can build different functions at the same time without stepping on each other.

Yes — some functions need others to test

You can't really test adminQuizNameUpdate until a quiz exists, and you can't make a quiz until a user is registered. Testing reveals a dependency order.

The resolution is a dependency graph: sketch which functions rely on which, build the roots first, and break up any circular dependencies so the team isn't deadlocked waiting on each other.

clear
│
register
register →
userDetails
│
quizCreate
quizCreate →
…etc
GANTT charts do the same job at the schedule level — they visualise task scheduling, communicate dependencies and let you track planned vs actual progress. They're great to know about, but not necessary in this course; a dependency sketch plus a task board is plenty.
Planning · sharing the load

Distributing tasks fairly (slides 18–19)

Fair doesn't mean identical — it means everyone has a meaningful role they're comfortable with. Assign specific roles, and remember that not every valuable task is highly technical.

Not all tasks need deep technical skill

Plenty of real, markable work sits around the code:

  • Project management
  • Deadline reminders
  • UI design
  • Brainstorming test cases
  • Usability testing
  • Writing documentation
  • Report writing
  • Reviewing the spec

Verbal agreements of equity

Don't assume the split is fair — ask. Three questions to say out loud: "Is everyone happy with their tasks?", "Are you comfortable with this workload?", "Does that seem fair?"

One catch in COMP1531. Documentation and other non-code roles are genuinely valuable, but documentation contribution is not a substitute for code contribution. Everyone still needs to write and merge real code.
Development · staying in sync

Frequent check-ins → standups (slides 26–36)

An iteration is roughly two weeks, and a full meeting every day is too heavy. The lighter answer is the standup: a frequent (often daily) short progress update where each person answers three key questions.

The three questions

  • What did I do?
  • What am I going to do?
  • What problems am I facing? (blockers)

Sync or async

Sync = in real time, e.g. a stand-up in person or on a call. Async = not in real time, e.g. a written update posted to your team channel. Either is fine — async suits busy, distributed student teams well.

Course expectation: at least 2 standups per week from each member, with attendance and contribution — including at least one time where you led the meeting and took the minutes.

Try it — async standup composer

Fill in the three questions and watch a clean, postable standup build itself. This is exactly the format you'd drop into your team channel.

no blockers? leave it empty — "none" is a perfectly good standup
Development · momentum

Getting work done on time (slides 37–43)

Deadlines slip for predictable reasons, and there are predictable counter-moves. A few small habits — and a little applied psychology — keep a team moving.

1

Always set deadlines

"Soon" is not a date. Attach a concrete due date to every task — vague asks like "do you mind making the model?" become real commitments only once a deadline is named.

2

Avoid the social diffusion effect

If a task is addressed to "the team", everyone assumes someone else will do it. Assign work to named people ("Mary/Jason: write the design-justification section") so responsibility can't diffuse away.

3

Exploit commitment bias

People follow through on things they've said out loud or written down. Get explicit, recorded commitments ("I'll finish 5.3–5.5 this week") and they're far more likely to happen.

4

Exploit the social facilitation effect

People work harder around others doing the same. Co-working sessions — even silent ones in a library or on a call — lift everyone's output.

5

Check in regularly and send reminders

A friendly nudge before a deadline costs nothing and catches problems early.

6

A team will not lead itself

Someone has to hold it together. Leadership here is a service role, not a power trip.

A team leader's job

  • Set goals & delegate tasks
  • Plan the timeline
  • Facilitate communication
  • Motivate and support the team
  • Monitor progress
  • Mediate conflict

A team leader does not have to

  • Have the best technical skills
  • Be a dictator
  • Carry a higher workload than everyone
  • Start fights with people
  • Be the most experienced or authoritative member
Be a better contributor (optional, but recommended). Be transparent and proactive — if a task is slipping, say so early. Embrace imposter syndrome — take the task you're unsure about; you'll learn on the way. Use the 80/20 rule — most of the marks come from a fraction of the effort, so spend yours where it lands. Practise, break problems down into a minimum reproducible example, and use your resources (search, read others' code, pair up, help sessions, the forum).
Review · doing it well

"Finished", code review & quality (slides 45–58)

Half of teamwork friction comes from a single hidden disagreement: what does "finished" mean? Pin down a shared definition of completion before you argue about whether something is done.

"Finished" = one click from merging

A merge request that is tested, reviewed, CI-passing and approved — genuinely ready to go onto master.

…not "it runs on my laptop"

Untested, unreviewed local code with a half-done-work.png still untracked is not finished — even if it technically runs.

Three ways to keep the standard high

Code review

A quality-assurance step (sync or async) on every merge request: share knowledge, catch bugs earlier, maintain standards, improve quality — and avoid a single point of failure where only one person understands a file.

Pair programming

Two developers, one keyboard. Real-time review and knowledge-sharing as you go.

Internal standards

Agree your own conventions so reviews are consistent and fast.

Flavours of pair programming

Unstructured

The pair trades off who leads, discussing decisions about the code as they go.

Driver / Navigator

One developer sets the architectural or strategic direction; the other implements those decisions as code.

Ping-pong

Control shifts rapidly back and forth between the two, like a game of ping pong — the software is the ball.

Create internal git standards. Read the marking criteria first — and if it's vague, add your own specificity. For example: commits follow a format like test: added login tests; branches start with the iteration like iter1/adminAuthLogin; and every merge request follows the same process — the original author is the assignee, another teammate reviews, and the original author merges. The git criteria rewards committing tests before implementation, meaningful commit messages, and at least 2 approved merge requests that bring your branch code to master.
Conflict · when it gets hard

Conflict management (slides 59–72)

Conflict is normal; unmanaged conflict is what sinks teams. Most arguments trace back to a short list of causes — strong conflicting opinions (often design decisions), people not listening or not getting to share, different rules for acceptable behaviour, unequal workload, unclear communication rules, and people missing meetings or deadlines.

Plan for it up front: the group contract. Assessed in iteration 0 (use the template in the repo), it answers the questions that cause fights later — when/where do we meet? where do minutes live? where do we communicate? what's a reasonable response time? how do we handle conflict? what does a member do if they get stuck? If a conflict can't be resolved through your contract, contact your tutor.

Making decisions as a group

Whether it's the kanban tool, an array-of-objects vs a single object, or naming a variable data vs dataStore — disagreement is constant. The healthy pattern isn't "loudest wins": let the minority voice make its case ("do you mind if I share why I think Jira is better?"), discuss, then commit as a group and move on.

If someone is slacking off — find the root cause

Motivation & understanding

Procrastination / low motivation: a private, candid chat; give them tasks they actually enjoy.

Doesn't grasp the deadline's importance: spell out the consequences of missing it.

Size & circumstances

Task feels overwhelming: break it into smaller pieces, checked weekly.

Genuine personal issues: redistribute their tasks and offer support. ("Heavy workload from other courses" is very rarely a valid excuse.)

The escalation ladder

01Communicate the issue clearly and politely with your group.
02Work together to solve it.
03If responses aren't constructive, contact your tutor privately.
Disappearing group members? Message them (e.g. on MS Teams) asking where they're at. If they don't reply within 48–72 hours, continue as if they won't reappear — if they come back having lost the chance to contribute, that's on them. Don't put yourself in a life-or-death scramble waiting on one person, and keep your team and your tutor informed throughout. Remember: tutors check real contribution via peer evaluation, scripts and git history.
Conflict · accountability

Evaluation & reflection (slides 73–80)

From iteration 1 onward (not iter0), the course asks each team to evaluate itself. This is where contribution becomes visible — and where honest, regular feedback keeps small problems small.

Teamwork evaluation

Rate each member, reviewed by your tutor, across:

  • Participation
  • Dependability
  • Team wellbeing
  • Work contribution
  • A free-text comment

Group & individual reflection

Individually: your most valuable contributions and what to improve next time. As a group: who did what, what went well, what didn't, and what to change. Reviewed by your tutor during the project demo.

The participation/dependability scale runs 1–7 — a normal, hard-working member sits around 4–5:

1not active
2minimum
3below exp.
4good
5high
6beyond
7superhero
Do you need to do everything in this lecture? No. The marking criteria sets a flexible minimum — meeting notes/minutes, an issues board, and standups (plus weekly check-in attendance and effective MS Teams use). Your group may add its own standards on top. Pick and choose the strategies that actually work for your team.

Past student questions worth thinking about

  • Communicating in a second language?
  • Communicating across an age gap or a knowledge gap?
  • Reconciling different individual goals — e.g. one member aiming for an HD, another for a Pass?
Active recall

Test yourself first

Try to answer before you flip. Each card is tagged to its part of the lecture.

Glossary

Keywords at a glance

Task board (kanban)
A project-management tool that tracks each task's description, status and assignee — showing progress at a glance across columns like To Do / Doing / Done.
Meeting minutes
A timestamped record of a meeting (agenda, decisions, action items) committed to the project-backend repo.
Dependency graph
A sketch of which functions rely on which, used to sequence work and break circular dependencies.
Standup
A frequent, short progress update answering: what I did, what I'll do, and my blockers.
Sync vs async
Sync = in real time (in-person/call); async = not in real time (a written post).
Blocker
Anything stopping you progressing — often a dependency on someone else's unfinished work.
Social diffusion effect
Responsibility "diffuses" when a task is owned by everyone and therefore no one. Counter it by assigning to named people.
Commitment bias
People follow through on commitments they've stated out loud or written down.
Social facilitation
People work harder in the presence of others doing the same — hence co-working sessions.
Definition of completion
A shared agreement on what "finished" means — ideally "one click from merging": tested, reviewed, approved.
Code review
A QA step on a merge request that shares knowledge, catches bugs and maintains standards.
Pair programming
Two developers, one keyboard — unstructured, driver/navigator, or ping-pong.
Group contract
An iteration-0 agreement on meetings, communication, response times and conflict handling.
Peer evaluation
Per-member ratings (participation, dependability, wellbeing, contribution) reviewed by your tutor from iter1 on.

One-screen summary

Good teamwork is deliberate, and it breaks into three phases. Plan: run tight meetings with an agenda and timestamped minutes, sketch a dependency graph to sequence work, distribute tasks fairly (not all are technical, but docs don't replace code), and track everything on a task board. Develop & review: keep momentum with standups (what I did / will do / blockers — 2+ per member per week), set deadlines and lean on commitment bias and social facilitation, lead the team as a service, then protect quality with a shared definition of completion, code review, pair programming and agreed git standards. Manage conflict: pre-empt it with a group contract, decide as a group by hearing the minority then committing, diagnose slacking by root cause, and escalate communicate → work together → tutor. From iter1, evaluate and reflect. You don't need all of it — meet the minimum (notes, issues board, standups) and pick what makes your team better.

TL;DR · plan (meetings + minutes on GitLab, dependency graph, fair task split, task board) · develop (standups: did/doing/blockers ×2 wk, deadlines + commitment bias + social facilitation, leader as service) · review (definition of completion = 1 click from merge, code review, pair programming, git standards) · conflict (group contract in iter0, hear minority then commit, fix slacking by root cause, escalate → tutor) · iter1+ peer eval + reflection · strategies optional — meet the minimum, choose what helps.

COMP1531 · 26T2 · Software Engineering Fundamentals · Week 2 — Lecture 1

Iteration 0 — from requirements to stubs, and splitting code across files

Two threads run through this session. First, the Unigotchi major project begins: Iteration 0 is about design, not implementation — read a user story, turn it into a function interface, write a stub, and move it through the issue → branch → merge-request workflow as a team. Second, a development skill you'll need immediately: importing across multiple files with default and named exports.

stub = a promise story → design → stub issues & merge requests merge conflicts import / export story-to-stub pipeline
01Story → stub pipeline 02What Iteration 0 is 03Starter code 04Reading a user story 05Story → design → stub 06Issues & merge requests 07Merge conflicts 08Teamwork habits 09Multi-file: why 10Importing libraries 11Default vs named 12Import playground
Play first

The whole of Iteration 0, in one path (requirement → design → stub → MR → merge)

This is the single most important skill of Iteration 0: taking an open-ended user story and turning it into a concrete function interface and a stub. Step through the pipeline for Story 1 — each stage is exactly what your tutor will walk through at the design check-in.

unigotchi — story_to_stub

Requirement → design → stub → MR → review → merge

Tap a stage to see how Story 1 becomes shippable code. Nothing here is implemented — Iteration 0 only proves the shape.

The mantra. A stub is a promise about the interface — the function name, its parameters, and a sample success return — with no real logic. Iteration 0 is design; implementation comes in Iteration 1. Iteration 0 is worth only 5% of the project mark, so it's the safe place to make mistakes and get your tutor's feedback.
The project

What Iteration 0 is (and isn't) (Iteration 0 deck · slides 1–2)

Unigotchi is the term-long major project — think Tamagotchi, but for a uni student who has to balance energy, happiness and academic progress to graduate. You're building the backend only (some future cohort imagines the front end). Iteration 0 is the setup iteration: understand the requirements, design the interfaces, agree how the team works, and write stubs.

This iteration is about

  • Understanding the requirements
  • Designing the function interfaces
  • Setting up how the team works together
  • Writing stub functions only

Deliverables (due in one week)

  • contract.md — the group contract
  • meeting minutes
  • issue board + merge requests
  • features.md — feature + interface design
  • data.md — proposed data structure
  • stub functions only
Don't implement the mechanics yet. If Iteration 0 is taking more than a couple of hours of real work, you're probably over-doing it — you can likely finish it in your lab plus an hour. The point isn't the code; it's getting everyone's Git set up and the team's habits in place so Iteration 1 starts at a sprint.
Where things live

The starter code & the spec (Iteration 0 deck · slide 3)

Your team has its own project-backend repo, pre-populated with templates and example data. The actual requirements live somewhere else — in a single, course-wide project-backend-spec repo, so that updates reach everyone at once.

project-backend/ contract.md # team agreement minutes-template.md features.md # main design doc data.md # proposed data shape src/ auth.js course.js dataStore.js exam.js other.js simulation.js universes/ universe1..4.json # example data
contract.md
Team agreement: meetings, communication, response times, conflict handling.
features.md
The main design doc — feature design rows plus the function interface table.
data.md
Your proposed data structure (enough for 1 user + 1 simulation).
src/*.js
Home for both the prescribed stubs and the ones you design.
universes/*.json
Example data to inspect while you design — e.g. what a universeData object looks like.
The spec is the source of truth — not the examples. The example universes are there only to help you picture the game while designing. When in doubt about a requirement, the spec wins.
Requirements

Reading a user story + acceptance criteria (Iteration 0 deck · slide 4)

A user story describes a need from a user's point of view; the acceptance criteria tell you how you'll know the design satisfies it. Stories here are deliberately open-ended — unlike the prescribed functions, they don't hand you the interface.

Story 1
As a student, I want to see all of my Unigotchi simulation instances, so that I can choose which simulation to inspect or continue.

Anatomy of a story

"As a student"who needs this?
"I want to see all…"what capability?
"so that I can choose…"why it matters
Acceptance criteriahow we know the design satisfies it

Which prescribed functions help?

simulationCreate(studentId, universeData)
simulationStatus(studentId, simulationId)

Neither returns all simulations for a student. Prescribed interfaces must not change — so when you need new behaviour, you design a new function.

Design

From story to design to stub (Iteration 0 deck · slides 5–6)

Three artefacts come out of one story: a feature design row (notes in features.md), a function interface (the contract), and a stub (sample code matching the interface). Here's all three for simulationList.

1 — Feature design row (features.md)

FeatureStoryDescriptionState / data needed
List simulation instancesStory 1Retrieve all simulations belonging to a student so they can choose which to inspectStudent records, simulation IDs, status, elapsed time

2 — Function interface

simulationList(studentId)

{
  simulations: [
    {
      simulationId: 1,
      simulationStatus: 'ACTIVE',
      timeElapsed: 0,
    }
  ]
}

Design trade-offs

  • simulationId — required by the AC
  • status + timeElapsed — useful summary
  • Not full course/exam data — this is a list/summary
  • Want detail? call simulationStatus later

3 — The stub (src/simulation.js)

// Return a summary list of all simulation
// instances belonging to a student.
function simulationList(studentId) {
  return {
    simulations: [
      {
        simulationId: 1,
        simulationStatus: 'ACTIVE',
        timeElapsed: 0,
      }
    ],
  };
}

A stub proves the shape, not the logic

  • No real behaviour
  • Just a sample object matching the interface
  • Design only the successful case — error handling waits for Iteration 1
Design as a group. The open-ended stories shape the whole project — whatever you design here gets implemented in Iteration 1 and influences Iteration 2. Split exploration if you like, but everyone should review and agree, because it affects everyone's future work.
Git workflow

GitLab issues & merge requests (Iteration 0 deck · slide 7)

Every piece of work is an issue, done on its own branch, integrated through a merge request that someone else reviews. The course requires a minimum of two merge requests per person into master — one from a prescribed stub, one from a designed stub.

A worked example

Issue[Iteration 0] Design and stub simulationList
Branchiter0-feat-simulation-list-stub
MR titleAdd Story 1 simulation list design and stub
MR bodyCloses #<issue>

Good practice

  • One issue per small task
  • One branch per issue / task
  • MR links to its issue (Closes #…)
  • Someone else reviews it
  • Creator merges after approval
  • No giant all-in-one MR
Why so much process for something this small? It's habit-building. Iteration 0 is easy on purpose, so by Iteration 2 — when things are genuinely complex — issues, branches and clean commits are muscle memory. And use MS Teams for communication: your tutor is in there and it's the regulated source of truth if a dispute ever arises.
When two branches collide

Resolving a merge conflict (Iteration 0 deck · slide 8)

Two teammates edit the same row on different branches. The first MR merges fine; the second now conflicts. Git marks the clashing region and asks you to decide the final content. Try it: pick which side wins.

features.md — resolve conflict

Accept current, incoming, or both

HEAD = your branch · origin/master = what's already merged. Never leave the <<< markers in the file.


            
unresolved — pick a side

          

        

      

      
Resolve locally first. Editors like VS Code colour-code the two sides and give you one-click "Accept current / incoming / both" buttons — pick an option rather than hand-deleting the ======= markers, which is easy to get wrong. The UI resolver struggles with big conflicts, so get comfortable resolving locally before Iteration 1. Best of all: resolve as a team, with both authors present.

Five habits & the whole path (Iteration 0 deck · slides 9–11)

The whole path

        Requirement → design → stub → MR → review → merge. ① Story: student wants to see all their simulations · ② AC: each needs a simulationId + a useful summary · ③ simulationStatus inspects one — can't list all · ④ prescribed functions must not change · ⑤ so design simulationList(studentId) · ⑥ add feature + interface rows to features.md, make an issue · ⑦ add the stub in src/simulation.js · ⑧ open a merge request · ⑨ someone else reviews · ⑩ merge into master.
      

    


    

    
    

      
Development · multi-file

      
Big projects ≠ one file (Multi-file deck · slides 1–2)

      
Most real software spans many files that need to interact — your own starter code already has around 20 JS files. To keep code clean you separate the logic into files and import only what you need. This half of the lecture is how that works in JavaScript.

      

        

          
Why?

          
Hundreds of files is normal. Separating logic lets you reuse functions, keep files focused, and let teammates work in parallel without stepping on each other.

        

        

          
What we'll cover

          
    
            
  • Importing libraries (built into Node)
    • 
            
  • Importing our own files (default vs named exports)
    • 
          

        

      

    


    
    

      
Standard libraries

      
Importing libraries (Multi-file deck · slides 3–4)

      
Just like C's #include, Node ships with libraries written by others that you don't need to install. The syntax — and how you use what you import — differs from C.

      

        

          
C

          
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  printf("Hello\n");
}

          
In C you call the imported function directly — printf(...).

        

        

          
JavaScript

          
import path from 'path';

console.log(path.resolve('./'));

          
In JS you often import an object and call a method on it — path.resolve(...), not resolve(...) directly.

        

      

      
The key difference. C gives you the function name to call straight away. In JS you import a binding (often an object) and reach its methods through it — so be mindful of how an imported thing is meant to be used.

    


    
    

      
Your own files

      
Default exports vs named exports (Multi-file deck · slides 5–13)

      
To use a function from another of your files, that file must first export it. There are two flavours — a single default export, or one-or-more named exports — and they import differently.

      

        

          
Default export — one thing per file

          
// lib.js
function manyString(repeat, str) { /* … */ }

export default manyString;

          
// main.js — name it whatever you like
import anyName from './lib.js';

console.log(anyName(5, 'hello '));

        

        

          
Named export — one or more things

          
// lib.js — note: NOT exporting an object
function manyString(repeat, str) { /* … */ }
function addBrackets(s) { return `(${s})`; }

export {
  manyString,
  addBrackets,
};

          
// main.js — destructure + alias with `as`
import { addBrackets, manyString as hi } from './lib.js';

        

      

      
Prefer named exports. They add flexibility — you can add more exports later — and by default callers reuse your function's real name (clearer code). You can still alias a named import with as when you already have a clashing name. And if you import many things, just break the { … } over multiple lines.


      
Two ways to grab everything

      

        

          
// pick specific names, alias as needed
import { add, divide as div } from './functions.js';

add(1, 2);
div(10, 2);

        

        

          
// namespace import — one object, all exports
import * as math from './functions.js';

math.add(1, 2);
math.divide(10, 2);

Glossary

      
Keywords at a glance

      

        
Stub
A function with the right name, parameters and a sample success return — but no real logic. Proves the interface's shape.

        
User story
A requirement from a user's view: as a [role], I want [capability], so that [reason].

        
Acceptance criteria
The conditions a design must meet to satisfy a story — how you know it's done right.

        
Function interface
The contract: name, parameters and return shape. Prescribed ones must not change.

        
features.md
Your design doc — feature design rows (planning) plus the function interface table.

        
Issue → branch → MR
One issue per task, one branch per issue, integrated by a merge request someone else reviews.

        
Merge conflict
Two branches changed the same lines; Git inserts <<< ======= >>> markers and you choose the final content.

        
HEAD vs origin/master
In a conflict, HEAD is your current branch; origin/master is what's already merged.

        
export default
Exports a single primary thing; imported without braces and renameable to any name.

        
Named export
export { a, b } — one or more things; imported with braces, aliased via as.

        
Namespace import
import * as m from './f.js' — gathers all exports onto one object, used as m.fn().

        
Default parameter types
In the spec: studentId is a string, simulationId a number, universeData an object.

      

    


    
    

      
One-screen summary

      
Iteration 0 is the Unigotchi project's design-only setup: understand requirements, design interfaces, agree how the team works, and write stubs (name + params + a sample success return, no logic). The core skill is turning an open-ended user story + acceptance criteria into a feature design row, a function interface, and a stub — designing a new function (e.g. simulationList) when prescribed ones don't fit, since prescribed interfaces must never change. Work flows through issues → branches → merge requests (≥2 MRs per person to master, reviewed by someone else, merged by the creator), and merge conflicts are resolved by choosing current/incoming/both — ideally together, locally. The second half is multi-file imports: like C's #include but JS imports a binding you reach methods on; use export default for the single main thing (no braces, free rename) or named exports for one-or-more utilities (braces, as to alias) — prefer named for flexibility.

      
TL;DR · Iteration 0 = design + stubs only (5% mark, safe to get wrong) · story + AC → feature row → interface → stub · design NEW functions, never change prescribed ones · issue→branch→MR, ≥2 MRs/person, someone else reviews, creator merges · conflicts: pick current/incoming/both, resolve locally & together · imports: default (one, no braces, any name) vs named (many, braces, alias with as) · prefer named exports · use MS Teams as the source of truth.

Package management with npm, and requirements engineering

      
Two threads. First, a practical tool: npm lets you pull in code other people wrote, and pins versions so your whole team — and a fresh clone — builds the exact same project. Package management · the problem

      
Why we need a package manager (Package deck · slides 2–5)

      
To use JavaScript fully you need code other people wrote — a library on the internet, not something built into Node. You google "how do I check if a date is valid", find date-fns, write the import… and it explodes. The library isn't on your machine, and Node doesn't know what a "module" is yet.

      

        
node — date_fns.js

        

          
Run the snippet

          
Toggle whether the project has been set up with npm. The code is identical — only the environment changes.

          

            
            
          

          

          

        

      

      
The two things you're missing. The error Cannot use import statement outside a module is about configuration (Node needs to be told this file is an ES module). The deeper problem is that date-fns isn't installed at all. npm fixes both: it sets the project up and downloads the dependency.

    


    
    

      
Package management · npm

      
npm and the package.json file (Package deck · slides 6–8)

      
npm — the Node Package Manager — installs automatically alongside Node. It manages your dependencies (also called modules or libraries — all the same thing). Its terminal command is just npm, and the libraries it can download live on the npmjs registry.

      

        

          
Setting up a repo

          
Run npm init once (if it hasn't been already). It asks a few questions — don't stress, you can change them later. Afterwards you'll see a package.json: your project's npm configuration file.

          
For 1531 we also add "type": "module" so the import syntax works.

        

        

          
package.json

          
// after `npm init`
{
  "name": "example",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "type": "module",   // ← 1531
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo ..."
  },
  "license": "ISC"
}

        

      

    


    
    

      
Package management · versions

      
Installing dependencies & reading versions (Package deck · slides 9–10)

      
Install with npm install date-fns. This downloads the most recent stable version and adds it to package.json — prefixed with a ^ or ~ symbol. Those symbols decide which future versions are allowed when someone runs npm install later. Play with the explorer to see what each range permits.

      

        
semver — range explorer

        

          
What does this version range allow?

          
Pick a prefix and an installed version. The widget computes the allowed range and tests candidate releases against it.

          

            

              
Prefix

              

                
                
                
              

              
Installed version

              

                ^
                
              

              
Allowed range

              

            

            

              
Candidate releases

              

            

          

        

      

      

        
PrefixMeaningExample 1.2.3Updates allowed

        
          
^ caretUp to the next major (left-most non-zero)>=1.2.3 <2.0.0minor + patch

          
~ tildeUp to the next minor>=1.2.3 <1.3.0patch only

          
none (exact)This version, nothing else1.2.3none

        
      

      
Why prefixes exist. Semantic versioning is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch = bug fixes, minor = backward-compatible features, major = breaking changes. ^ trusts that minor/patch won't break you; ~ is more cautious and only takes patches.

    


    
    

      
Package management · anatomy

      
What gets committed (and what never does) (Package deck · slides 11–13)

      
npm revolves around three things. Two are small text files you always commit; one is a big folder you never commit. Committing the right files is what makes your environment reproducible on a teammate's machine — and on your own after a fresh clone.

      

        
repo — npm anatomy

        

          
Fresh clone, then rebuild

          
A teammate clones the repo — the heavy node_modules/ isn't in git, so it's missing. Watch npm install read the two committed files and rebuild it.

          

          

          

            
            
            
          

        

      

      
The rule. package.json and package-lock.json → always committed. node_modules/ → never committed (it's recreated by npm install). The lock file pins exact versions so everyone — and every machine — installs the same thing.

    


    
    

      
Package management · scripts

      
Custom scripts (Package deck · slides 14–15)

      
A handy npm feature: you can add named commands to the "scripts" block of package.json and run them with npm run <name>. Scripts mix a little bash and json — the course covers them in depth later; for now you'll be told exactly what to put.

      

        

          
"scripts": {
  "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1",
  "bill": "echo 'Hi Bill!'"
}

        

        

          
# run your custom command
$ npm run bill

Hi Bill!

          
Define bill once, run it anywhere in the project. Later you'll wire scripts up to start servers, run linters and execute test suites.

        

      

    


    

    
    

      
Requirements · foundations

      
What is a requirement? (Requirements deck · slides 2–9)

      
The most important part of building a system is figuring out what you need to do. Requirements engineering sits at the very front of the Software Development Lifecycle — get it wrong and everything downstream is wrong too. The IEEE defines a requirement as a condition or capability needed by a user to solve a problem or achieve an objective.

      

        

          
A requirement is also…

          
    
            
  • An agreement of work to be completed by all stakeholders
    • 
            
  • A description of, and constraint on, a proposed system
    • 
          

        

        

          
Why they matter

          
    
            
  • Foundation for development
    • 
            
  • Drive cost and time
    • 
            
  • Basis for verification
    • 
            
  • Help manage scope
    • 
          

        

      

      
What makes a good requirement statement?

      
A model line: "The Online Banking System shall allow the Internet user to access her current account balance in less than 5 seconds." It (1) names the system under discussion, (2) uses a verb with a correct identifier — shall / may — and (3) states a positive end result.

      
🏆 The "top 10 worst requirements" — every one is too vague to test

      

        
#1"The system must have good usability"

        
#2"Response time should be less than X seconds"

        
#3"Round-the-clock availability"

        
#4"Work just like the previous one, but on a new platform"

        
#5"The system has to be bug-free"

        
#6"Reporting"

        
#7"Make it accessible"

        
#8"X cannot change"

        
#9"Easy to use"

        
#10"It has to be robust"

      

      
The common flaw. None of these can be verified. "Good usability" — measured how? "Bug-free" — impossible to prove. A requirement you can't test is a wish, not a requirement.

    


    
    

      
Requirements · classification

      
Functional vs non-functional (Requirements deck · slides 10–15)

      
Functional requirements describe what the system does — a specific capability or service. Non-functional requirements place a constraint on how it does it — usually a performance characteristic, often applying to the whole system rather than one feature. Classify each statement below.

      

        
classifier — functional or not?

        

          

            

            

              
              
            

            

            

              Score 0 / 0
              
            

          

        

      

      

        

          
Example pair

          
Functional: the system shall send a notification to all users whenever there's a new post or comment.

          
Non-functional: the system shall send those emails no later than 30 minutes after the activity.

        

        

          
Three families of non-functional

          
Product (efficiency, dependability, security), organisational (operational, development, environmental), and external (regulatory, ethical, legislative) requirements.

        

      

      
One-line test. Functional = what the system should do. Non-functional = how well it does it. Requirements should be both complete and consistent — and imprecise words like "search" cause trouble unless pinned down.

    


    
    

      
Requirements · the process

      
Requirements engineering, step by step (Requirements deck · slides 19–26)

      
Requirements don't appear out of thin air — we derive them. Requirements engineering is a set of activities for identifying a system's purpose, and a negotiation where stakeholders (end-users, managers, maintenance engineers, domain experts…) agree what they want. It follows four steps — though in practice they interleave and repeat.

      

        
re — process stepper

        

          

          

        

      

      
Why RE is hard. Requirements are often only understood once building starts; clients don't know what they want, or change their mind; developers don't know the domain; stakeholder access is limited; and people jump to solutions too early (the XY problem).

    


    
    

      
Requirements · use cases

      
Use cases (Use cases deck · slides 34–44)

      
Instead of listing each function, a use case specifies behaviour as the interaction between a user and the system: the user initiates actions, the system responds. They treat the system as a black box and stay at a high level. Because they read like storytelling, they're easy and natural to discuss with any stakeholder — great for brainstorming, not just documenting.

      

        

          
UC1 · Put an item for auction

          
Primary actor: Seller · Precondition: logged in

          Main success scenario
          
    
            
  1. Seller posts an item (category, description, picture)
    2. 
            
  2. System shows past prices of similar items
    3. 
            
  3. Seller sets starting bid and a close date
    4. 
            
  4. System accepts and posts the item
    5. 
          

          
Exception 2a: no past items of this category → system tells the seller.

        

        

          
UC: Withdraw cash (written list)

          
Primary actor: Customer · System as black box

          
    
            
  1. ATM asks customer for PIN
    2. 
            
  2. Customer enters PIN
    3. 
            
  3. ATM asks bank to verify PIN & account
    4. 
            
  4. Bank returns validity and balance
    5. 
            
  5. ATM asks what action they want
    6. 
            
  6. Customer requests a withdrawal amount
    7. 
            
  7. ATM dispenses money
    8. 
            
  8. ATM informs bank of the withdrawal
    9. 
          

        

      

      
How to write them. Requirements are usually phrased "The system shall…" or "should…". A full use case captures actors and goals, a main success scenario, plus failure conditions and how they're handled. They can be a written list or a diagram.

    


    
    

      
Requirements · user stories

      
User stories (User stories deck · slides 45–52)

      
A user story is a requirement told from the user's point of view — common in Agile, keeping the user at the centre. The shape is fixed: As a [role], I want [goal], so that [reason]. It carries just enough for developers to estimate the effort — avoiding detail that goes stale before work starts.

      

        
user-story builder

        

          
Build a story, then an acceptance criterion

          
Fill the three parts. Try a preset, then switch the acceptance-criteria style.

          

          

            

              

              

              

            

            

              
Generated story

              

              

                
                
              

              

            

          

        

      

      

        

          
Attributes

          
Written in non-technical language, focused on the customer, and goal-focused not feature-focused — describe the problem, not the solution.

        

        

          
Good stories are INVEST

          
Independent · Negotiable · Valuable · Estimable · Small · Testable.

        

      

    


    
    

      
Requirements · acceptance criteria

      
Acceptance criteria (User stories deck · slides 53–60)

      
Before a story is built, the customer writes an acceptance procedure: the conditions that must be met for them to accept the work — a way to "test" whether the story is satisfied. They're in natural language, can be refined before implementation, and should be written before coding starts.

      

        

          

            
Rule-based

            
Story: search for a hotel by city, name or street.

            
    
              
  • Search field sits in the top bar
    • 
              
  • Search runs on clicking "Search"
    • 
              
  • Placeholder reads "Where are you going?"
    • 
              
  • Accepts city, hotel name or street
    • 
              
  • Max 200 characters
    • 
            

          

          

            
Scenario-based (Given/When/Then)

            
Story: recover a forgotten password.

            
Given the user is on the login page
When they select "forgot password"
And enter a valid email
Then the system sends a recovery link

          

        

      

      

        
QuestionRule-basedScenario (G/W/T)

        
          
Works for any story?✓ generally yesonly when the story implies specific user actions

          
Higher-level system properties?✓ fine✗ awkward

          
Maps to an automated test?sometimes✓ more likely

        
      

      
Good criteria. Not too broad nor too narrow; minimise technical detail (the client must still understand them); write them before development. Acceptance tests check the criteria are met — they're black-box, and not all criteria map neatly to automated tests, so sometimes you set up a UAT environment for real users.

    


    
    

      
Requirements · validation

      
Verification vs validation & UAT (Validation deck · slides 64–69)

      
Two words that sound alike but mean different things. The clean mnemonic: verification checks the system was built right; validation checks the right system was built. Validation catches the expensive mistake — building exactly what was specified, when the spec was wrong.

      

        

          
Verification

          
Compares a product against its required characteristics — specified requirements, the design, the system itself.

          
"Will the system be built right?"

        

        

          
Validation

          
Gains confidence the system accomplishes its intended use, goals and objectives.

          
"Will the right system be built?"

        

      

      
How we validate

      

        
Requirements reviews
Examine the document to ensure it defines the right software.

        
Prototyping
Build something cheap to surface problems before committing resources.

      

      
User Acceptance Testing (UAT). ISTQB's formal testing against user needs and business processes, to decide whether to accept the system. Always black-box, run on the customer or user themselves, and either performance-based (hit a target) or stress testing. The aim of validation overall: catch problems before resources are committed.

    


    
    

      
Active recall

      
Test yourself first

      
Answer before you flip. Each card is tagged to its deck and slide.

      

    


    
    

      
Glossary

      
Keywords at a glance

      

        
npm
Node Package Manager — installs with Node, manages dependencies (= modules = libraries). Command: npm.

        
package.json
Project config + metadata, including the dependency list. Always committed. Created by npm init.

        
package-lock.json
Pins exact dependency versions so everyone installs the same thing. Always committed.

        
node_modules/
Where dependencies install locally. Never committed — rebuilt by npm install.

        
^ vs ~
^1.2.3 allows minor+patch (<2.0.0); ~1.2.3 allows patch only (<1.3.0).

        
Requirement
A condition or capability a user needs to solve a problem or meet an objective; an agreement among stakeholders.

        
Functional requirement
What the system does — a specific capability or service.

        
Non-functional requirement
A constraint on how well it does it — performance, availability, security; often system-wide.

        
Requirements engineering
Deriving requirements via elicitation → analysis → specification → validation (iterative, interleaved).

        
Use case
System behaviour as a user↔system interaction; black-box, story-like. Has actors, main success & failure scenarios.

        
User story
As a [role], I want [goal], so that [reason]. Good ones are INVEST.

        
Acceptance criteria
Conditions the customer accepts the story by. Rule-based or scenario (Given/When/Then). Written before coding.

        
Verification vs validation
Built the system right vs built the right system.

        
UAT
User Acceptance Testing — formal black-box testing against user needs to decide whether to accept the system.

      

    


    
    

      
One-screen summary

      
npm (installed with Node) lets you use libraries other people wrote: run npm init to create package.json, then npm install <pkg> to download a dependency and record it — prefixed with ^ (minor+patch updates) or ~ (patch only). Three artefacts: package.json and package-lock.json are always committed (the lock pins exact versions for reproducibility), while node_modules/ is never committed — a fresh clone rebuilds it with npm install. You can add named scripts and run them via npm run. The second thread is requirements engineering: figuring out what to build. A good requirement names the system, uses shall/may, states a positive end-result, and is testable — unlike "good usability". Requirements split into functional (what it does) and non-functional (how well). We derive them through elicitation → analysis → specification → validation, modelling with use cases (black-box user↔system interactions) and user stories (as a [role], I want [goal], so that [reason], ideally INVEST). Each story gets acceptance criteria — rule-based or Given/When/Then — written before coding and checked by black-box acceptance tests. Finally, verification (built right) differs from validation (right thing built), with UAT the formal acceptance test.

      
TL;DR · npm manages dependencies · npm init → package.json · npm install <pkg> · ^ = minor+patch, ~ = patch only · commit package.json + package-lock.json, NEVER node_modules · npm run <script> · requirement = testable condition a user needs · functional = what, non-functional = how well · RE = elicitation→analysis→specification→validation · use cases = black-box interactions · user story = as a [role], I want [goal], so that [reason] (INVEST) · acceptance criteria: rule-based or Given/When/Then, written first, black-box · verification = built right, validation = right thing built · UAT.

COMP1531 · 26T2 · Software Engineering Fundamentals · Week 3 — Lecture 1

      
Correctness — dynamic verification & code coverage

      
A bug shipped is a recall, an outage, a billion-dollar satellite lost on the pad. This lecture is about catching them before that — by running your code against tests and watching what it does. We treat functions as black boxes, write real tests with Vitest, lean on the contract to know what's worth testing, and use code coverage to find the lines our tests never touched.

      

        dynamic vs static
        black-box testing
        Vitest
        design by contract
        code coverage
        branch coverage
      

    

  


  

    

      01Why testing matters
      02Testing & its types
      03Dynamic vs static
      04Safety vs security

      07Vitest
