Correctness · motivation

      
Why writing tests is critical (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 2–5)

      
Tests exist to make sure an application behaves as expected and meets its requirements. Approaching testing the right way saves time, cost and major problems down the line. And in extreme cases, a single defect can degrade interconnected systems or cause genuinely serious harm — so it pays to understand how a language behaves in order to prevent bugs in the first place.

      

      
FunFact. An estimated 94% of spreadsheets contain an error — largely because people never verify their correctness. Testing isn't a formality; untested code is usually wrong code that nobody has caught yet.

      
What this lecture covers: abstraction & black boxes, design by contract, the Vitest framework, and software safety — then a second thread on measuring how much of your code your tests actually exercise (code coverage).

    


    
    

      
Correctness · testing

      
Testing in the lifecycle, and its many types (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 6–9)

      
Software testing is the process of evaluating and verifying that a product does what it's supposed to do. Its benefits — preventing bugs, reducing development cost, improving performance — are why many teams test the code as they write it. That's why the testing phase often runs parallel to development rather than strictly after it.

      
There are many different kinds of test — each answers a different question

      

        
Type of testThe question it answers

        
          
Acceptance testingDoes it meet the business requirements?

          
Integration testingAre the parts working well together?

          
Unit testingDo the individual methods work?

          
Usability testingIs it good to use?

          
Functional testingIs just the output correct?

          
Performance testingIs it fast enough?

        
      

      
Where this lecture sits. Testing is one phase of the SDLC (requirements → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance), but because teams test as they build, it overlaps heavily with development. Today we focus on dynamic verification — the run-it-and-watch kind.

    


    
    

      
Correctness · two kinds of verification

      
Dynamic vs static verification (Dynamic Verification deck · slide 10)

      
There are two broad ways to check that code is correct. Dynamic verification runs the program and observes what it actually does. Static verification reasons about the code without running it. The clean mnemonic: dynamic = run-time checks, static = compile-time checks.

      

        

          
Dynamic verification

          
Exercising and observing product behaviour — the system is executed with test data and its operational behaviour is observed.

          
"run-time checks"

        

        

          
Static verification

          
Checking properties of code without running it — type safety/correctness, control flows. TypeScript is a classic example.

          
"compile-time checks"

        

      

      
Static verification is usually considered more robust and reliable — but it's limited, because not everything can be verified statically. This course returns to static typing and linting later; today is all about the dynamic side. The two are complements, not rivals.

    


    
    

      
Correctness · safety

      
Safety is not security (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 11–14)

      
The goal of testing is to make software safe — which is a different thing from making it secure. Software becomes unsafe when unexpected or unintended behaviours are allowed to happen — like reading uninitialised memory or writing outside array bounds.

      

        

          
Safety

          
Prevention from accidental misuse. A user fat-fingers an input; the program shouldn't corrupt itself.

        

        

          
Security

          
Prevention from deliberate misuse. An attacker actively tries to break in or break things.

        

      

      

        
classify — safety or security?

        

          
Accidental or deliberate?

          
Read each scenario and decide whether testing for it is about safety (accidental misuse) or security (deliberate misuse).

          

            

            

              
              
            

            

            
0 / 0

          

        

      

      
"Thankfully we're using a normal, sensible language that would never let us do anything weird!" — said no one about JavaScript sincerely. The point of the joke: every language has sharp edges. Knowing your language's behaviour is how you prevent the bugs in the first place.

      
Memory safety: C vs JavaScript

      

        
AspectCJavaScript

        
          
Memory safe?✗ no✓ yes

          
Array bounds checking✗ none — write past the end freely✓ checked dynamically at runtime

          
Uninitialised / unallocated memorypointers can be dereferenced even if they point nowhere validaccess is prevented by runtime checks

          
The trade-offprioritises performance over memory safetyprioritises memory safety over performance

        
      

    


    
    

      
Correctness · scope of dynamic testing

      
Testing in the small vs in the large (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 16–18)

      
Dynamic testing is about making your program robust in the face of the real, inevitable things that go wrong while it's running. It falls into two broad categories — testing small isolated pieces, and testing big integrated systems. Tap a level to see what it covers.

      

        
scope of dynamic verification

        

          
From one function to the whole system

          
The wider the band, the more of the system each test exercises at once.

          

          

        

      

      
"Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of bugs" — Edsger W. Dijkstra. A passing test suite proves your tests didn't find a bug today; it can never prove none exist. That's exactly why coverage (part two) matters — it tells you where you haven't even looked.

    


    
    

      
Correctness · abstraction

      
Black boxes & the "is this even testing?" problem (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 19–24)

      
Faced with a function, your first instinct might be to sprinkle console.log calls and eyeball the output. That's a reasonable way to debug — but it isn't testing.

      

        

          
debugging — eyeballing output

          
function add_evens(limit) {
  // adds even numbers from 1 to the limit
  numbers = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < limit; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) numbers.push(i);
  }
  return numbers;
}

console.log(add_evens(12));
console.log(add_evens(7));
console.log(add_evens(-2));

        

        

          
You print, you squint, you decide it looks right. But:

          
    
            
  • Nothing checks the output automatically — you are the assertion.
    • 
            
  • It doesn't scale — you can't console.log forever across hundreds of functions.
    • 
            
  • That's debugging, not testing. Testing only counts once it scales and checks itself.
    • 
          

        

      

      
View every function as a black box

      
When we test, we treat the function as an abstraction — we don't care how it works inside, only that it behaves correctly at its boundary. Think about driving a car or using your PC: you care that it works, not how. So can you write tests against a stub that has no implementation yet?

      
Yes — and that's the whole point. You don't need to know how a function is implemented to test it; the implementation doesn't change what you want to happen. Write the tests against the contract, then make any implementation pass them. The hero widget at the top of this page proves it: swap the implementation and the same tests still judge it.

    



    
    

      
Correctness · the framework

      
Vitest: testing JavaScript at scale (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 25–30)

      
To test at scale you need a real framework. Vitest is a popular one for Node/JavaScript, and it installs with npm. Because it's only used for development and testing — never in production — you save it as a dev dependency.

      
# a dev-only dependency: not shipped to production
$ npm install --save-dev vitest


      

        

          
removeVowels.js — the black box

          

            
Pick an implementation

            
Same contract, different code inside. The tests on the right never change — they test the behaviour, not the implementation.

            

            
source under test

            

          

        

        

          
npm run test — vitest

          

            
Test results

            
Each row is one expect(...).toEqual(...) assertion. Green passes, red fails.

            

            

          

        

      


      

        

          
removeVowels.test.js

          
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { removeVowels } from './removeVowels.js';

describe('removeVowels', () => {
  test('deals with no vowels', () => {
    const example1 = removeVowels('bcd');
    expect(example1).toEqual('bcd');
  });
  test('deals with only vowels', () => {
    expect(removeVowels('aei')).toEqual('');
  });
  test('deals with complex words', () => {
    expect(removeVowels('cannot')).toEqual('cnnt');
  });
});

        

        

          
The structure of a test file

          
    
            
  • Outermost describe blocks group a broad area (e.g. auth).
    • 
            
  • Inner describe blocks group a particular function.
    • 
            
  • Inside those, a test for each property or use case you want to check.
    • 
            
  • Inside each test, one of Vitest's expect matchers does the actual checking.
    • 
          

          
Wiring it into npm. Add "test": "vitest run" to the "scripts" block of package.json. Now npm run test executes ./node_modules/.bin/vitest for you — no long path to remember.

        

      

    


    
    

      
Correctness · the contract

      
Design by contract (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 31)

      
When you test or implement a function, you're usually working from information that spells out the constraints on the inputs (and often the outputs). This documentation — the contract — comes in many forms, but it always tells you the same thing: what you do and don't need to worry about when writing tests.

      

        

          
design_contract.js

          
// Returns a new string with vowels removed
// Input is a non-empty string type
// Return type is another string
function removeVowels(string) {
  return 0;
}

// Calculates the factorial of a number
// Input is a number between 1 and 10
// Output is a positive number
function factorial(num) {
  return 0;
}

        

        

          
What the contract buys you

          
For factorial, the contract says the input is a number between 1 and 10. So you do not need to write tests for factorial(-3) or factorial(1000) — those are outside the contract. You're free to focus on the cases that are actually promised.

          
The contract narrows your job. Every constraint on the input is one less category of test you have to write. Read it before you write a single assertion.

        

      

    


    
    

      
Correctness · behaviour

      
Behaviour: defined, undefined & implementation-defined (Dynamic Verification deck · slides 32–34)

      
When we describe what a program does under certain conditions, we call it behaviour — and testing is essentially just testing behaviour. But it's not always possible to pin down every scenario from a spec: it isn't feasible to define every edge case, and some implementation details just aren't critical to the spec. That leaves two special categories.

      

        

          
Undefined behaviour

          
Not defined at all — the use case is beyond a reasonable scope of expectation and generally shouldn't occur in reasonable use. Example: the square root of −1.

        

        

          
Implementation-defined behaviour

          
Needs to be defined and considered, but it's up to the implementer to decide. Example: whether text input is treated as ASCII or UTF-8.

        

      

      

        
classify the behaviour

        

          
Which kind of behaviour is this?

          
Decide whether each scenario is defined, undefined, or implementation-defined behaviour.

          

            

            

              
              
              
            

            

            
0 / 0

          

        

      

    


    

    
    

      
Code coverage · the idea

      
What is coverage? (Code Coverage deck · slides 37–39)

      
You've written tests — but how do you know they actually test the code? Coverage answers one question: "out of all the code I wrote, how much did my tests actually check?" It's a general measure of how thorough your tests are — how much of your program's code is actually executed (or "covered") when you run them.

      

        

          
Test coverage

          
How much of the feature set is covered with tests. This is usually left to human judgement — there's no script that knows your feature list.

        

        

          
Code coverage

          
How much code is executed during testing. This can be computed and quantified with scripts — it's a hard number, e.g. books_server.js — Lines: 75% (30/40).

        

      

      
Coverage in Vitest

      
Vitest has built-in coverage support. Install the v8 coverage provider, and Vitest will run all your tests, record which lines, functions and branches executed, and produce a report — in the console and at coverage/index.html.

      
# install the coverage provider
$ npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-v8
# then open the HTML report
$ open coverage/index.html

      
example console output

      
--------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------
File          | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines | Uncovered Line #s
--------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------
All files     |   88.88 |     87.5 |     100 |   88.88 |
 grade.js     |   88.88 |     87.5 |     100 |   88.88 | 13
--------------|---------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------

    


    
    

      
Code coverage · interactive

      
The coverage explorer (Code Coverage deck · slides 42–45, 48)

      
Here's computeGrade(mark) — the classic 5-way grade function. Toggle test cases on and off and watch the coverage light up: green lines were executed, red lines were never reached. The four metrics update live. Try to hit 100% on all of them with the fewest tests.

      

        

          
computeGrade.js — line & branch coverage

          

            

          

        

        

          
your tests

          

            
Toggle test cases

            
Each button runs computeGrade(mark) with that input.

            

            

            

          

        

      

      
The lesson the widget teaches. One test (computeGrade(90)) gives you a function-coverage of 100% but leaves most lines red. It's what's not covered that matters — not the headline percentage. Add a mark in each band (e.g. 90, 80, 70, 55, 30) and every branch goes green.

    


    
    

      
Code coverage · branches

      
Branch coverage & the metrics that matter (Code Coverage deck · slides 44–46)

      
For any line that can jump to more than one other line — an if, a loop — branch coverage checks how many of the possible branches were actually taken. Vitest does this automatically. It's sometimes called edge coverage, because each branch is an edge in the program's control-flow graph.

      
      
The four common coverage metrics in Vitest

      

        
MetricWhat it measures

        
          
StatementsPercentage of all code statements executed

          
BranchesIf/else or switch-case paths covered

          
FunctionsHow many functions were called

          
LinesActual source-code lines covered

        
      

      

        
→
Code coverage is useful, but it's more important to look at what's not covered than at the coverage percentage itself.

        
→
Branch coverage is a more accurate measurement than statement coverage — prefer it. And like any measurement, understand what meaning to attach to it. (Want more? COMP3142 covers coverage types in depth.)

Glossary

      
Keywords at a glance

      

        
Dynamic verification
Exercising and observing product behaviour — running the system with test data. "Run-time checks".

        
Static verification
Checking properties of code without running it — type safety, control flow. "Compile-time checks", e.g. TypeScript.

        
Safety vs security
Safety = prevention from accidental misuse. Security = prevention from deliberate misuse.

        
Memory safety
JS prevents access to uninitialised/unallocated memory via runtime checks; C does not (no bounds checking).

        
Testing in the small
Unit testing — testing individual components (often single functions) in isolation.

        
Testing in the large
Module, integration & system tests — exposing defects in integrated systems.

        
Black-box testing
Testing a function as an abstraction — you don't need to know the implementation, only the behaviour.

        
Vitest
A popular JS/Node testing framework. Installed via npm install --save-dev vitest. Uses describe/test/expect.

        
Design by contract
Documentation of the constraints on inputs/outputs — tells you what you do and don't need to test.

        
Undefined behaviour
Behaviour not defined at all; beyond reasonable scope (e.g. √−1).

        
Implementation-defined behaviour
Must be considered, but left to the implementer (e.g. ASCII vs UTF-8 text).

        
Test coverage
How much of the feature set is tested — left to human judgement.

        
Code coverage
How much code is executed during testing — computed by scripts. Metrics: statements, branches, functions, lines.

        
Branch coverage
How many of the possible branches (if/else, loops) were taken. More accurate than statement coverage; aka edge coverage.

        
@vitest/coverage-v8
The Vitest coverage provider. Produces a report in the console and at coverage/index.html.

      

    


    
    

      
One-screen summary

      
Tests exist to make software safe — free of accidental, unintended behaviour (distinct from security, which is about deliberate misuse). Correctness is checked two ways: dynamic verification runs the code and observes behaviour ("run-time checks"), while static verification reasons without running ("compile-time checks", e.g. TypeScript). Dynamic testing spans the small (unit tests of isolated functions) to the large (module, integration, system tests) — but remember Dijkstra: testing shows the presence, not the absence, of bugs. We always treat a function as a black box: you can test a stub against its contract without knowing the implementation, and the contract's input constraints tell you what you don't need to test. Scattered console.logs are debugging, not testing — real testing scales and self-checks, which is why we use Vitest (npm install --save-dev vitest; describe → describe → test → expect; wired up as npm run test). Some behaviour is undefined (√−1) or implementation-defined (ASCII vs UTF-8). Finally, code coverage measures how much code your tests execute — statements, branches, functions, lines — via @vitest/coverage-v8. The headline percentage matters less than what's not covered, and branch coverage is the more accurate metric.

      
TL;DR · testing makes software SAFE (accidental) ≠ SECURE (deliberate) · dynamic = run-time checks, static = compile-time checks (TS) · small = unit, large = module/integration/system · "tests show presence not absence of bugs" (Dijkstra) · black box = test behaviour not implementation; you can test a stub · contract = input constraints tell you what NOT to test · console.log = debugging; testing must scale + self-check · Vitest: npm i --save-dev vitest, describe/test/expect, npm run test · undefined (√−1) vs impl-defined (ASCII/UTF-8) behaviour · code coverage = % of code executed: statements/branches/functions/lines · @vitest/coverage-v8 → coverage/index.html · look at what's NOT covered; branch coverage > statement coverage.

Iteration 1 — from stubs to working code

tests first — the red → green loop

      

        
Write the test before the implementation

        
The lecture's strongest advice: write your tests first. Walk the loop the demo walked — start with a failing test, write just enough code to pass it, then add the next edge case and watch it go red again. Tap a step or use the buttons.

Iteration 1 · the shift

      
What changes from Iteration 0 (transcript · “iteration one” intro)

      
Iteration 0 asked you to design: turn the spec into function interfaces and stubs, agree a contract, sketch your data store. Iteration 1 asks you to make that design semi-work — actual JavaScript and actual tests for the prescribed functions and the ones you designed. Everything cultural from Iteration 0 carries forward; the new thing is real code.

      

        
AspectIteration 0Iteration 1

        
          
CodeStubs only — empty functions returning placeholder valuesReal implementation and tests for every function

          
LanguageJavaScriptStill JavaScript — not TypeScript yet

          
Web serverNoneStill none — that's Iteration 2

          
Carries forwardGood git practice, teamwork, meeting minutes, and the contract you agreed as a team

          
Due—Monday of week 5 · no late submissions

        
      

      
Why Iteration 0 existed. Having already done the design, the issue board, the branching and the contract once, this “quite daunting workflow” is now closer to second nature — so you can spend your energy on writing good JavaScript and tests instead of re-learning the process.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · setup

      
What's new in your starter code (transcript · starter-code walkthrough)

      
A new merge request lands in your repo — for most groups it was auto-merged; if not, it's sitting in your merge requests (and if it conflicts, there's a forum post that walks you through resolving it). It brings four things worth knowing.

      

        
package.json
Marks the project as an ESM project and pins the test tooling — Vitest plus Vitest coverage. Don't edit those bits. You may add other packages.

        
echo.js + echo.test.js
A worked function and a very simple test, so you can see what a function and its test should look like. Copy it as your baseline.

        
data_store.js
The single place your functions read and write data. Use getData / setData to reach the store. The example object inside has made-up fields — it's an example, not the source of truth.

        
Stub files (e.g. auth.js)
The stubs you already had from Iteration 0 — this is where your implementation goes. Plus a few extra entries added to .gitignore.

      

      
Don't trust the example data store as a spec. Some fields in the sample data_store.js object are invented and may be wrong. Use it as a shape to copy, then read the spec for what your data store must actually hold. For most groups, what you designed as data.md in Iteration 0 is already enough.

      
Adding packages. You can add any package that helps you write better code. Before installing, glance at its weekly install count on npm — an unpopular package is more likely to be malicious. Popular ones can still be compromised, but it's far less likely.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · the model to copy

      
The echo example, read closely (transcript · echo.js / echo.test.js)

      
Everything you write in Iteration 1 follows the shape of echo: a function that validates its input, returns an error object when something's wrong, and otherwise returns the real result. Its test file shows how to import from Vitest, group tests with describe, write a happy-path case, and write error cases.

      

        

          
echo.js — validate, then return

          
export function echo(value) {
  if (typeof value === 'object' && value !== null
      && value.echo !== undefined) {
    return { error: {
      code: 'CANNOT_ECHO',
      message: 'Cannot echo an object with the property echo',
    } };
  }
  return { value };
}

        

        

          
echo.test.js — import, describe, expect

          
import { describe, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { echo } from './echo.js';

describe('echo', () => {
  test('returns the value', () => {
    expect(echo('hi')).toStrictEqual({ value: 'hi' });
  });
  test('errors on { echo: ... }', () => {
    expect(echo({ echo: 1 })).toStrictEqual({
      error: { code: expect.any(String), message: expect.any(String) },
    });
  });
});

        

      

      
Use toStrictEqual, not toEqual. JavaScript can be loose with types, and toStrictEqual checks the exact shape — that you got back the right structure, not just something loosely equal. For error cases you don't care about the exact message, so match it with expect.any(String).

      
Where things live is up to you. The course doesn't prescribe where your functions or tests go. A common choice from the demo: a tests/ directory with one test file per function, because test files get big. Group related cases with describe blocks.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · conventions

      
The error format & small conventions (transcript · errors & conventions)

      
Iteration 1 adds an errors column to the interface table you saw in Iteration 0 — the spec now tells you exactly which condition triggers which error. Each error carries a code and a message.

      

        
The error code
One or two words, written in ALL CAPS (e.g. INVALID_STUDENT_ID). For prescribed functions, use the course's predefined codes; for your designed functions, pick a course code or invent your own in the same style.

        
The message
Not marked — it could literally be empty and you'd pass. But a descriptive message (“Cannot echo an object with the property echo”) helps you debug, especially once you reach the web server in Iteration 2.

        
When two errors apply
For prescribed functions, return whichever error is listed first in the spec table. For your designed functions, order the checks so the most sensible one fires first.

        
Order your checks sensibly
Notice in the spec tables that “invalid student id” usually comes first — check whether someone is a student before checking what courses they're in.

      

      
You design the error cases now. In Iteration 0 you only had to design the happy case — the success return. Iteration 1 makes you think about an error case for every one of your designed functions too.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · defensive code

      
What you have to validate (transcript · universe validation)

      
The automarker will hand simulation_create objects that are deliberately broken — an object whose key is “Bob” and whose last name is “Spongebob”, anything at all. Your job is to raise the right error rather than quietly create a universe with garbage data, because bad data downstream breaks the gameplay.

      
// you can ASSUME you're handed an object — nothing else.
// everything inside it is suspect until you've checked it.
simulation_create({ "Bob": "Spongebob", courses: [ /* 7 of them… */ ] })
// → must raise an error, not build a broken universe

      
These are the kinds of rule the spec lays out — treat the list as a flavour of what to check, never as the real requirements:

      

        
Universe validation
Reject invalid universes in simulation_create. For example, a student can only be enrolled in up to six courses; many other field rules live in the spec.

        
Energy & happiness
Activities change a student's energy and happiness by defined amounts; some maths is involved (e.g. an energy change of three, three times, is nine). Get the arithmetic right.

        
Activity windows
Some activities make a student stop studying and do something else. Time windows are measured from when an activity ends, not when it starts.

        
Passing a course
A student passes a course once they've studied the required hours, and have passed at least two of the three exams while attempting all three.

        
Win / lose state
Graduate = passed every course. But if energy or happiness drops below zero, the student immediately drops out, no matter how many courses they passed.

        
Exam-take logic
If there's an exam_take function, don't auto-pass a student on study hours alone — wait until the exam is actually taken, then check the condition.

      

      
Read the spec, not these slides. The lecturer said it three times: this page only summarises. Every real rule, error and field is in the Iteration 1 spec — and the automarking universes will be different from any example, so never hard-code to the samples.

      
When the spec is silent, you may assume. Because you designed these functions, a weird edge case that isn't in the spec is yours to decide — coverage and a manual mark check the main behaviours, not obscure corners. If unsure, post on the forum and a tutor will confirm whether you can assume or whether you missed a line in the spec.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · teamwork

      
Dependencies & working in parallel (transcript · dependency chain)

      
Almost everything depends on simulation_create — if you're writing simulation_list, your tests will need a working simulation_create first. So before splitting the work, map the dependency chain and decide who does what, when.

      

        

          
Plan around the bottleneck

          
Since simulation_create blocks four other people, consider pair-programming it as a group, or giving it to whoever has the lightest load elsewhere this week — they then do less next week while everyone else catches up.

        

        

          
You're not actually blocked

          
Black-box tests let you write your tests before the dependency exists. They'll fail on your branch — that's fine. Pull the dependency's branch into yours when it's ready, then debug together. Just get core work into main early in week 5.

        

      

      
This is the point of black-box testing. You write the tests against the contract, not the implementation — so failing tests on a branch aren't a problem, they're expected. The course actively encourages writing tests before implementation.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · the loop

      
The workflow, step by step (transcript · workflow walkthrough)

      
It's the same shape as Iteration 0 — just harder, because now there's real code. Tap each step.

      

        
issue → branch → tests → implement → run → merge

        

          

          

        

      

      
Never leave failing tests or code in main. You lose marks for a broken master. Keep failing work on your own branch, fix it (or merge a teammate's fix into your branch) before you open the merge request into main. Push and pull regularly; prefer many small merge requests over one giant one.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · marking

      
Where the marks actually are (transcript · marking & automarking)

      
Here's the part that surprises people coming from COMP1511: a perfect solution can barely pass. A large slice of the mark is git, teamwork, meeting minutes and style — because the goal of this course isn't to write code, it's to write code in a team with industry tools.

      

        

          
Manual marks

          
Your designed functions are marked by hand — in the demo (you run your tests for your tutor) and outside class. Tutors also eyeball your implementation to make sure you didn't “cheat” with bare-minimum code that skips edge cases.

        

        

          
Automarks

          
Your tests (T) almost always score full marks because they pass. The course's hidden tests (I) run against your implementation. Then a coverage term feeds in — and it's the one that bites.

        

      

      
In the lecture's formula, coverage doesn't just add in — a term like (coverage + 10) is squared, so low coverage drags your whole mark down disproportionately. The slider below is illustrative (get the exact formula from the spec), but it shows the shape: the penalty for poor coverage grows much faster than the coverage gap itself.

      

        
why coverage is squared — illustrative

        

          

            

              
              
              
70% covered

              

              

            

            

              
relative mark impact (illustrative)

              

              
Each bar is a coverage level; height is the squared term. Notice how steeply the bars fall as coverage drops — that's why “just four tests per function” can crater an otherwise-correct submission.

            

          

        

      

      
Practical upshot. Write a test for every if branch so coverage stays high. And go slowly: students who do best aren't the strongest coders — they're the ones with clean git, full minutes, good style and a never-broken main.

    


    
    

      
Iteration 1 · logistics

      
Before you submit (transcript · submission & Q&A)

      

        
Run the dry run
A dry run checks the boring-but-fatal things — e.g. that simulation isn't misspelled in a function name. It checks plumbing, not correctness, so don't rely on it for behaviour.

        
The deadline is real
Monday of week 5, and there are no late submissions. With heavy dependencies, work steadily across the week and a half — don't leave it to the end.

        
Only main is marked
Automarking runs against whatever's in main/master. Code stranded on a branch won't be marked, so merge it in time.

        
JavaScript, not TypeScript
Iteration 1 is strictly JavaScript for both tests and implementation — even though the lecture introduced TypeScript.

        
Packages allowed
You may use any external packages you like (subject to the popularity sanity-check from §02).

        
Linting is optional
Optional but recommended — the config is already in your repo if you want it. It becomes compulsory in Iteration 2.

      

      
The order to actually work in. Merge the new starter code → satisfy the prescribed interface (write its tests first, then implement) → check coverage → merge → repeat for each of your self-designed functions (these can run in parallel). Finish with npm run coverage once everything passes.

Glossary

      
Keywords at a glance

      

        
Iteration 1
The second project milestone: write tests and implementation (in JavaScript) for the prescribed and designed functions. Due Monday of week 5.

        
Prescribed function
A function whose interface the course gives you (e.g. on the prescribed interface table). Marked partly by hidden automated tests.

        
Designed function
A function you designed yourself in Iteration 0. Manually marked by your tutor (demo + outside class).

        
data_store.js
The single module holding the universe's data; functions read/write it via getData/setData. The shipped example object has invented fields.

        
echo
The worked example function: validates input, returns an error object on bad input, otherwise the result. The template for every Iteration 1 function.

        
Error object
The return shape on failure: an ALL-CAPS one-or-two-word code plus an (unmarked) human message.

        
Tests-first / TDD
Writing the tests before the implementation. Encouraged here because black-box tests only depend on the contract.

        
toStrictEqual
The Vitest matcher that compares exact structure and types — preferred over toEqual for return objects.

        
Dependency chain
Which functions need which others first (e.g. everything needs simulation_create). Used to plan who works on what, when.

        
Dry run
A pre-submission check of plumbing (names, structure), not correctness — guards against fatal typos.

        
Coverage term
The squared coverage component of the automark; low coverage drags the whole mark down sharply.

        
Graduate / drop out
Win = pass every course. Lose = energy or happiness below zero, which forces an immediate drop-out regardless of courses passed.

      

    


    
    

      
One-screen summary

      
Iteration 1 turns your Iteration 0 design into running code: real tests and implementation, in JavaScript (not TypeScript), no web server yet, due Monday week 5 with no late submissions. The starter merge request adds a package.json (ESM, Vitest + coverage — don't edit), a worked echo.js/echo.test.js to copy, a data_store.js reached via getData/setData (its example fields are invented — trust the spec), and your Iteration 0 stub files. Every function follows echo's shape: validate, return an error object (ALL-CAPS code + unmarked message) on bad input, otherwise the result; test it with describe/test/expect and toStrictEqual. Write your tests first — black-box tests only need the contract, so failing tests on a branch are fine and you're never truly blocked by the simulation_create dependency. Validate defensively: the automarker hands you deliberately broken universes, so reject them (≤6 courses, energy/happiness rules, exam/course pass logic, drop-out below zero) — but read the spec, not the slides, and never hard-code to samples. Follow the loop: issue → branch → tests → implement → run → merge, and never break main. Finally, a huge share of marks is git, teamwork, minutes and style; the automark squares a coverage term, so a test per branch matters more than raw cleverness. Run the dry run and npm run coverage before you submit. Linting optional (compulsory in Iteration 2).

      
TL;DR · Iteration 1 = tests + implementation in JS (not TS), no web server, due Mon week 5, no late · starter MR: package.json (ESM, Vitest+coverage, don't edit) · echo.js/echo.test.js = the template · data_store.js via getData/setData, example fields are fake → trust the spec · every fn: validate → error object (ALL-CAPS code + unmarked message) or result · test with describe/test/expect + toStrictEqual · WRITE TESTS FIRST; black-box → failing branch tests are fine; not blocked by simulation_create · validate broken universes (≤6 courses, energy/happiness, 2-of-3 exams, drop-out below 0) · READ THE SPEC not slides; don't hard-code samples · issue→branch→tests→implement→run→merge; NEVER break main · marks: git/teamwork/minutes/style heavy; coverage term is SQUARED → test every branch · dry run + npm run coverage before submit · linting optional (compulsory iter 2).
